citations.quote: Let two finite microstate models from [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]] have nonempty state sets $\Omega_A,\Omega_B$, energies $E_A,E_B$ in joules, and the same $T>0$. Assume their declared composite model has state set $\Omega_A\times\Omega_B$ and energy $E_{AB}(x,y)=E_A(x)+E_B(y)$, with no interaction term. Under the canonical sampling assumption [[post-td-canonical-sampling]], the partition function factorizes as $Z_{AB}=Z_AZ_B$, the joint canonical law is $P_{AB}=P_AP_B$, the Gibbs entropy satisfies $S_{AB}=S_A+S_B$, and the statistical free-energy value satisfies $F_{AB}=F_A+F_B$.

Adopt the quantum Gibbs preparation of [[post-nrqm-many-body-canonical-equilibrium-ensemble]] for a finite list of independent modes at $T>0$. For a bosonic mode with excitation energy $\varepsilon>0$ joules, let $q=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$, $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$, and let $N$ be its dimensionless occupation number. Its partition trace and mean occupation are
$$Z_B=(1-q)^{-1},\qquad \langle N\rangle_B=\frac{q}{1-q}=\frac1{e^{\beta\varepsilon}-1}.$$
For a fermionic two-level occupation system with energies $0,\varepsilon$, the partition sum and excited-state occupation are
$$Z_F=1+q,\qquad \langle N\rangle_F=\frac{q}{1+q}=\frac1{e^{\beta\varepsilon}+1}.$$
For a finite independent collection, the corresponding partition traces multiply and each mode's marginal mean is the displayed one. These are exact model identities under the adopted preparation.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statement of isolated autonomous dynamics. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), which are the choice hypotheses of the cited spectral and group suppliers.

**(i) Energy operator.** An **isolated autonomous system** of the sector has a declared **energy operator** $H_{\mathrm{op}}:D(H_{\mathrm{op}})\subset H\to H$ that is self-adjoint ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]) and a declared energy unit in which its spectral coordinate is read. The energy operator is part of the model specification of the system; for a massive particle it is fixed by the kinematics postulate P5, and singular or unbounded model Hamiltonians require their own self-adjointness statements.

**(ii) Evolution.** The time evolution of the model is the strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group
$$U(t):=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tH_{\mathrm{op}}\Bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),\qquad U(t+s)=U(t)U(s),\quad U(t)^{*}=U(t)^{-1},$$
defined by the spectral calculus of the self-adjoint generator ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]], [[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]], [[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]). The energy unit enters the argument of the exponential so that $H_{\mathrm{op}}t/\hbar$ acts in the dimensionless spectral variable.

**(iii) State evolution.** A vector state evolves continuously, $\psi(t):=U(t)\psi(0)$ for every $\psi(0)\in H$, and the Schroedinger equation
$$i\hbar\,\frac{d}{dt}\psi(t)=H_{\mathrm{op}}\psi(t)$$
holds in the norm-differentiable sense exactly for initial vectors $\psi(0)\in D(H_{\mathrm{op}})$, where the derivative is the norm limit of the difference quotients; for other vectors the equation is not asserted, although the evolution remains continuous. A density-operator preparation evolves as $\rho(t)=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^{*}$, which is a density operator for every $t$ and satisfies $\operatorname{tr}\rho(t)=1$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]).

**(iv) Time-dependent families.** A prescribed time-dependent family $t\mapsto H(t)$ of self-adjoint operators is a different model assumption: a norm-continuous finite-dimensional Hermitian family is used only through the unitary two-time propagator that its family defines, and the exponential of the integral of $H(t)$ is not identified with that propagator unless the family commutes with itself at different times. The general unbounded time-dependent case requires a separate existence and domain theorem of its own and is not adopted by this postulate; the driven-dynamics page states its own assumptions for the models it treats.

**(v) Open systems.** A non-unitary evolution of the reduced description of a system coupled to an environment is an extension obtained from an explicitly chosen environment model and a declared reduction, not a replacement for clause (ii); no environment model is adopted by this postulate.

**(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the isolated-system idealization. They assert nothing about the origin of the energy operator of a concrete system, about the accuracy of the idealization for a laboratory preparation, or about which laboratory interactions realize an isolated evolution; those are tested identifications in the sense of P7.

**(a) Assigned energy observable.** Adopt the autonomous-dynamics postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]] (P4) for a declared isolated system whose state space is the model's [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. An **assigned energy observable** of the system is an assigned sharp observable $(H_{\mathrm{op}},u_H)$ in the sense of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (a), whose declared unit $u_H$ is an energy unit in the sense of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] (joules in the SI conventions fixed there). Thus $H_{\mathrm{op}}:D(H_{\mathrm{op}})\subset H\to H$ is densely defined and self-adjoint ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), with spectral projection-valued measure $E_H$ on the Borel sets of $\mathbb R$ under the choice hypotheses of [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]] ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and its outcome law in a preparation is the law of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (b). The assignment of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ is part of the model specification, as in clause (i) of P4; this definition asserts nothing about which laboratory quantity of a concrete system realizes it.

**(b) The unitary flow.** The **time evolution** or **flow** of the isolated system is the family
$$U(t):=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tH_{\mathrm{op}}\Bigr):=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}\,dE_H(\lambda)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),$$
the reading of clause (ii) of P4 in the spectral calculus of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ ([[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]); here $\hbar>0$ is the reduced Planck constant with its value and unit fixed by [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]], so that $tH_{\mathrm{op}}/\hbar$ is dimensionless. Equivalently, $U(t)=e^{itT}$ for the self-adjoint generator $T:=-H_{\mathrm{op}}/\hbar$ with $D(T)=D(H_{\mathrm{op}})$; the two readings agree by the uniqueness of the generator in Stone's theorem, and by [[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]] ([[lem-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-flow-calculus]] clause (a)) the family $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group: $U(0)=I$, $U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)$, $U(t)^{*}=U(t)^{-1}=U(-t)$ ([[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]).

**(c) Schroedinger picture.** The **Schroedinger-picture evolution** of a preparation is fixed by clause (iii) of P4. A state vector evolves by $\psi(t):=U(t)\psi(0)$ for every $\psi(0)\in H$, and the **state at time $t$** of the pure preparation $[\psi(0)]$ is the pure preparation $[\psi(t)]$, which is well defined because $U(t)$ is injective; a general preparation $\rho$, that is an element of the state space $D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]], evolves by
$$\rho(t):=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^{*},$$
the reading of clause (iii) of P4 in the density-operator vocabulary of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]] ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]). In this picture the assigned observables are held fixed at their assigned values and the preparation moves.

**(d) Heisenberg picture.** For a **bounded** assigned sharp observable $(A,u_A)$ — that is, an assigned sharp observable with $A\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), so that $A$ is self-adjoint and everywhere defined — the **Heisenberg representative** of $(A,u_A)$ at time $t$ is the pair $(A_H(t),u_A)$ with the same declared unit and
$$A_H(t):=U(t)^{*}AU(t)=U(-t)AU(t).$$
By [[lem-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-heisenberg-flow]] clauses (a) and (d), $A_H(t)$ is again bounded and self-adjoint with spectral projection-valued measure $E_{A_H(t)}(B)=U(-t)E_A(B)U(t)$, so $(A_H(t),u_A)$ is again an assigned sharp observable of the framework; in this picture the preparation is held fixed at its value at time $0$ and the observables move. The two pictures are two bookkeeping devices for the same model; the statement that they assign the same outcome laws is proved in the Heisenberg-picture theorem of this page, not assumed here.

**(e) Stationary preparations.** A preparation $\rho\in D(H)$ is **stationary** for the assigned energy observable when $\rho(t)=\rho$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$. A pure preparation $[\psi]$ is stationary when $[\psi(t)]=[\psi(0)]$ for every $t$, that is, when the evolved vector remains in the ray of $\psi$; the characterization of this condition by the eigenrays of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ is proved in the stationary-states theorem of this page, not assumed here. An **energy eigenstate** is a pure preparation of a unit eigenvector of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$, and a **stationary state** in the model is a stationary pure preparation; by that theorem the two notions coincide.

**(f) Energy-compatible observables.** An assigned sharp observable $(A,u_A)$ is **compatible with the energy**, or **energy-compatible**, when its spectral projection-valued measure and that of the energy commute strongly,
$$E_A(B)E_H(C)=E_H(C)E_A(B)\qquad\text{for all Borel }B,C\subseteq\mathbb R .$$
This is an equality of bounded operators on $H$, not a relation between formal commutators on a small domain; the phrase **conserved quantity** for an energy-compatible assigned observable is a claim about the time invariance of its outcome law and is established in the energy-conservation theorem of this page for bounded $A$.

**(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(f) record the readings of P4 together with P1 and P2 in the vocabulary of this page and fix the terminology used by the later pages of the category. They adopt no physical assumption beyond P4, P1 and P2 and the choice hypotheses of the cited mathematics, assert no dynamics for a prescribed time-dependent family or for an open system (clauses (iv) and (v) of P4 are separate model assumptions treated on their own pages), assert no measurement model, no apparatus realization and no empirical result, and make no claim that any laboratory system is exactly isolated.

The state therefore never reaches this Gibbs density under the declared unitary evolution.

citations.quote:
A finite statistical microstate model is a pair $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ where $\Omega$ is a finite nonempty set and $\epsilon:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ assigns a finite numerical energy to each microstate. The physical energy of $x\in\Omega$ is $E(x)=\epsilon(x)\,\mathrm J$, with its zero and any retained internal offsets fixed by the declared material model. Energies are evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame specified by [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], and $U$ is the corresponding macroscopic internal-energy coordinate of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Equal energy values at distinct elements of $\Omega$ count as distinct microstates.

When two such models are declared independent, their joint microstate set is the Cartesian product $\Omega_A\times\Omega_B$, and additivity of the microscopic energy is the explicit condition $\epsilon_{AB}(x,y)=\epsilon_A(x)+\epsilon_B(y)$. Independence and this energy equation are model data; they do not follow merely from the two systems being separated. The definition itself assigns no weights, temperature, probability law, or dynamics.

Let $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ be a finite microstate model with energies $E_x=\epsilon(x)\,\mathrm J$ from [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]. Let $T>0$, $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$, and $P_\beta(x)=e^{-\beta E_x}/Z(\beta)$ be the adopted preparation of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]]. With $\bar E_\beta=\sum_xP_\beta(x)E_x$, $\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)=\sum_xP_\beta(x)(E_x-\bar E_\beta)^2$, and $S_\beta=-k_{\mathrm B}\sum_xP_\beta(x)\log P_\beta(x)$, the finite partition sum is positive and
$$-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E_\beta,\qquad \partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E),\qquad S_\beta=k_{\mathrm B}(\log Z+\beta\bar E_\beta).$$
Consequently the statistical free-energy value $F_{\mathrm{stat}}:=-k_{\mathrm B}T\log Z$ satisfies $F_{\mathrm{stat}}=\bar E_\beta-TS_\beta$. The derivatives hold the finite state set and its energy list fixed. No equivalence with a macroscopic entropy or Helmholtz potential is asserted.

Let two finite microstate models from [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]] have nonempty state sets $\Omega_A,\Omega_B$, energies $E_A,E_B$ in joules, and the same $T>0$. Assume their declared composite model has state set $\Omega_A\times\Omega_B$ and energy $E_{AB}(x,y)=E_A(x)+E_B(y)$, with no interaction term. Under the canonical sampling assumption [[post-td-canonical-sampling]], the partition function factorizes as $Z_{AB}=Z_AZ_B$, the joint canonical law is $P_{AB}=P_AP_B$, the Gibbs entropy satisfies $S_{AB}=S_A+S_B$, and the statistical free-energy value satisfies $F_{AB}=F_A+F_B$.

citations.quote:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

derivations.claim:
At fixed $t$, differentiating the rational equation gives
$$
\frac{\partial p}{\partial v}=-\frac{24t}{(3v-1)^2}+\frac{6}{v^3}.
$$
At $t=0.9$ and $v=1$, this derivative is $-24(0.9)/4+6=0.6>0$.

The derivative is continuous near $(t,v)=(0.9,1)$ because $3v-1\ne0$ there. Hence it remains positive on some open neighborhood within $v>1/3$. Since $P=P_cp$ and $V=V_cv$ with positive scales, $(\partial P/\partial V)_T=(P_c/V_c)(\partial p/\partial v)_t>0$ there as well. This verifies a positive-slope branch of this phenomenological model only.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

Fix an integer spatial dimension $d\geq 1$, a reference length $\ell_0>0$, and a bounded measurable region $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$ with dimensionless volume $V=|\Lambda|$. Its physical region is $\ell_0\Lambda$. A finite positional configuration of $N$ classical point particles in $\Lambda$ is an unordered simple set $\omega=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subset\Lambda$; simple means that no point is repeated. Particle number $N$ is a dimensionless nonnegative integer and the physical number density corresponding to $N/V$ is $N/(\ell_0^dV)$.

A pair potential is an even measurable function $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where $\varphi(x)$ is the interaction energy in joules at physical displacement $\ell_0x$ and evenness means $\varphi(x)=\varphi(-x)$. For a labelled representative of $\omega$, define the positional pair energy
$$H_N(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\varphi(x_i-x_j),\qquad H_0=H_1=0.$$
If any pair is forbidden by the potential, its energy and hence $H_N$ are $+\infty$. This model contains no kinetic energy, internal molecular coordinates, quantum exchange terms, or external field.

The interaction is stable if there is a constant $B\geq0$, measured in joules, such that $H_N(\omega)\geq-BN$ for every finite simple configuration. It has a regular integrable tail if there are $R>0$ and a nonnegative nonincreasing measurable function $\psi:[R,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, measured in joules, such that $|\varphi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R$ and
$$\int_R^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)\,dr<\infty.$$
A stable potential with this tail condition is the stable regularly tempered class used for the free-cube results on this page. Superstability and a positive divergent core are stronger, separate hypotheses and are not implied by stability.

At temperature $T>0$, write $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in joules inverse. The activity $z>0$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity $\ell_0^{-d}$. A free-wall finite-volume model contains only positions in $\Lambda$ and uses $H_N$ above. A periodic model uses the declared periodic cell and sums its periodic-image pair interactions with each unordered pair counted once. These are distinct boundary preparations. The limits on this page are positional configurational limits and do not by themselves include a momentum integral or a full phase-space energy shell.

For a specified finite region and boundary preparation, take $T>0$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, and the positional energy in [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. For each fixed $N$, specialize the measurable-model canonical preparation of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] to the dimensionless positional configuration measure $\mu_{\Lambda,N}$; adopt the law
$$P_{\Lambda,N}^{\mathrm{can}}(d\omega)=Z_{\Lambda,N}^{-1}e^{-\beta H_N(\omega)}\mu_{\Lambda,N}(d\omega),\qquad Z_{\Lambda,N}=\int e^{-\beta H_N}\,d\mu_{\Lambda,N},$$
whenever $0<Z_{\Lambda,N}<\infty$. Separately adopt the grand-canonical law at activity $z>0$ to have weights $z^{N(\omega)}e^{-\beta H_{N(\omega)}(\omega)}$ relative to the same indistinguishable positional measures; its normalizer is $\Xi_\Lambda(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{\Lambda,N}$ when finite. Here $z$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity in [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]], and $\alpha=\log z$.

For the controlled positional shell of [[def-td-controlled-fixed-n-energy-shell]], adopt the conditional measure $M_n$ only when its shell has positive finite reference measure. These are probability-law preparations used to define the model. They are not derived from Hamiltonian trajectories, and they do not assert that a laboratory apparatus reaches any of them. The inverse-temperature-zero hard-core continuation is governed separately by [[def-td-retained-hard-core-zero-beta-preparation]].

Use the dimensionless coordinates, simple configurations, and pair potential of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. A sequence $(\Lambda_k)_{k\geq1}$ of bounded measurable regions is van Hove if $|\Lambda_k|\to\infty$ and, for every fixed $s>0$,
$$\frac{|\{x\in\Lambda_k:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Lambda_k)\leq s\}|}{|\Lambda_k|}\longrightarrow0.$$
This is an explicit condition on the boundary-layer volume; increasing volume alone does not imply it. A free wall permits particles only in $\Lambda_k$ and includes no exterior particles. A periodic wall uses the specified periodic cell and its image convention.

For the deterministic exterior class, let $C=[-1/2,1/2)^d$ and $\Lambda_n=[-n-1/2,n+1/2)^d$, with $V_n=|\Lambda_n|$. For a locally finite exterior configuration $\zeta\subset\mathbb R^d$, write $N_{C+i}(\zeta)=|\zeta\cap(C+i)|$. Given $t<\infty$, define
$$\Omega(t)=\left\{\zeta:\sum_{i\in\Lambda_n\cap\mathbb Z^d}N_{C+i}(\zeta)^2\leq tV_n\ \text{for every integer }n\geq0\right\}.$$
For an interior configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_n$, its exterior interaction is
$$W_n(\omega,\zeta)=\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{y\in\zeta\setminus\Lambda_n}\varphi(x-y),$$
interpreted as an extended-real sum. A positive infinite value has zero Boltzmann weight. The regular tail controls distant terms; the class $\Omega(t)$ is a fixed uniform bound on exterior cell counts, not permission for an arbitrary volume-filling external potential. The van Hove and uniformly tempered exterior conditions are separate boundary regimes.

Assume AC, as required by the current mathematical definition and its shape suppliers. Let $d\geq2$, $E_0=1\,\mathrm J$, $\widehat\varphi=\varphi/E_0$, and assume $\widehat\varphi$ is Borel measurable and superstable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. Use $\widehat H=H/E_0$ and $\widehat\beta=E_0(k_BT)^{-1}>0$ in the mathematical rates. Let $(\Lambda_k)$ be a van Hove sequence as in [[def-td-admissible-van-hove-and-tempered-exterior]]. First, for free walls, the positional grand pressure along $\Lambda_k$ converges to the free-cube pressure of [[pthm-td-stable-tempered-free-cube-grand-pressure]]. For any positive interior attainable density $\rho$ and exact integers $N_k$ with $N_k/|\Lambda_k|\to\rho$, the exact-$N_k$ free-wall canonical log-partition rate converges to the same cube canonical rate. These two shape statements require superstability and regularity; stability alone is not asserted to suffice for arbitrary van Hove shapes.

Second, strengthen the potential hypothesis: for some $r_0>0$, $\widehat\varphi(x)\geq\widehat\chi(\|x\|_\infty)>0$ whenever $0<\|x\|_\infty\leq r_0$, where $\widehat\chi$ is nonincreasing and $\int_0^{r_0}\widehat\chi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr=+\infty$. For each fixed $t<\infty$, the free-wall grand pressure in $\Lambda_n$ with exterior $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$ then converges uniformly in $\zeta$ to the same free-cube pressure. The exterior interaction is the deterministic positional term of [[def-td-admissible-van-hove-and-tempered-exterior]], not a volume-filling external field. This genuine divergent-core condition is the exact stronger hypothesis of the current exterior supplier; it is not inferred from superstability or replaced by a weaker source condition.

derivations.claim: Order the coordinates $0\leq x_1<\cdots<x_N\leq L$. The exclusion constraints are $x_{i+1}-x_i\geq a$. Apply the coordinatewise translation $x_i\mapsto y_i=x_i-(i-1)a$; each one-coordinate translation preserves Lebesgue measure [F5], so product measure is preserved. The ordered region becomes $0\leq y_1\leq\cdots\leq y_N\leq S$, where $S=L-(N-1)a$. The cube $[0,S]^N$ splits, up to equality sets of zero product measure, into $N!$ coordinate-order regions. Product-measure uniqueness makes these permutation chambers equal in measure, so the ordered region has volume $S^N/N!$. The full labeled allowed volume is $N!$ times this, and canonical division by $N!$ gives $Z(L,N;\beta)=S^N/N!$.

If $L=(N-1)a$, then $S=0$ and the transformed region is a null set; its integral is zero. If $L>(N-1)a$, then $S>0$ and the ordered region has positive product volume. Thus the maximal-density endpoint does not carry a positive canonical partition at exact close packing; the interior-only theorem [F2] makes no contrary assertion.

In one dimension, let the pair potential be infinite when the separation is less than $a>0$, and zero otherwise. For $N\geq1$ labeled rods in $[0,L]$, with canonical positional normalization $1/N!$, write $S=L-(N-1)a$. If $S>0$, translating the ordered coordinates by $y_i=x_i-(i-1)a$ gives

Thus the thermodynamic close-packing endpoint is approached by a sequence of zero-weight finite systems; it is not realized by a positive canonical partition. The interior canonical limit theorem makes no assertion at that endpoint.

In one dimension, let the pair potential be infinite when the separation is less than $a>0$, and zero otherwise. For $N\geq1$ labeled rods in $[0,L]$, with canonical positional normalization $1/N!$, write $S=L-(N-1)a$. If $S>0$, translating the ordered coordinates by $y_i=x_i-(i-1)a$ gives
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac{S^N}{N!}=\frac{(L-(N-1)a)^N}{N!},\qquad \beta>0.$$
If $S=0$, the allowed configuration set has zero Lebesgue measure and $Z(L,N;\beta)=0$. Along $N\to\infty$ with $L=(N-1)a$, the density $N/L\to1/a$ while every finite-volume partition is zero. Thus the thermodynamic close-packing endpoint is approached by a sequence of zero-weight finite systems; it is not realized by a positive canonical partition. The interior canonical limit theorem makes no assertion at that endpoint.

Let $I$ be a finite nonempty set of system types, $X_i$ a nonempty state set with chosen reference $r_i\in X_i$ for each $i\in I$, and $M$ a common meter state set with $z_0,z_1\in M$. Assume for every $i$ that the product state set $X_i\times M$ satisfies the hypotheses of [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]], with strict reference pair $(r_i,z_0)\prec\prec(r_i,z_1)$. Let $S_i$ be its normalized representation and put $\sigma_i(x):=S_i(x,z_0)$. In that product comparison, the unit product-state point mass satisfies $e_{(x,z_0)}\sim_s(1-\sigma_i(x))e_{(r_i,z_0)}+\sigma_i(x)e_{(r_i,z_1)}$, by [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]]. These product-state point masses are distinct from the shared state-and-meter compounds defined next.

Assume in addition a **common-meter compatibility interface**. Let $\mathcal Y$ contain disjoint families of raw state tags $a_{i,x}$, raw type-reference tags $\rho_i$, and two distinct raw meter tags $\zeta_0,\zeta_1$. Using the unit point masses on these tags, write $e_{r_i}:=e_{\rho_i}$ and $e_{z_j}:=e_{\zeta_j}$, and define $u_{i,x}:=e_{a_{i,x}}+e_{z_0}$. Thus $u_{i,x}$ is an explicit mass-two state-and-fixed-meter compound; it is not a unit tag. Compounds over $\mathcal Y$ use the finite-support convention of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]], and their signed comparison is the one in [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]]. Require the exact substitution

$$u_{i,x}\sim_s e_{r_i}+(1-\sigma_i(x))e_{z_0}+\sigma_i(x)e_{z_1}\qquad(i\in I,\ x\in X_i),$$

finite substitutions to compose, and the fixed reference sum $\sum_iT_ie_{r_i}$ to cancel when type totals agree. Both sides of this signed substitution have total coefficient two, even when $\sigma_i(x)$ lies outside $[0,1]$. Require the common meter point masses to satisfy $e_{z_0}\preceq e_{z_1}$ and not $e_{z_1}\preceq e_{z_0}$. These are hypotheses on the comparison algebra, not consequences of separate numerical meter readings.

For positive coefficients $t_{ik}$ on a finite collection of type-$i$ states $x_{ik}$, define $T_i:=\sum_k t_{ik}$ and $T:=\sum_iT_i$. Put $C_0:=\sum_{i,k}t_{ik}e_{a_{i,x_{ik}}}$ and $C:=\sum_{i,k}t_{ik}u_{i,x_{ik}}=C_0+T e_{z_0}$. Thus $C_0$ is the state compound of mass $T$ and $C$ is its fixed-meter encoding of mass $2T$. Empty collections give $T=0$ and $C_0=C=0$. Define

$$\Sigma(C):=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_k t_{ik}\sigma_i(x_{ik}).$$

For two such compounds $C,D$ with the same type-total vector $(T_i)_{i\in I}$, the common comparison satisfies $C\preceq D$ exactly when $\Sigma(C)\le\Sigma(D)$. Equivalently, the same order criterion holds for the state compounds $C_0,D_0$ after canceling their common $T e_{z_0}$. The index family is finite; no arbitrary-index choice or infinite decomposition is asserted.

Let $X$ be nonempty and suppose its finite-support compounds carry the comparison structure of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] over the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. If there are $x_0,x_1\in X$ with $x_0\preceq x_1$ and not $x_1\preceq x_0$, define $S(x):=\sup L_x$ using [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]]. Then $S:X\to\mathbb R$ is normalized by $S(x_0)=0$, $S(x_1)=1$, and for all equal-mass compounds $A=\sum_i a_i e_{x_i}$ and $B=\sum_j b_j e_{y_j}$,

$$A\preceq B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_i a_iS(x_i)\le\sum_j b_jS(y_j).$$

Thus $S$ is an additive extensive representation on finite compounds. If no strict pair exists, CH instead makes every equal-mass pair of compounds equivalent, and any constant state function gives a (degenerate) additive representation. No concavity, continuity, or physical law follows without additional hypotheses.

derivations.claim: Both compounds have type-total vector $(1,1)$, so [F1] applies. Their calibrated values are $\Sigma(C)=1+1/3=4/3$ and $\Sigma(D)=0+3=3$. Since $4/3\le3$, [F1] gives $C\preceq D$. The theorem also cancels their common $2e_{z_0}$, giving $C_0\preceq D_0$. The value $3$ is permitted by [F2]; the representation theorem imposes no unit-interval bound on arbitrary states.

Reversing the comparison would require $3\le4/3$, which is false; hence this particular comparison is strict. No separate per-type numerical reading is treated as a proof of common-meter compatibility; that remains the stated hypothesis.

citations.quote: For finite random variables $M,R$ with joint law $p(m,r)$ and marginals $p_M,p_R$, use the entropy definition $H(Y)$ of [[lem-tdmath-conditional-memory-entropy]] for $Y=M,R,(M,R)$. Define $I(M;R):=\sum_{p(m,r)>0}p(m,r)\log\frac{p(m,r)}{p_M(m)p_R(r)}$. Then $I(M;R)=H(M)+H(R)-H(M,R)=H(M)-H(M|R)\ge0$, with equality exactly when $p(m,r)=p_M(m)p_R(r)$ for every pair.

Let $M$ and $R$ take values in finite sets under a joint probability law $p(m,r)\ge0$ with $\sum_{m,r}p(m,r)=1$. For any finite random variable $Y$ with law $p_Y$, define its Shannon entropy by $H(Y):=-\sum_{y:p_Y(y)>0}p_Y(y)\log p_Y(y)$; for a pair, $H(M,R)$ means this definition applied to its joint law. Put $a_r:=\sum_m p(m,r)$ and, when $a_r>0$, $q(m|r):=p(m,r)/a_r$. Thus $H(R)=-\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r\log a_r$. Define $H(M|R):=\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r[-\sum_{m:q(m|r)>0}q(m|r)\log q(m|r)]$. Then $H(M,R)=H(R)+H(M|R)$ and $H(M|R)\ge0$.

derivations.claim: Both marginals are uniform, so their entropies are $-2(1/2)\log(1/2)=\log2$. The joint law has two positive entries of size $1/2$, so $H(M,R)=\log2$.
Conditional on either value of $R$, $M$ is determined, so its conditional law has one probability $1$ and one $0$; therefore $H(M|R)=0$. Substituting these values into [F1] gives $I(M;R)=\log2$.

citations.quote: Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$; then $(p_i)$ is a countable probability law. For any real observable $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

derivations.claim: Every summand is $g_ne^{-\beta E_n}=1$, so the first $N$ terms sum to $N$ for every $N$; their supremum is infinite.
Thus $Z(\beta)=+\infty$, which violates the finite-normalization condition in [F1]; no normalized canonical probabilities $p_n$ are defined.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. Write $\overline{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ with its usual order and extended addition; in a convex combination set $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ and $\lambda\cdot(+\infty)=+\infty$ for $\lambda>0$. A function $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **proper** when it never takes the value $-\infty$ and its effective domain

$$\operatorname{dom}f:=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:f(x)<+\infty\}$$

is nonempty. It is **convex** when

$$f((1-t)x+ty)\le (1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d,\ t\in[0,1]).$$

It is **lower semicontinuous** when each weak sublevel set $\{x:f(x)\le a\}$ is closed in the Euclidean topology, for every $a\in\mathbb R$. Its **epigraph** is

$$\operatorname{epi}f:=\{(x,r)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R:f(x)\le r\}.$$

On this page “closed proper convex” means proper, convex, and lower semicontinuous in these conventions. The pairing of $p,x\in\mathbb R^d$ is the Euclidean inner product $\langle p,x\rangle$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be proper in the sense of [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]. Its **Fenchel conjugate** is $f^*:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,

$$f^*(p):=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}\bigl(\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)\bigr).$$

The supremum is taken in $\overline{\mathbb R}$; its defining set is nonempty and consists of real numbers, so $f^*(p)\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. The **biconjugate** is an extended-real expression that may also take $-\infty$ when its defining supremum is over the empty set:

$$f^{**}(x):=\sup_{\{p\in\mathbb R^d:f^*(p)<+\infty\}}\bigl(\langle p,x\rangle-f^*(p)\bigr),$$

with the convention $\sup\varnothing=-\infty$. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, the **subdifferential** is

$$\partial f(x):=\{p\in\mathbb R^d:f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle p,y-x\rangle\text{ for every }y\in\mathbb R^d\};$$

set $\partial f(x)=\varnothing$ for $x\notin\operatorname{dom}f$. A vector in $\partial f(x)$ is a subgradient at $x$. All pairings use [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ use the conventions of [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]. Then $f$ is convex if and only if $\operatorname{epi}f$ is a convex subset of $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, and $f$ is lower semicontinuous if and only if $\operatorname{epi}f$ is closed.

Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be proper, let $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, and let $p\in\mathbb R^d$. Then $f^*(p)\ge\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)$. Equality holds exactly when $p\in\partial f(x)$, equivalently when $x$ attains the supremum defining $f^*(p)$; in that case the supremum is finite.

Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be closed, proper, and convex, let $p\in\mathbb R^d$, and define $g(x)=f(x)-\langle p,x\rangle$. Assume $g$ is **coercive**, meaning that for every $M\in\mathbb R$ there is $R>0$ such that $\|x\|_2\ge R$ implies $g(x)>M$. Then $g$ has a finite global minimum at some $x_*\in\operatorname{dom}f$. The supremum defining $f^*(p)$ is finite and attained at $x_*$, and $p\in\partial f(x_*)$. No uniqueness is asserted.

Since $0\leq I(S;X_G)\leq H(S)<\infty$, divide by $|G|$ and take the cube limit [F2]; $H(S)/|G|\to0$, so $I(P_\theta)=\theta I(P)+(1-\theta)I(R)$. The expectation defining $\rho$ is affine. derivations.claim: In one unit cell, the conditional distribution of point positions given the count is identical for $Q_z$ and $Q_1$. The ratio of their count probabilities at $n$ is $$\frac{e^{-z}z^n/n!}{e^{-1}/n!}=e^{1-z}z^n.$$ Thus this is the Radon–Nikodym density on that cell.

The cube $\Lambda_m=[0,m)^d$ is the disjoint union of $m^d$ unit cells. Independence in [F1] makes the finite-cube density the product of the cell densities: $$h_m(\omega)=e^{(1-z)m^d}z^{N_{\Lambda_m}(\omega)}.$$

The count $N_{\Lambda_m}$ is Poisson with mean $zm^d$ by [F1]. Directly from its mass function and the exponential series, $$E_PN_{\Lambda_m}=e^{-zm^d}\sum_{n\geq1}n\frac{(zm^d)^n}{n!}=zm^d e^{-zm^d}\sum_{k\geq0}\frac{(zm^d)^k}{k!}=zm^d.$$ Therefore [F2] gives $$\frac{D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})}{m^d}=\frac{E_P\log h_m}{m^d}=1-z+z\log z$$ for every positive integer $m$.
Taking the cube limit in [F2] yields $I(Q_z)=1-z+z\log z$. At $z=1$ the value is zero, the reference-law baseline.

Let $A$ be a finite set of reaction channels, let $r\in\mathbb N$, let $\nu_a\in\mathbb R^r$ be the output-minus-input type vector of channel $a$, and let $d_a\in\mathbb R$ be a finite lower bound on its already calibrated entropy change. There exists an offset vector $b\in\mathbb R^r$ satisfying

$$b\cdot\nu_a+d_a\ge0\qquad(a\in A)$$

if and only if every $\lambda\in\mathbb R^A$ with $\lambda_a\ge0$ and $\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_a\nu_a=0$ satisfies $\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_ad_a\ge0$. If an actual transition has entropy change $\Delta\sigma_a\ge d_a$, such a vector guarantees $\Delta\sigma_a+b\cdot\nu_a\ge0$. The criterion is exact for the finite lower-bound inequalities; it does not claim necessity for actual transitions when $d_a$ is only a loose bound.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb N$ be finite, let $c_j\in\mathbb R^n$ and $h_j\in\mathbb R$ for $0\le j<m$. The finite system

$$c_j\cdot b\ge h_j\qquad(0\le j<m)$$

has a solution $b\in\mathbb R^n$ if and only if every $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$ with $\lambda_j\ge0$ and $\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jc_j=0$ satisfies $\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jh_j\le0$. Dot products and sums are finite. This includes empty rows, empty variables, and an empty inequality family.

Directly, the two inequalities would require $b_1-b_2\ge2$ and $-b_1+b_2\ge-1$, equivalently $b_1-b_2\le1$. Adding the original inequalities gives $0\ge1$, a contradiction. This is the positive-right-side zero-left certificate of [F2].

Fix a nonempty set $X$ and the compounds of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. A **comparison relation** $\preceq$ is defined only for pairs $(A,B)$ with $m(A)=m(B)$. Write $A\sim B$ when both $A\preceq B$ and $B\preceq A$; this is equivalence, not equality of coefficient functions. The following are explicit hypotheses on $\preceq$:

1. **Preorder:** $A\preceq A$, and $A\preceq B\preceq C$ implies $A\preceq C$.
2. **Composition consistency:** $A\preceq B$ implies $A+C\preceq B+C$ for every compound $C$.
3. **Positive scaling:** $A\preceq B$ implies $tA\preceq tB$ for every real $t>0$.
4. **Splitting and recombination:** for $x\in X$, $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, the one-state compound $te_x$ is equivalent to $se_x+(t-s)e_x$.

Let $C\ge1$ be the number of components and $P\ge1$ the number of phases. Use common positive real coordinates $T,p$, expressed in fixed units if they are given a physical interpretation, and, for each phase $\alpha$, an interior composition vector

$$x^\alpha\in\Omega_C:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},$$

with the convention $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $\Omega_1=\{0\}$. The final component fraction is $1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$. The ambient coordinate domain $U=(0,\infty)^2\times\Omega_C^P$ is open in $\mathbb R^n$, where $n=2+P(C-1)$. For each phase $\alpha$ and component $i$, let $\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)$ be a real-valued $C^1$ coordinate function; these are mathematical maps and no thermodynamic potential or physical realization is assumed.

For $P\ge2$, define the $q=C(P-1)$ coexistence equations

$$F_{i,\alpha}(T,p,x^1,\ldots,x^P)=\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)-\mu_i^1(T,p,x^1)=0\quad(1\le i\le C,\ 2\le\alpha\le P).$$

At a solution $z_*\in U$, assume some $q\times q$ derivative minor of $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is invertible. Then the local solution set is a graph of dimension

$$n-q=2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)=C-P+2.$$

For $P=1$ there are no coexistence equations and the coordinate domain itself has dimension $n=C+1=C-P+2$. In a specified reactive variant with $R\ge1$, let $\nu^1,\ldots,\nu^R\in\mathbb R^C$ be linearly independent dimensionless stoichiometric vectors and add the $R$ affinity equations $A_r=\sum_{i=1}^C\nu_i^r\mu_i^1=0$. If the combined equation map has an invertible $(q+R)\times(q+R)$ derivative minor at a solution and $q+R\le n$, its local zero set has dimension

$$n-q-R=C-P+2-R.$$

These are conditional local dimensions under the displayed nonsingular-minor assumptions. No dimension formula follows at singular solutions, on composition boundaries, or from equation counting alone; no empirical or general physical phase rule is asserted.

derivations.claim: For $C=P=2$, there are $n=2+2(2-1)=4$ coordinates and $q=2(2-1)=2$ equations. Since each $\mu_i^\alpha$ is identically zero, both differences $\mu_i^2-\mu_i^1$ equal zero at every point of $U$. Thus the zero set is exactly the open set $U$, which is locally parameterized by its four original coordinates.

The derivative of each identically zero equation is the zero covector, so the equation Jacobian has rank zero and no $2\times2$ minor is invertible. Therefore [L1] does not apply; the example does not contradict its regular dimension count, and it shows why equation count alone does not determine local dimension.

citations.quote: Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$; then $(p_i)$ is a countable probability law. For any real observable $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

Let $I,E_i,g_i,J,Z$ be as in [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]. Suppose that for every compact interval $K\subset J$ there is a summable sequence $a_i\ge0$ such that $g_i(1+|E_i|^2)\exp(-\beta E_i)\le a_i$ for every $i\in I$ and $\beta\in K$. Then $Z$ is positive, finite, and $C^2$ on $J$, with $Z'(\beta)=-\sum_i g_iE_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ and $Z''(\beta)=\sum_i g_iE_i^2\exp(-\beta E_i)$. The probabilities $p_i$ are normalized; their mean $\bar E$ and variance are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. Moreover $H_g(p)=\log Z+\beta\bar E$, and its defining series is absolutely convergent.

derivations.claim: Direct summation gives $Z=1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}=1+q$, hence $p_1=q/(1+q)$ and $p_0=1/(1+q)$.

The finite weighted sum gives $\bar E=\varepsilon p_1=\varepsilon q/(1+q)$. The second centered moment is $p_0(0-\bar E)^2+p_1(\varepsilon-\bar E)^2=\varepsilon^2q/(1+q)^2$, which is positive because $q\in(0,1)$. The values also agree with the finite-list derivative identities of [F2].

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. Write $\overline{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ with its usual order and extended addition; in a convex combination set $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ and $\lambda\cdot(+\infty)=+\infty$ for $\lambda>0$. A function $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **proper** when it never takes the value $-\infty$ and its effective domain

$$\operatorname{dom}f:=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:f(x)<+\infty\}$$

is nonempty. It is **convex** when

$$f((1-t)x+ty)\le (1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d,\ t\in[0,1]).$$

It is **lower semicontinuous** when each weak sublevel set $\{x:f(x)\le a\}$ is closed in the Euclidean topology, for every $a\in\mathbb R$. Its **epigraph** is

$$\operatorname{epi}f:=\{(x,r)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R:f(x)\le r\}.$$

On this page “closed proper convex” means proper, convex, and lower semicontinuous in these conventions. The pairing of $p,x\in\mathbb R^d$ is the Euclidean inner product $\langle p,x\rangle$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be proper in the sense of [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]. Its **Fenchel conjugate** is $f^*:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,

$$f^*(p):=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}\bigl(\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)\bigr).$$

The supremum is taken in $\overline{\mathbb R}$; its defining set is nonempty and consists of real numbers, so $f^*(p)\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. The **biconjugate** is an extended-real expression that may also take $-\infty$ when its defining supremum is over the empty set:

$$f^{**}(x):=\sup_{\{p\in\mathbb R^d:f^*(p)<+\infty\}}\bigl(\langle p,x\rangle-f^*(p)\bigr),$$

with the convention $\sup\varnothing=-\infty$. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, the **subdifferential** is

$$\partial f(x):=\{p\in\mathbb R^d:f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle p,y-x\rangle\text{ for every }y\in\mathbb R^d\};$$

set $\partial f(x)=\varnothing$ for $x\notin\operatorname{dom}f$. A vector in $\partial f(x)$ is a subgradient at $x$. All pairings use [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ use the conventions of [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]. Then $f$ is convex if and only if $\operatorname{epi}f$ is a convex subset of $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, and $f$ is lower semicontinuous if and only if $\operatorname{epi}f$ is closed.

Let $n\ge1$, let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $z\notin E$. Then there are a nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^n$ and a real $c$ such that

$$\langle u,e\rangle\le c<\langle u,z\rangle\qquad(e\in E).$$

Thus an affine hyperplane strictly separates the point from the entire set.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be closed, proper, and convex in the sense of [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]. With the Fenchel conjugate and biconjugate of [[def-tdmath-fenchel-transform-and-subgradient]], one has

$$f^{**}(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^d).$$

derivations.claim: The domain is $[0,\infty)$, so it is nonempty and $f$ is proper. Its epigraph is $E=\{(y,s):y\ge0,\ s\ge0\}$, a nonempty closed convex set; [F3] therefore makes $f$ closed and convex. The point $(-1,0)$ lies outside $E$. With $u=(-1,0)$ and $c=0$, every $(y,s)\in E$ satisfies $\langle u,(y,s)\rangle=-y\le0<1=\langle u,(-1,0)\rangle$, so this is the strict vertical separator; its height coefficient is zero.

For $p\le0$ and $y\ge0$, $py\le0$, with equality at $y=0$, so $f^*(p)=0$. For $p>0$, given any real $M$ choose $y>\max\{0,M/p\}$; then $py>M$, so the defining supremum is $+\infty$. Therefore $\operatorname{dom}f^*=(-\infty,0]$.
At $x=-1$, the biconjugate is $\sup_{p\le0}(-p-f^*(p))=\sup_{p\le0}(-p)=+\infty$: for every real bound $M$, the admissible choice $p=-\max\{M,0\}-1$ gives $-p>M$. Thus $f^{**}(-1)=f(-1)$.

For each $k\ge0$ and $y\ge0$, $\ell_k(y)=-ky\le0=f(y)$, so $\ell_k$ is an affine minorant. Its value at $-1$ is $k$, and the conjugate choice $p=-k$ has $f^*(-k)=0$, so the same family realizes arbitrarily large dual values at the point outside the domain. The conclusion is consistent with the full equality in [L2].

Let $s,r\ge1$, let $\nu\in\mathbb R^{s\times r}$ be a stoichiometric matrix (column $k$ gives the signed species-amount change per unit extent of reaction $k$), and let $n^0\in[0,\infty)^s$ be initial species amounts. Extents $\xi\in\mathbb R^r$ are measured in one fixed amount unit, so $n(\xi)=n^0+\nu\xi$ has species amounts in that same unit; $\nu$ is dimensionless. The feasible extent set is the polyhedron

$$\mathcal F=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^r:n^0+\nu\xi\in[0,\infty)^s\}.$$

At $\xi_*\in\mathcal F$, let $J=\{j:n^0_j+(\nu\xi_*)_j=0\}$ be the active species set. Define the Bouligand tangent cone $T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$ to consist of all $h\in\mathbb R^r$ for which there are $t_k>0$ with $t_k\to0$ and $h_k\to h$ such that $\xi_*+t_kh_k\in\mathcal F$. Then

$$T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)=\{h\in\mathbb R^r:(\nu h)_j\ge0\text{ for every }j\in J\}.$$

If $U\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ is open with $\xi_*\in U$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable with a local minimum at $\xi_*$ relative to $\mathcal F\cap U$, then $Df(\xi_*)h\ge0$ for every $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$. Conversely, if $U$ is convex and $f$ is convex and differentiable on $U$, this directional inequality for every $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$ implies $f(\xi)\ge f(\xi_*)$ for every $\xi\in\mathcal F\cap U$. If a potential $\Phi$ is differentiable on an open neighborhood of the relevant amounts and $f(\xi)=\Phi(n^0+\nu\xi)$, define $\mu_j=\partial\Phi/\partial n_j$; then

$$Df(\xi_*)h=\sum_{j=1}^s\mu_j(\nu h)_j=(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu)\cdot h.$$

The tangent-cone and optimality claims are mathematical deductions. They do not assert that a particular physical system obeys this model or is at equilibrium.

derivations.claim: The species-amount vector is $n(\xi)=n^0+\nu\xi=(2-2\xi,1-\xi,2\xi)^{\mathsf T}$. Nonnegativity of its third component requires $\xi\ge0$, and nonnegativity of its first two components requires $\xi\le1$; hence the feasible set is exactly $[0,1]$.

The elemental count matrix is $D=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&2\\0&2&1\end{pmatrix}$, with first row counting hydrogen atoms and second row oxygen atoms per molecule. Direct multiplication gives $D\nu=(-4+4,-2+2)^{\mathsf T}=(0,0)^{\mathsf T}$, so every change $n(\xi)-n^0=\nu\xi$ preserves both atom totals.

At $\xi_*=0$, only the water component is zero. Its directional change is $(\nu h)_3=2h$, so [L1] gives $T_{\mathcal F}(0)=\{h:2h\ge0\}=[0,\infty)$. A negative direction is infeasible because it would make the water amount $2\xi$ negative.

For $\Phi(n)=n_3$, the induced function is $f(\xi)=\Phi(n(\xi))=2\xi$. Its derivative at $0$ is $Df(0)h=2h\ge0$ for every feasible tangent $h\ge0$, and $f(\xi)\ge f(0)$ for every $\xi\in[0,1]$. This verifies the boundary first-order condition and minimum directly for this chosen mathematical objective.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

derivations.claim: Expand the square in the product integral and use [A1]: $\int_\Omega\int_\Omega(w(x)-w(y))^2\,dy\,dx=2|\Omega|\int_\Omega w^2-2(\int_\Omega w)^2=2|\Omega|\int_\Omega w^2$. The integrand is continuous, so [F2] justifies the repeated integrals.

For $x,y\in\Omega$, define $z^{(0)}=x$ and $z^{(i)}=(y_1,\ldots,y_i,x_{i+1},\ldots,x_d)$ for $1\le i\le d$, and set $\delta_i=w(z^{(i-1)})-w(z^{(i)})$. Then $w(x)-w(y)=\sum_i\delta_i$ and $d\sum_i\delta_i^2-(\sum_i\delta_i)^2=\sum_{i<j}(\delta_i-\delta_j)^2\ge0$.

Fix $i$ and the other coordinates. By [F1], $\delta_i$ is the integral of $h=\partial_iw$ over the interval between $x_i$ and $y_i$. If the endpoints differ, let $\bar h$ be the average of $h$ on that interval. Nonnegativity of $\int(h-\bar h)^2$ gives $(\int h)^2\le |x_i-y_i|\int h^2$; if they agree, $\delta_i=0$. Since $|x_i-y_i|\le L_i$, in both cases $\delta_i^2\le L_i\int_0^{L_i}|\partial_iw(z_1,\ldots,z_{i-1},s,z_{i+1},\ldots,z_d)|^2\,ds$.

Integrate the last bound over $x,y$. The $x_i,y_i$ integrations contribute $L_i^2$, the displayed segment bound contributes $L_i$, each unused variable from a pair $x_j,y_j$ with $j\ne i$ contributes $L_j$, and the remaining variables and $s$ give $\int_\Omega|\partial_iw|^2$. By [F2], this yields $\int_\Omega\int_\Omega\delta_i^2\,dy\,dx\le |\Omega|L_i^2\int_\Omega|\partial_iw|^2$.

By step 1.2 and the finite squared-sum inequality, the double integral in step 1.1 is at most $d\sum_i\int_\Omega\int_\Omega\delta_i^2\,dy\,dx$. Apply step 2.1, divide by $2|\Omega|>0$, and use $\sum_iL_i^2|\partial_iw|^2\le(\max_iL_i^2)|\nabla w|^2$ pointwise. This gives both stated inequalities with the displayed $C_\Omega$.

citations.quote: Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$; then $(p_i)$ is a countable probability law. For any real observable $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

Let $I,E_i,g_i,J,Z$ be as in [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]. Suppose that for every compact interval $K\subset J$ there is a summable sequence $a_i\ge0$ such that $g_i(1+|E_i|^2)\exp(-\beta E_i)\le a_i$ for every $i\in I$ and $\beta\in K$. Then $Z$ is positive, finite, and $C^2$ on $J$, with $Z'(\beta)=-\sum_i g_iE_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ and $Z''(\beta)=\sum_i g_iE_i^2\exp(-\beta E_i)$. The probabilities $p_i$ are normalized; their mean $\bar E$ and variance are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. Moreover $H_g(p)=\log Z+\beta\bar E$, and its defining series is absolutely convergent.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

For real random variables $X$ and $Y$ on one finite probability space, define
$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2],\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
The **standard deviation** of $X$ is $\sigma_X:=\operatorname{Var}(X)^{1/2}$, using the unique nonnegative square root supplied by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. Variance is nonnegative because its defining random variable is pointwise nonnegative and expectation is a sum with nonnegative weights.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

derivations.claim: Let $S_N=\sum_{n=0}^Nq^n$. Multiplying this finite sum by $1-q$ gives $(1-q)S_N=1-q^{N+1}$. Since $q=e^{-\gamma}$ for $\gamma>0$, [F5] gives $q^{N+1}\to0$; hence $Z=(1-q)^{-1}$ and the weights $(1-q)q^n$ sum to one. On a compact $\gamma$-interval $[b,B]\subset(0,\infty)$, set $a_n=(1+n^2)e^{-bn}$. Then $a_{n+1}/a_n=e^{-b}(1+(n+1)^2)/(1+n^2)\to e^{-b}<1$. Choose $c$ with $e^{-b}<c<1$; for all sufficiently large $n$, $a_{n+1}\le ca_n$, so the tail is bounded by a convergent geometric series. Thus $\sum_n(1+n^2)e^{-\gamma n}\le\sum_na_n<\infty$, which is the local envelope required by [F1].

With $Z(\gamma)=(1-e^{-\gamma})^{-1}$, [F1] gives $\mathbb E n=-\partial_\gamma\log Z=q/(1-q)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(n)=\partial_\gamma^2\log Z=q/(1-q)^2$. Substitution $q=e^{-\gamma}$ and [F4] justify the parameter derivatives. Therefore $\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(n)}/\mathbb E n=1/\sqrt q\to1$ as $q\uparrow1$.

The fermionic partition sum is $1+q$; its two probabilities are $1/(1+q)$ and $q/(1+q)$. Their finite weighted sums give mean $q/(1+q)$ and variance $q/(1+q)^2$, equal to the mean times one minus the mean.
These are calculations for the two specified probability laws only; no independence, physical preparation, or measured fluctuation claim is used.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$; then $(p_i)$ is a countable probability law. For any real observable $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2],\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

With fixed numerical length and energy units, the canonical positional partition is
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}dq_1\cdots dq_N,\quad Z(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
where $\beta>0$, and the grand partition is $\Xi(L;a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$ for numerical activity $a>0$.

For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, define
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(e^\alpha,\beta),$$
whose existence is [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]].

For free and periodic cubes define
$$Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}\!\left[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,bc}}\right],\qquad bc\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{per}\}.$$
Then the limit $p_Q(z,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}$ exists, is independent of $bc$, and
$$p_Q(z,\beta)=-\min_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
The minimizer set is nonempty and compact in the local-tame topology $\tau_L$.

Define its **periodized empirical field**
$$R_{L,\omega}:=\frac1{L^d}\int_{\Lambda_L}\delta_{T_x\omega^{(L)}}\,dx.$$
The integral is the push-forward of normalized Lebesgue measure on $\Lambda_L$ under $x\mapsto T_x\omega^{(L)}$.

For $L>0$ and a finite configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$ with $N(\omega)=N$, the measure $R_{L,\omega}$ of [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]] is a stationary probability law of finite intensity and
$$\rho(R_{L,\omega})=\frac{N}{L^d}.$$
For any probability law $C_L$ on finite configurations in $\Lambda_L$ with $E_{C_L}N<\infty$, its empirical-field barycenter $\bar C_L$ is also a stationary probability law of finite intensity and $\rho(\bar C_L)=E_{C_L}N/L^d$.

derivations.claim: The canonical law is the grand law conditioned on $N=N_L$, since the grand weight on the $N_L$ sector differs from the canonical density only by the constant activity factor $z^{N_L}$. Its conditioning probability is $$G^b_{L,z,\beta}(N=N_L)=\frac{z^{N_L}e^{-L^d}Z_b(L,N_L;\beta)}{Z_{Q,b}(L;z,\beta)}.$$ Divide the logarithm by $L^d$. The numerator terms tend to $\rho\log z+F_\beta(\rho)-1$ by the assumed canonical rate and [F1]; the denominator tends to $p_Q(z,\beta)$. By [F2]–[F3], $p_Q(z,\beta)=F_\beta(\rho)+\rho\log z-1$, so $$L^{-d}\log G^b_{L,z,\beta}(N=N_L)\longrightarrow0.$$ Thus the exact-number conditioning event has subexponential, positive grand probability for all sufficiently large $L$.

Let $U$ be an open $\tau_L$ neighborhood of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$ and set $F=U^c$. The good rate in [L1] has zero set exactly $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$. Its infimum on the closed set $F$ is strictly positive: otherwise a sequence in $F$ with rates tending to zero would lie in a compact rate sublevel, have a limit in $F$, and by lower semicontinuity that limit would be a zero of the rate outside $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$. The large-deviation upper bound therefore gives some $c>0$ with $$\limsup_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log G^b_{L,z,\beta}\{R_{L,\omega}\in F\}\leq-c.$$

Conditioning on $N=N_L$ yields $$C^b_{L,N_L}\{R_{L,\omega}\notin U\}\leq \frac{G^b_{L,z,\beta}\{R_{L,\omega}\in F\}}{G^b_{L,z,\beta}(N=N_L)}.$$ The numerator decays exponentially by step 1.2 and the denominator has zero exponential rate by step 1.1, so the ratio tends to zero. This proves concentration on every neighborhood of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$. If the minimizer is unique, these neighborhood bounds are exactly convergence in probability in $\tau_L$.

Let $\beta,z>0$, let $\rho>0$ be an interior attainable density, and choose $\alpha=\log z$ supporting the free canonical rate $F_\beta$ at $\rho$. For either free or periodic boundary condition $b$, let $C^b_{L,N_L}$ be the exact-$N_L$ canonical law and $G^b_{L,z,\beta}$ the grand-canonical law using the same finite-volume energy, where $N_L/L^d\to\rho$. Assume
$$L^{-d}\log Z_b(L,N_L;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho).$$
Let $R_{L,\omega}$ be the periodized empirical field of [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]], and let
