citations.quote: Let $I$ be a finite or countably infinite set with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$, and let $\ell^2(I):=\{x:I\to\mathbb C:\sum_i|x_i|^2<\infty\}$ with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_i x_i\overline{y_i}$, linear in the first variable. Write $u_i$ for the coordinate unit vector at $i$. The diagonal multiplication operator $H_E$ is the linear operator with domain $D(H_E):=\{x\in\ell^2(I):\sum_i|E_ix_i|^2<\infty\}$ and action $(H_Ex)_i:=E_ix_i$. Its domain is part of the operator data in the sense of [[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: Every finitely supported sequence belongs to $D(H_E)$. For $x\in\ell^2(I)$, the tails of its square-sum can be made arbitrarily small, so finite-coordinate truncations converge in norm to $x$; finite-support vectors are therefore dense in $\ell^2(I)$.

For $x,y\in D(H_E)$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] makes $\sum_i|E_ix_i\overline{y_i}|$ finite, and reality of $E_i$ gives $\langle H_Ex,y\rangle=\sum_iE_ix_i\overline{y_i}=\langle x,H_Ey\rangle$. Thus $H_E$ is symmetric.

If $y\in D(H_E^*)$, there is $z\in\ell^2(I)$ such that $\langle H_Ex,y\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle$ for every $x\in D(H_E)$. Taking $x=u_i$ gives $E_i\overline{y_i}=\overline{z_i}$, hence $z_i=E_iy_i$ for every $i$; since $z\in\ell^2(I)$, $y\in D(H_E)$ and $H_E^*y=H_Ey$. Conversely symmetry in step 1.2 shows every $y\in D(H_E)$ is in $D(H_E^*)$ with that value. Therefore $D(H_E^*)=D(H_E)$ and $H_E^*=H_E$.

$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

derivations.claim: Fix $x\in C$. Openness of $C$ and continuity of $\lambda\mapsto\lambda x$ give an open interval $K_x\subset(0,\infty)$ around $1$ with $\lambda x\in C$ for $\lambda\in K_x$. Define $g:K_x\to\mathbb R$ by $g(\lambda)=f(\lambda x)$. By [F1], $g'(1)=Df(x)[x]$. This ambient derivative exists even if $1$ is an endpoint of the interval $J_x$ on which homogeneity is assumed.

Since $J_x$ is a nondegenerate interval containing $1$, it contains points $\lambda\ne1$ arbitrarily close to $1$, also lying in $K_x$. For these points, homogeneity and $g(1)=f(x)$ give $(g(\lambda)-g(1))/(\lambda-1)=f(x)$. The ambient derivative in step 1.1 exists, so its limit along this possibly one-sided set is $g'(1)=f(x)$. Therefore $f(x)=Df(x)[x]$, and writing the total derivative in Euclidean coordinates gives $Df(x)[x]=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\partial_j f(x)$.

Step 2.1: the coordinate formula is the total derivative evaluated on x and includes the one-dimensional case.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Suppose that for every $x\in C$ there is a nondegenerate interval $J_x\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $1$ such that $\lambda x\in C$ and $f(\lambda x)=\lambda f(x)$ for every $\lambda\in J_x$. Here nondegenerate means that $J_x$ contains a point different from $1$; $1$ may be an endpoint. Then

$$f(x)=Df(x)[x]=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\,\partial_j f(x)\qquad(x\in C).$$

The radial identity need only hold on one side of $1$: openness of $C$ and $C^1$ regularity supply an ambient derivative, and the interval makes $1$ a nonisolated point at which that derivative is determined by the radial identity. This uses the same function on the same domain; it asserts nothing about a family of functions on different tagged domains.

citations.quote: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable with $f_n\le f_{n+1}$ and $f_n\to f$ pointwise. Then $\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu$, including infinite values. Also, for measurable $f,g\ge0$, $\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu$. For every $c\ge0$, $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$; the integral is also linear on real integrable functions.

derivations.claim: Set $h_k:=\inf_{n\ge k}f_n$. For each real $a$, $\{h_k<a\}=\bigcup_{n\ge k}\{f_n<a\}$, so $h_k$ is measurable by the sigma-algebra closure in [F1]. The sequence $h_k$ is increasing and its pointwise limit is $\liminf_n f_n$, which is measurable since $\{\lim_kh_k>a\}=\bigcup_k\{h_k>a\}$.

For every $n\ge k$, monotonicity gives $\int h_k\le\int f_n$, so $\int h_k\le\inf_{n\ge k}\int f_n$. Taking $k\to\infty$ and applying monotone convergence to $h_k$ yields $\int\liminf f_n=\lim_k\int h_k\le\lim_k\inf_{n\ge k}\int f_n=\liminf_n\int f_n$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable with $f_n\le f_{n+1}$ and $f_n\to f$ pointwise. Then $\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu$, including infinite values. Also, for measurable $f,g\ge0$, $\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu$. For every $c\ge0$, $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$; the integral is also linear on real integrable functions.

citations.quote: Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$; then $(p_i)$ is a countable probability law. For any real observable $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

derivations.claim: Factor $e^{-\beta E_0}$ from the partition sum to obtain $Z=e^{-\beta E_0}(g+\sum_{i:E_i>E_0}e^{-\beta(E_i-E_0)})$. Every gap is positive, and there are finitely many, so the parenthesized sum tends to $g$. Thus each ground probability tends to $1/g$ and every excited probability tends to zero.

Ground-state entropy terms tend to $-g(1/g)\log(1/g)=\log g$. For an excited state with gap $\Delta_i>0$, step 1.1 gives $p_i=O(e^{-\beta\Delta_i})$ and $\log p_i=-\beta\Delta_i-\log D(\beta)$, where $D(\beta):=g+\sum_{j:E_j>E_0}e^{-\beta(E_j-E_0)}\to g>0$ by step 1.1, so $\log D(\beta)$ is bounded by continuity of $\log$; hence $|p_i\log p_i|=O((1+\beta)e^{-\beta\Delta_i})\to0$ by [F3]. The excited sum is finite, so its limit is zero and the total entropy tends to $\log g$.

citations.quote:
Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with finite slope $P_i(x)$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

Let $X$ be a set of state labels. A **tagged scalable compound over $X$** is a function $c:X\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ whose support $\operatorname{supp}(c):=\{x\in X:c(x)\ne0\}$ is finite. The coefficient is a dimensionless formal amount; state labels retain their tags, so equal coefficients on different labels do not identify those labels. Compounds are equal exactly when their coefficient functions are equal.

For compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, define composition and nonnegative scaling pointwise by $(c+d)(x):=c(x)+d(x)$ and $(tc)(x):=t c(x)$. The zero function is the empty compound; in particular $0c=0$. Comparison axioms involving scaling still require a strictly positive scalar unless explicitly stated otherwise. The **mass** of $c$ is the finite sum $m(c):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)$. It is dimensionless bookkeeping mass, not thermodynamic mass or energy. The compound is positive when $m(c)>0$.

For every state label $x\in X$, the **unit-state compound** $e_x$ is the coefficient function with $e_x(y)=1$ if $y=x$ and $e_x(y)=0$ otherwise. Its support is $\{x\}$, so it is a tagged compound. In compound comparisons, a state label $x$ denotes $e_x$. Every compound has the canonical finite decomposition $c=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)e_x$, with an empty sum when $c=0$; coefficients on this support are strictly positive. The mass-one property $m(e_x)=1$ and the equivalence $m(c)=0\Longleftrightarrow c=0$ are proved in [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

The formula for mass is independent of the chosen finite set containing the support, and composition and scaling obey $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]] proves these assertions.

For every tagged scalable compound $c$, the mass in [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] is independent of the finite summation set used. For any compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; $m(0)=0$. For every $x\in X$, the unit-state compound $e_x$ has $m(e_x)=1$. A compound has zero mass if and only if it is the empty compound.

Let $u,v$ be finite-support real coefficient maps on the tagged state labels of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] with equal total coefficient. For a typed state $x$, compound notation uses the represented map $\mathsf{J}(x)$ from [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]; its raw unit point mass is $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. Signed maps still use the ordinary total of their raw coefficients, exactly the bookkeeping mass of the represented nonnegative maps. Put $d=v-u$, $d^+(x)=\max(d(x),0)$ and $d^-(x)=\max(-d(x),0)$. Define $u\preceq_s v$ to mean $d^-\prec d^+$ under the compound relation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Write $u\sim_s v$ when both $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s u$. These are formal signed comparison maps, not physical negative amounts. The positive and negative parts are finite-support compounds of equal mass. If $u\sim_s v$, then $cu\sim_s cv$ for every real $c$: positive $c$ uses scaling, $c=0$ is reflexivity, and negative $c$ swaps the positive and negative parts while equivalence supplies both comparison directions. This Definition introduces the signed notation; ordinary-order compatibility and the signed-order laws are proved separately.

derivations.claim: Assume $A+C\prec B+C$ and $m(C)>0$. Scaling by $1/n$ gives $A/n+C/n\prec B/n+C/n$. Define $E_j=(n-j)A/n+jB/n+C/n$ for $j=0,\ldots,n$. For $j<n$, add the common spectator $(n-j-1)A/n+jB/n$ to the scaled comparison to obtain $E_j\prec E_{j+1}$. Transitivity yields $A+C/n=E_0\prec E_n=B+C/n$. Stability with bases $A,B$, fixed positive spectators $C,C$, and $\epsilon_n=1/n$ gives $A\prec B$. If $m(C)=0$, nonnegativity gives $C=0$ and the implication is immediate. Conversely, consistency gives $A+C\prec B+C$ from $A\prec B$.

For equal-total signed maps $u,v$, the difference $d=v-u$ has finite support and total coefficient zero, so $m(d^+)=m(d^-)$. If $u,v$ are nonnegative, their pointwise common part $k(x)=\min\{u(x),v(x)\}$ gives $u=k+d^-$ and $v=k+d^+$. Cancellation in step 1.1 proves $u\prec v$ exactly when $d^-\prec d^+$, which by [F2] is $u\preceq_s v$; adding a common signed map leaves $d$ unchanged by [F2].

If $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s w$, [F2] identifies these with comparisons of $(v-u)^-$ to $(v-u)^+$ and $(w-v)^-$ to $(w-v)^+$. Consistency combines them. Their pointwise common minimum cancels by step 1.1, leaving $(w-u)^-\prec(w-u)^+$, which [F2] identifies as $u\preceq_s w$. The same finite-sum argument proves closure under addition; reflexivity follows from reflexivity of the zero compound.

It is lower regular if a nonnegative nonincreasing $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfies
$$\phi(x)\geq-\psi(|x|_\infty),\qquad \int_0^\infty\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty.$$
It is regular if it is lower regular and, for some $R<\infty$, $\phi(x)\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ whenever $|x|_\infty\geq R$.

derivations.claim: Since $\psi$ is nonincreasing, $0\leq g^d\psi(g)\leq \frac{d}{1-2^{-d}}\int_{g/2}^{g}r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr$ for $g>2R_0$: on $[g/2,g]$, $\psi(r)\geq\psi(g)$, and integration of $r^{d-1}$ gives the displayed coefficient. Both the interval integral and the tail integral in $\eta(g)$ tend to zero as $g\to\infty$, so $\eta(g)\to0$.

For $m\geq2$ and $r\in[(m-1)g,mg]$, monotonicity gives $\psi(r)\geq\psi(mg)$ and $r^{d-1}\geq((m-1)g)^{d-1}$. Hence $$ \int_{(m-1)g}^{mg}r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr\geq g^d(m-1)^{d-1}\psi(mg). $$ Since $m^{d-1}\leq2^{d-1}(m-1)^{d-1}$, summing over disjoint intervals yields $\sum_{m\geq2}m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq2^{d-1}g^{-d}\int_g^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr$. The $m=1$ term equals $g^{-d}g^d\psi(g)$, so adding it proves the stated bound because $2^{d-1}\geq1$.

For integer $m\geq\lceil R_0+3\rceil$, monotonicity gives $\psi(r)\geq\psi(m-1)$ on $[m-2,m-1]$, so $\int_{m-2}^{m-1}r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr\geq(m-2)^{d-1}\psi(m-1)$. Since $m^{d-1}\leq c_d(m-2)^{d-1}$ for these $m$, summing over disjoint unit intervals proves $\sum_{m\geq\lceil R_0+3\rceil} m^{d-1}\psi(m-1)<\infty$.

For each integer $k\geq1$, let $G_k$ be the least integer greater than $2R_0$ such that $\eta(g)\leq k^{-2d}$ for every $g\geq G_k$; it exists by step 1.1 and the well-ordering of the positive integers. Choose a strictly increasing sequence $L_k$ with $L_k\geq kG_k$ and $L_k\geq k^2$. For $\ell\geq L_1$, let $k(\ell)=\max\{k:L_k\leq\ell\}$ and $g(\ell)=\ell/k(\ell)$. Then $k(\ell)\to\infty$, $g(\ell)\geq G_{k(\ell)}$ and $g(\ell)\geq k(\ell)$, while $g(\ell)/\ell=1/k(\ell)$. Therefore $$ \left(\frac{\ell}{g(\ell)}\right)^d\eta(g(\ell))\leq k(\ell)^d k(\ell)^{-2d}=k(\ell)^{-d}\to0. $$ This gives all three gap limits.

Fix distinct points $x,y$ in a finite configuration and a period $L>0$. For $|k|_\infty$ larger than $2|x-y|_\infty/L+2R_0/L$, the triangle inequality gives $|x-y+Lk|_\infty\geq L|k|_\infty/2>2R_0$. Grouping lattice indices by $m=|k|_\infty$ and applying the sum bound of step 1.2 with gap $g=L/2$ shows $\sum_k|\phi(x-y+Lk)|<\infty$ whenever $L/2>2R_0$. There are finitely many remaining images; any $+\infty$ term makes the periodic energy $+\infty$ by definition, while otherwise their finite sum is well-defined. This proves the periodic-image convention used in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]] for all sufficiently large $L$.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $d\geq1$ and let $\phi$ be a regular potential with a nonnegative nonincreasing envelope $\psi:[R_0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, where $R_0<\infty$ and $\int_{R_0}^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr<\infty$. Thus $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ for $|x|_\infty\geq R_0$. For $g>2R_0$ set
$$\eta(g)=g^d\psi(g)+\int_g^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr.$$
Then $\eta(g)\to0$ and
$$\sum_{m=1}^\infty m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq 2^{d-1}g^{-d}\eta(g).$$
Moreover, there is a choice $g(\ell)>0$, for all sufficiently large real $\ell$, such that $g(\ell)\to\infty$, $g(\ell)/\ell\to0$, and
$$\left(\frac{\ell}{g(\ell)}\right)^d\eta(g(\ell))\longrightarrow0.$$
For every fixed finite configuration and all sufficiently large periods $L$, the noncoincident periodic-image tail $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d,\ |k|_\infty\geq K_0}|\phi(x-y+Lk)|$ is absolutely convergent. The tail of the cell envelope $\psi(|j|_\infty-1)$ over all sufficiently large integer offsets is summable. This lemma is a deterministic tail estimate; it uses no superstability or thermodynamic-limit conclusion.

boundaries.evidence: Statement the chosen tail gap is positive and tends to infinity, and g>2R_0 is used only in its tail regime. No estimate divides by a zero gap; an empty block contributes zero without division by its count.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the integral defining $h(t)=\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$ exists. Continuity of $f$ gives $h'(t)=f(t)$ on $(0,T)$: the difference quotient error is bounded by $\sup_{|s-t|\le|r|}|f(s)-f(t)|$, which tends to zero as $r\to0$. Also $h$ is continuous on $[0,T]$. The hypothesis gives $h'\le Lh$, so [F2]–[F3] yield $g'(t)\le0$ for $g(t)=e^{-Lt}h(t)$ on $(0,T)$. The mean value theorem makes $g$ nonincreasing; since $g(0)=0$ and $g\ge0$, $g\equiv0$ and $h\equiv0$.

For any $t>0$, the nonnegative continuous function $f$ has integral $h(t)=0$. If $f(t_0)>0$ at any $t_0>0$, continuity gives a positive lower bound on a nonempty subinterval of $[0,t_0]$, contradicting $h(t_0)=0$. At $t=0$ the assumed inequality gives $f(0)\le0$; nonnegativity gives $f(0)=0$. Hence $f\equiv0$.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, writing $d = n + 1 - m$
for the number of terms,

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $M$ and $R$ take values in finite sets under a joint probability law $p(m,r)\ge0$ with $\sum_{m,r}p(m,r)=1$. For any finite random variable $Y$ with law $p_Y$, define its Shannon entropy by $H(Y):=-\sum_{y:p_Y(y)>0}p_Y(y)\log p_Y(y)$; for a pair, $H(M,R)$ means this definition applied to its joint law. Put $a_r:=\sum_m p(m,r)$ and, when $a_r>0$, $q(m|r):=p(m,r)/a_r$. Thus $H(R)=-\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r\log a_r$. Define $H(M|R):=\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r[-\sum_{m:q(m|r)>0}q(m|r)\log q(m|r)]$. Then $H(M,R)=H(R)+H(M|R)$ and $H(M|R)\ge0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Define $\phi(t):=t-1-\log t$ for $t>0$. Its derivative is $1-1/t$, nonpositive on $(0,1]$ and nonnegative on $[1,\infty)$; the mean-value theorem [F4] gives $\phi(t)\ge\phi(1)=0$, with equality only at $t=1$. Thus $-\log t\ge1-t$, strictly unless $t=1$.
Expanding the finite logarithmic sum gives $I(M;R)=H(M)+H(R)-H(M,R)$; applying [F2] rewrites it as $H(M)-H(M|R)$.

Put $q(m,r):=p_M(m)p_R(r)$. For $p(m,r)>0$, $q(m,r)>0$ by [F1], and step 1.1 with $t=q/p$ gives $p\log(p/q)\ge p-q$. Summing over the support of $p$ yields $I(M;R)\ge1-\sum_{p>0}q\ge0$. Equality forces $q=p$ on the support and no $q$-mass outside it, hence equality at every pair; conversely independence makes each positive logarithm zero.

Fix a positive integer $d$ and use the Euclidean space $\mathbb R^d$ with norm
$\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A
pair potential is an even Borel-measurable function
$\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ whose image is contained in
$\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. Here $\overline{\mathbb R}$ is the extended real
line ([[def-extended-reals]]). Borel measurability means the inverse image of
each Borel subset of $\overline{\mathbb R}$ belongs to the Borel sigma-algebra
generated by open sets in the Euclidean topology on $\mathbb R^d$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Even means $\phi(-x)=\phi(x)$. The value
$+\infty$ represents a forbidden pair separation. Coordinates and
potential values are numerical values in fixed reference length and energy
units.

A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

$0\le e^{-\beta U_N}\le e^{\beta BN}$, with the value $0$ when $U_N=+\infty$.
Fact [F7] makes the integrand and its restriction to $\Lambda_L^N$
measurable. For every simple minorant of this restricted integrand, [L1]
bounds its integral by the integral of the constant $e^{\beta BN}$ on
$\Lambda_L^N$.

The box and product-measure formulas [F2, F3] give
$\lambda_d^{\otimes N}(\Lambda_L^N)=L^{dN}$. Thus
$Z_{L,N}\le(ae^{\beta B}L^d)^N/N!=(QL^d)^N/N!$ for $N\ge1$, and this
also holds for $N=0$ since $Z_{L,0}=1$.

Summing the nonnegative terms by [F6] and using [F4] gives
$1\le\Xi_L\le\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}(QL^d)^N/N!=e^{QL^d}$; the lower bound is
the empty-configuration term.

By [F8], $KL^d<n_L\le KL^d+1$. If $N>n_L$, then $N>KL^d$, so
$1\le e^{N-KL^d}$. Therefore
$$\sum_{N>n_L}Z_{L,N}\le e^{-KL^d}\sum_{N>n_L}\frac{(eQL^d)^N}{N!}\le e^{-KL^d}e^{eQL^d}=e^{(eQ-K)L^d}\le e^{-L^d}.$$
The second inequality extends a nonnegative partial tail to the full
exponential series; the equality uses [F5], and the last inequality follows
from $K>eQ+1$ and [F5].

$\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}$ and the finite tail from $n_L+1$ through $M$.

$\Xi_L=\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}+\sum_{N>n_L}Z_{L,N}$; subtraction is valid because

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $d\ge1$, let $\phi$ be a stable pair
potential as in [[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]] with
stability constant $B$, and fix $a,\beta>0$. In fixed reference length and
energy units, put $\Lambda_L=[0,L]^d$ and define, for $N\ge1$,
$$Z_{L,N}:=\frac{a^N}{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta U_N(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}\,d\lambda_d^{\otimes N},$$
where $\lambda_d$ is Lebesgue measure restricted to the Borel subsets of
$\mathbb R^d$, $\lambda_d^{\otimes N}$ is its $N$-fold product measure. The
integrand uses the ordinary real exponential when $U_N<+\infty$ and is defined
to be $0$ when $U_N=+\infty$. Also,
$\int_{\Lambda_L^N}f\,d\lambda_d^{\otimes N}$ abbreviates the nonnegative
integral of $f\mathbf1_{\Lambda_L^N}$ on the full product space, using
[[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]. Set $Z_{L,0}=1$.
Define $\Xi_L:=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}Z_{L,N}$ as the nonnegative extended sum of
[[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]. For $L\ge1$ put
$Q:=a e^{\beta B}$. Choose any real $K>eQ+1$ and set
$$n_L:=\lfloor K L^d\rfloor+1.$$
which satisfies $K L^d<n_L\le K L^d+1$ by the integer-part lemma
[[lem-integer-part]]. Let
$\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}:=\sum_{N=0}^{n_L}Z_{L,N}$. Then
$$1\le\Xi_L\le e^{Q L^d},\qquad \sum_{N>n_L}Z_{L,N}\le e^{-L^d},\qquad \Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge(1-e^{-L^d})\Xi_L.$$

The integrand is $L\mathbb Z^d$-periodic in $x$. The translated cube $\Lambda_L+y$ is another fundamental region for this lattice; partitioning it and $\Lambda_L$ into their finitely many translated intersections and using translation invariance of Lebesgue measure gives equal integrals. For each fixed $q\in\omega$, the sets $\Lambda_L+Lk$ partition $\mathbb R^d$ up to null boundaries. Translating variables in each integral therefore makes the inner sum of integrals equal to $|A|$. $$\rho(\bar C_L)=E_{C_L}[R_{L,\omega}(N_{[0,1)^d})]=E_{C_L}N/L^d<\infty.$$

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.

derivations.claim: The natural numbers are nonempty. If they had an upper bound, completeness [F1] would give $s=\sup\mathbb N$. The number $s-1$ cannot be an upper bound, so some $n\in\mathbb N$ satisfies $n>s-1$. Then $n+1>s$, while $n+1\in\mathbb N$, contradicting that $s$ is an upper bound. Thus the natural numbers are unbounded above.

Each $n+1$ is positive, so $\epsilon_n>0$; since $n+2>n+1$, ordered-field division by positive denominators gives $1/(n+2)<1/(n+1)$. Given $\eta>0$, unboundedness from step 1.1 supplies $N\in\mathbb N$ with $N+1>1/\eta$. For all $n\ge N$, $0<\epsilon_n\le1/(N+1)<\eta$, which is the definition of convergence to zero.

Fix a nonempty set $X$ and the compounds of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. A **comparison relation** $\preceq$ is defined only for pairs $(A,B)$ with $m(A)=m(B)$. Write $A\sim B$ when both $A\preceq B$ and $B\preceq A$; this is equivalence, not equality of coefficient functions. The following are explicit hypotheses on $\preceq$:

1. **Preorder:** $A\preceq A$, and $A\preceq B\preceq C$ implies $A\preceq C$.
2. **Composition consistency:** $A\preceq B$ implies $A+C\preceq B+C$ for every compound $C$.
3. **Positive scaling:** $A\preceq B$ implies $tA\preceq tB$ for every real $t>0$.
4. **Splitting and recombination:** for $x\in X$, $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, the one-state compound $te_x$ is equivalent to $se_x+(t-s)e_x$.
5. **Stability:** for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive compounds $Z_0,Z_1$ with $m(Z_0)=m(Z_1)$, and a sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to $0$, if $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\preceq B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for every $n$, then $A\preceq B$.
6. **Comparison hypothesis (CH):** for every equal-mass pair $A,B$, either $A\preceq B$ or $B\preceq A$ (or both).

These are mathematical assumptions, not conclusions about a physical system. No antisymmetry, continuity, convexity, or strict comparison is included. Strict comparison means $A\preceq B$ and not $B\preceq A$.

Let $u,v:X\to\mathbb R$ be finite-support real coefficient maps with equal total coefficient $\sum_xu(x)=\sum_xv(x)$. These signed maps are formal comparison notation, not compounds. Put $d:=v-u$ and define $d^+(x):=\max\{d(x),0\}$ and $d^-(x):=\max\{-d(x),0\}$. Then $d^+,d^-$ are nonnegative finite-support compounds of equal mass, as verified in [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]. Define

$$u\preceq_s v\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d^-\preceq d^+,$$

using the compound comparison relation of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]. Thus positive coefficients of $v-u$ remain on the right and negative coefficients move to the left. Signed notation is never a claim that a negative amount of a physical system exists.

Under [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]], for equal-mass compounds $A,B,C$, $A+C\preceq B+C$ if and only if $A\preceq B$. The signed relation of [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] is well-defined; on nonnegative equal-mass maps it agrees with $\preceq$, is invariant under adding the same finite-support signed map to both sides, and is transitive and closed under adding two comparisons.

derivations.claim: Put $\delta:=\mu-\lambda$. The coefficient difference is $R_\mu-R_\lambda=\delta(e_{x_1}-e_{x_0})$ and has total zero. If $\delta>0$, its negative and positive parts are $\delta e_{x_0}$ and $\delta e_{x_1}$; if $\delta<0$, they are $(-\delta)e_{x_1}$ and $(-\delta)e_{x_0}$; if $\delta=0$, both are zero.

If $\delta=0$, reflexivity gives $R_\lambda\preceq_sR_\mu$. If $\delta>0$, [F1] reduces this comparison to $\delta e_{x_0}\preceq\delta e_{x_1}$, which follows by positive scaling of $x_0\preceq x_1$ by $\delta$. Hence $\lambda<\mu$ implies $R_\lambda\preceq_sR_\mu$.

If $\delta<0$ and $R_\lambda\preceq_sR_\mu$, [F1] gives $(-\delta)e_{x_1}\preceq(-\delta)e_{x_0}$. Positive scaling by $1/(-\delta)$ would imply $x_1\preceq x_0$, contrary to [A1]. Thus this comparison fails when $\lambda>\mu$. The three cases prove the equivalence.
