Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with finite slope $P_i(x)$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

For two simple domains $\Gamma_i\subset\mathbb R^{n_i+1}$ and $\Gamma_j\subset\mathbb R^{n_j+1}$, write their coordinates $(u_i,v_i)$ and $(u_j,v_j)$. Their thermal-join domain is

$$\Delta_{ij}:=\{(u,v_i,v_j):\exists u_i,u_j,\ (u_i,v_i)\in\Gamma_i,\ (u_j,v_j)\in\Gamma_j,\ u=u_i+u_j\}.$$

The joined simple type is a distinct formal tag with amount function $\nu_{\Delta_{ij}}=\nu_{\Gamma_i}+\nu_{\Gamma_j}$ and weight $w_{\Delta_{ij}}=w_{\Gamma_i}+w_{\Gamma_j}$, as defined in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Encode the separated pair by $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and a joined coordinate $Z$ by $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(Z)$. Their bookkeeping masses agree, and their aggregate composition functions agree. These encoded maps and their raw tags remain distinct. Positive coordinate-scaled copies use the reversible preparation transport of that definition; nested joins preserve their finite primitive amount function under reassociation and permutation. The empty type contributes the zero map.

Write $J_{ij}(x,y)$ for the join state with the summed energy coordinate and the unchanged work coordinates. A compound pair $(x,y)$ and $J_{ij}(x,y)$ have the same total energy and work coordinates but are distinct tagged objects. Define $x\sim_T y$ exactly when $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(J_{ij}(x,y))$ are accessible in both directions. Nested joins use the declared reassociation and permutation identifications.

Assume every finite join is itself a simple domain satisfying [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. The contact hypotheses are mathematical assumptions on the common relation: (T1) $(x,y)\prec J_{ij}(x,y)$; (T2) every join state has at least one reversible split into component states at its stated coordinates, and the equal-state split of any state into positive scaled copies of itself is reversible; (T3) $\sim_T$ is transitive; (T4) for every simple state $x$ there are states $x_0,x_1$ in its domain with $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ and $x_0\sim_T x_1$; (T5) for every ordered pair of simple systems, every $x$ in the first and every work coordinate $v$ in the second's projection $\rho(\Gamma_j):=\{v:\exists u,(u,v)\in\Gamma_j\}$, there is a state $y$ with work coordinate $v$ and $x\sim_T y$.

For the completed calibrator branch, add (C1) **join coherence**: whenever $x\sim_T y$, the join state $J_{ij}(x,y)$ is thermally equivalent to each of $x$ and $y$ under the nested-join identifications. The coordinate sum in the definition alone does not assert C1. In later theorem statements, T1–T5 and C1 are explicitly listed as hypotheses; they are not treated as established physical laws.
Under T1–T3 and the equal-state reversible split in [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]], if $x\sim_T y$ then $s x\sim_T t y$ for every $s,t>0$.

Let $u,v$ be finite-support real coefficient maps on the tagged state labels of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] with equal total coefficient. For a typed state $x$, compound notation uses the represented map $\mathsf{J}(x)$ from [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]; its raw unit point mass is $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. Signed maps still use the ordinary total of their raw coefficients, exactly the bookkeeping mass of the represented nonnegative maps. Put $d=v-u$, $d^+(x)=\max(d(x),0)$ and $d^-(x)=\max(-d(x),0)$. Define $u\preceq_s v$ to mean $d^-\prec d^+$ under the compound relation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Write $u\sim_s v$ when both $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s u$. These are formal signed comparison maps, not physical negative amounts. The positive and negative parts are finite-support compounds of equal mass. If $u\sim_s v$, then $cu\sim_s cv$ for every real $c$: positive $c$ uses scaling, $c=0$ is reflexivity, and negative $c$ swaps the positive and negative parts while equivalence supplies both comparison directions. This Definition introduces the signed notation; ordinary-order compatibility and the signed-order laws are proved separately.

Under A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for compounds $A,B$ with $m(A)=m(B)$ and every finite spectator compound $C$, $A+C\prec B+C$ if and only if $A\prec B$. Consequently, for finite-support signed maps $u,v$ of equal total coefficient, define $u\preceq_s v$ by $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$. This relation is well-defined, agrees with $\prec$ on nonnegative maps, is invariant under adding a common signed map, is transitive, and is closed under addition of two comparisons. No comparison hypothesis is used.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], the sectors are nested: if $y\in A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$; equality holds when $y\in\partial A_x$, and $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ when $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$. For every $x,y\in\Gamma_i$, either $x\prec y$ or $y\prec x$ (possibly both). Strict comparison is exactly interior membership: $x\prec\prec y$ if and only if $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$.

derivations.claim: For $0\le\lambda<\mu\le1$, the signed difference $R_\mu-R_\lambda=(\mu-\lambda)(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))$ has positive part $(\mu-\lambda)\mathsf{J}(x_1)$ and negative part $(\mu-\lambda)\mathsf{J}(x_0)$. Since $x_0\prec x_1$, positive scaling and [F2] give $R_\lambda\prec R_\mu$. A reverse comparison would, by [F2] and inverse positive scaling, give $x_1\prec x_0$, contrary to strictness. Thus the reference states are strictly ordered by parameter.

For $0<\lambda<1$, [F1] makes $(1-\lambda)x_0$ and $\lambda x_1$ thermally equivalent. By the definition of thermal equivalence, their compound is reversible with its join state. The equal-state split makes $((1-\lambda)x,\lambda x)$ reversible with its join state and with $x$. Both join states belong to the join of two scaled copies of the same simple domain, so [F3] compares them. The endpoint cases use $R_0=x_0$ and $R_1=x_1$ directly. Hence $R_\lambda$ and $x$ are comparable for every $\lambda\in[0,1]$.

Let $L=\{\lambda\in[0,1]:R_\lambda\prec x\}$. The strict endpoint comparison $x_0\prec x$ puts $0$ in $L$. Step 1.1 and transitivity make $L$ downward closed. Let $s=\sup L$. If $s>0$, then $s-1/n\in L$ for every sufficiently large $n$. Since $R_{s-1/n}+(1/n)x_1=R_s+(1/n)x_0$, consistency yields $R_s+(1/n)x_0\prec x+(1/n)x_1$. Stability with bases $R_s,x$ and fixed spectators $x_0,x_1$ gives $R_s\prec x$. If $s=0$, this comparison is the given $x_0\prec x$.

If $s<1$, then $s+1/n\notin L$ for every sufficiently large $n$. Step 1.2 gives comparability and the definition of $L$ excludes $R_{s+1/n}\prec x$, so $x\prec R_{s+1/n}$. The identity $R_{s+1/n}+(1/n)x_0=R_s+(1/n)x_1$ and stability yield $x\prec R_s$. If $s=1$, the strict strip gives $x\prec R_1$; together with step 2.1 this would imply $x_1\prec x$, contrary to $x\prec\prec x_1$. Thus $s<1$, and step 2.1 and the preceding stability comparison give $R_s\sim x$.

The equivalence $R_s\sim x$ also excludes $s=0$, because $R_0=x_0$ and $x_0\not\sim x$, and excludes $s=1$ by strictness of $x\prec\prec x_1$. If $R_t\sim x$ for another $t$, transitivity gives $R_s\sim R_t$; step 1.1 then forces $s=t$. Hence the parameter is unique and lies in $(0,1)$.

citations.quote:
Fix a nonempty set $X$ and the compounds of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. A **comparison relation** $\preceq$ is defined only for pairs $(A,B)$ with $m(A)=m(B)$. Write $A\sim B$ when both $A\preceq B$ and $B\preceq A$; this is equivalence, not equality of coefficient functions. The following are explicit hypotheses on $\preceq$:

1. **Preorder:** $A\preceq A$, and $A\preceq B\preceq C$ implies $A\preceq C$.
2. **Composition consistency:** $A\preceq B$ implies $A+C\preceq B+C$ for every compound $C$.
3. **Positive scaling:** $A\preceq B$ implies $tA\preceq tB$ for every real $t>0$.
4. **Splitting and recombination:** for $x\in X$, $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, the one-state compound $te_x$ is equivalent to $se_x+(t-s)e_x$.
5. **Stability:** for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive compounds $Z_0,Z_1$ with $m(Z_0)=m(Z_1)$, and a sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to $0$, if $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\preceq B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for every $n$, then $A\preceq B$.
6. **Comparison hypothesis (CH):** for every equal-mass pair $A,B$, either $A\preceq B$ or $B\preceq A$ (or both).

These are mathematical assumptions, not conclusions about a physical system. No antisymmetry, continuity, convexity, or strict comparison is included. Strict comparison means $A\preceq B$ and not $B\preceq A$.

Let $X$ be a set of state labels. A **tagged scalable compound over $X$** is a function $c:X\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ whose support $\operatorname{supp}(c):=\{x\in X:c(x)\ne0\}$ is finite. The coefficient is a dimensionless formal amount; state labels retain their tags, so equal coefficients on different labels do not identify those labels. Compounds are equal exactly when their coefficient functions are equal.

For compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, define composition and nonnegative scaling pointwise by $(c+d)(x):=c(x)+d(x)$ and $(tc)(x):=t c(x)$. The zero function is the empty compound; in particular $0c=0$. Comparison axioms involving scaling still require a strictly positive scalar unless explicitly stated otherwise. The **mass** of $c$ is the finite sum $m(c):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)$. It is dimensionless bookkeeping mass, not thermodynamic mass or energy. The compound is positive when $m(c)>0$.

For every state label $x\in X$, the **unit-state compound** $e_x$ is the coefficient function with $e_x(y)=1$ if $y=x$ and $e_x(y)=0$ otherwise. Its support is $\{x\}$, so it is a tagged compound. In compound comparisons, a state label $x$ denotes $e_x$. Every compound has the canonical finite decomposition $c=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)e_x$, with an empty sum when $c=0$; coefficients on this support are strictly positive. The mass-one property $m(e_x)=1$ and the equivalence $m(c)=0\Longleftrightarrow c=0$ are proved in [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

The formula for mass is independent of the chosen finite set containing the support, and composition and scaling obey $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]] proves these assertions.

For every tagged scalable compound $c$, the mass in [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] is independent of the finite summation set used. For any compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; $m(0)=0$. For every $x\in X$, the unit-state compound $e_x$ has $m(e_x)=1$. A compound has zero mass if and only if it is the empty compound.

Let $u,v:X\to\mathbb R$ be finite-support real coefficient maps with equal total coefficient $\sum_xu(x)=\sum_xv(x)$. These signed maps are formal comparison notation, not compounds. Put $d:=v-u$ and define $d^+(x):=\max\{d(x),0\}$ and $d^-(x):=\max\{-d(x),0\}$. Then $d^+,d^-$ are nonnegative finite-support compounds of equal mass, as verified in [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]. Define

$$u\preceq_s v\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d^-\preceq d^+,$$

using the compound comparison relation of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]. Thus positive coefficients of $v-u$ remain on the right and negative coefficients move to the left. Signed notation is never a claim that a negative amount of a physical system exists.

Under [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]], for equal-mass compounds $A,B,C$, $A+C\preceq B+C$ if and only if $A\preceq B$. The signed relation of [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] is well-defined; on nonnegative equal-mass maps it agrees with $\preceq$, is invariant under adding the same finite-support signed map to both sides, and is transitive and closed under adding two comparisons.

Let $x_0,x_1\in X$ satisfy $x_0\preceq x_1$ and not $x_1\preceq x_0$. For every real $\lambda$, define the signed unit-mass reference map $R_\lambda:=(1-\lambda)e_{x_0}+\lambda e_{x_1}$. For all $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$,

$$R_\lambda\preceq_s R_\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda\le\mu.$$

The parameters need not lie in $[0,1]$; outside that interval $R_\lambda$ is signed notation, not a compound.
In the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$, the sequence $\epsilon_n:=1/(n+1)$, $n\in\mathbb N$, is positive, strictly decreasing, and converges to zero.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.

derivations.claim: Suppose no positive integer $n$ satisfies $(n+1)e_{x_0}\preceq ne_{x_1}+e_x$. Both sides have mass $n+1$, so CH gives $ne_{x_1}+e_x\preceq(n+1)e_{x_0}$. Scale by $1/n$ to obtain $e_{x_1}+n^{-1}e_x\preceq e_{x_0}+n^{-1}e_{x_0}$. Apply stability to the sequence $\epsilon_n=1/n$, with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and spectators $e_x,e_{x_0}$, each of mass one. It yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, contradicting strictness. Thus some $n$ has $(n+1)e_{x_0}\preceq ne_{x_1}+e_x$, which by [F2] is $R_{-n}\preceq_s e_x$; hence $-n\in L_x$.

Suppose $L_x$ is unbounded above. For each positive integer $n$, unboundedness supplies $\lambda\in L_x$ with $\lambda>n$; [F3] gives $R_n\preceq_sR_\lambda$, and transitivity gives $n\in L_x$. By [F2], $R_n\preceq_s e_x$ is the compound comparison $e_{x_0}+n e_{x_1}\preceq e_x+n e_{x_0}$. Scaling by $1/n$ gives $e_{x_1}+n^{-1}e_{x_0}\preceq e_{x_0}+n^{-1}e_x$. Stability with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and spectators $e_{x_0},e_x$ now yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, again a contradiction. Therefore $L_x$ is bounded above.

If $\lambda\in L_x$ and $\mu\le\lambda$, [F3] gives $R_\mu\preceq_sR_\lambda$; signed transitivity and $R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x$ imply $\mu\in L_x$. Thus $L_x$ is downward closed. By steps 1.1 and 1.2 it is nonempty and bounded above, so [F5] supplies the real number $s:=\sup L_x$.

For each $n$, $s-1/n$ is not an upper bound of $L_x$, so some $\lambda\in L_x$ has $\lambda>s-1/n$. Downward closure gives $s-1/n\in L_x$. Consistency then gives $R_s+n^{-1}e_{x_0}\preceq_s e_x+n^{-1}e_{x_1}$, because $R_{s-1/n}+n^{-1}e_{x_1}=R_s+n^{-1}e_{x_0}$. Let $K:=R_s^-$. Adding the fixed nonnegative map $K$ to both sides converts this signed comparison into the compound comparisons $R_s^++n^{-1}e_{x_0}\preceq e_x+K+n^{-1}e_{x_1}$. Their bases have equal mass because $m(R_s^+)-m(K)=1$. Stability with spectators $e_{x_0},e_{x_1}$ yields $R_s^+\preceq e_x+K$, that is, $R_s\preceq_s e_x$.

Since $s$ is an upper bound, $s+1/n\notin L_x$. CH therefore gives $e_x\preceq_s R_{s+1/n}$. Add $n^{-1}e_{x_0}$ to both sides and use $R_{s+1/n}+n^{-1}e_{x_0}=R_s+n^{-1}e_{x_1}$. Adding $K=R_s^-$ converts the result to equal-mass compounds $e_x+K+n^{-1}e_{x_0}\preceq R_s^++n^{-1}e_{x_1}$. Stability with the same positive unit-mass spectators yields $e_x+K\preceq R_s^+$, or $e_x\preceq_sR_s$. Together with step 3.1 this proves $R_s\sim_s e_x$ and the claimed attainment.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Assume [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] on compounds over a nonempty state set $X$, a strict reference pair $x_0\preceq x_1$ with not $x_1\preceq x_0$, and the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. For $x\in X$ define

$$L_x:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R:R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x\}.$$

Then $L_x$ is nonempty, bounded above, and downward closed. Its supremum $S(x):=\sup L_x$ is a real number and satisfies $R_{S(x)}\sim_s e_x$. Stability is used to prove attainment; no continuity of states or order is assumed.

3.1 proves R_s <=_s e_x.
4.1 proves e_x <=_s R_s.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$, let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $z\notin E$. Then there are a nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^n$ and a real $c$ such that

$$\langle u,e\rangle\le c<\langle u,z\rangle\qquad(e\in E).$$

Thus an affine hyperplane strictly separates the point from the entire set.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.

   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,

here.

derivations.claim: Choose affine coordinates identifying $H$ with $\mathbb R^k$. Convexity of $C$ makes its closure $K$ convex: approximate any two points of $K$ by sequences in $C$ and pass to the limit in each convex combination. Since $z\in\partial_H K$, choose $z_m\notin K$ with $z_m\to z$. By [F1], for each $m$ there are $u_m\ne0$ and $c_m$ with $u_m\cdot q\le c_m<u_m\cdot z_m$ for all $q\in K$. Normalize $u_m$ to unit length; [F3] places these vectors on the compact unit sphere, which is compact by [F2], so a subsequence converges to a unit vector $u$. [F2] and [F3] provide the convergent subsequence.

For every $q\in K$, the inequalities give $u_m\cdot(q-z_m)<0$. Along the convergent subsequence, continuity of the Euclidean inner product yields $u\cdot(q-z)\le0$. The limit vector has unit length, so its functional is nonzero and supports $K$, hence $C$, at $z$.

If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine hull $H$ of dimension at most $d-2$, its orthogonal complement has dimension at least two. Choose two nonparallel nonzero normals $n_1,n_2$ orthogonal to the direction space of $H$. For each $j$, the hyperplane $\{q:n_j\cdot(q-z)=0\}$ contains $H$ and therefore supports $C$ at $z$. The two hyperplanes are distinct because their normals are not parallel.

derivations.claim: For $P\ll Q$ with density $h$, the negative part of $h\log h$ is integrable because $-u\log u\leq1/e$ for $0\leq u\leq1$; the density definition is therefore unambiguous. Also $u\log u\geq u-1$ for $u\geq0$, so $D(P\Vert Q)=\int h\log h\,dQ\geq\int(h-1)\,dQ=0$. If $P\not\ll Q$, the defined value is $+\infty\geq0$.

For bounded $\phi$, let $Q_\phi$ have density $e^\phi/Q(e^\phi)$ relative to $Q$. When $P\ll Q$ and $D(P\Vert Q)<\infty$, the density logarithm identity gives $D(P\Vert Q_\phi)=D(P\Vert Q)-P(\phi)+\log Q(e^\phi)\geq0$ by step 1.1. Thus every variational test is at most $D(P\Vert Q)$; the same upper bound is immediate if $D=+\infty$. If $P\not\ll Q$, choose a measurable $Q$-null set $N$ with $P(N)>0$ and use $\phi=t\mathbf1_N$: then $Q(e^\phi)=1$ and $P(\phi)=tP(N)\to\infty$.

In the remaining case $P\ll Q$, let $h=dP/dQ$ and set $\phi_m=\max(-m,\min(m,\log h))$, taking $\phi_m=-m$ on $\{h=0\}$. Then $e^{\phi_m}\to h$ and $e^{\phi_m}\leq1+h$, so [F4] gives $Q(e^{\phi_m})\to1$. The negative part of $h\phi_m$ is bounded by $1/e$, and its positive part increases to $(h\log h)^+$; hence [F4] gives $P(\phi_m)=\int h\phi_m\,dQ\to D(P\Vert Q)$, including when the positive entropy part is infinite. Combining this with step 2.1 proves the variational identity.

If $T$ is measurable, every bounded test $\psi$ on the target pulls back to the bounded test $\psi\circ T$ on the source, and $Q(e^{\psi\circ T})=(Q\circ T^{-1})(e^\psi)$ while $P(\psi\circ T)=(P\circ T^{-1})(\psi)$. Taking suprema in step 3.1 proves the restriction inequality.

For a conditioning observation $R$, applying the variational identity pointwise to the conditional density $k_R(r,y)$ shows $$G(R)=\sup_{\phi\in B_b}\left(E_P\phi(R,Y)-E_P\!\left[\log\int e^{\phi(R,y)}Q_Y(dy)\right]\right),$$ where the tests range over bounded measurable functions of $(R,Y)$. The upper bound follows from step 2.1 for each conditional law; the reverse bound follows by using the jointly measurable bounded truncations of $\log k_R$ from step 3.1 and then [F3]–[F4]. When $R$ is a measurable function of $S$, every test depending on $(R,Y)$ is an admissible test depending on $(S,Y)$ with the same objective value, since the $Q_Y$ normalizer still depends only on $R$. Thus $G(R)\leq G(S)$; nonnegativity is step 1.1 applied conditionally.

Suppose $P_{XY}$ has density $h(x,y)$ relative to $Q_X\otimes Q_Y$. Put $h_X(x)=\int h(x,y)Q_Y(dy)$. By [F3], $h_X$ is a density for $P_X$. Where $0<h_X(x)<\infty$, [F2] supplies the conditional density $k(x,y)=h(x,y)/h_X(x)$ relative to $Q_Y$; elsewhere use its supplied filler. On the full $P_X$-measure set of finite positive $h_X$, $h=h_Xk$ and $\log h=\log h_X+\log k$ $P_{XY}$-almost everywhere. Integrating this identity, with nonnegative conditional entropies and finite total entropy, gives the displayed chain rule. If a restriction entropy is infinite, step 4.1 makes the joint entropy infinite as well, so no subtraction of two infinite terms is used.

Steps 1.1–1.3 prove nonnegativity and the variational identity, step 4.1 proves restriction monotonicity, step 5.1 proves the product chain rule, and step 4.2 proves monotonicity under additional conditioning.

Assume AC. Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on one measurable space and use $D(P\Vert Q)$ as defined in [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]. Then
$$D(P\Vert Q)=\sup_{\phi\in B_b}\left(P(\phi)-\log Q(e^\phi)\right),$$
where $B_b$ is the set of bounded real measurable functions. In particular $D\geq0$. If $T$ is measurable, then $D(P\circ T^{-1}\Vert Q\circ T^{-1})\leq D(P\Vert Q)$.

For standard-Borel spaces $X,Y$, probability reference measures $Q_X,Q_Y$, and a joint probability $P_{XY}\ll Q_X\otimes Q_Y$ with finite $D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)$, let $P_{Y|X=x}$ be the conditional law supplied by [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. Then
$$D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)=D(P_X\Vert Q_X)+\int_X D(P_{Y|X=x}\Vert Q_Y)\,P_X(dx).$$
More generally, for nested standard-Borel observations $R$ and $S$ with $R$ a measurable function of $S$, and a fixed probability reference $Q_Y$ for a further variable $Y$, the conditional increments
$$G(R):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|R}\Vert Q_Y)\right],\qquad G(S):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|S}\Vert Q_Y)\right]$$
satisfy $0\leq G(R)\leq G(S)$ whenever the joint relative entropy is finite.

Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with finite slope $P_i(x)$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for every simple state $x$, the forward sector $A_x=\{y\in\Gamma_i:x\prec y\}$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$. For collinear $y=tx+(1-t)z$, $0<t<1$, $y\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$, and $x\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$.

Let $C$ be a nonempty convex set in a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$ of dimension $k\ge1$, let $\operatorname{aff}C=H$, and put $K=\overline{C}^{\,H}$. If $z\in\partial_H K$ (that is, $z\in K$ and every relative neighborhood of $z$ meets $H\setminus K$), then there is a nonzero linear functional $\ell$ on the translation space of $H$ such that $\ell(q-z)\le0$ for all $q\in C$. If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine dimension at most $d-2$, then every $z\in C$ has at least two distinct ambient supporting hyperplanes containing $\operatorname{aff}C$.

Let $C$ be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$. Its relative interior $\operatorname{ri}_H C$ is the interior in $H=\operatorname{aff}C$. Then $\operatorname{ri}_H C$ is nonempty. If $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$, $y\in\overline{C}^{\,H}$, and $0\le t<1$, then $(1-t)w+ty\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$.

derivations.claim: Suppose $A_x$ has empty ambient interior. If $d=1$, S1 supplies a strict successor $y\ne x$; convexity puts the nondegenerate interval between $x$ and $y$ in $A_x$, contradicting empty interior. Thus take $d\ge2$. The affine hull of $A_x$ has dimension at most $d-1$. If its dimension were at most $d-2$, [F2] would give two distinct supporting hyperplanes at $x$, contradicting S2. Hence its affine hull is a hyperplane $H$; this $H$ supports $A_x$ at every point, including $x$.

By S1 choose $y$ with $x\prec\prec y$. Then $y\in A_x$ and $x\notin A_y$. Transitivity gives $A_y\subseteq A_x\subseteq H$. If $A_y$ had affine dimension at most $d-2$, [F2] would again give multiple ambient supports at $y$, contrary to S2. Thus $\operatorname{aff}A_y=H$.

Choose $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H A_y$ by [F3]. The segment from $w$ to $x$ is contained in $H\cap\Gamma_i$ by convexity of both sets, starts in $A_y$, and ends outside $A_y$. Its intersection with $A_y$ is closed by relative closedness [F1], so it has a last point $z$ before $x$. Points immediately after $z$ on this segment lie outside $A_y$ and, because $A_y$ is closed in the open set $\Gamma_i$, outside $\overline{A_y}^{\,H}$. Thus $z\in\partial_H\overline{A_y}^{\,H}$. The support statement [F2] supplies a nonzero functional on $H$ whose zero hyperplane supports $A_y$ at $z$.

Extend this functional to the ambient Euclidean space by taking its normal vector in the direction space of $H$. Its zero hyperplane contains the within-$H$ support and is not $H$ itself. Since $z\in A_y$, transitivity gives $A_z\subseteq A_y$, so the extended plane supports $A_z$ at $z$; the plane $H$ also supports $A_z$. These are distinct, contradicting S2 at $z$. Therefore $A_x$ has nonempty ambient interior.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

Let $X$ be a set of state labels. A **tagged scalable compound over $X$** is a function $c:X\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ whose support $\operatorname{supp}(c):=\{x\in X:c(x)\ne0\}$ is finite. The coefficient is a dimensionless formal amount; state labels retain their tags, so equal coefficients on different labels do not identify those labels. Compounds are equal exactly when their coefficient functions are equal.

For compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, define composition and nonnegative scaling pointwise by $(c+d)(x):=c(x)+d(x)$ and $(tc)(x):=t c(x)$. The zero function is the empty compound; in particular $0c=0$. Comparison axioms involving scaling still require a strictly positive scalar unless explicitly stated otherwise. The **mass** of $c$ is the finite sum $m(c):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)$. It is dimensionless bookkeeping mass, not thermodynamic mass or energy. The compound is positive when $m(c)>0$.

For every state label $x\in X$, the **unit-state compound** $e_x$ is the coefficient function with $e_x(y)=1$ if $y=x$ and $e_x(y)=0$ otherwise. Its support is $\{x\}$, so it is a tagged compound. In compound comparisons, a state label $x$ denotes $e_x$. Every compound has the canonical finite decomposition $c=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)e_x$, with an empty sum when $c=0$; coefficients on this support are strictly positive. The mass-one property $m(e_x)=1$ and the equivalence $m(c)=0\Longleftrightarrow c=0$ are proved in [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

The formula for mass is independent of the chosen finite set containing the support, and composition and scaling obey $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]] proves these assertions.

For every tagged scalable compound $c$, the mass in [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] is independent of the finite summation set used. For any compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; $m(0)=0$. For every $x\in X$, the unit-state compound $e_x$ has $m(e_x)=1$. A compound has zero mass if and only if it is the empty compound.

Fix a nonempty set $X$ and the compounds of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. A **comparison relation** $\preceq$ is defined only for pairs $(A,B)$ with $m(A)=m(B)$. Write $A\sim B$ when both $A\preceq B$ and $B\preceq A$; this is equivalence, not equality of coefficient functions. The following are explicit hypotheses on $\preceq$:

1. **Preorder:** $A\preceq A$, and $A\preceq B\preceq C$ implies $A\preceq C$.
2. **Composition consistency:** $A\preceq B$ implies $A+C\preceq B+C$ for every compound $C$.
3. **Positive scaling:** $A\preceq B$ implies $tA\preceq tB$ for every real $t>0$.
4. **Splitting and recombination:** for $x\in X$, $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, the one-state compound $te_x$ is equivalent to $se_x+(t-s)e_x$.
5. **Stability:** for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive compounds $Z_0,Z_1$ with $m(Z_0)=m(Z_1)$, and a sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to $0$, if $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\preceq B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for every $n$, then $A\preceq B$.
6. **Comparison hypothesis (CH):** for every equal-mass pair $A,B$, either $A\preceq B$ or $B\preceq A$ (or both).

These are mathematical assumptions, not conclusions about a physical system. No antisymmetry, continuity, convexity, or strict comparison is included. Strict comparison means $A\preceq B$ and not $B\preceq A$.

Let $u,v:X\to\mathbb R$ be finite-support real coefficient maps with equal total coefficient $\sum_xu(x)=\sum_xv(x)$. These signed maps are formal comparison notation, not compounds. Put $d:=v-u$ and define $d^+(x):=\max\{d(x),0\}$ and $d^-(x):=\max\{-d(x),0\}$. Then $d^+,d^-$ are nonnegative finite-support compounds of equal mass, as verified in [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]. Define

$$u\preceq_s v\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d^-\preceq d^+,$$

using the compound comparison relation of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]. Thus positive coefficients of $v-u$ remain on the right and negative coefficients move to the left. Signed notation is never a claim that a negative amount of a physical system exists.

derivations.claim: For equal-total $u,v$, $d=v-u$ has finite support and total sum zero. Pointwise $d=d^+-d^-$, so finite-sum linearity gives $m(d^+)-m(d^-)=0$; both maps are finite-support and nonnegative. Thus the definition in [F2] compares equal-mass compounds. If $u,v$ are nonnegative, set $k(x)=\min\{u(x),v(x)\}$; then $u=k+(v-u)^-$ and $v=k+(v-u)^+$.

Suppose $A+C\preceq B+C$ and $m(C)>0$. For each positive integer $n$, pointwise addition gives $A=n(A/n)$ and $B=n(B/n)$. Scaling the given comparison by $1/n$ gives $A/n+C/n\preceq B/n+C/n$. By composition consistency, replace the $n$ copies of $A/n$ one at a time by $B/n$, keeping the already replaced copies, the remaining copies, and $C/n$ as spectators; after all replacements, $A+C/n\preceq B+C/n$. Apply stability with $Z_0=Z_1=C$ and $\epsilon_n=1/n$ to obtain $A\preceq B$. If $m(C)=0$, nonnegativity implies $C=0$ and the conclusion is the premise itself. Conversely, $A\preceq B$ gives $A+C\preceq B+C$ by consistency.

For nonnegative $u,v$, step 1.1 gives $u=k+(v-u)^-$ and $v=k+(v-u)^+$. Cancellation from step 1.2 shows $u\preceq v$ exactly when $(v-u)^-\preceq(v-u)^+$, which is $u\preceq_s v$. For general signed maps, adding a common map leaves $v-u$ unchanged, so it leaves signed comparison unchanged.

If $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s w$, then consistency combines $(v-u)^-\preceq(v-u)^+$ and $(w-v)^-\preceq(w-v)^+$ into a comparison between the sums of their negative and positive parts. The two sums have a common pointwise minimum; cancel it by step 1.2. The remaining maps are precisely $(w-u)^-$ and $(w-u)^+$, so $u\preceq_s w$. The same sum-and-cancel argument applied to two independent signed comparisons proves closure under their addition; reflexivity follows from $0\preceq0$.

citations.quote:
Define
$$H_\phi(\omega)=\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset\omega}\phi(x-y),\qquad H_\phi(\varnothing)=0.$$
The sum is over unordered two-point subsets, so every term is evaluated at a nonzero separation; if any term is $+\infty$, the sum is $+\infty$.

For $g>2R_0$ set
$$\eta(g)=g^d\psi(g)+\int_g^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr.$$
Then $\eta(g)\to0$ and
$$\sum_{m=1}^\infty m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq 2^{d-1}g^{-d}\eta(g).$$
Moreover, there is a choice $g(\ell)>0$, for all sufficiently large real $\ell$, such that $g(\ell)\to\infty$, $g(\ell)/\ell\to0$, and
$$\left(\frac{\ell}{g(\ell)}\right)^d\eta(g(\ell))\longrightarrow0.$$
For every fixed finite configuration and all sufficiently large periods $L$, the noncoincident periodic-image tail $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d,\ |k|_\infty\geq K_0}|\phi(x-y+Lk)|$ is absolutely convergent.

derivations.claim: Write $N_i=N_{C_i}(\omega)$. The negative part of each pair potential is bounded both by $2B_s$ and, at large separation, by the lower-regular envelope. Set $\Psi_j$ to a finite constant on the finitely many near-cell offsets and to the envelope evaluated at $|j|_\infty-1$ on the remaining offsets. The shell count $|\{j:|j|_\infty=m\}|\leq c_dm^{d-1}$ and the cell-envelope conclusion of [F2] give $\sum_j\Psi_j<\infty$. Since $N_iN_j\leq(N_i^2+N_j^2)/2$, the total negative pair contribution is at most $C\sum_iN_i^2$ for a finite $C$.

In case (i), choose $k_0$ with $1/k_0<r_1$. For $k\geq k_0$, partition one unit cell into $k^d$ half-open cubes of side $1/k$, put $\chi_k=\chi(1/k)$, and $\Delta\chi_k=\chi_k-\chi_{k-1}\geq0$. If the cell contains $N$ points, the identity $\sum_jn_j^2-N=2\sum_j\binom{n_j}{2}$ and nonnegativity of $\sum_j(n_j-N/k^d)^2$ give at least $\frac12(N^2/k^d-N)$ same-subcube pairs at scale $k$. A fixed pair counted at scale $k$ has separation $s<1/k$, hence $k<1/s$; summing its nonnegative weights over all scales where it is counted is at most $\sum_{k=k_0}^{\lfloor1/s\rfloor}\Delta\chi_k\leq\chi(s)$. Thus the positive core energy in the cell dominates the sum of these weighted pair counts. With $K_N=\lfloor(N/2)^{1/d}\rfloor$, each $k\leq K_N$ satisfies $N^2/k^d-N\geq N^2/(2k^d)$, so the core energy is at least $$ \frac{N^2}{4}\sum_{k=k_0}^{K_N}\frac{\Delta\chi_k}{k^d}. $$ Summation by parts writes the coefficient as an initial constant plus $\sum_{k=k_0}^{K_N-1}\chi_k(k^{-d}-(k+1)^{-d})$; and $k^{-d}-(k+1)^{-d}\geq d/(2^{d+1}k^{d+1})$. The series $\sum_k\chi(1/k)k^{-d-1}$ diverges: on dyadic intervals $[2^{-j-1},2^{-j}]$, monotonicity bounds the integral above by $C_d2^{-jd}\chi(2^{-j-1})$, while the corresponding block $2^{j+1}\leq k<2^{j+2}$ contributes at least $c_d2^{-jd}\chi(2^{-j-1})$ to that series. The divergent core integral therefore forces the displayed coefficient to tend to infinity.

In case (i), sum the cell core bound from step 1.2 and subtract the negative-pair bound from step 1.1. The resulting coefficient of $N_i^2$ tends to infinity with $N_i$. Above a finite threshold it dominates $2CN_i^2$; below that threshold its possible negative remainder is bounded by a constant times $N_i$. Taking $h(N)$ to be half the positive cell lower bound above the threshold and zero below it gives a nondecreasing extended-valued function with $h(N)/N^2\to\infty$ and $H_\phi\geq\sum_i h(N_i)-bN$.

In case (ii), choose $k$ with $1/k<r_h$ and partition every unit cell into $k^d$ subcubes. A finite-energy configuration has at most one point in each subcube, so $N_i\leq k^d$ for every $i$. Define $h(N)=0$ for $N\leq k^d$ and $h(N)=+\infty$ for $N>k^d$. If any cell exceeds this occupancy, the configuration has a forbidden pair and $H_\phi=+\infty$; otherwise stability gives $H_\phi\geq-BN=\sum_i h(N_i)-BN$. This proves the hard-core alternative.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Assume the potential of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]] is stable and regular. In addition, assume either (i) $\chi:(0,r_1]\to(0,\infty)$ is finite-valued and nonincreasing, $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_1$, and $\int_0^{r_1}\chi(r)r^{d-1}dr=+\infty$; or (ii) there is a hard-core radius $r_h>0$ such that $\phi(x)=+\infty$ whenever $|x|_\infty<r_h$. Then there are a nonnegative nondecreasing $h:\mathbb N_0\to[0,+\infty]$ with $h(0)=0$ and $h(N)/N^2\to+\infty$, and a constant $b<\infty$, such that
$$H_\phi(\omega)\geq\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}h(N_{C_i}(\omega))-bN(\omega).$$
The hard-core alternative permits $h(N)=+\infty$ above the finite packing capacity of a unit cell. This is stronger than ordinary superstability and is not inferred from stability or regularity alone.

boundaries.evidence: Statement the near-core radius and positive core envelope determine positive subdivision scales. The h(N)/N^2 limit is taken through positive large N; zero occupation is handled by h(0)=0.

citations.quote: It is superstable in the Georgii splitting convention if $\phi=\phi_s+\phi_r$, where $\phi_s$ is stable and $\phi_r\geq0$ everywhere and, for some $r_0,\delta>0$, $\phi_r(x)\geq\delta$ whenever $|x|_\infty\leq r_0$.

derivations.claim:
Choose an integer $k\geq1$ with $1/k\leq r_0$. Partition each unit cell $C_i$ into $k^d$ half-open subcubes of side $1/k$, and denote their occupancies by $n_{i,j}$, $1\leq j\leq k^d$. Distinct points in one subcube have $|x-y|_\infty<1/k\leq r_0$, so their repulsive pair energy is at least $\delta$. Therefore
$$H_{\phi_r}(\omega)\geq\frac{\delta}{2}\sum_{i,j}n_{i,j}(n_{i,j}-1).$$
Writing $\bar n=N_{C_i}(\omega)/k^d$, nonnegativity of $\sum_j(n_{i,j}-\bar n)^2$ expands to $\sum_j n_{i,j}^2\geq N_{C_i}(\omega)^2/k^d$, and $\sum_{i,j}n_{i,j}=N(\omega)$. Thus $H_{\phi_r}(\omega)\geq\frac{\delta}{2k^d}\sum_iN_{C_i}^2-\frac\delta2N$.

The stable part obeys $H_{\phi_s}(\omega)\geq-B_sN$. Add this inequality to step 1.1 and take $A=\delta/(2k^d)$ and $B=B_s+\delta/2$. This proves the cell-quadratic bound. If any term is $+\infty$, the inequality holds in the extended order; otherwise all sums are finite.

citations.quote:
Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with finite slope $P_i(x)$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

For two simple domains $\Gamma_i\subset\mathbb R^{n_i+1}$ and $\Gamma_j\subset\mathbb R^{n_j+1}$, write their coordinates $(u_i,v_i)$ and $(u_j,v_j)$. Their thermal-join domain is

$$\Delta_{ij}:=\{(u,v_i,v_j):\exists u_i,u_j,\ (u_i,v_i)\in\Gamma_i,\ (u_j,v_j)\in\Gamma_j,\ u=u_i+u_j\}.$$

The joined simple type is a distinct formal tag with amount function $\nu_{\Delta_{ij}}=\nu_{\Gamma_i}+\nu_{\Gamma_j}$ and weight $w_{\Delta_{ij}}=w_{\Gamma_i}+w_{\Gamma_j}$, as defined in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Encode the separated pair by $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and a joined coordinate $Z$ by $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(Z)$. Their bookkeeping masses agree, and their aggregate composition functions agree. These encoded maps and their raw tags remain distinct. Positive coordinate-scaled copies use the reversible preparation transport of that definition; nested joins preserve their finite primitive amount function under reassociation and permutation. The empty type contributes the zero map.

Write $J_{ij}(x,y)$ for the join state with the summed energy coordinate and the unchanged work coordinates. A compound pair $(x,y)$ and $J_{ij}(x,y)$ have the same total energy and work coordinates but are distinct tagged objects. Define $x\sim_T y$ exactly when $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(J_{ij}(x,y))$ are accessible in both directions. Nested joins use the declared reassociation and permutation identifications.

Assume every finite join is itself a simple domain satisfying [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. The contact hypotheses are mathematical assumptions on the common relation: (T1) $(x,y)\prec J_{ij}(x,y)$; (T2) every join state has at least one reversible split into component states at its stated coordinates, and the equal-state split of any state into positive scaled copies of itself is reversible; (T3) $\sim_T$ is transitive; (T4) for every simple state $x$ there are states $x_0,x_1$ in its domain with $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ and $x_0\sim_T x_1$; (T5) for every ordered pair of simple systems, every $x$ in the first and every work coordinate $v$ in the second's projection $\rho(\Gamma_j):=\{v:\exists u,(u,v)\in\Gamma_j\}$, there is a state $y$ with work coordinate $v$ and $x\sim_T y$.

For the completed calibrator branch, add (C1) **join coherence**: whenever $x\sim_T y$, the join state $J_{ij}(x,y)$ is thermally equivalent to each of $x$ and $y$ under the nested-join identifications. The coordinate sum in the definition alone does not assert C1. In later theorem statements, T1–T5 and C1 are explicitly listed as hypotheses; they are not treated as established physical laws.

Assume [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and T1–T4 of [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]] for every finite join. For any one simple type $\Gamma_i$, every two finite compounds of its scaled copies with the same total coefficient mass are comparable. Thus CH holds on all multiple scaled products of that type. No entropy across different material types is asserted here.

Let $X$ be nonempty and suppose its finite-support compounds carry the comparison structure of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] over the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. If there are $x_0,x_1\in X$ with $x_0\preceq x_1$ and not $x_1\preceq x_0$, define $S(x):=\sup L_x$ using [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]]. Then $S:X\to\mathbb R$ is normalized by $S(x_0)=0$, $S(x_1)=1$, and for all equal-mass compounds $A=\sum_i a_i e_{x_i}$ and $B=\sum_j b_j e_{y_j}$,

$$A\preceq B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_i a_iS(x_i)\le\sum_j b_jS(y_j).$$

Thus $S$ is an additive extensive representation on finite compounds. If no strict pair exists, CH instead makes every equal-mass pair of compounds equivalent, and any constant state function gives a (degenerate) additive representation. No concavity, continuity, or physical law follows without additional hypotheses.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], each simple domain has one orientation sign $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$, constant across the domain, such that at fixed work coordinate $v$, $x\prec y$ exactly when $\varepsilon_i(u_y-u_x)\ge0$. In coordinates oriented so $\varepsilon_i=1$, for each $x\in\Gamma_i$ the projection $\rho_x$ of $\partial_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ onto work coordinates is open and connected; the boundary is the graph $(u_x(v),v)$ of a $C^1$ function with locally Lipschitz derivative

$$Du_x(v)=-P_i(u_x(v),v).$$

If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y=A_x$ and their boundary graphs agree.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be finite and convex. For every $x_0\in U$, there are a neighborhood $V$ of $x_0$ and $L<\infty$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|$ for all $x,y\in V$. The same conclusion holds for finite concave functions by applying the result to $-f$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], the sectors are nested: if $y\in A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$; equality holds when $y\in\partial A_x$, and $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ when $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$. For every $x,y\in\Gamma_i$, either $x\prec y$ or $y\prec x$ (possibly both). Strict comparison is exactly interior membership: $x\prec\prec y$ if and only if $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$.

Let a family of simple domains satisfy [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], and suppose every pair has an admitted simple thermal join satisfying T1 and T2 of [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Then the fixed-work orientation signs from [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]] agree throughout the family. One common affine proof-coordinate convention $u'=\varepsilon u$, $\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, therefore makes each fixed-work accessibility order increase with $u'$ and preserves the energy-sum formula for joins. This is a mathematical coordinate convention; it does not change a physical energy quantity or assert a sign of a measured temperature.

derivations.claim: Use [F7]'s common mathematical energy orientation for the proof coordinates. Apply [F2] using [F1] after dividing represented coefficient maps by the fixed positive type weight $w_\Gamma$, as specified in [A1]. Multiply the resulting unit-state entropy by $w_\Gamma$ to evaluate represented states; this positive factor preserves all same-type order comparisons. Write $S(x)$ for that represented-state value. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] and additivity imply concavity: for $0<t<1$, accessibility of $(tx,(1-t)y)$ to $tx+(1-t)y$ gives $tS(x)+(1-t)S(y)\le S(tx+(1-t)y)$. By [F3], $S$ is strictly increasing in energy at fixed work coordinate.

Fix a work coordinate $v$ and let $J_v:=\{u:(u,v)\in\Gamma\}$, an open interval. The restriction $s_v(u)=S(u,v)$ is finite, concave, continuous by [F4], and strictly increasing by [F3]. For an interior $u$, concavity makes the right secant slopes nonincreasing as the secant endpoint moves right, and the left secant slopes monotone as the endpoint approaches $u$; hence the one-sided derivative limits $s'_{v,+}(u)$ and $s'_{v,-}(u)$ exist. Choose $a<u<b$ in $J_v$: the secants to $a,b$ bound those limits, so they are finite, and concavity gives $s'_-\ge s'_+$. Monotonicity gives nonnegative slopes. If $s'_+(u)=0$, then for every $z>u$ concavity bounds $(s_v(z)-s_v(u))/(z-u)\le s'_+(u)=0$, contradicting strict increase. Thus $s'_-\ge s'_+>0$. Define $\Theta(u,v)=[1/s'_{v,-}(u),1/s'_{v,+}(u)]$, a nonempty compact interval of positive finite reciprocal slopes.

Suppose the second alternative fails, so each adiabat contains one thermal-equivalence class. By [F1]–[F2], $A_x=\{y:S(y)\ge S(x)\}$. Continuity of $S$ and strict increase in energy at fixed work coordinate imply that every point with $S=\sigma$ has arbitrarily nearby points with larger and smaller entropy; hence each entropy level $E_\sigma=\{x:S(x)=\sigma\}$ is a forward-sector boundary. The supposition makes each $E_\sigma$ lie in one thermal class. Let $R=S(\Gamma)$ and, for each thermal class $C_\alpha$, put $R_\alpha=\{S(x):x\in C_\alpha\}$. These sets partition $R$: two distinct classes cannot share a level under the supposition. The range $R$ is an interval, since any two points of the convex domain are joined by a segment and the continuous entropy takes every intermediate value along it.

Fix $x=(u_1,v_1)$ and $y=(u_2,v_2)$ of this same simple type, and let $U=u_1+u_2$. The admissible energy splits form the open interval $D=\{w:(U-w,v_1)\in\Gamma,\ (w,v_2)\in\Gamma\}$, which contains $u_2$. Define $g(w)=s_{v_1}(U-w)+s_{v_2}(w)$. For the join state $J(x,y)$, T2 gives an admissible split $q$ whose pair is reversible with the join. For every other split $p$, T1 gives $p\prec J(x,y)\prec q$, so $p\prec q$. The pair states $p,q$ are finite compounds of two copies of this same simple type; [F1]–[F2] and their entropy representation therefore give $g(p)\le g(q)$. Thus $q$ maximizes $g$. If the initial split $x,y$ is reversible with the join, it is equivalent to $q$; entropy representation gives equal entropy, so it too maximizes $g$. Conversely, if $u_2$ maximizes $g$, then $g(u_2)=g(q)$, and [F1]–[F2] make the initial pair reversible with $q$; composing with $q\sim J(x,y)$ shows $x\sim_T y$. For a concave function at an interior point, maximality is equivalent to $g'_+(u_2)\le0\le g'_-(u_2)$: right secants are bounded above by the right derivative and left secants below by the left derivative. Here
$g'_+(u_2)=-s'_{v_1,-}(u_1)+s'_{v_2,+}(u_2),\qquad
g'_-(u_2)=-s'_{v_1,+}(u_1)+s'_{v_2,-}(u_2).$
The two inequalities are exactly $s'_{v_1,+}(u_1)\le s'_{v_2,-}(u_2)$ and $s'_{v_2,+}(u_2)\le s'_{v_1,-}(u_1)$, which say the positive slope intervals intersect; reciprocal reverses their endpoints, so this is equivalent to $\Theta(x)\cap\Theta(y)\ne\varnothing$.

Let $T_\alpha$ be one thermal class. The compact intervals $\Theta(x)$, $x\in T_\alpha$, pairwise intersect by step 2.1. For any finite subfamily, pairwise intersection implies common intersection: the largest left endpoint is no greater than the smallest right endpoint, since the intervals attaining those two endpoints intersect. Fix $x_0\in T_\alpha$; the sets $\Theta(x)\cap\Theta(x_0)$ are closed subsets of the compact interval $\Theta(x_0)$ and have the finite-intersection property. Compactness [F5] gives a common point, so $I_\alpha:=\bigcap_{x\in T_\alpha}\Theta(x)$ is a nonempty compact interval. If distinct classes had intersecting common intervals, representatives $x,y$ would have intersecting $\Theta$ intervals and would be thermally equivalent by step 2.1, a contradiction. Thus the intervals $I_\alpha$ for distinct classes are disjoint and strictly ordered on the real line; use this as the order of the classes.

For each work coordinate $v$, strict continuity of $s_v$ maps the open interval $J_v$ onto an open interval $R_v\subset R$. On $R_v$, the level-to-class map is nondecreasing: as $u$ increases, concavity makes both one-sided slopes nonincreasing, so both endpoints of $\Theta(u,v)$ are nondecreasing. If two such intervals $\Theta$ are disjoint, monotonicity of both endpoints forces the earlier interval to lie strictly below the later one; by step 3.1, this is the class order. The local class maps agree on overlaps of $R_v$ because each entropy level lies in one class. The open intervals $R_v$ cover $R$. Any compact subinterval of $R$ has a finite subcover by these intervals by [F5]; its intersection graph is connected, since otherwise the connected subinterval would be split into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets. Chaining the local orders through overlaps proves that the class map is nondecreasing on all of $R$.

Fix $\sigma\in R_\alpha$ and $x\in E_\sigma$. T4 gives $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ with $x_0\sim_T x_1$. Entropy representation gives $S(x_0)<\sigma<S(x_1)$, and their levels belong to the same class $R_\alpha$. The global nondecreasing order from step 4.1 forces every level between them, including an open neighborhood of $\sigma$, into $R_\alpha$. Thus each class set is open in the interval $R$. Since these disjoint open sets partition connected $R$, only one nonempty class exists. Under the supposition, all states are thermally equivalent, proving the dichotomy.

For the completed calibrator branch, add (C1) **join coherence**: whenever $x\sim_T y$, the join state $J_{ij}(x,y)$ is thermally equivalent to each of $x$ and $y$ under the nested-join identifications. The coordinate sum in the definition alone does not assert C1. In later theorem statements, T1–T5 and C1 are explicitly listed as hypotheses; they are not treated as established physical laws.

derivations.claim: Let $x$ be any typed state and $s>0$. The state $z=(1+s)x$ in the scaled type has the equal-state reversible split with fractions $1/(1+s)$ and $s/(1+s)$; its two components are exactly $x$ and $sx$.
