citations.quote: Let $\mathcal G$ be a set of formal type labels closed under the formal operations $(\Gamma,\Gamma')\mapsto\Gamma\times\Gamma'$ and $(t,\Gamma)\mapsto t\Gamma$ for every real $t>0$. Let $F:=\mathbb R^{(\mathcal G)}$ be the vector space of finite-support real functions on $\mathcal G$, and let $e_\Gamma$ be the function equal to $1$ at $\Gamma$ and $0$ elsewhere.

**The two boundary cases.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, so $n = 0$ is a genuine
case. Since $0 = \varnothing$, the set $F^{0} = F^{\varnothing}$ has exactly one
element, the empty function; that element is $0_{F^{0}}$, so $F^{0}$ is the
**zero space** $\{0_{F^{0}}\}$, not the empty set. For $n = 1$ we have
$1 = \{0\}$, and the map $F^{1} \to F$ sending $x$ to its single coordinate $x_0$
is a bijection satisfying $(x+y)_0 = x_0 + y_0$ and $(\lambda x)_0 = \lambda x_0$;
we use it to read $F^{1}$ as $F$ where convenient. (No general notion of
isomorphism of vector spaces is available on this page, and none is claimed here:
what is asserted is exactly the displayed bijection and the two displayed
equations.)

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), with additive identity $0_F$, multiplicative
identity $1_F$, and the field axioms as stated there. A **vector space over $F$**,
also called an **$F$-vector space**, consists of
$$\forall x\,\forall y\,\exists z\,\forall t\,\bigl(t \in z \leftrightarrow (t = x \vee t = y)\bigr)$$

of the language of set theory ([[def-language-of-set-theory]]): for any set $x$
there is a set $y$ whose elements are exactly the sets $z$ belonging to some
member $s$ of $x$.

$$\exists I\,\Bigl(\exists e\,\bigl(e \in I \wedge \neg\exists t\,(t \in e)\bigr) \wedge \forall y\,\bigl(y \in I \to \exists s\,(s \in I \wedge \forall t\,(t \in s \leftrightarrow (t \in y \vee t = y)))\bigr)\Bigr)$$
$$\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,\bigl(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p))\bigr).$$
The **Axiom of Power Set** is the sentence

$$\forall \bar p\,\forall A\,\Bigl(\forall z\,\bigl(z \in A \to \exists! w\,\varphi(z,w,\bar p)\bigr) \to \exists B\,\forall w\,\bigl(w \in B \leftrightarrow \exists z\,(z \in A \wedge \varphi(z,w,\bar p))\bigr)\Bigr).$$

Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. By
[[lem-ordered-pairs-lie-in-the-double-power-set]] every ordered pair $(a,b)$ with
$a \in A$ and $b \in B$ is an element of $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B))$, so
[[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]] applied inside that set produces the
**Cartesian product**

derivations.claim: The set of all functions $\mathcal G\to\mathbb R$ exists and is a vector space by [F2]. Separation [F4] selects the functions whose support is finite, so $F$ is a set. It contains zero; if $c,d\in F$, then $\operatorname{supp}(c+d)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(c)\cup\operatorname{supp}(d)$, a finite union, and $\operatorname{supp}(tc)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(c)$ for every scalar $t$. Thus $F$ is a linear subspace of the function space by [F3], hence a real vector space.

The index sets $\mathcal G\times\mathcal G$ and $\mathbb R_{>0}\times\mathcal G$ exist by [F4]. Replacement applied to the two displayed relation maps in [F1] gives the set $\mathcal R$; each relation vector has support of size at most three and lies in $F$. The family of finite subsets of $\mathcal R$ is a subset of its power set, and the coefficient functions on each such finite subset form sets by [F2] and [F4]. Replacement under finite summation therefore gives the set $N\subseteq F$ of all finite linear combinations.

The zero vector is in $N$ as the empty sum. If $u,v\in N$, write each as a finite combination of relation vectors; their sum is the finite combination on the union of those two finite index sets, adding coefficients where an index repeats. For $t\in\mathbb R$, $tu$ is obtained by multiplying every coefficient by $t$. Hence $N$ is closed under addition and scalar multiplication and is a linear subspace of $F$ by [F3].

Define $c\sim d$ on $F$ exactly when $c-d\in N$. Since $0\in N$, $N$ is closed under negatives (take scalar $-1$), and under addition, this relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Each class $[c]=\{d\in F:d-c\in N\}$ is a subset of $F$ by separation; replacement on the set $F$ gives the quotient set of these classes.

If $c\sim c'$ and $d\sim d'$, then $(c+d)-(c'+d')=(c-c')+(d-d')\in N$; and for any scalar $t$, $tc-tc'=t(c-c')\in N$. Therefore $[c]+[d]:=[c+d]$ and $t[c]:=[tc]$ do not depend on representatives. The quotient map $c\mapsto[c]$ preserves zero, addition and scalar multiplication; applying it to each vector-space identity in $F$ proves all vector-space axioms in $F/N$. Every generator in $\mathcal R$ lies in $N$, so its class is zero and the two displayed relations hold.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$, let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $z\notin E$. Then there are a nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^n$ and a real $c$ such that

$$\langle u,e\rangle\le c<\langle u,z\rangle\qquad(e\in E).$$

Thus an affine hyperplane strictly separates the point from the entire set.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

derivations.claim: Let $T=\overline{\{a(q-x):a\ge0,\ q\in K\}}$. This is a closed convex cone. If a nonzero functional $\ell$ is nonnegative on $T$, then it is nonnegative on $K-x$, so its zero plane through $x$ supports $K$. Uniqueness in the hypothesis makes that plane the plane with normal $n$; the inward sign forces $\ell=c n\cdot(\,\cdot\,)$ for some $c>0$.

The support at $x$ gives $T\subseteq\{w:n\cdot w\ge0\}$. If $v$ with $n\cdot v>0$ were outside $T$, strict separation [F1] of $v$ from the cone would give a nonzero functional $\ell$ nonnegative on $T$ and negative at $v$: the separating bound is zero because $0\in T$ and $T$ is a cone. Step 1.1 then makes $\ell$ a positive multiple of $n$, contradicting $n\cdot v>0$. Thus the open half-space $n\cdot w>0$ lies in $T$, and each such $v$ is an interior point of $T$.

Fix such $v$. Since $v\in\operatorname{int}T$, choose $d+1$ affinely independent vectors in a small ball about $v$ whose simplex contains a neighborhood of $v$. Approximate each vector by a nonzero cone generator $g_j=a_j(q_j-x)$ with $a_j>0$, $q_j\in K$. Sufficiently close approximations preserve affine independence and keep $v$ in the simplex interior, so a neighborhood $N$ of $v$ lies in the simplex of the $g_j$. For each $w\in N$, write $w=\sum_j\theta_j(w)a_j(q_j-x)$ with $\theta_j(w)\ge0$ and $\sum_j\theta_j(w)=1$. Shrink $N$ so its closure is a closed bounded neighborhood of $v$ contained in that simplex. Barycentric coordinates vary continuously there; by [F3] the closure is compact, so $A:=\sup_{w\in N}\sum_j\theta_j(w)a_j<\infty$.

Choose $\delta>0$ with $\delta A<1$. For $0<t<\delta$ and each $w\in N$, $x+tw=(1-t\sum_j\theta_j a_j)x+\sum_j t\theta_j a_j q_j$ is a convex combination of points of $K$, hence lies in $K$ by [F4]. Therefore $x+tN\subset K$, so a neighborhood of $x+tv$ lies in $K$ and $x+tv\in\operatorname{int}K$.

citations.quote:
Fix a working system of constitution $c$ and a closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(c)$ with equilibrium endpoints as in [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. A cycle of the working system is such a record with $x_P^-=x_P^+$; the reservoirs and work store need not return to their initial energy states.

An ideal thermal reservoir $b$ has an energy interval $J_b\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in joules and a finite entropy function $S_b:J_b\to\mathbb R$ measured in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. On the energy interval admitted for a cycle, assume the exact affine law
$
S_b(E_b)=s_{b,0}+\frac{E_b}{T_b}
$
for a constant $s_{b,0}$ and fixed $T_b>0$ kelvins. Thus $S_b'(E_b)=1/T_b$ in the interior and every admitted endpoint change is exactly $\Delta S_b=\Delta E_b/T_b$. This constant is the absolute thermodynamic temperature under [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. The affine entropy law on the admitted interval is the ideal-bath model; a finite reservoir whose temperature changes is outside this definition.

An ideal work store is a named auxiliary with an energy coordinate $E_w$ measured in joules and an assigned entropy $S_w(E_w)=s_w$ constant on the energy interval used by the cycle. It exchanges only mechanical work and no matter or heat. Its energy may change, while its entropy change is zero by this model definition.

A two-reservoir cycle contains one working-system cycle, one hot bath at $T_h$, one cold bath at $T_c$, and the ideal work store. They lie inside one isolated outer boundary in the sense of [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]], so the full compound has no external matter or energy transfer. There are no unlisted heat, work, matter, kinetic-energy, or external-potential-energy changes. The admitted process and transfer signs are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The model declares the endpoint entropy split
$
S_{\mathrm{tot}}=S_{\mathrm{ws}}(x_{\mathrm{ws}})+S_h(E_h)+S_{\mathrm{cold}}(E_c)+S_w(E_w),
$
where $S_{\mathrm{ws}}$ is the working-system entropy and the bath and work-store functions are those defined here. This additive constituent split is assumed to be one admitted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] and is the entropy supplied to [[post-td-macroscopic-second-law]]; $S_w$ contributes zero change. Reversibility of the full record is as in [[def-td-reversible-process]].

When the second law is applied to the cycle, the model also supplies an admitted closed process record for the full compound. At both endpoints its constituent preparations, with the declared contact controls locked or insulated, are an equilibrium macrostate for that record; its separately tracked center-of-mass kinetic and external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change. This total-compound record is the input to the second law; the working-system record $P$ is the input to its first-law balance.

In the heat-engine mode, the positive magnitudes $Q_h,Q_c$ in joules mean respectively heat taken from the hot bath into the working system and heat rejected by the working system to the cold bath; accordingly $\Delta E_h=-Q_h$, $\Delta E_c=Q_c$, $Q[P]=Q_h-Q_c$, and work output is $W_{\mathrm{out}}=-W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]$. In the refrigerator mode, $Q_c>0$ is heat taken from the cold bath into the working system, $Q_h>0$ is heat rejected to the hot bath, so $\Delta E_c=-Q_c$, $\Delta E_h=Q_h$, $Q[P]=Q_c-Q_h$, and work input is $W_{\mathrm{in}}=W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]$. These are idealized model conventions, not claims that a particular apparatus realizes the cycle.

For every admitted $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ with equilibrium endpoints $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$, fixed material constitution, zero change in center-of-mass kinetic energy, and zero change in separately tracked external-field potential energy in the fixed chart selected by the process model, the adopted model balance is
$$U_c(x_P^+)-U_c(x_P^-)=Q[P]+W_{\mathrm{on}}[P],$$
where $U_c$ is the dimensioned energy-coordinate map of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]].

Here the internal-energy coordinate is evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame as in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], while $Q[P]$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]$ are the protocol transfers defined by [[def-td-process-and-protocol]], in joules as in [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The sign convention is positive $Q$ into the system and positive $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ for work done on it. If $P$ is adiabatic, its defining condition is $Q[P]=0$, so the same adopted balance gives $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]=U_c(x_P^+)-U_c(x_P^-)$.

This equation is an adopted physical postulate of the stated framework. It is not deduced here from a mechanical model or from experimental observations. Records with matter exchange or nonzero changes in omitted kinetic or external-field energy require a separately specified balance and are outside this item.

For every admitted closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ of an isolated compound, assume its declared outer boundary is isolated throughout, its material constitution is fixed, its center-of-mass kinetic and separately tracked external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change, and both endpoint preparations are equilibrium macrostates. Include every named auxiliary and work device in the compound, and restrict to constituent splits for which [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] supplies the additive total entropy. where $S_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the sum of the constituent entropies in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. The process record and the zero-change conditions are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The process may pass through nonequilibrium configurations; this postulate compares endpoint entropies only and assigns no entropy function to those intermediate configurations.

For an admitted reversible operation in the sense of [[def-td-reversible-process]], adopt zero total entropy change. An admitted irreversible adiabatic operation may have a strictly positive entropy increase, but strict increase is not required for every irreversible operation. The postulate does not state monotonicity for an open compound, an externally driven process, a subsystem that exchanges energy with an omitted environment, or every microscopic trajectory.

derivations.claim: The working system returns to its initial state, so $\Delta U=0$. Applying [F2] with [F1] gives $0=Q_h-Q_c-W_{\mathrm{out}}$, hence $W_{\mathrm{out}}=Q_h-Q_c$ and $\eta=1-Q_c/Q_h$.

The hot bath loses energy $Q_h$, the cold bath gains $Q_c$, and their entropy slopes are constant. Thus their entropy changes are $-Q_h/T_h$ and $Q_c/T_c$. The working system and work store have zero entropy change, so [F3] gives
$
-\frac{Q_h}{T_h}+\frac{Q_c}{T_c}=\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}\ge0.
$
Since $Q_h,T_c,T_h>0$, step 1.2 implies $Q_c/Q_h\ge T_c/T_h$. Substituting into step 1.1 yields $\eta\le 1-T_c/T_h$. Equality in this algebraic bound holds exactly when $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}=0$.
If the full admitted cycle is reversible, [F3] gives $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}=0$, so step 2.1 is saturated. No converse about reversibility follows from the entropy calculation.

Let an admitted heat-engine cycle in the sense of [[def-td-reservoir-cycle]] operate between fixed ideal-bath temperatures $0<T_c<T_h$, absorb $Q_h>0$, reject $Q_c>0$, and deliver $W_{\mathrm{out}}>0$. Define its efficiency by $\eta=W_{\mathrm{out}}/Q_h$. Then

Equality holds exactly when the total entropy change of the isolated compound is zero. In particular, a reversible cycle in the stated boundary model saturates the bound; zero entropy change is not here asserted to imply full reversibility.

citations.quote:
Let $C$ be the open positive-temperature domain of a local C2 energy representation $\mathcal U_c(s,V,n)$ for a fixed material constitution $c$, with $V>0$, $n_j>0$, and conjugates $T=\mathcal U_{c,s}$, $p=-\mathcal U_{c,V}$, and $\mu_j=\mathcal U_{c,n_j}$. Let $W\subseteq C$ be open. In addition to the framework suppliers, assume the **same-tag homogeneity hypothesis**: for every $q=(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in W$ there is an $\varepsilon_q\in(0,1)$ such that

$$\mathcal U_c(\lambda s,\lambda V,\lambda n_1,\ldots,\lambda n_r)=\lambda\mathcal U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$$

for every $\lambda>0$ with $|\lambda-1|<\varepsilon_q$ and $\lambda q\in C$. Then, throughout $W$,

$$\mathcal U_c=Ts-pV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j,$$

and on the same chart

$$s\,dT-V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j=0.$$

The same-tag hypothesis is supplied, in particular, when the inverse states $\Psi(q):=(\mathcal U_c(q),V,n)$ for $q\in W$ lie in the designated common-law cone of [[post-td-common-bulk-constitutive-law]], expressed in physical SI coordinate values using the fixed unit conversion. On this branch the adopted entropy transport implies the energy homogeneity locally by uniqueness of the local inverse; no global inverse or global energy-domain cone is assumed. These are conditional model deductions. The general tagged relation in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] alone does not identify the scaled system with one fixed constitutive law.

Let $P=(I_P,x_P^-,x_P^+,z_P,\kappa_P,r_P)$ be an admitted closed process record as defined in [[def-td-process-and-protocol]], with equilibrium endpoints $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$. The record is **reversible relative to its declared boundary and protocol** when the model also admits a reverse record $P^{\mathrm{rev}}$ for the same system and material constitution, starting at $x_P^+$ and ending at $x_P^-$, such that every auxiliary and device state specified by the protocol is restored to its initial state and every signed boundary transfer is reversed. In particular,

$$Q[P^{\mathrm{rev}}]=-Q[P],\qquad W_{\mathrm{on}}[P^{\mathrm{rev}}]=-W_{\mathrm{on}}[P].$$

If the protocol records additional transfer channels, their signed values must likewise be negatives of their forward values. A record that is slow is not reversible merely because it is slow; it must satisfy the reverse-record condition above. Reversibility is therefore relative to what the model includes inside the boundary and which reverse controls it admits.

For every admitted closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ of an isolated compound, assume its declared outer boundary is isolated throughout, its material constitution is fixed, its center-of-mass kinetic and separately tracked external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change, and both endpoint preparations are equilibrium macrostates. Include every named auxiliary and work device in the compound, and restrict to constituent splits for which [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] supplies the additive total entropy. The adopted macroscopic second law is

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^+)-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^-)\ge0,$$

where $S_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the sum of the constituent entropies in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. The process record and the zero-change conditions are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The process may pass through nonequilibrium configurations; this postulate compares endpoint entropies only and assigns no entropy function to those intermediate configurations.

For an admitted reversible operation in the sense of [[def-td-reversible-process]], adopt zero total entropy change. An admitted irreversible adiabatic operation may have a strictly positive entropy increase, but strict increase is not required for every irreversible operation. The postulate does not state monotonicity for an open compound, an externally driven process, a subsystem that exchanges energy with an omitted environment, or every microscopic trajectory.

Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

Fix a material constitution $c$ with finite species list $(1,\ldots,r)$ and a local energy representation $U_c=U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]]. Here $s$ is entropy in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, $V>0$ is volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, each $n_j>0$ is in $\mathrm{mol}$, $U_c$ is in joules, and the conjugates are $T=U_{c,s}$ in kelvins, $p=-U_{c,V}$ in pascals, and $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The derivatives hold every other listed natural coordinate fixed; the physical-coordinate and rest-frame conventions are those of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and [[def-td-si-quantities]].

For an open chart, a **local Legendre transformation** means the following partial transformation of $U_c$: select one or more of its extensive coordinates $q$, take their conjugate coordinates $x=D_qU_c$, and use only a neighborhood on which $(q,z)\mapsto(x,z)$, with $z$ the untransformed coordinates, has a $C^1$ inverse. Such a neighborhood is a valid local transform chart in the sense of [[def-td-response-functions]]. No inverse or potential as a function of the proposed natural coordinates is asserted outside that chart.

On their respective valid charts define the enthalpy, Helmholtz potential, Gibbs potential, and grand potential by

$$H_c:=U_c+pV,\qquad F_c:=U_c-Ts,\qquad G_c:=U_c-Ts+pV,\qquad \Omega_c:=U_c-Ts-\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j.$$

Their natural-coordinate charts are respectively $(s,p,n)$, $(T,V,n)$, $(T,p,n)$, and $(T,V,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r)$. In the volume transform the conjugate coordinate is $-p=U_{c,V}$, which accounts for the plus sign in $H_c$ and $G_c$; in the chemical transform the conjugates are $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$, which accounts for the minus signs in $\Omega_c$. All four potentials have units of joules. A displayed differential or global convex-duality characterization is not part of this definition; critical, coexistence, and other non-C2 boundaries are excluded.

On a valid local energy-representation chart from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]], let $s,V,n_j,U,T,p,\mu_j$ and the potentials $H,F,G,\Omega$ be as defined in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. On every open neighborhood where the corresponding natural-coordinate maps have their stated $C^1$ inverses, the potentials are C2 and their differentials are

$$dU=T\,ds-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dH=T\,ds+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$dF=-s\,dT-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dG=-s\,dT+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$d\Omega=-s\,dT-p\,dV-\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j.$$

All differentials are local state-function differentials. They do not assert that heat or work is an exact differential on process space.

Let $C$ be the open positive-temperature domain of a local C2 energy representation $\mathcal U_c(s,V,n)$ for a fixed material constitution $c$, with $V>0$, $n_j>0$, and conjugates $T=\mathcal U_{c,s}$, $p=-\mathcal U_{c,V}$, and $\mu_j=\mathcal U_{c,n_j}$. Let $W\subseteq C$ be open. In addition to the framework suppliers, assume the **same-tag homogeneity hypothesis**: for every $q=(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in W$ there is an $\varepsilon_q\in(0,1)$ such that

$$\mathcal U_c(\lambda s,\lambda V,\lambda n_1,\ldots,\lambda n_r)=\lambda\mathcal U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$$

for every $\lambda>0$ with $|\lambda-1|<\varepsilon_q$ and $\lambda q\in C$. Then, throughout $W$,

$$\mathcal U_c=Ts-pV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j,$$

and on the same chart

$$s\,dT-V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j=0.$$

The same-tag hypothesis is supplied, in particular, when the inverse states $\Psi(q):=(\mathcal U_c(q),V,n)$ for $q\in W$ lie in the designated common-law cone of [[post-td-common-bulk-constitutive-law]], expressed in physical SI coordinate values using the fixed unit conversion. On this branch the adopted entropy transport implies the energy homogeneity locally by uniqueness of the local inverse; no global inverse or global energy-domain cone is assumed. These are conditional model deductions. The general tagged relation in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] alone does not identify the scaled system with one fixed constitutive law.

Let $1\le q\le n$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Suppose $F(x_*)=0$ and some $q\times q$ minor of the derivative matrix $DF(x_*)$ is invertible. This nonsingular-minor hypothesis is the explicit full-row-rank condition used here. If $q<n$, then after permuting coordinates $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\mathbb R^q$, there are open neighborhoods $P$ of $u_*$ and $Q$ of $v_*$ and a unique $C^1$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$ such that

$$F(u,v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=\varphi(u)\qquad((u,v)\in P\times Q).$$

Its derivative is

$$D\varphi(u)=-D_vF(u,\varphi(u))^{-1}D_uF(u,\varphi(u)).$$

Thus the local zero set is a graph over $n-q$ free coordinates. If $q=n$, the zero is locally isolated, so the local graph dimension is zero. Here “local graph dimension $k$” means a local graph parameterized by an open subset of $\mathbb R^k$, with a singleton counted as dimension zero.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: By [F3], bilateral energy, volume, and species exchange give common $T_0,p_0$ and $\mu_\alpha=\mu_\beta$ at the attained interior coexistence point. Apply [F5] separately to the two phase branches using [A1]: $G_i/n_i=\mu_i$ for $i=\alpha,\beta$. Thus $F(T_0,p_0):=g_\beta(T_0,p_0)-g_\alpha(T_0,p_0)=0$.

On each branch, hold the amount $n_i$ fixed while varying $(T,p)$. By [F2] and [F4], $d(G_i/n_i)=-s_i\,dT+v_i\,dp$. Consequently $F_T=-(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$ and $F_p=v_\beta-v_\alpha$ at $(T_0,p_0)$. The nonzero-volume-jump hypothesis makes $F_p\ne0$.

Apply [L1] to $F=g_\beta-g_\alpha$ on $O$. It gives a unique local C1 graph $p=p(T)$ satisfying $F(T,p(T))=0$. Differentiating this identity using [L2] gives $0=F_T+F_p\,p'(T)$. Substitution of the derivatives from step 1.2 yields
$$
p'(T_0)=\frac{s_\beta-s_\alpha}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}.
$$
The same calculation applies at every point of the shrunken coexistence interval with nonzero $\Delta v$.

For the reversible latent-heat clause, the system entropy change when $n$ moles are converted is $n(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$. By [A2], the total entropy change of system and reservoir is zero and the reservoir contributes $-Q/T$, so $Q/T=n(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$. Dividing by $n>0$ gives $\ell_{\alpha\to\beta}:=Q/n=T(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$. Let $P=(I_P,x_P^-,x_P^+,z_P,\kappa_P,r_P)$ be an admitted closed process record as defined in [[def-td-process-and-protocol]], with equilibrium endpoints $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$. The record is **reversible relative to its declared boundary and protocol** when the model also admits a reverse record $P^{\mathrm{rev}}$ for the same system and material constitution, starting at $x_P^+$ and ending at $x_P^-$, such that every auxiliary and device state specified by the protocol is restored to its initial state and every signed boundary transfer is reversed. In particular,

$$Q[P^{\mathrm{rev}}]=-Q[P],\qquad W_{\mathrm{on}}[P^{\mathrm{rev}}]=-W_{\mathrm{on}}[P].$$

If the protocol records additional transfer channels, their signed values must likewise be negatives of their forward values. A record that is slow is not reversible merely because it is slow; it must satisfy the reverse-record condition above. Reversibility is therefore relative to what the model includes inside the boundary and which reverse controls it admits.

For every admitted closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ of an isolated compound, assume its declared outer boundary is isolated throughout, its material constitution is fixed, its center-of-mass kinetic and separately tracked external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change, and both endpoint preparations are equilibrium macrostates. Include every named auxiliary and work device in the compound, and restrict to constituent splits for which [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] supplies the additive total entropy. The adopted macroscopic second law is

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^+)-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^-)\ge0,$$

where $S_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the sum of the constituent entropies in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. The process record and the zero-change conditions are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The process may pass through nonequilibrium configurations; this postulate compares endpoint entropies only and assigns no entropy function to those intermediate configurations.

For an admitted reversible operation in the sense of [[def-td-reversible-process]], adopt zero total entropy change. An admitted irreversible adiabatic operation may have a strictly positive entropy increase, but strict increase is not required for every irreversible operation. The postulate does not state monotonicity for an open compound, an externally driven process, a subsystem that exchanges energy with an omitted environment, or every microscopic trajectory.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a material constitution $c$ with finite species list $(1,\ldots,r)$ and a local energy representation $U_c=U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]]. Here $s$ is entropy in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, $V>0$ is volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, each $n_j>0$ is in $\mathrm{mol}$, $U_c$ is in joules, and the conjugates are $T=U_{c,s}$ in kelvins, $p=-U_{c,V}$ in pascals, and $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The derivatives hold every other listed natural coordinate fixed; the physical-coordinate and rest-frame conventions are those of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and [[def-td-si-quantities]].

For an open chart, a **local Legendre transformation** means the following partial transformation of $U_c$: select one or more of its extensive coordinates $q$, take their conjugate coordinates $x=D_qU_c$, and use only a neighborhood on which $(q,z)\mapsto(x,z)$, with $z$ the untransformed coordinates, has a $C^1$ inverse. Such a neighborhood is a valid local transform chart in the sense of [[def-td-response-functions]]. No inverse or potential as a function of the proposed natural coordinates is asserted outside that chart.

On their respective valid charts define the enthalpy, Helmholtz potential, Gibbs potential, and grand potential by

$$H_c:=U_c+pV,\qquad F_c:=U_c-Ts,\qquad G_c:=U_c-Ts+pV,\qquad \Omega_c:=U_c-Ts-\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j.$$

Their natural-coordinate charts are respectively $(s,p,n)$, $(T,V,n)$, $(T,p,n)$, and $(T,V,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r)$. In the volume transform the conjugate coordinate is $-p=U_{c,V}$, which accounts for the plus sign in $H_c$ and $G_c$; in the chemical transform the conjugates are $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$, which accounts for the minus signs in $\Omega_c$. All four potentials have units of joules. A displayed differential or global convex-duality characterization is not part of this definition; critical, coexistence, and other non-C2 boundaries are excluded.

Let $\Omega_{\rm per}=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$ with opposite faces identified, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval in seconds, and let $f(x,v,t)\ge0$ be a one-particle number density for $x\in\Omega_{\rm per}$, $v\in\mathbb R^3$, and $t\in I$. With $x$ in metres and $v$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $f$ has units $\mathrm{s^3\,m^{-6}}$ relative to $d^3x\,d^3v$; its moments used below are assumed finite. Periodic boundary conditions are imposed in $x$.

Adopt the incoming molecular-chaos closure: at a collision location and time, the incoming two-particle velocity density used in the collision term is $f(x,v,t)f(x,w,t)$. This is a one-sided factorization assumption; no factorization of the outgoing pair and no derivation from reversible many-particle mechanics is asserted.

For the elastic data $Q_{\rm el},\nu$ of [[def-td-regular-elastic-collision-model]], adopt a collision operator $Q_\nu(f)$, with units of $f$ per second, satisfying for every measurable test function $\varphi$ for which the integrals converge absolutely,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\varphi(v)Q_\nu(f)(x,v,t)\,d^3v=\frac14\int_{Q_{\rm el}}\big(f(x,v',t)f(x,w',t)-f(x,v,t)f(x,w,t)\big)\big(\varphi(v)+\varphi(w)-\varphi(v')-\varphi(w')\big)\,d\nu.$$
The adopted kinetic equation is
$$\partial_t f+v\cdot\nabla_x f=Q_\nu(f).$$
The equation and weak collision identity are model postulates. This item does not assert a hard-sphere Boltzmann–Grad limit, propagation of chaos, or universal equilibration.

Fix a particle mass $m_p>0$ in kilograms and velocity space $V=\mathbb R^3$ with components in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The elastic collision set is
$$Q_{\rm el}=\{(v,w,v',w')\in V^4:v+w=v'+w',\ |v|^2+|w|^2=|v'|^2+|w'|^2\}.$$
Thus each allowed event conserves momentum $m_p(v+w)$ and kinetic energy $m_p(|v|^2+|w|^2)/2$. Equip $Q_{\rm el}$ with the Borel sets generated by its relative topology.

Collision-rate data consist of a nonnegative, countably additive, $\sigma$-finite Borel measure $\nu$ on these Borel sets. It is invariant under exchanging $v$ with $w$, exchanging $v'$ with $w'$, and exchanging the incoming pair $(v,w)$ with the outgoing pair $(v',w')$: for each of these maps $S$ and Borel set $E$, $\nu(S^{-1}E)=\nu(E)$. This is the three-dimensional physical restriction of the collision set and exchange conventions in [[def-tdmath-elastic-collision-kernel]], with $\sigma$-finiteness stated explicitly for the product integrals used by the entropy theorem. Its physical units and rate normalization are chosen so the associated weak collision operator has units of density per second. The measure is a declared model input; no differential cross section or microscopic limit is inferred from this Definition.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

Let $\Omega=\mathbb T^d$ be a spatial rectangle with opposite faces identified, $d\ge2$, and let $I$ be an open time interval. Suppose $f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\times I\to(0,\infty)$ is $C^1$ in space and time and $C^2$ in velocity. Fix a positive reference density $f_{\rm ref}$ with the same units as $f$. Assume $f$, $f|v|^2$, and $f|\log(f/f_{\rm ref})|$ are integrable, and assume an integrable envelope on every compact time interval justifying differentiation of the entropy integral and every displayed collision integral. Let $Q$ and the symmetric collision measure $\nu$ satisfy the weak identity in [[def-tdmath-elastic-collision-kernel]] for tests $1$ and $\log(f/f_{\rm ref})$, with absolute convergence, and suppose
$$\partial_t f+v\cdot\nabla_r f=Q(f).$$
Then for $H[f](t)=\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\log(f/f_{\rm ref})\,dv\,dr$,
$$\frac{d}{dt}H[f](t)=-\frac14\int_\Omega\int_{Q_{\rm el}}(A-B)(\log A-\log B)\,d\nu\,dr\le0,\qquad A=f(r,v,t)f(r,w,t),\quad B=f(r,v',t)f(r,w',t).$$
The integrand is nonnegative because $\log$ is strictly increasing. Equality in the entropy-production integral holds exactly when $A=B$ for $\nu$-almost every collision at almost every $r$. Under the additional assumptions that $\nu$ is locally finite, has full support on $Q_{\rm el}$, and $f$ is positive and $C^2$ in $v$, this balance implies for almost every $r$ that
$$\log(f(r,v,t)/f_{\rm ref})=\alpha(r,t)+b(r,t)\cdot v+\frac{\lambda(r,t)}2|v|^2.$$
If $f(r,\cdot,t)$ is integrable over $\mathbb R^d$, then $\lambda(r,t)<0$, so its velocity profile is Maxwellian. Conversely, every profile of this form has zero collision entropy production. The weak collision identity is an explicit model hypothesis; this is not a derivation from reversible many-particle mechanics or a PDE existence theorem.

derivations.claim:
Set $H(t)=\int_{\Omega_{\rm per}}\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\log(f/f_{\rm ref})\,d^3v\,d^3x$. The hypotheses match [L1]: the spatial dimension is $d=3$, the opposite-face identification is periodic, the density is positive with the required regularity and moments, [A3] supplies the dominated differentiation and absolute convergence conditions, and [A1] supplies the kinetic equation and weak identity. The collision measure is symmetric by [F1]; its $\sigma$-finiteness in [A3] permits the product-space integrals. Thus [L1] gives
$$H'(t)=-\frac14\int_{\Omega_{\rm per}}\int_{Q_{\rm el}}(A-B)\log\!\left(\frac AB\right)\,d\nu\,d^3x\le0,$$
and its equality condition applies at each time where the derivative and production integral are defined.

By definition $S_{\rm kin}=-k_BH$, and $k_B>0$ by [F2]. Multiplying the identity in step 1.1 by $-k_B$ reverses its sign and yields the displayed entropy-production formula with nonnegative right-hand side. Since the multiplier is strictly positive, $S'_{\rm kin}(t)=0$ holds exactly when the production integral vanishes; the equality characterization in [L1] gives $A=B$ for $\nu$-almost every collision at almost every spatial point. This remains a conditional model deduction and uses no outgoing-pair molecular-chaos assumption.

citations.quote:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

For each admitted material constitution $c$, the model adopts a finite scalar function

$$S_c:D_c\longrightarrow\mathbb R\ \text{with values measured in }\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}},$$

on the equilibrium state domain $D_c$ of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. This framework treats $S_c$ as primitive constitutive data: its existence and form are assumed, not derived from the word entropy, statistical mechanics, or experimental evidence.

On every specified convex region $C\subseteq D_c$ in the dimensionless coordinates of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], $S_c$ is continuous and concave, meaning that for all $x,y\in C$ and every $\alpha\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]),

$$S_c((1-\alpha)x+\alpha y)\ge (1-\alpha)S_c(x)+\alpha S_c(y).$$

The domain assumptions are local to the material and region named; no unlisted coordinate tuple is presumed physically realizable. The input of $S_c$ is the represented state $\pi_c(e)$; when the function is written using physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, those coordinates mean the SI values whose dimensionless numerical tuple is $\pi_c(e)$. For independent separated macroscopic systems $A,B$ admitted by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], entropy is additive under that postulate's composition map $\kappa_{AB}$:

$$S_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=S_A(x_A)+S_B(x_B).$$

On each separately designated open, single-phase chart in the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, assume the numerical representative of $S_c$ is $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: its first and second coordinate partial derivatives exist and are continuous. The partial derivative $S_U$ at fixed $V,n_1,\ldots,n_r$ is the ordinary partial derivative in the $U$ coordinate, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and is assumed finite and strictly positive. The numerical chart input uses $\hat U=U/(1\,\mathrm J)$; consequently $S_U=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial S_c/\partial\hat U$ and has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. The other physical coordinates are similarly represented using the fixed SI units of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. For the tagged bulk family with scaling maps $\delta_\lambda$ and domains $B_{c,\lambda}$ from [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], also adopt, for every admitted $\lambda>0$ and $x\in B_{c,\lambda}$,

$$S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(\delta_\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x).$$

This is a bulk homogeneity assumption for tagged scaled systems, not exact finite-size scaling for every body. Lieb–Yngvason develop a different accessibility-based route in which entropy is represented from additional operational hypotheses; this framework does not claim that their derivation proves the present primitive entropy postulate.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty compact, $d\ge1$, and $a:K\to\mathbb R$ continuous. Define $a_{\rm mix}$ as in [[def-tdmath-mixture-generator-space-and-energy]]. Then for every $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$ the infimum defining $a_{\rm mix}(x)$ is attained by a Borel probability measure supported on at most $d+1$ points. The function $a_{\rm mix}$ is lower semicontinuous and convex on $\operatorname{conv}K$, and is the greatest convex function on $\operatorname{conv}K$ bounded above by $a$ on $K$. Minimizing over all Borel probabilities on $K$ gives the same attained value as minimizing over finite mixtures. This is a mathematical compactness result; it makes no phase-preparation or equilibrium postulate.

derivations.claim:
By [A1], each generator is a declared model state and feasible mixtures obey the model's exact totals. By [L2], $|s(x)|\le M$ on $K$ for some finite $M$. Every open subset of $\mathbb R$ has open preimage under the continuous map $s$, and preimages preserve complements and countable unions, so preimages of Borel sets are Borel; hence $s$ is Borel measurable. For any feasible probability measure $P$ and any nonnegative simple function $\varphi\le |s|$, write $\varphi=\sum_j c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ on disjoint Borel sets; then
$$
\int_K\varphi\,dP=\sum_jc_jP(A_j)\le M\sum_jP(A_j)\le M P(K)=M.
$$
By the integral definition [F2], $\int_K|s|\,dP\le M$, so $s$ is integrable. Set $a=-s$; it is continuous and integrable, and the signed-integral definition gives $\int_Ka\,dP=-\int_Ks\,dP$. The barycenter constraint is unchanged, so minimizing $\int_Ka\,dP$ over the same feasible set is equivalent to maximizing $\int_Ks\,dP$.

By definition of $\operatorname{conv}K$, there are finitely many $x_i\in K$ and nonnegative weights $\theta_i$ with $\sum_i\theta_i=1$ and $\bar x=\sum_i\theta_ix_i$. Then $P_0:=\sum_i\theta_i\delta_{x_i}$ is a Borel probability measure with coordinatewise barycenter $\bar x$, so the fixed-barycenter feasible set is nonempty under the model assumption.

Apply the exact current statement of [L1] to $K$, $a$, and $\bar x$. Conditional on the batch-12 proof defects being resolved and its accepted proof supporting that statement, it supplies a minimizing Borel probability measure $P_*$ supported on at most $d+1$ points. By step 1.1, this same $P_*$ maximizes the physical entropy functional. No finite phase menu was assumed.

Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty compact, $d\ge1$, and $a:K\to\mathbb R$ continuous. Define $a_{\rm mix}$ as in [[def-tdmath-mixture-generator-space-and-energy]]. Then for every $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$ the infimum defining $a_{\rm mix}(x)$ is attained by a Borel probability measure supported on at most $d+1$ points. The function $a_{\rm mix}$ is lower semicontinuous and convex on $\operatorname{conv}K$, and is the greatest convex function on $\operatorname{conv}K$ bounded above by $a$ on $K$. Minimizing over all Borel probabilities on $K$ gives the same attained value as minimizing over finite mixtures. This is a mathematical compactness result; it makes no phase-preparation or equilibrium postulate.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: [[thm-tdmath-compact-continuous-mixture-attainment]]: For nonempty compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ with $d\ge1$ and continuous $a:K\to\mathbb R$, every fixed barycenter $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$ has an attained minimum of $\int_Ka\,dP$ over all Borel probability measures with that barycenter; a minimizer can be chosen atomic on at most $d+1$ points. Its current batch-12 carrier has this exact statement and is registered as a draft. Its proof has unresolved completion defects recorded in batch-13 cross-batch evidence: step 5.1 cites nonexistent step 2.2, and step 4.1 uses uniform continuity and a finite Borel partition without a supporting proof or cited supplier.

citations.quote:
Fix a constitution $c$ and a smooth physical-coordinate chart in $D_c$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], with fixed amounts $n=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ and $T,p$ as in [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. A **valid response chart** is an open neighborhood on which the relevant independent coordinates used below have a $C^1$ inverse to the physical $(U,V)$ coordinates; a $C^1$ diffeomorphism has a $C^1$ inverse on open neighborhoods by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The existence of such a chart is a hypothesis for a response derivative, not a consequence of this definition. The derivatives use the indicated natural variables and hold all other listed coordinates fixed.

The **constant-volume heat capacity** and **constant-pressure heat capacity** of the whole system are, where the derivatives exist and are finite,

$$C_V:=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_{V,n},\qquad H:=U+pV,\qquad C_p:=\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Here $H$ is the enthalpy in joules; both heat capacities are in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, not per mole. The **isothermal compressibility** and **isobaric thermal expansion coefficient** are

$$\kappa_T:=-\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_{T,n},\qquad \alpha_p:=\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Since $V>0$ and the coordinates use SI units ([[def-td-si-quantities]]), $\kappa_T$ has units $\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$ and $\alpha_p$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. This definition asserts no sign for any response, no identity among them, and no finite value at a critical or otherwise singular chart.

Fix a constitution $c$, a positive-temperature local energy chart with entropy coordinate $s$ and physical volume $V>0$, and fixed amounts $n=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)$. The energy representation and pressure on this chart are those of [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]] and the response-chart conventions are those of [[def-td-response-functions]]. Where $(s,V,n)\mapsto(s,p,n)$ has a C1 local inverse, define the **isentropic compressibility** of the whole system by

$$\kappa_S:=-\frac1V\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_{s,n}.$$

The entropy $s$ is held fixed, as are all amounts $n_j$. Since $V$ is in $\mathrm{m^3}$ and $p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$ ([[def-td-si-quantities]]), $\kappa_S$ has units $\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$. This definition asserts no sign, finiteness, or existence outside the specified inverse chart; in particular it does not assign a value at a singular or critical response point.

Let $U,H,F,G,\Omega$ and their natural-coordinate charts be as in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]], with the exact differentials supplied by [[pthm-td-potential-differentials]]. Assume each potential is C2 on its named open chart. Every pair of conjugate coefficients in its exact differential has equal cross derivatives. Explicitly, with all unlisted natural coordinates held fixed, for each species $i,j$:

- From $U(s,V,n)$: $T_V|_{s,n}=-p_s|_{V,n}$; $T_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,s}|_{V,n}$; $-p_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,V}|_{s,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{s,V}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{s,V}$.
- From $H(s,p,n)$: $T_p|_{s,n}=V_s|_{p,n}$; $T_{n_j}|_{s,p,n}=\mu_{j,s}|_{p,n}$; $V_{n_j}|_{s,p,n}=\mu_{j,p}|_{s,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{s,p}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{s,p}$.
- From $F(T,V,n)$: $s_V|_{T,n}=p_T|_{V,n}$; $s_{n_j}|_{T,V,n}=-\mu_{j,T}|_{V,n}$; $-p_{n_j}|_{T,V,n}=\mu_{j,V}|_{T,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{T,V}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{T,V}$.
- From $G(T,p,n)$: $-s_p|_{T,n}=V_T|_{p,n}$; $-s_{n_j}|_{T,p,n}=\mu_{j,T}|_{p,n}$; $V_{n_j}|_{T,p,n}=\mu_{j,p}|_{T,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{T,p}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{T,p}$.
- From $\Omega(T,V,\mu)$: $s_V|_{T,\mu}=p_T|_{V,\mu}$; $s_{\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,T}|_{V,\mu}$; $p_{\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,V}|_{T,\mu}$; and $n_{i,\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,\mu_i}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne i}}$.

On an open C2 Helmholtz chart $F(T,V,n)$ at fixed composition $n$, suppose $T>0$, $V>0$, the response coordinates $(T,p,n)$ have the local inverse required by [[def-td-response-functions]], and $\kappa_T>0$. Then

$$C_p-C_V=\frac{TV\alpha_p^2}{\kappa_T}.$$

Here $C_V,C_p$ are the whole-system heat capacities, $\alpha_p=V^{-1}(\partial V/\partial T)_{p,n}$, and $\kappa_T=-V^{-1}(\partial V/\partial p)_{T,n}$, all as in [[def-td-response-functions]]. The formula is a conditional model identity, not an empirical law or a claim at singular response points.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: From [F1] and [F3], the differential of entropy at fixed $n$ is $ds=(C_V/T)\,dT+p_T|_{V,n}\,dV$. Along an isentrope $ds=0$, the valid chart therefore gives $T_V|_{s,n}=-T p_T|_{V,n}/C_V$.
Differentiate $p(T,V,n)$ along the same isentrope using [F5]: $p_V|_{s,n}=p_V|_{T,n}+p_T|_{V,n}T_V|_{s,n}=p_V|_{T,n}-T(p_T|_{V,n})^2/C_V$.

From [F1] and the response inverse, $p_V|_{T,n}=-1/(V\kappa_T)$ and $p_T|_{V,n}=\alpha_p/\kappa_T$. Thus [F4] is equivalently $C_p-C_V=-T(p_T|_{V,n})^2/p_V|_{T,n}$. Substitution into step 2.1 yields $p_V|_{s,n}=p_V|_{T,n}(C_p/C_V)$. Since $p_V|_{T,n}<0$ and $C_V>0$, [F4] also gives $C_p=C_V-T(p_T|_{V,n})^2/p_V|_{T,n}\ge C_V>0$, hence $p_V|_{s,n}<0$.
Use the definitions [F1]–[F2] and step 3.1: $\kappa_T/\kappa_S=p_V|_{s,n}/p_V|_{T,n}=C_p/C_V$. All denominators are nonzero by the stated positivity and valid-chart hypotheses.
