Then $Z$ is $C^2$, $-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E_\beta$, $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$, and the dimensionless Gibbs entropy is finite with
$$-\sum_i p_i\log p_i=\log Z+\beta\bar E_\beta.$$
Thus $F_{\mathrm{stat}}=-k_{\mathrm B}T\log Z=\bar E_\beta-TS_\beta$ for $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$. A lower bound on the energies alone does not supply the summable envelope or finite partition function.

citations.quote:
Use the finite-alphabet, bounded, translation-invariant finite-range lattice model of [[def-tdmath-bounded-finite-range-lattice]], with physical interaction energies in joules, inverse temperature $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}>0$, and partition sum $Z_L(\beta)$. Suppose each site represents a fixed cell of volume $v_0>0$ in $\mathrm{m^3}$. Define the reduced log-partition density $p_L=L^{-d}\log Z_L$ and the lattice pressure convention $P_L=(k_{\mathrm B}T/v_0)p_L$ in pascals. Then $p_L$ and $P_L$ have finite limits as $L\to\infty$. If a second boundary-energy model on the same configuration sets differs pointwise by at most $C_bL^{d-1}$ joules for fixed $C_b$, it has the same limit.

The pressure convention in this statement is assigned to this lattice model. Equating it with a derivative-based macroscopic pressure or a measured mechanical pressure requires a separate model identification.

For the lattice models of [[thm-tdmath-finite-range-lattice-pressure-limit]], write $p_L(\gamma)=L^{-d}\log Z_L(\gamma)$ and let $p(\gamma)=\lim_Lp_L(\gamma)$ on an open interval $J\subseteq(0,\infty)$. At finite $L$, use the canonical law $\mathbb P_{\gamma,L}(s):=e^{-\gamma H_L(s)}/Z_L(\gamma)$ and its finite expectation $\mathbb E_{\gamma,L}$. If $p$ is differentiable at $\beta\in J$, then $\mathbb E_{\beta,L}[H_L]/L^d\to e:=-p'(\beta)$. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there are $c>0$ and $L_0$ such that for $L\ge L_0$, $\mathbb P_{\beta,L}(|H_L/L^d-e|\ge\varepsilon)\le2e^{-cL^d}$. No energy-density limit is asserted at a nondifferentiability point.

Assign a positive temperature $T$ in kelvins and the exact framework constant $k_{\mathrm B}$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ from [[def-td-si-quantities]], and put $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. For a finite microstate model $(\Omega,\epsilon)$, adopt the canonical preparation
$$P_\beta(x)=\frac{e^{-\beta E(x)}}{Z(\beta)},\qquad Z(\beta)=\sum_{x\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E(x)}.$$
Here $Z$ is dimensionless, positive, and finite because $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty.

The same adopted law may be assigned to a specified countable state model with its stated enumeration and energy list, or to a measurable model $(X,\Sigma,\mu,E)$ with a dimensionless reference measure $\mu$ and measurable energy $E:X\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$, only when $0<Z(\beta)<\infty$ for the declared series or integral. In those cases $P_\beta(i)=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$ or the probability density is $p_\beta=e^{-\beta E}/Z$ relative to $\mu$. The countable and integral conventions are those of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]] and [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] at their actual current draft statements.

This is an adopted statistical-mechanical preparation rule. It is not derived from the macroscopic thermodynamic laws, a finite bath, entropy maximization, or a time-evolution equation. It does not assert that a physical sample has this preparation; that identification is an additional model assumption to be tested against a specified preparation and apparatus.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

derivations.claim: The finite-volume energy law and $p_L$ in [F1]–[F2] match the model and probability hypotheses of [L1]. The condition $\beta>0$ and differentiability at $\beta$ are exactly those in [A1].

Applying [L1] yields $\mathbb E_{\beta,L}[H_L]/L^d\to -p'(\beta)=e$ and, for each fixed $\varepsilon>0$, a constant $c>0$ and threshold $L_0$ with the stated two-tail exponential estimate. The result is a model probability statement and is silent at pressure nondifferentiability.

If $p$ is differentiable at $\beta\in J_\beta$, set $e=-p'(\beta)$ in joules per site. Then the canonical mean energy density satisfies $\mathbb E_{\beta,L}[H_L]/L^d\to e$, and for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exist $c>0$ and $L_0$ such that

citations.quote:
In addition to the general tagged bulk family of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and its entropy law in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], designate a common-constitutive-law bulk branch as follows. Fix a material constitution $c$ with an ordered species list and fixed intensive constitutive parameters. Let $C\subseteq D_c$ be a nonempty open single-phase chart in the fixed dimensionless SI numerical coordinates of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and [[def-td-si-quantities]], and assume it is a positive cone: $\lambda x\in C$ for all $x\in C$ and $\lambda>0$. Use the adopted $C^2$ entropy with $S_{c,U}>0$ on this chart.

For every $\lambda>0$, admit scaling of every $x\in C$, so $C\subseteq B_{c,\lambda}$, and retain the distinct scaled-system tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. The image $C^{(\lambda)}:=\delta_\lambda(C)$ is a chart in $D_{c^{(\lambda)}}$. Adopt a coordinate-preserving material-law transport $j_{c,\lambda}:C^{(\lambda)}\to C$ defined in numerical coordinates by $j_{c,\lambda}(y)=y$, and adopt entropy preservation under that transport:

$$S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(y)=S_c(j_{c,\lambda}(y))\qquad(y\in C^{(\lambda)}).$$

The transport identifies the constitutive numerical law used for bodies in this branch; it does not equate their physical identities or material tags. It presumes a common ordered species list, units, internal-energy reference and entropy calibration. Fixed material parameters in this branch exclude a hidden size parameter whose independent variation changes the law. Combined with the existing tagged entropy law, this adopted transport gives the same-function relation

$$S_c(\lambda x)=S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(\delta_\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x)\qquad(x\in C,\ \lambda>0).$$

This is additional idealized constitutive information for the designated bulk branch. It is not implied by coordinate additivity, SI units, the general tagged relation, or the existence of local equilibrium charts. No empirical proof, finite-size error bound, or assertion for surface-sensitive, interacting long-range or self-gravitating bodies is supplied. Euler and Gibbs–Duhem identities are conditional deductions on this branch, not part of the postulate's source review.

Let $A$ and $B$ be two named subsystems with disjoint physical regions as in [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]], combined as a compound system $A\sqcup B$ inside a declared outer boundary. The model's admitted separated pairs form a specified subset $\mathcal C_{AB}\subseteq D_A\times D_B$ using [[def-subset-and-proper-subset]] and [[def-cartesian-product]]. For every pair $(x_A,x_B)\in\mathcal C_{AB}$, the composition map $\kappa_{AB}:\mathcal C_{AB}\to D_{A\sqcup B}$ is a function ([[def-function-space]]) adopted so the dimensioned coordinates of its output satisfy
$$U_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=U_A(x_A)+U_B(x_B),\qquad V_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=V_A(x_A)+V_B(x_B),\qquad n_{A\sqcup B,j}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=n_{A,j}(x_A)+n_{B,j}(x_B).$$
Here each coordinate function is the dimensioned map of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] for its material constitution, with SI units as in [[def-td-si-quantities]].

Here “extensive coordinates” means precisely the named coordinates declared additive by this postulate. Amount coordinates are aligned by species label; when a species is absent from one subsystem, its zero amount is in a separately declared composition boundary, not the positive-mole chart of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. This is an idealized composition rule: cross-interface and long-range interaction energy is omitted from $U_{A\sqcup B}$, rather than asserted to vanish in nature. The postulate does not assert that every pair of subsystem states is physically admissible.

The framework's bulk family is a tagged family of material types. For each dimensionless scale $\lambda>0$ the model may designate a tag $c^{(\lambda)}$ and a subset $B_{c,\lambda}\subseteq D_c$ of states admitting a scaled copy, with inclusion as in [[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]. For $x=(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n_1,\ldots,\hat n_r)\in B_{c,\lambda}$, the scaling map is the function $\delta_\lambda:B_{c,\lambda}\to D_{c^{(\lambda)}}$ ([[def-function-space]]) given by $\delta_\lambda(x)=(\lambda\hat U,\lambda\hat V,\lambda\hat n_1,\ldots,\lambda\hat n_r)$. The tag matters: $c^{(\lambda)}$ is not silently identified with $c$. This postulate specifies the coordinate scaling model and energy additivity only; it does not postulate entropy additivity or exact scaling for every finite physical body.

This is an adopted physical composition rule, not a deduction from SI units or from the mathematics of Cartesian products.

For each admitted material constitution $c$, the model adopts a finite scalar function

$$S_c:D_c\longrightarrow\mathbb R\ \text{with values measured in }\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}},$$

on the equilibrium state domain $D_c$ of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. This framework treats $S_c$ as primitive constitutive data: its existence and form are assumed, not derived from the word entropy, statistical mechanics, or experimental evidence.

On every specified convex region $C\subseteq D_c$ in the dimensionless coordinates of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], $S_c$ is continuous and concave, meaning that for all $x,y\in C$ and every $\alpha\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]),

$$S_c((1-\alpha)x+\alpha y)\ge (1-\alpha)S_c(x)+\alpha S_c(y).$$

The domain assumptions are local to the material and region named; no unlisted coordinate tuple is presumed physically realizable. The input of $S_c$ is the represented state $\pi_c(e)$; when the function is written using physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, those coordinates mean the SI values whose dimensionless numerical tuple is $\pi_c(e)$. For independent separated macroscopic systems $A,B$ admitted by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], entropy is additive under that postulate's composition map $\kappa_{AB}$:

$$S_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=S_A(x_A)+S_B(x_B).$$

On each separately designated open, single-phase chart in the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, assume the numerical representative of $S_c$ is $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: its first and second coordinate partial derivatives exist and are continuous. The partial derivative $S_U$ at fixed $V,n_1,\ldots,n_r$ is the ordinary partial derivative in the $U$ coordinate, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and is assumed finite and strictly positive. The numerical chart input uses $\hat U=U/(1\,\mathrm J)$; consequently $S_U=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial S_c/\partial\hat U$ and has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. The other physical coordinates are similarly represented using the fixed SI units of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. No differentiability, strict concavity, or positive $S_U$ is asserted outside those charts. This item does not itself define a thermometer calibration or claim a temperature law.

For the tagged bulk family with scaling maps $\delta_\lambda$ and domains $B_{c,\lambda}$ from [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], also adopt, for every admitted $\lambda>0$ and $x\in B_{c,\lambda}$,

$$S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(\delta_\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x).$$

This is a bulk homogeneity assumption for tagged scaled systems, not exact finite-size scaling for every body. Lieb–Yngvason develop a different accessibility-based route in which entropy is represented from additional operational hypotheses; this framework does not claim that their derivation proves the present primitive entropy postulate.

Let $c$ be a material constitution, let $r$ be its finite number of named species, and let $(U_0,V_0,n_{0,1},\ldots,n_{0,r})$ lie in an open single-phase chart $\Omega$ of physical SI coordinate values, with $U$ in joules, $V>0$ in cubic metres, and each $n_j>0$ in moles ([[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], [[def-td-si-quantities]]). The chart is the image of an open subset of the dimensionless domain $D_c$ under the fixed diagonal unit conversion $(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n)\mapsto(U,V,n)$. Write $S_c(U,V,n)$ for the entropy on $D_c$ composed with the inverse unit conversion; its physical-coordinate partials include those unit factors as specified in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Assume this representative is $C^2$ and $S_{c,U}(U_0,V_0,n_0)>0$. Then there are open neighborhoods of $(S_c(U_0,V_0,n_0),V_0,n_0)$ and $(U_0,V_0,n_0)$ on which the equation

$$S_c(U,V,n)=s$$

has a unique solution $U=\mathcal U_c(s,V,n)$ of class $C^2$. On this local chart,

$$\mathcal U_{c,s}=T_c,\qquad \mathcal U_{c,V}=-p_c,\qquad \mathcal U_{c,n_j}=\mu_{c,j},$$

with the intensive functions defined by [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. This is a local representation only: it asserts neither global injectivity or domain coverage nor differentiability at a nonsmooth phase boundary.

On a valid local energy-representation chart from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]], let $s,V,n_j,U,T,p,\mu_j$ and the potentials $H,F,G,\Omega$ be as defined in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. On every open neighborhood where the corresponding natural-coordinate maps have their stated $C^1$ inverses, the potentials are C2 and their differentials are

$$dU=T\,ds-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dH=T\,ds+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$dF=-s\,dT-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dG=-s\,dT+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$d\Omega=-s\,dT-p\,dV-\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j.$$

All differentials are local state-function differentials. They do not assert that heat or work is an exact differential on process space.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Suppose that for every $x\in C$ there is a nondegenerate interval $J_x\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $1$ such that $\lambda x\in C$ and $f(\lambda x)=\lambda f(x)$ for every $\lambda\in J_x$. Here nondegenerate means that $J_x$ contains a point different from $1$; $1$ may be an endpoint. Then

$$f(x)=Df(x)[x]=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\,\partial_j f(x)\qquad(x\in C).$$

The radial identity need only hold on one side of $1$: openness of $C$ and $C^1$ regularity supply an ambient derivative, and the interval makes $1$ a nonisolated point at which that derivative is determined by the radial identity. This uses the same function on the same domain; it asserts nothing about a family of functions on different tagged domains.

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

A finite statistical microstate model is a pair $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ where $\Omega$ is a finite nonempty set and $\epsilon:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ assigns a finite numerical energy to each microstate. The physical energy of $x\in\Omega$ is $E(x)=\epsilon(x)\,\mathrm J$, with its zero and any retained internal offsets fixed by the declared material model. Energies are evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame specified by [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], and $U$ is the corresponding macroscopic internal-energy coordinate of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Equal energy values at distinct elements of $\Omega$ count as distinct microstates.

When two such models are declared independent, their joint microstate set is the Cartesian product $\Omega_A\times\Omega_B$, and additivity of the microscopic energy is the explicit condition $\epsilon_{AB}(x,y)=\epsilon_A(x)+\epsilon_B(y)$. Independence and this energy equation are model data; they do not follow merely from the two systems being separated. The definition itself assigns no weights, temperature, probability law, or dynamics.

Assign a positive temperature $T$ in kelvins and the exact framework constant $k_{\mathrm B}$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ from [[def-td-si-quantities]], and put $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. For a finite microstate model $(\Omega,\epsilon)$, adopt the canonical preparation
$$P_\beta(x)=\frac{e^{-\beta E(x)}}{Z(\beta)},\qquad Z(\beta)=\sum_{x\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E(x)}.$$
Here $Z$ is dimensionless, positive, and finite because $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty.

The same adopted law may be assigned to a specified countable state model with its stated enumeration and energy list, or to a measurable model $(X,\Sigma,\mu,E)$ with a dimensionless reference measure $\mu$ and measurable energy $E:X\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$, only when $0<Z(\beta)<\infty$ for the declared series or integral. In those cases $P_\beta(i)=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$ or the probability density is $p_\beta=e^{-\beta E}/Z$ relative to $\mu$. The countable and integral conventions are those of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]] and [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] at their actual current draft statements.

This is an adopted statistical-mechanical preparation rule. It is not derived from the macroscopic thermodynamic laws, a finite bath, entropy maximization, or a time-evolution equation. It does not assert that a physical sample has this preparation; that identification is an additional model assumption to be tested against a specified preparation and apparatus.

For a finite microstate model and a declared energy value $E_0$ in joules and resolution $\delta\ge0$ in joules, define the admitted window
$$\Omega_{E_0,\delta}:=\{x\in\Omega:|E(x)-E_0|\le\delta\}.$$
When this set is nonempty, adopt the uniform preparation $P(x)=|\Omega_{E_0,\delta}|^{-1}$ on it and zero outside. Its dimensionless Boltzmann entropy is $\log|\Omega_{E_0,\delta}|$, and its physical entropy convention is $k_{\mathrm B}\log|\Omega_{E_0,\delta}|$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. A zero-width window is allowed only when it contains at least one microstate.

For a continuous classical model, when the hypotheses and normalization in [[def-td-regular-hamiltonian-shell-preparation]] hold, the microcanonical preparation is the normalized shell measure $\nu_{\hat E}$ defined there. These finite-window and regular-shell rules are adopted model preparations. They do not assert Hamiltonian ergodicity, equality with long-time averages, canonical sampling, or equilibration.

Let $I$ be a finite nonempty subsystem state set, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $|E_i|\le L$ for $L\ge0$, and let the dimensionless bath entropy $s_B$ be $C^2$ on an open interval $U$ containing $[u_0-L,u_0+L]$, with $|s_B''(u)|\le M$ on that closed interval for $M\ge0$. Use one energy unit for $E_i,u_0,L$, so $\beta=s_B'(u_0)$ has inverse-energy units and $M$ has inverse-energy-squared units; $\delta=ML^2/2$ is dimensionless. Put $Z:=\sum_{j\in I}e^{-\beta E_j}$ and $q_i:=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$. Suppose the joint shell weights induce the normalized subsystem law $p_i:=e^{s_B(u_0-E_i)}/\sum_{j\in I}e^{s_B(u_0-E_j)}$. Then $|s_B(u_0-E_i)-s_B(u_0)+\beta E_i|\le\delta$ for every $i$, and $\sum_i|p_i-q_i|\le e^{2\delta}-1$.

derivations.claim: With $|E_x|\le L$, every bath argument $u_0-E_x$ lies in the stated interval. The curvature bound and $\beta=s'_B(u_0)$ therefore match the hypotheses of [L1], including the dimensionless remainder scale $\delta=ML^2/2$. The shell weights in [F3] are exactly the weights required by [L1], and the finite canonical comparison is [F2].

Applying [L1] to these matched inputs gives $|s_B(u_0-E_x)-s_B(u_0)+\beta E_x|\le\delta$ for each state and $\sum_x|P_B(x)-P_C(x)|\le e^{2\delta}-1$. The claim is conditional on the actual shell-weight rule and the draft mathematical supplier, not on bath size alone.

Let the subsystem have a finite nonempty state set $\Omega$ and internal energies $E_x$ in joules with $|E_x|\le L$. A bath has a dimensionless shell entropy $s_B(u)$, defined on an open interval containing $[u_0-L,u_0+L]$ in joules, with $s_B\in C^2$ and $|s_B''(u)|\le M$ there; the model adopts $\beta=s'_B(u_0)>0$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$ and $T=(k_{\mathrm B}\beta)^{-1}$. Assume weak additive coupling and microcanonical shell sampling induce subsystem weights $P_B(x)\propto e^{s_B(u_0-E_x)}$. Let $P_C(x)=e^{-\beta E_x}/Z$ be the corresponding canonical law. With $\delta=ML^2/2$ (dimensionless), the shell log-weight remainder obeys
$$|s_B(u_0-E_x)-s_B(u_0)+\beta E_x|\le\delta,$$
and the normalized laws satisfy
$$\sum_{x\in\Omega}|P_B(x)-P_C(x)|\le e^{2\delta}-1.$$
This is an $\ell^1$ probability-vector bound; it does not assert a universal error or a thermodynamic limit.

A bath has a dimensionless shell entropy $s_B(u)$, defined on an open interval containing $[u_0-L,u_0+L]$ in joules, with $s_B\in C^2$ and $|s_B''(u)|\le M$ there; the model adopts $\beta=s'_B(u_0)>0$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$ and $T=(k_{\mathrm B}\beta)^{-1}$. Assume weak additive coupling and microcanonical shell sampling induce subsystem weights $P_B(x)\propto e^{s_B(u_0-E_x)}$. Let $P_C(x)=e^{-\beta E_x}/Z$ be the corresponding canonical law. With $\delta=ML^2/2$ (dimensionless), the shell log-weight remainder obeys
$$|s_B(u_0-E_x)-s_B(u_0)+\beta E_x|\le\delta,$$
and the normalized laws satisfy
$$\sum_{x\in\Omega}|P_B(x)-P_C(x)|\le e^{2\delta}-1.$$
This is an $\ell^1$ probability-vector bound; it does not assert a universal error or a thermodynamic limit.

citations.quote:
A finite statistical microstate model is a pair $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ where $\Omega$ is a finite nonempty set and $\epsilon:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ assigns a finite numerical energy to each microstate. The physical energy of $x\in\Omega$ is $E(x)=\epsilon(x)\,\mathrm J$, with its zero and any retained internal offsets fixed by the declared material model. Energies are evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame specified by [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], and $U$ is the corresponding macroscopic internal-energy coordinate of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Equal energy values at distinct elements of $\Omega$ count as distinct microstates.

When two such models are declared independent, their joint microstate set is the Cartesian product $\Omega_A\times\Omega_B$, and additivity of the microscopic energy is the explicit condition $\epsilon_{AB}(x,y)=\epsilon_A(x)+\epsilon_B(y)$. Independence and this energy equation are model data; they do not follow merely from the two systems being separated. The definition itself assigns no weights, temperature, probability law, or dynamics.

Assign a positive temperature $T$ in kelvins and the exact framework constant $k_{\mathrm B}$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ from [[def-td-si-quantities]], and put $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. For a finite microstate model $(\Omega,\epsilon)$, adopt the canonical preparation
$$P_\beta(x)=\frac{e^{-\beta E(x)}}{Z(\beta)},\qquad Z(\beta)=\sum_{x\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E(x)}.$$
Here $Z$ is dimensionless, positive, and finite because $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty.

The same adopted law may be assigned to a specified countable state model with its stated enumeration and energy list, or to a measurable model $(X,\Sigma,\mu,E)$ with a dimensionless reference measure $\mu$ and measurable energy $E:X\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$, only when $0<Z(\beta)<\infty$ for the declared series or integral. In those cases $P_\beta(i)=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$ or the probability density is $p_\beta=e^{-\beta E}/Z$ relative to $\mu$. The countable and integral conventions are those of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]] and [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] at their actual current draft statements.

This is an adopted statistical-mechanical preparation rule. It is not derived from the macroscopic thermodynamic laws, a finite bath, entropy maximization, or a time-evolution equation. It does not assert that a physical sample has this preparation; that identification is an additional model assumption to be tested against a specified preparation and apparatus.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

derivations.claim: Since $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty and every $e^{-\beta E_x}>0$, the finite sum $Z=\sum_xe^{-\beta E_x}$ is strictly positive and finite. The weights $P_\beta(x)$ therefore sum to one by their definition.

Differentiating the finite sum term by term using [F3] gives $Z'=-\sum_xE_xe^{-\beta E_x}$ and $Z''=\sum_xE_x^2e^{-\beta E_x}$. Applying [F4] yields $-\partial_\beta\log Z=-(Z'/Z)=\bar E_\beta$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=Z''/Z-(Z'/Z)^2=\sum_xP_\beta(x)E_x^2-\bar E_\beta^2=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$.

For each $x$, $\log P_\beta(x)=-\beta E_x-\log Z$. Substituting this into the finite entropy sum gives $S_\beta=-k_{\mathrm B}\sum_xP_\beta(x)\log P_\beta(x)=k_{\mathrm B}(\beta\bar E_\beta+\log Z)$. Since $\beta k_{\mathrm B}=1/T$, rearrangement gives $\bar E_\beta-TS_\beta=-k_{\mathrm B}T\log Z=F_{\mathrm{stat}}$.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ be a finite microstate model with energies $E_x=\epsilon(x)\,\mathrm J$ from [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]. Let $T>0$, $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$, and $P_\beta(x)=e^{-\beta E_x}/Z(\beta)$ be the adopted preparation of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]]. With $\bar E_\beta=\sum_xP_\beta(x)E_x$, $\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)=\sum_xP_\beta(x)(E_x-\bar E_\beta)^2$, and $S_\beta=-k_{\mathrm B}\sum_xP_\beta(x)\log P_\beta(x)$, the finite partition sum is positive and
$$-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E_\beta,\qquad \partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E),\qquad S_\beta=k_{\mathrm B}(\log Z+\beta\bar E_\beta).$$
Consequently the statistical free-energy value $F_{\mathrm{stat}}:=-k_{\mathrm B}T\log Z$ satisfies $F_{\mathrm{stat}}=\bar E_\beta-TS_\beta$. The derivatives hold the finite state set and its energy list fixed. No equivalence with a macroscopic entropy or Helmholtz potential is asserted.

citations.quote:
Take $\Omega$ to be a finite nonempty microstate set as in [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]: distinct elements count as distinct microstates, and the physical energy values are finite and measured in joules in the declared rest frame. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and stage energy functions $E_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ for $k=0,\ldots,m$, with the energy offsets fixed by the declared protocol model. Fix inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$. The finite partition sum and canonical probability vector at stage $k$ are $Z_k=\sum_{i\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E_k(i)}$ and $\pi_k(i)=e^{-\beta E_k(i)}/Z_k$. Since $\Omega$ is nonempty and finite and each energy is finite, $0<Z_k<\infty$ and $\pi_k$ is a strictly positive probability vector.

A transition kernel at stage $k$ is a matrix $K_k(i,j)\ge0$ with $\sum_{j\in\Omega}K_k(i,j)=1$. In the forward stage order, the energy changes instantaneously from $E_{k-1}$ to $E_k$ while the state is still $i_{k-1}$; the subsequent bath transition samples $i_k$ using $K_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$ at fixed energy $E_k$. A path is $\omega=(i_0,\ldots,i_m)\in\Omega^{m+1}$. For an initial law $\mu_0$, its path probability is $P_F(\omega)=\mu_0(i_0)\prod_{k=1}^mK_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$.

Work on the system is positive when energy is supplied to it, and heat into the system is positive when a bath transition raises its energy. Define $W(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_{k-1})-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})]$ and $Q_{\mathrm{in}}(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_k)-E_k(i_{k-1})]$, both in joules. Define $F_k=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_k$ and $\Delta F=F_m-F_0=-\beta^{-1}\log(Z_m/Z_0)$. These are finite-model quantities; their physical interpretation is conditional on the adopted preparation and transition assumptions.

A finite rate model consists of a finite nonempty state set $S$ and rates $q_{ij}\ge0$ in seconds$^{-1}$ for $i
e j$. Set $q_{ii}=-\sum_{j
e i}q_{ij}$. A row probability vector is $p=(p_i)_{i\in S}$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$. Its time-dependent law $p(t)$ follows the continuous-time master equation $\dot p_i=\sum_{j
e i}[p_jq_{ji}-p_iq_{ij}]$. A strictly positive normalized vector $\pi$ is a detailed-balance law when $\pi_iq_{ij}=\pi_jq_{ji}$ for every distinct pair. Its undirected rate graph has an edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $\pi_iq_{ij}>0$; detailed balance makes this equivalent to $\pi_jq_{ji}>0$.

For a discrete transition kernel $K$ on a finite state set, $\pi$-detailed balance means $\pi_iK(i,j)=\pi_jK(j,i)$ for every pair. If $\pi$ is strictly positive, this identity pairs the supports of forward and reversed transitions. A rate model or a reversible kernel is a mathematical/physical model class; no observed trajectory is asserted by the definition.

For a protocol of [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], fix a bath temperature $T_b>0$ kelvin and set $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T_b)^{-1}$ in joules$^{-1}$, using the exact constant and SI conventions of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The finite-state clause of the adopted [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] then gives the stage-zero law $\pi_0(i)=e^{-\beta E_0(i)}/Z_0$; adopt that the initial microstate is drawn from this law, so $\mu_0=\pi_0$. Here $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty and $E_0(i)$ is finite, so $0<Z_0<\infty$ as required by that clause. This is a model premise about the preparation distribution. It does not follow from the finite partition-sum definition, does not assert that an arbitrary system equilibrates in finite time, and does not report a measured preparation. The countable-state and measure-integral branches of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] are not used.

For the protocol in [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], adopt, at each stage $k=1,\ldots,m$, the stationarity condition $\sum_{i\in\Omega}\pi_k(i)K_k(i,j)=\pi_k(j)$ for every $j\in\Omega$. This says that if the bath transition begins with law $\pi_k$ at fixed energy $E_k$, it ends with the same law. It is a physical modeling assumption for this protocol family, not a consequence of the transition-kernel definition and not an assertion that the kernel mixes every initial law to $\pi_k$.
For every path $\omega=(i_0,\ldots,i_m)$ of [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], the endpoint energy change is $E_m(i_m)-E_0(i_0)=W(\omega)+Q_{\mathrm{in}}(\omega)$, with the stated sign convention.

derivations.claim: Define the reverse path law by starting with $\pi_m(i_m)$ and, in reverse order, using $K_k(i_k,i_{k-1})$ at fixed energy $E_k$ before undoing that quench. By detailed balance, if $K_k(i_{k-1},i_k)>0$ then $K_k(i_k,i_{k-1})>0$, because $\pi_k$ is strictly positive. Thus positive forward paths pair with positive reverse paths.

On a paired path, divide the endpoint Gibbs weights and use detailed balance for each transition: $P_F(\omega)/P_R(\omega^R)=[\pi_0(i_0)/\pi_m(i_m)]\prod_{k=1}^m[\pi_k(i_k)/\pi_k(i_{k-1})]$. Substituting $\pi_k(i)=e^{-\beta E_k(i)}/Z_k$ and collecting terms gives $\log(P_F/P_R)=\beta[E_m(i_m)-E_0(i_0)-Q_{\mathrm{in}}]+\log(Z_m/Z_0)=\beta(W-\Delta F)$ by [F3].

The reversed quench at stage $k$ occurs at state $i_{k-1}$, so its work term is $E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})-E_k(i_{k-1})=-[E_k(i_{k-1})-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})]$; summing proves $W_R(\omega^R)=-W(\omega)$. Summing the path ratio over the finite set of paths with $W=w$ proves the stated distribution identity.

Equal energy values at distinct elements of $\Omega$ count as distinct microstates.

When two such models are declared independent, their joint microstate set is the Cartesian product $\Omega_A\times\Omega_B$, and additivity of the microscopic energy is the explicit condition $\epsilon_{AB}(x,y)=\epsilon_A(x)+\epsilon_B(y)$. Independence and this energy equation are model data; they do not follow merely from the two systems being separated. The definition itself assigns no weights, temperature, probability law, or dynamics.

Assign a positive temperature $T$ in kelvins and the exact framework constant $k_{\mathrm B}$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ from [[def-td-si-quantities]], and put $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. For a finite microstate model $(\Omega,\epsilon)$, adopt the canonical preparation
$$P_\beta(x)=\frac{e^{-\beta E(x)}}{Z(\beta)},\qquad Z(\beta)=\sum_{x\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E(x)}.$$
Here $Z$ is dimensionless, positive, and finite because $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty.

The same adopted law may be assigned to a specified countable state model with its stated enumeration and energy list, or to a measurable model $(X,\Sigma,\mu,E)$ with a dimensionless reference measure $\mu$ and measurable energy $E:X\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$, only when $0<Z(\beta)<\infty$ for the declared series or integral. In those cases $P_\beta(i)=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$ or the probability density is $p_\beta=e^{-\beta E}/Z$ relative to $\mu$. The countable and integral conventions are those of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]] and [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] at their actual current draft statements.

This is an adopted statistical-mechanical preparation rule. It is not derived from the macroscopic thermodynamic laws, a finite bath, entropy maximization, or a time-evolution equation. It does not assert that a physical sample has this preparation; that identification is an additional model assumption to be tested against a specified preparation and apparatus.

Let $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ be a finite microstate model with energies $E_x=\epsilon(x)\,\mathrm J$ from [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]. Let $T>0$, $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$, and $P_\beta(x)=e^{-\beta E_x}/Z(\beta)$ be the adopted preparation of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]]. With $\bar E_\beta=\sum_xP_\beta(x)E_x$, $\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)=\sum_xP_\beta(x)(E_x-\bar E_\beta)^2$, and $S_\beta=-k_{\mathrm B}\sum_xP_\beta(x)\log P_\beta(x)$, the finite partition sum is positive and
$$-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E_\beta,\qquad \partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E),\qquad S_\beta=k_{\mathrm B}(\log Z+\beta\bar E_\beta).$$
Consequently the statistical free-energy value $F_{\mathrm{stat}}:=-k_{\mathrm B}T\log Z$ satisfies $F_{\mathrm{stat}}=\bar E_\beta-TS_\beta$. The derivatives hold the finite state set and its energy list fixed. No equivalence with a macroscopic entropy or Helmholtz potential is asserted.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

derivations.claim: For every $t>0$, [F4] gives $\log t\le t-1$, with equality only at $t=1$: for $t>1$, integrate $1/u<1$ on $(1,t)$; for $0<t<1$, integrate $1/u>1$ on $(t,1)$ and reverse the endpoints. For every $x$ with $r_x>0$, apply this to $t=q_x/r_x$ to obtain $r_x\log(r_x/q_x)\ge r_x-q_x$. Summing over the support of $r$ gives $D:=\sum_{x:r_x>0}r_x\log(r_x/q_x)\ge1-\sum_{x:r_x>0}q_x\ge0$. Equality forces full support and $r_x=q_x$ for every state.

Using [F3] and the fixed-mean condition [A1], $D=\sum_{x:r_x>0}r_x\log r_x+\beta\bar E+\log Z$. Therefore $S(r)=k_{\mathrm B}(\beta\bar E+\log Z-D)\le k_{\mathrm B}(\beta\bar E+\log Z)=S(q)$ by the finite identity in [F3]. Equality holds only when $D=0$, which by step 1.1 is equivalent to $r=q$. This proves the unique maximum.

Take $\Omega$ to be a finite nonempty microstate set as in [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]: distinct elements count as distinct microstates, and the physical energy values are finite and measured in joules in the declared rest frame. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and stage energy functions $E_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ for $k=0,\ldots,m$, with the energy offsets fixed by the declared protocol model. Fix inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$. The finite partition sum and canonical probability vector at stage $k$ are $Z_k=\sum_{i\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E_k(i)}$ and $\pi_k(i)=e^{-\beta E_k(i)}/Z_k$. Since $\Omega$ is nonempty and finite and each energy is finite, $0<Z_k<\infty$ and $\pi_k$ is a strictly positive probability vector.

A transition kernel at stage $k$ is a matrix $K_k(i,j)\ge0$ with $\sum_{j\in\Omega}K_k(i,j)=1$. In the forward stage order, the energy changes instantaneously from $E_{k-1}$ to $E_k$ while the state is still $i_{k-1}$; the subsequent bath transition samples $i_k$ using $K_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$ at fixed energy $E_k$. A path is $\omega=(i_0,\ldots,i_m)\in\Omega^{m+1}$. For an initial law $\mu_0$, its path probability is $P_F(\omega)=\mu_0(i_0)\prod_{k=1}^mK_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$.

Work on the system is positive when energy is supplied to it, and heat into the system is positive when a bath transition raises its energy. Define $W(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_{k-1})-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})]$ and $Q_{\mathrm{in}}(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_k)-E_k(i_{k-1})]$, both in joules. Define $F_k=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_k$ and $\Delta F=F_m-F_0=-\beta^{-1}\log(Z_m/Z_0)$. These are finite-model quantities; their physical interpretation is conditional on the adopted preparation and transition assumptions.

For a protocol of [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], fix a bath temperature $T_b>0$ kelvin and set $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T_b)^{-1}$ in joules$^{-1}$, using the exact constant and SI conventions of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The finite-state clause of the adopted [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] then gives the stage-zero law $\pi_0(i)=e^{-\beta E_0(i)}/Z_0$; adopt that the initial microstate is drawn from this law, so $\mu_0=\pi_0$. Here $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty and $E_0(i)$ is finite, so $0<Z_0<\infty$ as required by that clause. This is a model premise about the preparation distribution. It does not follow from the finite partition-sum definition, does not assert that an arbitrary system equilibrates in finite time, and does not report a measured preparation. The countable-state and measure-integral branches of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] are not used.

For the protocol in [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], adopt, at each stage $k=1,\ldots,m$, the stationarity condition $\sum_{i\in\Omega}\pi_k(i)K_k(i,j)=\pi_k(j)$ for every $j\in\Omega$. This says that if the bath transition begins with law $\pi_k$ at fixed energy $E_k$, it ends with the same law. It is a physical modeling assumption for this protocol family, not a consequence of the transition-kernel definition and not an assertion that the kernel mixes every initial law to $\pi_k$.

Assign a positive temperature $T$ in kelvins and the exact framework constant $k_{\mathrm B}$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ from [[def-td-si-quantities]], and put $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. For a finite microstate model $(\Omega,\epsilon)$, adopt the canonical preparation
$$P_\beta(x)=\frac{e^{-\beta E(x)}}{Z(\beta)},\qquad Z(\beta)=\sum_{x\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E(x)}.$$
Here $Z$ is dimensionless, positive, and finite because $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty.

In those cases $P_\beta(i)=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$ or the probability density is $p_\beta=e^{-\beta E}/Z$ relative to $\mu$. The countable and integral conventions are those of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]] and [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] at their actual current draft statements.

derivations.claim: For $k\ge1$ and $j\in\Omega$, define $S_k(j)$ by the finite sum over $i_0,\ldots,i_{k-1}\in\Omega$ of $\pi_0(i_0)\prod_{\ell=1}^kK_\ell(i_{\ell-1},i_\ell)e^{-\beta W_k}$, with $i_k=j$ and $W_k=\sum_{\ell=1}^k[E_\ell(i_{\ell-1})-E_{\ell-1}(i_{\ell-1})]$; put $S_0(j)=\pi_0(j)$. Partitioning this finite sum by the state $i=i_{k-1}$ gives $S_k(j)=\sum_iS_{k-1}(i)e^{-\beta(E_k(i)-E_{k-1}(i))}K_k(i,j)$. The canonical preparation gives the base $S_0(j)=\pi_0(j)=(Z_0/Z_0)\pi_0(j)$ by [A1] and the finite branch of [L1].
For the induction step fix $k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and suppose $S_{k-1}(i)=(Z_{k-1}/Z_0)\pi_{k-1}(i)$ for every $i$.

Substitute this hypothesis in the recurrence from step 1.1. Since $\pi_{k-1}(i)=e^{-\beta E_{k-1}(i)}/Z_{k-1}$, the previous-stage Boltzmann factor cancels against the quench factor, giving $S_k(j)=(Z_k/Z_0)\sum_i\pi_k(i)K_k(i,j)=(Z_k/Z_0)\pi_k(j)$ by [A2]. This proves the induction step at each stage.

The base and induction step establish $S_k(j)=(Z_k/Z_0)\pi_k(j)$ for all stages. At $k=m$, summing over terminal states and using normalization of $\pi_m$ gives $\mathbb E_F[e^{-\beta W}]=Z_m/Z_0$. By $\Delta F=-\beta^{-1}\log(Z_m/Z_0)$, this equals $e^{-\beta\Delta F}$.

citations.quote:
**(a) Adopted readings and framework data.** Adopt the state and composition
postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]] (P1), the observable
and probability postulate
[[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] (P2), the
autonomous-dynamics postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]]
(P4) and the preparation and apparatus postulate
[[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]] (P7), together with the
Boltzmann-constant and temperature conventions of
[[def-nrqm-many-body-framework-entropy-and-free-energy]]. Declare one of the
following model readings of the same **adopted Gibbs assignment**:

(i) a fixed-$N$ model of
[[def-nrqm-many-body-framework-declared-fixed-n-model]], on its sector space,
with Gibbs generator $G:=H_N^\sigma$; or

(ii) a separately declared number-variable mode model, such as a one-mode
bosonic Fock space, a fermionic occupation space, or a declared countable
independent-mode space, with its declared assigned observables and energy
operator $H$. The model declares a self-adjoint Gibbs generator $G$ on that
space: either $G=H$, or a separately supplied self-adjoint realization of the
effective generator $G=H-\mu\mathcal N$, where $\mathcal N$ is the declared
particle-number operator and $\mu\in\mathbb R$ is an assigned chemical
potential in joules. The subtraction is an operator with its supplied domain,
not an assertion that a formal unbounded difference is self-adjoint.

In either reading assume $G$ is bounded below and give its spectral PVM
$E_G$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]],
[[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Let $T>0$ be an assigned temperature in
kelvin and let $\beta:=1/(k_BT)$ in $\mathrm J^{-1}$ with the assigned
Boltzmann constant $k_B$. The Gibbs assignment to either model, and the
chemical-potential identification in (ii), are additional physical
preparation assumptions made here; they are not derived from P1-P4 or from
the fixed-$N$ construction. In (ii) no restriction on the assigned real
$\mu$ is imposed beyond the declared generator and trace existence
conditions; the mode-specific convergence conditions are proved separately.
For reading (ii), $G$ specifies the Gibbs weights. If the assigned autonomous
dynamics is generated by $H$, stationarity of the Gibbs density requires its
separate dynamical or commutation hypotheses; this assignment does not
identify $H-\mu\mathcal N$ with the physical evolution generator.
The physical Helmholtz free-energy vocabulary of the entropy definition
continues to apply only to its stated nonzero finite-sector class and is not
extended to every effective generator by this postulate.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of
the spectral calculus.

**(b) Existence hypothesis and the Gibbs preparation.** The model assumes
that the **partition trace is strictly positive and finite**:
$$0<Z:=\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta G}<\infty,$$
where $\operatorname{Tr}B:=\sum_{f\in\mathcal B}\langle Bf,f\rangle$ for a
bounded positive $B$ and an orthonormal basis $\mathcal B$, with value allowed
to be $+\infty$. Such a basis exists under the declared AC by the maximal
orthonormal-family argument using [[thm-zorn]] and the zero-complement
criterion of [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]].
This trace is basis independent: for $C:=B^{1/2}$ of
[[thm-positive-square-root]], the defining sum is
$\sum_{f\in\mathcal B}\|Cf\|^2$, whose invariance is
[[thm-hilbert-schmidt-norm-is-basis-independent]]. When the sum is finite,
$C$ is Hilbert-Schmidt ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]), so $B=C^2$ is
trace class by [[thm-trace-class-iff-product-of-two-hilbert-schmidt-operators]],
and its ordinary trace is this same diagonal sum by
[[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]. Apply this to the bounded positive operator $e^{-\beta G}$, since the
declared Gibbs generator $G$ is bounded below. The model
adopts as the **canonical** or **Gibbs preparation** of the declared model
at temperature $T$ the density operator
$$\rho_\beta:=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta G}.$$
If the sector is zero-dimensional, its partition trace is $Z=0$, no
trace-one density exists, and no canonical density or equilibrium free
energy is assigned. On a nonzero finite-dimensional model space, $Z$ is a
positive finite sum $\sum_je^{-\beta E_j}$ over the eigenvalues of $G$; no energy
sign restriction is needed. There $\rho_\beta$ is the canonical operator of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-finite-gibbs-free-energy-minimum]], and the
strict positivity and finiteness hypothesis is automatic. In reading (i),
$Z=Z_N$ and this is precisely the finite-sector Gibbs assignment.

Outside the finite-dimensional class the existence hypothesis is a genuine
restriction. For a declared non-interacting fixed-$N$ model with a supplied
countably infinite orthonormal eigenmode basis and real mode energies
$\varepsilon_j$ bounded below, the complete construction and trace criterion
of [[lem-nrqm-many-body-fixed-n-countable-mode-partition-criterion]] give
$Z_N=h_N(q)$ for bosonic statistics or $Z_N=e_N(q)$ for fermionic statistics,
where $q_j=e^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}$ and $h_N,e_N$ are the corresponding
nonnegative occupation-series sums. For every fixed $N\ge1$, either trace is
finite exactly when $\sum_jq_j<\infty$. This is a trace on the fixed-$N$
sector and permits negative mode energies.

For the separately declared full bosonic Fock models of reading (ii),
the single-mode calculation of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-single-mode-thermal-trace]] and the product
criterion of [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-countable-mode-product-criterion]]
provide the separate mathematical full-Fock traces, with their original
positive mode-energy hypotheses: they sum over every particle number,
including the vacuum, giving $(1-e^{-\beta\varepsilon})^{-1}$ for one mode
and $\prod_j(1-e^{-\beta\varepsilon_j})^{-1}$ for countably many modes.
Their physical Gibbs reading is the additional assignment of (a)(ii), not a
consequence of a mathematical trace formula. Those full-Fock traces are not
substituted for the fixed-$N$ partition trace of reading (i).

**(c) The equilibrium assumption and thermal means.** The model **assumes**
that, for a declared sample of the species at the assigned temperature $T$
and in the absence of further preparation information, the preparation
description of the sample is $\rho_\beta$ in the sense of P1. For an assigned
sharp observable $(A,u_A)$ with spectral PVM $E_A$, define its outcome law
$\mu_{\rho_\beta}^A(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta E_A(B))$ as in
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (b).
If and only if the absolute first moment is finite,
$$\int_{\mathbb R}|a|\,d\mu_{\rho_\beta}^A(a)<\infty,$$
the model defines the **thermal mean** at temperature $T$ by
$$\langle A\rangle_\beta:=\int_{\mathbb R}a\,d\mu_{\rho_\beta}^A(a),$$
read in the assigned unit $u_A$. For bounded $A$ this equals
$\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta A)=\operatorname{tr}(A\rho_\beta)$. For
unbounded $A$, if the mean exists and the literal product $A\rho_\beta$ is
defined on the whole Hilbert space and is trace class, the mean also equals
$\operatorname{tr}(A\rho_\beta)$ and
$\operatorname{tr}(\overline{\rho_\beta A})$; these conditional product
identities are proved by the density eigenexpansion in
[[lem-nrqm-many-body-spectral-mean-and-defined-trace-product]]. First-moment
existence alone imposes no such product or operator-square-domain condition.
When the absolute first moment is infinite the model asserts no finite
thermal mean. The identification of the parameter $T$ with the thermodynamic temperature of a
sample, and of $\beta$ with its inverse temperature, is part of this
assumption; the stated conservation and equilibrium properties of
$\rho_\beta$ under the flow of P4, and the extremal property of $\rho_\beta$
among preparations, are separate conditional results of this pair.

**(d) Motivation and status.** The assumption is motivated, but not
established, by the maximum-entropy reasoning of the cited sources: among
preparations with a prescribed mean energy, the Gibbs weights maximize the
entropy functional, and the finite-dimensional comparison theorem makes
$\rho_\beta$ the minimizer of the corresponding functional built from $G$.
Its physical Helmholtz free-energy reading applies in the stated finite
fixed-sector class; an effective-generator interpretation in a different
mode model is a separate declared reading. That reasoning is
an argument inside mathematical statistics and thermodynamics; it does not
derive the physical assumption that a sample is described by $\rho_\beta$.
The postulate is an **adopted** statistical-mechanical assumption of the
model, in the sense of the content model's distinction between adopted
assumptions and derived consequences.

**(e) Scope.** The postulate asserts nothing about how a sample reaches the
Gibbs preparation; in particular it asserts no thermalization, no equilibration
time, no ergodicity, no master-equation or Markov approximation, no
thermodynamic limit, no pressure, volume or phase-transition structure, and
no measured temperature or expectation. The requirement $0<Z<\infty$ is part
of the assumption; the model does not define a canonical preparation when
$Z=0$ or the partition trace diverges. Any comparison with a laboratory sample requires the
declared preparation, isolation, detection and sampling models of P7, and
agreement of a thermal prediction with data is evidence about the combined
model and apparatus assumptions, not a proof of the framework or of this
postulate.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\omega>0$ and
$\beta>0$ be real parameters, let $F(\mathbb C)$ be the one-mode Fock space
with its complete orthonormal family $(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ and number
operator $N$ as in [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-fixed-mode-number-law]]
and [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-number-operator-domain]], and define the
operator $G_\beta\in\mathcal B(F(\mathbb C))$ by
$$G_\beta e_n:=e^{-\beta\omega n}e_n\qquad(n\in\mathbb N)$$
together with bounded linear extension. Then:

(a) $G_\beta$ is a bounded self-adjoint positive operator with $\|G_\beta\|=1$,
and $G_\beta=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb N}e^{-\beta\omega n}\,\mathrm{id}$ on the
Fock sectors ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]]);

(b) the series of weights converge,
$$Z(\beta):=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}e^{-\beta\omega n}=\frac1{1-e^{-\beta\omega}},\qquad \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}n\,e^{-\beta\omega n}=\frac{e^{-\beta\omega}}{(1-e^{-\beta\omega})^2};$$

(c) $G_\beta$ is trace class with
$\|G_\beta\|_1=\operatorname{tr}G_\beta=Z(\beta)$
([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);

(d) $\rho_\beta:=G_\beta/Z(\beta)$ is a density operator on $F(\mathbb C)$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]), and its
number expectation, defined by the absolutely convergent spectral sum
$\langle N\rangle_\beta:=\sum_{n}n\,e^{-\beta\omega n}/Z(\beta)$, equals
$$\langle N\rangle_\beta=\frac{e^{-\beta\omega}}{1-e^{-\beta\omega}}=\frac1{e^{\beta\omega}-1};$$
more generally $\sum_nn^k e^{-\beta\omega n}<\infty$ for every $k\ge1$.

The parameter $\beta$ is a positive real parameter of the model; its
identification with an inverse temperature, and the interpretation of
$\rho_\beta$ as a physical thermal state, are additional physical assumptions
not asserted here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\varepsilon>0$ and $\beta>0$ be real parameters, let $\mathfrak h$ be a
two-dimensional complex Hilbert space with orthonormal basis
$(u_0,u_1)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]),
and let $H:=T_{u_1,u_1}\varepsilon=\varepsilon\,T_{u_1,u_1}$ be the
self-adjoint operator with eigenvalues $0$ on $\mathbb Cu_0$ and
$\varepsilon$ on $\mathbb Cu_1$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]). Let
$$Z:=\sum_{j=0}^{1}e^{-\beta E_j},\qquad \rho_\beta:=\frac1Z\sum_{j=0}^{1}e^{-\beta E_j}T_{u_j,u_j},\qquad s(\rho):=-\sum_{i:\,w_i>0}w_i\log w_i$$
be the partition sum, canonical operator and entropy of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-finite-gibbs-free-energy-minimum]] clause
(a), with $E_0=0$, $E_1=\varepsilon$ and $w_i$ the eigenvalues of a density
operator $\rho$ on $\mathfrak h$ ([[def-natural-logarithm]]). Then:

(a) $Z=1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}\in(1,2)$, and
$$\rho_\beta=\frac1Z\bigl(T_{u_0,u_0}+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}T_{u_1,u_1}\bigr)$$
is a density operator on $\mathfrak h$ that is not the maximally mixed state
$\tfrac12\mathrm{id}$;

(b) the mean energy is the exact identity
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)=\frac{\varepsilon e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}{Z}=\frac{\varepsilon}{e^{\beta\varepsilon}+1},\qquad 0<\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)<\frac{\varepsilon}{2};$$

(c) the entropy and free energy satisfy
$$s(\rho_\beta)=\log Z+\frac{\beta\varepsilon}{e^{\beta\varepsilon}+1}=\log\bigl(1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}\bigr)+\frac{\beta\varepsilon\,e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}{1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}},\qquad 0\le s(\rho_\beta)<\log 2,$$
and, with $F:=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$,
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)-\beta^{-1}s(\rho_\beta)=F ;$$

(d) *scope*: clauses (a)-(c) are exact algebraic identities for the
declared two-dimensional Hilbert space and the two real parameters
$\varepsilon,\beta>0$; no temperature, thermodynamic, equilibrium or
measurement interpretation is asserted, and the parameter $\beta$ carries no
physical dimension in this lemma.

Adopt the canonical equilibrium-ensemble postulate
[[post-nrqm-many-body-canonical-equilibrium-ensemble]] for the mode models
declared below, the state and probability postulates P1, P2
([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]) in the readings of
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] and
[[pthm-nrqm-observables-preparation-moments]], and the
identical-particle and spin postulate P6
([[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]]); assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Temperatures are assigned as in
[[def-nrqm-many-body-framework-entropy-and-free-energy]], so that
$\beta=1/(k_BT)$ in $\mathrm J^{-1}$. Declare the occupation readouts as assigned sharp observables $(N,1)$ and $(N_-,1)$, with unit particle-count, which is dimensionless. The total particle-number operator $\mathcal N$ in the countable-mode reading has the same unit; every occupation mean and higher number moment below is read in the corresponding dimensionless count unit. Then:

(a) *single bosonic mode*: let $F(\mathbb C)$ be the one-mode Fock space with
number operator $N$ and orthonormal number basis $(e_n)$
([[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-fixed-mode-number-law]],
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-number-operator-domain]]), let
$\varepsilon>0$ and let the model declare the energy operator $H:=\varepsilon N$
on $F(\mathbb C)$; the model's canonical preparation at temperature $T$ is
$\rho_\beta=e^{-\beta H}/Z$ with $Z=(1-e^{-\beta\varepsilon})^{-1}$, the
number readout $N$ is an assigned sharp observable with finite thermal mean
$$\langle N\rangle_\beta=\frac1{e^{\beta\varepsilon}-1}=\frac1{e^{\varepsilon/(k_BT)}-1},$$
and all moments $\langle N^k\rangle_\beta$, $k\ge1$, are finite;

(b) *single fermionic orbital and grand-canonical shift*: on
$\mathfrak h=\mathbb C^2$ with occupation operator $N_-$ and
$\varepsilon_1,\mu\in\mathbb R$, the model's canonical (grand-canonical)
preparation $F=Z^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^1e^{-\beta(\varepsilon_1-\mu)k}T_{u_k,u_k}$
has $Z=1+e^{-\beta(\varepsilon_1-\mu)}$, $\operatorname{tr}F=1$, and occupation mean
$$\langle N_-\rangle=\frac1{e^{\beta(\varepsilon_1-\mu)}+1};$$
the same formula is the model's thermal mean when $\mu=0$ and
$\varepsilon_1>0$;

(c) *countably many independent modes*: let $(\varepsilon_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq(0,\infty)$
and $\mu\in\mathbb R$, and let the model declare the free-mode energies
$\varepsilon_j$ (one mode case of clause (a)) with the product reading of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-countable-mode-product-criterion]]; then the
bosonic product partition is finite exactly when
$\sum_je^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}<\infty$ and $\mu<\inf_j\varepsilon_j$, and
the fermionic product partition is finite exactly when
$\sum_je^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}<\infty$; in the finite cases the products
equal $\prod_j(1-e^{-\beta(\varepsilon_j-\mu)})^{-1}$ and
$\prod_j(1+e^{-\beta(\varepsilon_j-\mu)})$ respectively;

(d) *dilute remainders*: for $q=e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}$ the model's
occupation means satisfy the exact identities
$$\frac q{1-q}=q+\frac{q^2}{1-q}\quad(\text{bosonic},\ 0<q<1),\qquad \frac q{1+q}=q-\frac{q^2}{1+q}\quad(\text{fermionic},\ q>0),$$
so both differ from $q$ by at most $q^2/(1-q)$ and $q^2/(1+q)$
respectively;

(e) *scope*: clauses (a)-(d) are conditional statements about the declared
mode models together with the adopted ensemble assignment; they assert no
thermodynamic limit, no continuum of radiation modes, no Bose-Einstein
condensation, no measured occupation number, and no thermalisation of a
sample. All numerical equalities are exact identities of the declared
finite-mode (or product) models at the assigned temperature.

Let two finite microstate models from [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]] have nonempty state sets $\Omega_A,\Omega_B$, energies $E_A,E_B$ in joules, and the same $T>0$. Assume their declared composite model has state set $\Omega_A\times\Omega_B$ and energy $E_{AB}(x,y)=E_A(x)+E_B(y)$, with no interaction term. Under the canonical sampling assumption [[post-td-canonical-sampling]], the partition function factorizes as $Z_{AB}=Z_AZ_B$, the joint canonical law is $P_{AB}=P_AP_B$, the Gibbs entropy satisfies $S_{AB}=S_A+S_B$, and the statistical free-energy value satisfies $F_{AB}=F_A+F_B$.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$, $\vartheta$ for the four independent dimension symbols of length, duration, mass and electric charge. A **dimension** is an element of $\mathbb Q^{4}$, written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$ with $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb Q$; products and inverses of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, and the dimensionless dimension $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}\vartheta^{0}$ is abbreviated $1$. The conventions assign to each quantity of the framework a dimension $[X]$, subject to $[XY]=[X][Y]$, $[X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1}$ and $[dX/du]=[X][u]^{-1}$, with sums meaningful only between quantities of equal dimension, in which case the sum carries that dimension. For a rational power $q$, dimension powers mean $[X]^q=\ell^{qa}\tau^{qb}\mu^{qc}\vartheta^{qd}$ when $[X]=\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$. Rational exponents include the half-integer wave-function dimensions in clause (d); the integer-exponent dimensions form the subgroup $\mathbb Z^4$. These are consistency requirements on the conventions, not laws of nature.

For extensions using temperature, adjoin an independent dimension symbol $\Theta$: the enlarged group is $\mathbb Q^4\times\mathbb Q$, written $\ell^a\tau^b\mu^c\vartheta^d\Theta^e$, with the same componentwise rules. The preceding group embeds by $e=0$, so all previously assigned dimensions are preserved. Temperature has dimension $\Theta$, the Boltzmann constant has dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}\Theta^{-1}$, and entropy in joules per kelvin has that same dimension; a dimensionless entropy remains dimensionless. This convention does not assign a temperature or an entropy to any system.

**(b) Reference units.** The **metre** (m), **second** (s), **kilogram** (kg) and **coulomb** (C) are the reference units of length, duration, mass and charge; a quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\mathrm s^{b}\mathrm kg^{c}\mathrm C^{d}$. Coordinates of an inertial frame are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinates $x_{i}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; slice distances of the arena are read in metres. In the temperature extension the reference unit of $\Theta$ is the kelvin (K), so the general reference unit gains a factor $\mathrm K^e$.

**(c) Defining constants of the current SI.** The framework keeps $\hbar$ explicit. In the current SI the constants $h$, $c$ and $e$ are exact defining constants, with the values $h=6{,}626\,070\,15\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=2{,}99792458\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$ and $e=1{,}602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}$ C, and $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. These are real scalar constants with dimensions and units $[h]=[\hbar]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (J s), $[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ (m s$^{-1}$), and $[e]=\vartheta$ (C). The vacuum permeability $\mu_{0}$ is a positive real scalar that is experimentally determined in the current SI, with $[\mu_{0}]=\mu\ell\vartheta^{-2}$ (N A$^{-2}$ = H m$^{-1}$); $\varepsilon_{0}:=(\mu_{0}c^{2})^{-1}$ is a positive real scalar with $[\varepsilon_{0}]=\mu^{-1}\ell^{-3}\tau^{2}\vartheta^{2}$ (F m$^{-1}$). These are unit-convention statements of the SI, not measurements reported by this framework; $c$ enters the framework only through the separate radiation assumptions adopted on their own pages, not in the nonrelativistic spacetime of [[def-nrqm-framework-newtonian-spacetime]].

**(d) Dimensions and types of the framework's quantities.** The dimension map is fixed on the following quantities.

1. State quantities: a position wave function of a system with $d$ spatial dimensions and $r$ internal components is an almost-everywhere equivalence class in $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ with dimension $\ell^{-d/2}$, its norm $\|\psi\|$ is dimensionless, and an abstract normalized state and the density operators of the state postulate are dimensionless.
2. Probability: the outcome probability $\mu(B)$ of the observable postulate is a dimensionless number; a position density $|\psi|^{2}$ has dimension $\ell^{-d}$; a momentum wave function normalized against $\mathrm d^{d}p$ has dimension $(\mu\ell\tau^{-1})^{-d/2}$; an amplitude for a finite outcome is a dimensionless complex number, while an amplitude read against a detector coordinate carries the square-root of the inverse of the detector measure.
3. Frame parameters ([[def-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations]]): $[b]=\tau$, $[a_{i}]=\ell$, $[v_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $[R_{ij}]=1$.
4. Mechanical quantities: action $[\hbar]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; energy and the Hamiltonian eigenvalues $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$; momentum $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$; position components $\ell$; angular momentum and spin $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; mass $\mu$; velocity of a free spinless model $\ell\tau^{-1}$; force $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$; a real potential energy $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.
5. Probability current: in the ordinary continuous-field regime, fix an integer $d\ge1$, an open spatial region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$. A **probability current density** is a declared continuous map $j:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^d$, whose spatial components have dimension $\ell^{1-d}\tau^{-1}$ and reference unit $\mathrm m^{1-d}\mathrm s^{-1}$. At fixed time it is a spatial vector field; its signed normal component is read as probability transported per unit spatial $(d-1)$-area and time. Explicitly, for a flat face $S=\{x:x_k=a,\ a_i\le x_i\le b_i\ (i\ne k)\}\subset\Omega$, with $a_i<b_i$ and chosen normal $n=\epsilon e_k$, $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, define its **signed probability flux** at $t\in I$ as $\Phi_S(t):=\epsilon\int_{\prod_{i\ne k}[a_i,b_i]}j_k(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1},a,x_{k+1},\ldots,x_d,t)\prod_{i\ne k}dx_i$. Here $e_k$ is the $k$th coordinate unit vector and the integral uses $(d-1)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure; for $d=1$ this means $\Phi_{\{a\}}(t)=\epsilon j(a,t)$. The flux has dimension $\tau^{-1}$ and unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$; positive sign means transport in the chosen normal direction. Fluxes through curved surfaces, or currents with weaker regularity, require separately specified surface measures or traces. This fixes the quantity type and flux convention; it supplies neither a current associated to an arbitrary $L^2$ state nor a conservation or detector law. Each dynamical model supplies its current construction and balance hypotheses.
6. Electric quantities of the model parameters: charge has dimension $\vartheta$; a magnetic moment has dimension $\ell^{2}\vartheta\tau^{-1}$, equivalently $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm T^{-1}$, and a gyromagnetic parameter $\gamma$ in the relation $\boldsymbol\mu=\gamma\mathbf S$ has dimension $\mu^{-1}\vartheta$, equivalently $\mathrm s^{-1}\mathrm T^{-1}$; these quantities appear only in the model assumptions that introduce them.
7. Statistical quantities: a mean has the dimension of its outcome coordinate, a variance the square of it and a standard deviation it; a mean, variance or higher moment exists only when the corresponding moment of the outcome probability is finite, so a symbolic average is not a number unless that integrability is established. Angles and phases are dimensionless under the radian convention.
8. Quantities of later extension assumptions - radiation frequencies and energies, electric dipole moments, cross sections, temperatures and entropies - are declared with their dimensions and units by the items that introduce those assumptions, under the rules fixed here; they are not part of the present list.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any model parameter is fixed by this item: no mass, charge, spin label, potential or measured constant is asserted, and natural-unit shorthand (for example setting $\hbar=1$ or $c=1$) is read as an abbreviation for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored.

derivations.claim: For one bosonic mode, [F2] gives $Z_B=(1-q)^{-1}$ and $\langle N\rangle_B=q/(1-q)$; for $q=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$, multiplication of numerator and denominator by $e^{\beta\varepsilon}$ gives $q/(1-q)=1/(e^{\beta\varepsilon}-1)$. The unit convention in [F6] makes the exponent dimensionless.
For one fermionic occupation, [F3] gives $Z_F=1+q$ and upper-level probability $q/(1+q)$; multiplying numerator and denominator by $e^{\beta\varepsilon}$ gives $q/(1+q)=1/(e^{\beta\varepsilon}+1)$.

For a finite independent collection, apply [F5] repeatedly to factor the full partition trace into the product of its one-mode factors. Summing the product law over all other mode labels leaves each single-mode marginal unchanged, so the means in steps 1.1–1.2 apply componentwise.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Adopt the quantum Gibbs preparation of [[post-nrqm-many-body-canonical-equilibrium-ensemble]] for a finite list of independent modes at $T>0$. For a bosonic mode with excitation energy $\varepsilon>0$ joules, let $q=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$, $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$, and let $N$ be its dimensionless occupation number. Its partition trace and mean occupation are
$$Z_B=(1-q)^{-1},\qquad \langle N\rangle_B=\frac{q}{1-q}=\frac1{e^{\beta\varepsilon}-1}.$$
For a fermionic two-level occupation system with energies $0,\varepsilon$, the partition sum and excited-state occupation are
$$Z_F=1+q,\qquad \langle N\rangle_F=\frac{q}{1+q}=\frac1{e^{\beta\varepsilon}+1}.$$
For a finite independent collection, the corresponding partition traces multiply and each mode's marginal mean is the displayed one. These are exact model identities under the adopted preparation.

Take $\Omega$ to be a finite nonempty microstate set as in [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]: distinct elements count as distinct microstates, and the physical energy values are finite and measured in joules in the declared rest frame. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and stage energy functions $E_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ for $k=0,\ldots,m$, with the energy offsets fixed by the declared protocol model. Fix inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$. The finite partition sum and canonical probability vector at stage $k$ are $Z_k=\sum_{i\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E_k(i)}$ and $\pi_k(i)=e^{-\beta E_k(i)}/Z_k$. Since $\Omega$ is nonempty and finite and each energy is finite, $0<Z_k<\infty$ and $\pi_k$ is a strictly positive probability vector.

A transition kernel at stage $k$ is a matrix $K_k(i,j)\ge0$ with $\sum_{j\in\Omega}K_k(i,j)=1$. In the forward stage order, the energy changes instantaneously from $E_{k-1}$ to $E_k$ while the state is still $i_{k-1}$; the subsequent bath transition samples $i_k$ using $K_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$ at fixed energy $E_k$. A path is $\omega=(i_0,\ldots,i_m)\in\Omega^{m+1}$. For an initial law $\mu_0$, its path probability is $P_F(\omega)=\mu_0(i_0)\prod_{k=1}^mK_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$.

Work on the system is positive when energy is supplied to it, and heat into the system is positive when a bath transition raises its energy. Define $W(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_{k-1})-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})]$ and $Q_{\mathrm{in}}(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_k)-E_k(i_{k-1})]$, both in joules. Define $F_k=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_k$ and $\Delta F=F_m-F_0=-\beta^{-1}\log(Z_m/Z_0)$. These are finite-model quantities; their physical interpretation is conditional on the adopted preparation and transition assumptions.

derivations.claim: Insert the intermediate energies and telescope: $E_m(i_m)-E_0(i_0)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_k)-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})]$.
For each $k$, split the summand as $E_k(i_{k-1})-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})+E_k(i_k)-E_k(i_{k-1})$. Summing the first terms gives $W(\omega)$ and the second terms give $Q_{\mathrm{in}}(\omega)$.
