Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice and the canonical Gibbs-preparation assumption [[post-nrqm-many-body-canonical-equilibrium-ensemble]]. Restrict to its $G=H$ branch: the declared energy operator $H$ is self-adjoint, bounded below, and measured in joules; $T>0$ is in kelvins, $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ is in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$, and $K_\beta=e^{-\beta H}$ has $0<Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta<\infty$. Suppose also that on an open interval $J_\beta\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $\beta$, every compact $C\subset J_\beta$ admits a summable family $a_j\ge0$ with $(1+|E_j|^2)e^{-\gamma E_j}\le a_j$ for all energy eigenvalues $E_j$ and $\gamma\in C$. For the adopted density $\rho_\beta=K_\beta/Z_\beta$, the mean and variance of $H$ are finite and
$$-\partial_\beta\log Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta H),\qquad \partial_\beta^2\log Z_\beta=\operatorname{Var}_{\rho_\beta}(H),\qquad S_{\mathrm{vN}}(\rho_\beta)=k_{\mathrm B}\bigl(\log Z_\beta+\beta\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta H)\bigr).$$
Thus $F_{\mathrm{stat}}=-k_{\mathrm B}T\log Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta H)-T S_{\mathrm{vN}}(\rho_\beta)$. This statement does not extend the Helmholtz interpretation to an effective generator $H-\mu\mathcal N$.

Fix a constitution $c$ and a smooth physical-coordinate chart in $D_c$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], with fixed amounts $n=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ and $T,p$ as in [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. A **valid response chart** is an open neighborhood on which the relevant independent coordinates used below have a $C^1$ inverse to the physical $(U,V)$ coordinates; a $C^1$ diffeomorphism has a $C^1$ inverse on open neighborhoods by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The existence of such a chart is a hypothesis for a response derivative, not a consequence of this definition. The derivatives use the indicated natural variables and hold all other listed coordinates fixed.

The **constant-volume heat capacity** and **constant-pressure heat capacity** of the whole system are, where the derivatives exist and are finite,

$$C_V:=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_{V,n},\qquad H:=U+pV,\qquad C_p:=\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Here $H$ is the enthalpy in joules; both heat capacities are in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, not per mole. The **isothermal compressibility** and **isobaric thermal expansion coefficient** are

$$\kappa_T:=-\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_{T,n},\qquad \alpha_p:=\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Since $V>0$ and the coordinates use SI units ([[def-td-si-quantities]]), $\kappa_T$ has units $\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$ and $\alpha_p$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. This definition asserts no sign for any response, no identity among them, and no finite value at a critical or otherwise singular chart.

On a valid local energy-representation chart from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]], let $s,V,n_j,U,T,p,\mu_j$ and the potentials $H,F,G,\Omega$ be as defined in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. On every open neighborhood where the corresponding natural-coordinate maps have their stated $C^1$ inverses, the potentials are C2 and their differentials are

$$dU=T\,ds-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dH=T\,ds+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$dF=-s\,dT-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dG=-s\,dT+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$d\Omega=-s\,dT-p\,dV-\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j.$$

All differentials are local state-function differentials. They do not assert that heat or work is an exact differential on process space.

Let $U,H,F,G,\Omega$ and their natural-coordinate charts be as in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]], with the exact differentials supplied by [[pthm-td-potential-differentials]]. Assume each potential is C2 on its named open chart. Every pair of conjugate coefficients in its exact differential has equal cross derivatives. Explicitly, with all unlisted natural coordinates held fixed, for each species $i,j$:

- From $U(s,V,n)$: $T_V|_{s,n}=-p_s|_{V,n}$; $T_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,s}|_{V,n}$; $-p_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,V}|_{s,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{s,V}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{s,V}$.
- From $H(s,p,n)$: $T_p|_{s,n}=V_s|_{p,n}$; $T_{n_j}|_{s,p,n}=\mu_{j,s}|_{p,n}$; $V_{n_j}|_{s,p,n}=\mu_{j,p}|_{s,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{s,p}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{s,p}$.
- From $F(T,V,n)$: $s_V|_{T,n}=p_T|_{V,n}$; $s_{n_j}|_{T,V,n}=-\mu_{j,T}|_{V,n}$; $-p_{n_j}|_{T,V,n}=\mu_{j,V}|_{T,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{T,V}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{T,V}$.
- From $G(T,p,n)$: $-s_p|_{T,n}=V_T|_{p,n}$; $-s_{n_j}|_{T,p,n}=\mu_{j,T}|_{p,n}$; $V_{n_j}|_{T,p,n}=\mu_{j,p}|_{T,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{T,p}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{T,p}$.
- From $\Omega(T,V,\mu)$: $s_V|_{T,\mu}=p_T|_{V,\mu}$; $s_{\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,T}|_{V,\mu}$; $p_{\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,V}|_{T,\mu}$; and $n_{i,\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,\mu_i}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne i}}$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

derivations.claim: At fixed $V,n$, $U=F+Ts$ and $F_T=-s$ from [F2], so the product rule [F5] gives $C_V=U_T|_{V,n}=T s_T|_{V,n}$. At fixed $p,n$, $dH=T\,ds+V\,dp$ from [F2], hence $C_p=H_T|_{p,n}=T s_T|_{p,n}$.

Differentiating $p(T,V(T,p,n),n)=p$ in $T$ at fixed $p,n$ gives $p_T|_{V,n}+p_V|_{T,n}V_T|_{p,n}=0$. The response inverse in the hypothesis makes these derivatives valid, and [F1] gives $p_V|_{T,n}=-1/(V\kappa_T)$. Thus $p_T|_{V,n}=\alpha_p/\kappa_T$.
Along a constant-$p$, fixed-$n$ curve, [F4] gives $s_T|_{p,n}=s_T|_{V,n}+s_V|_{T,n}V_T|_{p,n}$. Subtract the two identities in step 1.1 and use [F3] to obtain $C_p-C_V=T p_T|_{V,n}V_T|_{p,n}$.

Substitute $p_T|_{V,n}=\alpha_p/\kappa_T$ and $V_T|_{p,n}=V\alpha_p$ into step 2.1 to obtain $C_p-C_V=TV\alpha_p^2/\kappa_T$. Since $\kappa_T>0$, no zero denominator is used. The units are $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ on both sides because $\mathrm{Pa\,m^3=J}$.

A finite statistical microstate model is a pair $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ where $\Omega$ is a finite nonempty set and $\epsilon:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ assigns a finite numerical energy to each microstate. The physical energy of $x\in\Omega$ is $E(x)=\epsilon(x)\,\mathrm J$, with its zero and any retained internal offsets fixed by the declared material model. Energies are evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame specified by [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], and $U$ is the corresponding macroscopic internal-energy coordinate of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Equal energy values at distinct elements of $\Omega$ count as distinct microstates.

When two such models are declared independent, their joint microstate set is the Cartesian product $\Omega_A\times\Omega_B$, and additivity of the microscopic energy is the explicit condition $\epsilon_{AB}(x,y)=\epsilon_A(x)+\epsilon_B(y)$. Independence and this energy equation are model data; they do not follow merely from the two systems being separated. The definition itself assigns no weights, temperature, probability law, or dynamics.

Assign a positive temperature $T$ in kelvins and the exact framework constant $k_{\mathrm B}$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ from [[def-td-si-quantities]], and put $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. For a finite microstate model $(\Omega,\epsilon)$, adopt the canonical preparation
$$P_\beta(x)=\frac{e^{-\beta E(x)}}{Z(\beta)},\qquad Z(\beta)=\sum_{x\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E(x)}.$$
Here $Z$ is dimensionless, positive, and finite because $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty.

The same adopted law may be assigned to a specified countable state model with its stated enumeration and energy list, or to a measurable model $(X,\Sigma,\mu,E)$ with a dimensionless reference measure $\mu$ and measurable energy $E:X\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$, only when $0<Z(\beta)<\infty$ for the declared series or integral. In those cases $P_\beta(i)=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$ or the probability density is $p_\beta=e^{-\beta E}/Z$ relative to $\mu$. The countable and integral conventions are those of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]] and [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] at their actual current draft statements.

This is an adopted statistical-mechanical preparation rule. It is not derived from the macroscopic thermodynamic laws, a finite bath, entropy maximization, or a time-evolution equation. It does not assert that a physical sample has this preparation; that identification is an additional model assumption to be tested against a specified preparation and apparatus.

Let $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ be a finite microstate model with energies $E_x=\epsilon(x)\,\mathrm J$ from [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]. Let $T>0$, $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$, and $P_\beta(x)=e^{-\beta E_x}/Z(\beta)$ be the adopted preparation of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]]. With $\bar E_\beta=\sum_xP_\beta(x)E_x$, $\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)=\sum_xP_\beta(x)(E_x-\bar E_\beta)^2$, and $S_\beta=-k_{\mathrm B}\sum_xP_\beta(x)\log P_\beta(x)$, the finite partition sum is positive and
$$-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E_\beta,\qquad \partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E),\qquad S_\beta=k_{\mathrm B}(\log Z+\beta\bar E_\beta).$$
Consequently the statistical free-energy value $F_{\mathrm{stat}}:=-k_{\mathrm B}T\log Z$ satisfies $F_{\mathrm{stat}}=\bar E_\beta-TS_\beta$. The derivatives hold the finite state set and its energy list fixed. No equivalence with a macroscopic entropy or Helmholtz potential is asserted.

derivations.claim: For every $(x,y)\in\Omega_A\times\Omega_B$, $e^{-\beta E_{AB}(x,y)}=e^{-\beta E_A(x)}e^{-\beta E_B(y)}$. Reindexing the finite sum over the Cartesian product therefore gives $Z_{AB}=(\sum_xe^{-\beta E_A(x)})(\sum_ye^{-\beta E_B(y)})=Z_AZ_B$. Dividing the product weight by $Z_AZ_B$ gives $P_{AB}(x,y)=P_A(x)P_B(y)$.

Since each probability is positive, $\log P_{AB}(x,y)=\log P_A(x)+\log P_B(y)$. Summing against $P_A(x)P_B(y)$ and using the finite normalizations yields $S_{AB}=S_A+S_B$. The mean energy is $\bar E_{AB}=\bar E_A+\bar E_B$ by the same finite factorization, so $F_{AB}=\bar E_{AB}-TS_{AB}=F_A+F_B$.

Assume their declared composite model has state set $\Omega_A\times\Omega_B$ and energy $E_{AB}(x,y)=E_A(x)+E_B(y)$, with no interaction term. citations.quote:
Let $\mathcal F$ be the explicitly declared feasible endpoint set of an isolated compound whose constituents are independent separated macroscopic systems, as defined in [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. For this route, adopt the physical criterion that any endpoint tuple the model classifies as a stable equilibrium under these fixed totals, retained partitions, and permitted exchanges satisfies

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^{\mathrm{eq}})=\max_{x\in\mathcal F}S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x),\qquad S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}S_{c_i}(x_i),$$

Here $\max$ means that $x^{\mathrm{eq}}\in\mathcal F$ and $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^{\mathrm{eq}})\ge S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x)$ for every $x\in\mathcal F$, using maximum in the sense of [[def-max-min]]. The finite sum is as in [[def-finite-sum]], and the summands are those of the separated macroscopic constituents under [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Whenever the stable-equilibrium label is used, attainment is assumed: at least one maximizing endpoint lies in $\mathcal F$. If $\mathcal F$ is empty or the entropy supremum is not attained, this item supplies no equilibrium state.

“Global” refers to every endpoint in this exact $\mathcal F$, not just nearby states, states reachable by a restricted short-time dynamics, or states on a selected branch. A local maximum that is not global, or a long-lived preparation trapped by kinetic barriers, is not declared stable equilibrium by this postulate. No uniqueness or relaxation dynamics is assumed.

Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

Fix a finite list of named subsystems $s_1,\ldots,s_m$, where $m\in\mathbb N$ and $m\ge1$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), each having its own equilibrium state domain $D_{c_i}$ as defined in [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Their separated endpoint state space is the Cartesian product ([[def-cartesian-product]])

$$\mathcal D:=D_{c_1}\times\cdots\times D_{c_m}.$$

An **isolated compound** is the system consisting of those subsystems and any named auxiliaries or work devices included inside a declared outer boundary, with no matter or energy transfer across that outer boundary during the admitted process, in the sense of [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]]. Transfers between constituents are internal to the compound. Its total energy and other extensive coordinates use the composition convention of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. The additive entropy sum applies only when the constituent split is admitted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] as a collection of independent separated macroscopic systems; an interacting compound outside that scope needs its own total-entropy model.

For specified totals and retained barriers, an **equilibrium feasible set** is the model-declared subset $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal D$ of endpoint tuples satisfying those totals and exactly the exchange permissions in the declared protocol. derivations.claim: Fix any pair $\alpha,\beta$ and an allowed energy transfer. For any fixed nonzero increment $h$ joules, bilateral local feasibility supplies the curve $U_\alpha(t)=U_\alpha^*+th$, $U_\beta(t)=U_\beta^*-th$ for all sufficiently small $t$ of either sign, with all other coordinates fixed. The total entropy along this curve has a local maximum at $t=0$ by [A1]. Its derivative exists by [F2]; the right difference quotients are nonpositive and the left difference quotients are nonnegative, so the derivative is zero. By additivity and [L1], this derivative is $h(S_{\alpha,U}-S_{\beta,U})$. Since $h\ne0$, $S_{\alpha,U}=S_{\beta,U}$.
By [F3], $S_{\alpha,U}=1/T_\alpha$ and $S_{\beta,U}=1/T_\beta$. Both temperatures are finite and positive, so equality of the reciprocals gives $T_\alpha=T_\beta$.

If volume transfer is permitted, take a nonzero increment $k$ in $\mathrm{m^3}$ and vary $V_\alpha(t)=V_\alpha^*+tk$, $V_\beta(t)=V_\beta^*-tk$ with both signs feasible. The same local-maximum quotient argument gives $k(S_{\alpha,V}-S_{\beta,V})=0$, hence $S_{\alpha,V}=S_{\beta,V}$. By [F3], $p_\alpha/T_\alpha=p_\beta/T_\beta$. When energy transfer is also permitted, step 2.1 gives equal positive temperatures, so $p_\alpha=p_\beta$. These are derivative pressures; a mechanical piston interpretation requires its separately declared coupling.

If species $j$ is transferable, vary its mole amounts by $n_{\alpha,j}(t)=n_{\alpha,j}^*+tq$ and $n_{\beta,j}(t)=n_{\beta,j}^*-tq$ for a nonzero increment $q$ in moles. Both signs are feasible. The same quotient argument gives $q(S_{\alpha,n_j}-S_{\beta,n_j})=0$, hence equal entropy partials. By [F3], $\mu_{\alpha,j}/T_\alpha=\mu_{\beta,j}/T_\beta$. If energy transfer is also permitted, step 2.1 gives equal positive temperatures and therefore equal chemical potentials.

Every pair was arbitrary, so the asserted pairwise equalities hold for all named phases and only for the channels whose bilateral feasibility was assumed. If $P=1$, there are no pairs and the conditions are vacuous. No derivative equality follows for a retained or boundary coordinate because its required two-sided feasible curve is absent.

Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},

$$T_c:=\frac{1}{S_{c,U}},\qquad p_c:=T_cS_{c,V},\qquad \mu_{c,j}:=-T_cS_{c,n_j}.$$

The entropy unit is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, the energy $U$ is in joules, $V$ is in cubic metres, and $n_j$ is in moles ([[def-td-si-quantities]]). Thus $S_{c,U}$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$, $T_c$ is finite and positive in kelvins, $S_{c,V}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$ and $p_c$ has units pascals, and $S_{c,n_j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\mu_{c,j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. If a microscopic model instead uses a dimensionless particle count $N_j=N_{\!A}n_j$, the corresponding per-particle chemical potential is $\mu_{c,j}/N_{\!A}$ joules, with the exact SI Avogadro constant from [[def-td-si-quantities]].

These are scalar state functions of the stated rest-frame equilibrium chart. The pressure in this definition is a derivative-defined conjugate; identifying it with force per area requires a separate adopted mechanical coupling. Neither an empirical thermometer calibration nor any equation of state is supplied by this definition.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer spatial dimension $d\geq 1$, a reference length $\ell_0>0$, and a bounded measurable region $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$ with dimensionless volume $V=|\Lambda|$. Its physical region is $\ell_0\Lambda$. A finite positional configuration of $N$ classical point particles in $\Lambda$ is an unordered simple set $\omega=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subset\Lambda$; simple means that no point is repeated. Particle number $N$ is a dimensionless nonnegative integer and the physical number density corresponding to $N/V$ is $N/(\ell_0^dV)$.

A pair potential is an even measurable function $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where $\varphi(x)$ is the interaction energy in joules at physical displacement $\ell_0x$ and evenness means $\varphi(x)=\varphi(-x)$. For a labelled representative of $\omega$, define the positional pair energy
$$H_N(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\varphi(x_i-x_j),\qquad H_0=H_1=0.$$
If any pair is forbidden by the potential, its energy and hence $H_N$ are $+\infty$. This model contains no kinetic energy, internal molecular coordinates, quantum exchange terms, or external field.

The interaction is stable if there is a constant $B\geq0$, measured in joules, such that $H_N(\omega)\geq-BN$ for every finite simple configuration. It has a regular integrable tail if there are $R>0$ and a nonnegative nonincreasing measurable function $\psi:[R,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, measured in joules, such that $|\varphi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R$ and
$$\int_R^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)\,dr<\infty.$$
A stable potential with this tail condition is the stable regularly tempered class used for the free-cube results on this page. Superstability and a positive divergent core are stronger, separate hypotheses and are not implied by stability.

At temperature $T>0$, write $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in joules inverse. The activity $z>0$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity $\ell_0^{-d}$. A free-wall finite-volume model contains only positions in $\Lambda$ and uses $H_N$ above. A periodic model uses the declared periodic cell and sums its periodic-image pair interactions with each unordered pair counted once. These are distinct boundary preparations. The limits on this page are positional configurational limits and do not by themselves include a momentum integral or a full phase-space energy shell.

Use the periodic boxes $\Lambda_n$ and positional energy of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]], and the exact-$N$ measure $\mu_{\Lambda_n,N}$ of [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]]. Given $N_n\in\mathbb N$, a reduced configuration-energy center $e\in\mathbb R$ joules per dimensionless reference volume, and a width $\delta_n>0$ in the same units, define
$$S_n(N_n,e,\delta_n)=\{\omega\subset\Lambda_n:|\omega|=N_n,\ |H_{N_n}^{\mathrm{per}}(\omega)/V_n-e|\leq\delta_n\}.$$
When $0<\mu_{\Lambda_n,N_n}(S_n)<\infty$, the uniform positional shell law is
$$M_n(A)=\frac{\mu_{\Lambda_n,N_n}(A\cap S_n)}{\mu_{\Lambda_n,N_n}(S_n)}.$$
A shrinking energy-density shell uses some specified sequence $\delta_n\downarrow0$. Its total energy width is $2\delta_nV_n$, which is $o(V_n)$ but need not be microscopic or bounded. Existence of a normalizing shell and the existence of a suitable shrinking sequence are separate theorem obligations. This is not a surface measure on an exact-energy hypersurface and not a phase-space shell for $K(p)+H_N^{\mathrm{per}}$.

For a specified finite region and boundary preparation, take $T>0$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, and the positional energy in [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. For each fixed $N$, specialize the measurable-model canonical preparation of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] to the dimensionless positional configuration measure $\mu_{\Lambda,N}$; adopt the law
$$P_{\Lambda,N}^{\mathrm{can}}(d\omega)=Z_{\Lambda,N}^{-1}e^{-\beta H_N(\omega)}\mu_{\Lambda,N}(d\omega),\qquad Z_{\Lambda,N}=\int e^{-\beta H_N}\,d\mu_{\Lambda,N},$$
whenever $0<Z_{\Lambda,N}<\infty$. Separately adopt the grand-canonical law at activity $z>0$ to have weights $z^{N(\omega)}e^{-\beta H_{N(\omega)}(\omega)}$ relative to the same indistinguishable positional measures; its normalizer is $\Xi_\Lambda(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{\Lambda,N}$ when finite. Here $z$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity in [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]], and $\alpha=\log z$.

For the controlled positional shell of [[def-td-controlled-fixed-n-energy-shell]], adopt the conditional measure $M_n$ only when its shell has positive finite reference measure. These are probability-law preparations used to define the model. They are not derived from Hamiltonian trajectories, and they do not assert that a laboratory apparatus reaches any of them. The inverse-temperature-zero hard-core continuation is governed separately by [[def-td-retained-hard-core-zero-beta-preparation]].

Fix the selected stable regularly tempered pair model, $T>0$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, and activity $z>0$. For the superstable branch, require an explicit decomposition $\varphi=\varphi_s+\varphi_r$ where $\varphi_s$ is stable and there is a $\delta>0$ such that $\varphi_r(x)\geq\delta\mathbf 1_{\{|x|\leq\delta\}}$. This is an additional model hypothesis, not a consequence of stability alone.

A probability law $P$ on locally finite simple configurations is stationary if it is invariant under every spatial translation. Let $P_{\Lambda_L}$ and $Q_{\Lambda_L}$ be its restriction and the unit-intensity Poisson reference of [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]] to a centered cube $\Lambda_L$. For probability measures $P_0,Q_0$, define $D(P_0\|Q_0)=\int \log(dP_0/dQ_0)\,dP_0$ if $P_0$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $Q_0$, and $D=+\infty$ otherwise. Let $C=[-1/2,1/2)^d$ and define $\rho(P)=P(N_C)$. On stationary laws for which the finite limits exist, define
$$I(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{D(P_{\Lambda_L}\|Q_{\Lambda_L})}{|\Lambda_L|},\qquad \Phi(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{P(H_{\Lambda_L}^{\mathrm{free}})}{|\Lambda_L|}.$$
For $\beta>0$, use the stationary laws with finite $I(P)$ and $\Phi(P)$ and adopt, at the selected $(\varphi,\beta,z)$, that
$$\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{P}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}=\{P^\ast\}.$$

For the $\beta=0$ branch, require a nonempty hard-core displacement set $B=\{x:\varphi(x)=+\infty\}$ and use [[def-td-retained-hard-core-zero-beta-preparation]]. Restrict to stationary laws supported on hard-admissible configurations with finite $I(P)$ and adopt, at the selected $z$, that
$$\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{P}\{I(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}=\{P^\ast\}.$$
These are two explicit parameter-specific physical model restrictions. They do not assert uniqueness for every activity or temperature, do not apply at coexistence when the minimizer set has several elements, and do not infer uniqueness from thermodynamic smoothness.

Assume AC. Fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$, use the Euclidean norm $|\cdot|_2$ from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], define $|x|_\infty=\max_j|x_j|$, and use the numerical coordinate conventions in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. A finite configuration is a finite subset $\omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with no repeated points; its number of points is $N(\omega)$. A pair potential is an even Borel function, measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra generated by open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]), $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where even means $\phi(-x)=\phi(x)$. Define
$$H_\phi(\omega)=\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset\omega}\phi(x-y),\qquad H_\phi(\varnothing)=0.$$
The sum is over unordered two-point subsets, so every term is evaluated at a nonzero separation; if any term is $+\infty$, the sum is $+\infty$.

The potential is stable if some $B\geq0$ satisfies $H_\phi(\omega)\geq-BN(\omega)$ for every finite configuration. It is superstable in the Georgii splitting convention if $\phi=\phi_s+\phi_r$, where $\phi_s$ is stable and $\phi_r\geq0$ everywhere and, for some $r_0,\delta>0$, $\phi_r(x)\geq\delta$ whenever $|x|_\infty\leq r_0$. It is lower regular if a nonnegative nonincreasing $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfies
$$\phi(x)\geq-\psi(|x|_\infty),\qquad \int_0^\infty\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty.$$
It is regular if it is lower regular and, for some $R<\infty$, $\phi(x)\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ whenever $|x|_\infty\geq R$. These are the conventions used for the interacting results on this page. A genuine divergent positive core is the separate additional condition that some nonincreasing $\chi:(0,r_1]\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_1$ and $\int_0^{r_1}\chi(r)r^{d-1}dr=+\infty$; it is not implied by superstability.

For $L>0$ put $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, $V_L=L^d$, and let $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}$ be $H_\phi$ for configurations restricted to $\Lambda_L$. For sufficiently large periodic cubes, periodize $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$ by $\omega^{\mathrm{per}}=\{x+Lk:x\in\omega,\ k\in\mathbb Z^d\}$ and set
$$H_{L,\mathrm{per}}(\omega)=\frac12\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{y\in\omega^{\mathrm{per}},\ y\ne x}\phi(y-x),$$
interpreting the value as $+\infty$ if a positive infinite term occurs. The far image sum is absolutely convergent for all sufficiently large $L$ by [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]; this is the image convention used below. With fixed numerical length and energy units, the canonical positional partition is
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}dq_1\cdots dq_N,\quad Z(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
where $\beta>0$, and the grand partition is $\Xi(L;a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$ for numerical activity $a>0$. The normalized unit-intensity Poisson version is $Z_Q(L;z,\beta)=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,\mathrm{free}}}]$; since the Poisson density contributes $e^{-V_L}$, $\Xi(L;z,\beta)=e^{V_L}Z_Q(L;z,\beta)$. A physical pressure identification is not part of this mathematical definition.

For a stationary probability law $P$ on the configuration space of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], write $\rho(P)=E_PN_{[0,1)^d}$. When the limit exists, write
$$\mathcal E(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}E_PH_{L,\mathrm{free}},\qquad I(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}D(P_{\Lambda_L}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L}).$$
The cited results below establish existence under their stated hypotheses; this definition does not assume it for every stationary law.

Assume the superstable regular model of [[thm-tdmath-periodic-fixed-n-limit]], an interior density $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, and differentiability of $\beta\mapsto F_\beta(\rho)$ at $\beta>0$. Put $e=-\partial_\beta F_\beta(\rho)$. Suppose the grand variational minimizer at a supporting activity $z>0$ is a singleton $P_*$. Let $R_{L,\omega}$ be the periodized empirical field of [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]]. There exists a specified sequence $\delta_L\downarrow0$ such that the uniform positional shell law
$$Q_{\Lambda_L}\!\left(\,\cdot\ \middle|\ N=N_L,\ \left|H_{L,\mathrm{per}}/L^d-e\right|\leq\delta_L\right)$$
is eventually defined, and its empirical field converges in probability in $\tau_L$ to $P_*$. The free and periodic exact-$N$ canonical empirical fields and the matching periodic grand-canonical empirical field converge in probability to the same limit. The energy width $2\delta_LL^d=o(L^d)$; no arbitrary prescribed width or zero-width surface measure is asserted.

Assume the superstable regular interaction of [[thm-tdmath-continuum-variational-pressure]], $\beta>0$, and an interior attainable density $\rho>0$. For integers $N_L$ with $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, let $Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta)$ be the $1/N_L!$-normalized positional partition on the periodized cube, with the image convention of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. Then
$$L^{-d}\log Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho),$$
the same rate as the free cube. Let $C^{\mathrm{per}}_{L,N_L}$ be the periodic exact-$N_L$ canonical law and $R_{L,\omega}$ its periodized empirical field from [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]]. For any finite supporting activity $z>0$ of $F_\beta$ at $\rho$, these empirical fields concentrate in every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood of the minimizer set of $I+\beta\Phi-\rho\log z$. A singleton minimizer gives convergence in probability in $\tau_L$.

Assume the superstable regular model of [[thm-tdmath-continuum-variational-pressure]], $\beta>0$, and an interior attainable density $\rho>0$. Let $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, let $C_{L,N_L}$ be the free-boundary positional canonical law with exactly $N_L$ particles, and let $R_{L,\omega}$ be its periodized empirical field from [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]]. Choose any finite supporting activity $z>0$ of $F_\beta$ at $\rho$ and set
$$\mathcal M_{z,\beta}:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
For every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$,
$$C_{L,N_L}\{\omega:R_{L,\omega}\in U\}\longrightarrow1.$$
If $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}=\{P_*\}$, then $R_{L,\omega}\to P_*$ in probability in $\tau_L$. This is local observable equivalence for a uniformly sampled bulk location; it makes no claim about the raw finite-box law at a fixed origin or about uniqueness for every interaction.

Assume AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, and HB as in [[thm-tdmath-local-tame-entropy-compactness]]. Let $L\to\infty$ and let $C_L$ be probability laws on finite configurations in $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, invariant under every translation modulo $L\mathbb Z^d$. Write $Q_L$ for unit-intensity Poisson measure and suppose
$$c_L=L^{-d}D(C_L\Vert Q_L),\qquad \sup_L c_L<\infty.$$
Let $\widetilde C_L$ be the law of the periodic continuation. Then $\widetilde C_L=E_{C_L}R_{L,\omega}$; these laws are stationary and are relatively sequentially compact in $\tau_L$ as $L\to\infty$. Their local counts are uniformly integrable. Along any convergent subsequence with limit $P$,
$$I(P)\leq\liminf_L c_L.$$
If the empirical fields $R_{L,\omega}$ converge in probability in $\tau_L$ to a fixed $P_*$, then $\widetilde C_L\to P_*$ in $\tau_L$, including expectations of every measurable local $f$ with $|f|\leq b(1+N_A)$ for bounded $A$. This concerns periodic continuation, not the zero extension of a configuration outside its fundamental cube.

derivations.claim: The Borel superstable regular assumptions match [L0], and the hypotheses in the Statement match [L1]–[L3], including exact particle number, periodic boundary, interior density, differentiability, finite supporting $\alpha$, and singleton minimizer [A2]. [L2] fixes the periodic canonical rate. The periodic canonical conclusion uses [L1] and [L2]; the free-box result [L3] is not substituted for a periodic law. The carrier [L1] explicitly concerns positional pair energy, so [F1]–[F2] identify the physical shell with its positional shell law without adding kinetic energy; the chain rule gives $e/E_0=-\partial_{\widehat\beta}F$, and $\widehat\delta_n=\delta_n/E_0$ converts its numerical energy window to joules.

By [L1], canonical energy concentration permits construction of a sequence $\widehat\delta_n\downarrow0$ such that the shell has positive measure eventually and its uniform conditional law, the exact-$N$ canonical law, and the matching grand law have empirical fields converging in probability to $P^\ast$. Each periodic preparation is translation-invariant on its torus. Their finite-volume entropy densities are bounded: the canonical normalization, supporting activity and bounded canonical mean energy give this for the canonical law; for the shell, its entropy is the negative logarithm of its Poisson event probability, bounded using its eventually high canonical probability and the energy window; the grand pressure identity gives the grand bound. Apply [L4] to transfer all three empirical-field limits to their periodically continued laws for local tame observables. Set $\delta_n=E_0\widehat\delta_n$; therefore the physical shell widths shrink in joules per reference volume and expectations converge for each stated bounded-region observable of at-most-linear count growth.

Choose a finite supporting activity parameter $\alpha$ for $F$ at $\rho$ and set $z=e^\alpha>0$; assume the corresponding stationary grand variational minimizer is the singleton $P^\ast$ as in [[post-td-grand-variational-phase-uniqueness]].

Then there exists a constructed sequence $\delta_n\downarrow0$ for which the periodic exact-$N_n$ canonical positional law, the periodic grand-canonical law at $(\alpha,\beta)$, and the uniform positional shell law of [[def-td-controlled-fixed-n-energy-shell]] on
$$N=N_n,\qquad |H_{N_n}^{\mathrm{per}}/V_n-e|\leq\delta_n$$
all converge locally to $P^\ast$. Convergence means convergence of expectations for every measurable local observable $f$ supported in a bounded region and satisfying $|f|\leq c(1+N_A)$ there. The shell sequence is constructed from canonical concentration; arbitrary preassigned shrinking widths, exact zero-width surfaces, full phase-space shells involving kinetic momentum, and a conclusion at nonunique minimizers are not asserted.

Here local observables are evaluated on the periodic continuation of the prepared torus configuration. This is the same periodic boundary preparation, with no new physical sampling assumption; a configuration is not extended by the empty configuration outside its fundamental cube.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$, a canonical chart with physical coordinates $q_i$ in metres and $p_i$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, and the corresponding dimensionless coordinates $\hat q_i=q_i/(1\,\mathrm m)$ and $\hat p_i=p_i/(1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}})$. Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ be the open domain of the numerical vector $\hat x=(\hat q,\hat p)$, let $\hat H:O	o\mathbb R$ be the numerical energy map with physical energy $H=(1\,\mathrm J)\hat H$, and require $\hat H$ to have continuous partial derivatives through order two. A specified open interval $J_E\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a regular compact-shell band when $\hat H^{-1}(K)$ is compact in $O$ for every compact $K\subset J_E$ and $
abla\hat H$ is nonzero at every point of $\hat H^{-1}(J_E)$.

For $\hat E\in J_E$, the energy shell is $\Sigma_{\hat E}:=\{x\in O:\hat H(x)=\hat E\}$. The graph-chart definition of the weighted shell integral is [[def-tdmath-regular-energy-shell]]: in a local graph chart $x_i=h(z,\hat E)$, its coarea measure is $d\mu_{\hat E}=dA_{\hat E}/|
abla\hat H|$, with graph-area factor and gradient in the dimensionless Euclidean coordinates. Set $D(\hat E):=\int_{\Sigma_{\hat E}}d\mu_{\hat E}$ and admit the preparation only when $\Sigma_{\hat E}
e\varnothing$ and $0<D(\hat E)<\infty$. Its normalized shell law is $
u_{\hat E}(A):=D(\hat E)^{-1}\mu_{\hat E}(A\cap\Sigma_{\hat E})$. The current draft theorem [[thm-tdmath-regular-energy-shell-measure]] proves the coarea identity, chart independence and positive finite shell mass under its stated $C^2$, compact-regular-band hypotheses; its statement and proof are present, while its acceptance remains unresolved. Multiplying the unnormalized shell measure by a fixed positive phase-volume normalization does not change $
u_{\hat E}$.

For a finite microstate model and a declared energy value $E_0$ in joules and resolution $\delta\ge0$ in joules, define the admitted window
$$\Omega_{E_0,\delta}:=\{x\in\Omega:|E(x)-E_0|\le\delta\}.$$
When this set is nonempty, adopt the uniform preparation $P(x)=|\Omega_{E_0,\delta}|^{-1}$ on it and zero outside. Its dimensionless Boltzmann entropy is $\log|\Omega_{E_0,\delta}|$, and its physical entropy convention is $k_{\mathrm B}\log|\Omega_{E_0,\delta}|$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. A zero-width window is allowed only when it contains at least one microstate.

For a continuous classical model, when the hypotheses and normalization in [[def-td-regular-hamiltonian-shell-preparation]] hold, the microcanonical preparation is the normalized shell measure $\nu_{\hat E}$ defined there. These finite-window and regular-shell rules are adopted model preparations. They do not assert Hamiltonian ergodicity, equality with long-time averages, canonical sampling, or equilibration.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(M,\omega)$ be a smooth $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold and $H\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, with Hamiltonian field defined by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$. Wherever its local flow $\phi_t$ is defined, it preserves the symplectic form and the volume measure $m$ determined by $\omega^n/n!$. No completeness is asserted. For a region $R$ on which a nonzero-time map $T=\phi_\tau$ and all its iterates are defined, $T$ is a measure-preserving transformation. If $m(R)<\infty$, then for every measurable $E\subseteq R$, almost every point of $E$ returns to $E$ infinitely often under forward iteration.

If $m(R)=1$ and $T$ is ergodic, then for every $f\in L^1(R,m)$ the averages $N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}f(T^jx)$ converge almost everywhere and in $L^1$ to $\int_Rf\,dm$. Without ergodicity, the limit is the invariant conditional expectation supplied by Birkhoff's theorem, not necessarily the space mean. Finally, if each stated time map $\phi_t$ is a diffeomorphism of a finite invariant region $R$, a density $p_0\ge0$ with $\int_Rp_0\,dm=1$ and $\int_R|p_0\log p_0|\,dm<\infty$ transports by $p_t=p_0\circ\phi_{-t}$ with conserved fine-grained entropy $-k_B\int_Rp_t\log p_t\,dm$, using $0\log0=0$. Volume preservation alone does not imply ergodicity or a time-average/ensemble identity.

Assume AC. Let $O\subset\mathbb R^{2n}$ be open with its canonical symplectic form, let $H\in C^2(O,\mathbb R)$, and let $J\subset\mathbb R$ be open. Suppose $\nabla H\ne0$ on $H^{-1}(J)$ and $H^{-1}(K)$ is compact in $O$ for every compact $K\subset J$. Define $\mu_E$ by [[def-tdmath-regular-energy-shell]]. Then for every nonnegative Borel $f$ compactly supported in $H^{-1}(J)$,
$$\int_Of(x)\,dx=\int_J\mu_E(f)\,dE.$$
For every $E\in J$ with nonempty shell $\Sigma_E=H^{-1}(\{E\})$, $0<\mu_E(1)<\infty$, and $\widehat\mu_E=\mu_E/\mu_E(1)$ is a probability measure. Let $\phi_t$ be a Hamiltonian flow map defined as a diffeomorphism on a full compact energy band containing $\Sigma_E$ and preserving that band. Then $\widehat\mu_E$ is invariant under $\phi_t$ for every such regular $E$. Critical levels and noncompact bands are outside this statement.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [A2], the canonical Hamiltonian data, smoothness, and full-band invertible flow match the hypotheses of [L1]–[L2]. Energy is conserved along each flow line because $\frac{d}{dt}\hat H(\phi_t(x))=d\hat H(X_{\hat H})=\hat\omega(X_{\hat H},X_{\hat H})=0$; the global-flow condition is an assumption, not a consequence of local equations.

The draft suppliers [L1] and [L2] give volume preservation and shell-measure invariance for the matched model in step 1.1. Normalization by the positive finite shell mass preserves invariance, and [F2] assigns that normalized measure as the preparation. Hence $\nu_{\hat E}(\phi_t^{-1}(A))=\nu_{\hat E}(A)$. This deduction remains conditional while both suppliers lack current Step 1 readiness.

Let a physical Hamiltonian model satisfy [[def-td-regular-hamiltonian-shell-preparation]] on a nonempty compact regular energy band, and adopt its normalized shell law by [[post-td-microcanonical-sampling]]. In addition to the definition's $C^2$ regularity, assume its numerical Hamiltonian $\hat H$ is $C^\infty$ and its Hamiltonian flow $\phi_t$ is an invertible smooth map of the whole band for every $t\in\mathbb R$. Then, conditional on the current batch-12 draft mathematical interfaces [[thm-tdmath-hamiltonian-measure-and-recurrence]] and [[thm-tdmath-regular-energy-shell-measure]], every shell probability $
u_{\hat E}$ is invariant:
$$
u_{\hat E}(\phi_t^{-1}(A))=
u_{\hat E}(A)$$
for every Borel set $A\subseteq\Sigma_{\hat E}$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$. This result asserts no ergodicity, time-average equality, or thermalization.

citations.quote:
On a valid local energy-representation chart from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]], let $s,V,n_j,U,T,p,\mu_j$ and the potentials $H,F,G,\Omega$ be as defined in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. On every open neighborhood where the corresponding natural-coordinate maps have their stated $C^1$ inverses, the potentials are C2 and their differentials are

$$dU=T\,ds-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dH=T\,ds+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$dF=-s\,dT-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dG=-s\,dT+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$d\Omega=-s\,dT-p\,dV-\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j.$$

All differentials are local state-function differentials. They do not assert that heat or work is an exact differential on process space.

Let $U,H,F,G,\Omega$ and their natural-coordinate charts be as in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]], with the exact differentials supplied by [[pthm-td-potential-differentials]]. Assume each potential is C2 on its named open chart. Every pair of conjugate coefficients in its exact differential has equal cross derivatives. Explicitly, with all unlisted natural coordinates held fixed, for each species $i,j$:

- From $U(s,V,n)$: $T_V|_{s,n}=-p_s|_{V,n}$; $T_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,s}|_{V,n}$; $-p_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,V}|_{s,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{s,V}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{s,V}$.
- From $H(s,p,n)$: $T_p|_{s,n}=V_s|_{p,n}$; $T_{n_j}|_{s,p,n}=\mu_{j,s}|_{p,n}$; $V_{n_j}|_{s,p,n}=\mu_{j,p}|_{s,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{s,p}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{s,p}$.
- From $F(T,V,n)$: $s_V|_{T,n}=p_T|_{V,n}$; $s_{n_j}|_{T,V,n}=-\mu_{j,T}|_{V,n}$; $-p_{n_j}|_{T,V,n}=\mu_{j,V}|_{T,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{T,V}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{T,V}$.
- From $G(T,p,n)$: $-s_p|_{T,n}=V_T|_{p,n}$; $-s_{n_j}|_{T,p,n}=\mu_{j,T}|_{p,n}$; $V_{n_j}|_{T,p,n}=\mu_{j,p}|_{T,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{T,p}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{T,p}$.
- From $\Omega(T,V,\mu)$: $s_V|_{T,\mu}=p_T|_{V,\mu}$; $s_{\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,T}|_{V,\mu}$; $p_{\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,V}|_{T,\mu}$; and $n_{i,\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,\mu_i}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne i}}$.

Fix a constitution $c$ and a smooth physical-coordinate chart in $D_c$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], with fixed amounts $n=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ and $T,p$ as in [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. A **valid response chart** is an open neighborhood on which the relevant independent coordinates used below have a $C^1$ inverse to the physical $(U,V)$ coordinates; a $C^1$ diffeomorphism has a $C^1$ inverse on open neighborhoods by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The existence of such a chart is a hypothesis for a response derivative, not a consequence of this definition. The derivatives use the indicated natural variables and hold all other listed coordinates fixed.

The **constant-volume heat capacity** and **constant-pressure heat capacity** of the whole system are, where the derivatives exist and are finite,

$$C_V:=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_{V,n},\qquad H:=U+pV,\qquad C_p:=\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Here $H$ is the enthalpy in joules; both heat capacities are in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, not per mole. The **isothermal compressibility** and **isobaric thermal expansion coefficient** are

$$\kappa_T:=-\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_{T,n},\qquad \alpha_p:=\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Since $V>0$ and the coordinates use SI units ([[def-td-si-quantities]]), $\kappa_T$ has units $\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$ and $\alpha_p$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. This definition asserts no sign for any response, no identity among them, and no finite value at a critical or otherwise singular chart.

Fix a material constitution $c$ with finite species list $(1,\ldots,r)$ and a local energy representation $U_c=U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]]. Here $s$ is entropy in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, $V>0$ is volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, each $n_j>0$ is in $\mathrm{mol}$, $U_c$ is in joules, and the conjugates are $T=U_{c,s}$ in kelvins, $p=-U_{c,V}$ in pascals, and $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The derivatives hold every other listed natural coordinate fixed; the physical-coordinate and rest-frame conventions are those of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and [[def-td-si-quantities]].

For an open chart, a **local Legendre transformation** means the following partial transformation of $U_c$: select one or more of its extensive coordinates $q$, take their conjugate coordinates $x=D_qU_c$, and use only a neighborhood on which $(q,z)\mapsto(x,z)$, with $z$ the untransformed coordinates, has a $C^1$ inverse. Such a neighborhood is a valid local transform chart in the sense of [[def-td-response-functions]]. No inverse or potential as a function of the proposed natural coordinates is asserted outside that chart.

On their respective valid charts define the enthalpy, Helmholtz potential, Gibbs potential, and grand potential by

$$H_c:=U_c+pV,\qquad F_c:=U_c-Ts,\qquad G_c:=U_c-Ts+pV,\qquad \Omega_c:=U_c-Ts-\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j.$$

Their natural-coordinate charts are respectively $(s,p,n)$, $(T,V,n)$, $(T,p,n)$, and $(T,V,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r)$. In the volume transform the conjugate coordinate is $-p=U_{c,V}$, which accounts for the plus sign in $H_c$ and $G_c$; in the chemical transform the conjugates are $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$, which accounts for the minus signs in $\Omega_c$. All four potentials have units of joules. A displayed differential or global convex-duality characterization is not part of this definition; critical, coexistence, and other non-C2 boundaries are excluded.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

derivations.claim: At fixed $n$, write $ds=s_T|_{p,n}\,dT+s_p|_{T,n}\,dp$ in [F1]. The enthalpy $H$ and chart are those of [F4]. Since $C_p=H_T|_{p,n}$ and $dH=T\,ds+V\,dp$, the coefficient of $dT$ gives $C_p=T s_T|_{p,n}$. Therefore $dH=C_p\,dT+(T s_p|_{T,n}+V)\,dp$.
Substitute the Maxwell relation [F2] into step 1.1 to obtain $dH=C_p\,dT+(V-T V_T|_{p,n})\,dp$.
Along a curve of constant $H$ and fixed $n$, step 2.1 gives $0=C_p\,dT+(V-T V_T|_{p,n})\,dp$. The assumed $(H,p,n)$ chart and $C_p>0$ therefore give $\mu_{JT}=(T V_T|_{p,n}-V)/C_p$.
Substitute $V_T|_{p,n}=V\alpha_p$ from [F3] to obtain $\mu_{JT}=V(T\alpha_p-1)/C_p$. Its units are $\mathrm{K\,Pa^{-1}}$ by [F5].

boundaries.reason:
On a C2 Gibbs chart $G(T,p,n)$ at fixed composition $n$, with $T>0$, $V>0$, finite $C_p>0$, and a valid local inverse between $(T,p,n)$ and $(H,p,n)$, define the **Joule-Thomson coefficient** by

$$\mu_{JT}:=\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial p}\right)_{H,n}.$$

Then

$$\mu_{JT}=\frac{T(\partial V/\partial T)_{p,n}-V}{C_p}=\frac{V(T\alpha_p-1)}{C_p},$$

where $\alpha_p=V^{-1}(\partial V/\partial T)_{p,n}$ and $C_p=(\partial H/\partial T)_{p,n}$ are the response functions of [[def-td-response-functions]]. Boundary empty: The statement concerns a specified local state chart and has no empty-chart physical instance.

On a C2 Gibbs chart $G(T,p,n)$ at fixed composition $n$, with $T>0$, $V>0$, finite $C_p>0$, and a valid local inverse between $(T,p,n)$ and $(H,p,n)$, define the **Joule-Thomson coefficient** by

$$\mu_{JT}:=\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial p}\right)_{H,n}.$$

Then

$$\mu_{JT}=\frac{T(\partial V/\partial T)_{p,n}-V}{C_p}=\frac{V(T\alpha_p-1)}{C_p},$$

where $\alpha_p=V^{-1}(\partial V/\partial T)_{p,n}$ and $C_p=(\partial H/\partial T)_{p,n}$ are the response functions of [[def-td-response-functions]]. This is a local derivative identity. It does not prove that a real throttle is isenthalpic or that a particular substance cools under expansion.

citations.quote: Fix integers $d\ge1$, $L\ge1$, a finite alphabet $\mathcal A$ of cardinality $q\ge1$, and a finite, possibly empty, list of interaction shapes $S_a\subset\mathbb Z^d$, each nonempty and contained in $[-R,R]^d$ for some integer $R\ge0$. $\|\Phi_a\|_\infty$ is finite because its domain is finite. For each shape let $\Phi_a:\mathcal A^{S_a}\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded interaction function. Set $J_0:=\sum_a\|\Phi_a\|_\infty$. On $\Lambda_L:=\{1,\ldots,L\}^d$, define the free-boundary energy $H_L(s):=\sum_a\sum_{x:x+S_a\subseteq\Lambda_L}\Phi_a((s_{x+u})_{u\in S_a})$, for configurations $s\in\mathcal A^{\Lambda_L}$. For $\beta>0$, define the finite partition sum $Z_L(\beta):=\sum_{s\in\mathcal A^{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_L(s)}$ and normalized log-partition density $p_L(\beta):=L^{-d}\log Z_L(\beta)$.

For every fixed $\beta>0$, the sequence $p_L(\beta)$ of [[def-tdmath-bounded-finite-range-lattice]] has a finite limit as $L\to\infty$. If another finite-volume energy $\widetilde H_L$ on the same configurations satisfies $\sup_s|\widetilde H_L(s)-H_L(s)|\le C_bL^{d-1}$ for a constant $C_b$ independent of $L$, define $\widetilde Z_L(\beta):=\sum_{s\in\mathcal A^{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta\widetilde H_L(s)}$ and $\widetilde p_L(\beta):=L^{-d}\log\widetilde Z_L(\beta)$. Then $\widetilde p_L$ has the same limit. The result covers finite-alphabet, bounded, translation-invariant finite-range interactions on cubic boxes; it asserts no continuum-particle or long-range limit.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

Assign a positive temperature $T$ in kelvins and the exact framework constant $k_{\mathrm B}$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ from [[def-td-si-quantities]], and put $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. For a finite microstate model $(\Omega,\epsilon)$, adopt the canonical preparation
$$P_\beta(x)=\frac{e^{-\beta E(x)}}{Z(\beta)},\qquad Z(\beta)=\sum_{x\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E(x)}.$$
Here $Z$ is dimensionless, positive, and finite because $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty.

The same adopted law may be assigned to a specified countable state model with its stated enumeration and energy list, or to a measurable model $(X,\Sigma,\mu,E)$ with a dimensionless reference measure $\mu$ and measurable energy $E:X\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$, only when $0<Z(\beta)<\infty$ for the declared series or integral. In those cases $P_\beta(i)=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$ or the probability density is $p_\beta=e^{-\beta E}/Z$ relative to $\mu$. The countable and integral conventions are those of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]] and [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] at their actual current draft statements.

This is an adopted statistical-mechanical preparation rule. It is not derived from the macroscopic thermodynamic laws, a finite bath, entropy maximization, or a time-evolution equation. It does not assert that a physical sample has this preparation; that identification is an additional model assumption to be tested against a specified preparation and apparatus.

derivations.claim: The finite lattice data in [F1] and $\beta>0$ match the model hypotheses of [F2]. Thus $p_L=L^{-d}\log Z_L$ converges to a finite $p_\infty$; the same supplier gives the identical limit for the stated boundary perturbation. By [F4], these finite partition sums give the adopted lattice canonical law.

Since $v_0$ and $T$ are fixed along the volume sequence, multiplying by the constant $k_{\mathrm B}T/v_0$ preserves convergence: $P_L=(k_{\mathrm B}T/v_0)p_L\to(k_{\mathrm B}T/v_0)p_\infty$. The factor has units of pressure by [F3]. This proves only the declared lattice pressure convention.

Suppose each site represents a fixed cell of volume $v_0>0$ in $\mathrm{m^3}$. Define the reduced log-partition density $p_L=L^{-d}\log Z_L$ and the lattice pressure convention $P_L=(k_{\mathrm B}T/v_0)p_L$ in pascals. Then $p_L$ and $P_L$ have finite limits as $L\to\infty$. A finite rate model consists of a finite nonempty state set $S$ and rates $q_{ij}\ge0$ in seconds$^{-1}$ for $i
e j$. Set $q_{ii}=-\sum_{j
e i}q_{ij}$. A row probability vector is $p=(p_i)_{i\in S}$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$. Its time-dependent law $p(t)$ follows the continuous-time master equation $\dot p_i=\sum_{j
e i}[p_jq_{ji}-p_iq_{ij}]$. A strictly positive normalized vector $\pi$ is a detailed-balance law when $\pi_iq_{ij}=\pi_jq_{ji}$ for every distinct pair. Its undirected rate graph has an edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $\pi_iq_{ij}>0$; detailed balance makes this equivalent to $\pi_jq_{ji}>0$.

For a discrete transition kernel $K$ on a finite state set, $\pi$-detailed balance means $\pi_iK(i,j)=\pi_jK(j,i)$ for every pair. If $\pi$ is strictly positive, this identity pairs the supports of forward and reversed transitions. A rate model or a reversible kernel is a mathematical/physical model class; no observed trajectory is asserted by the definition.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Put $c=1+\max_i\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}$ and $P=I+Q/c$, where $Q=(q_{ij})$. Then $P$ has nonnegative entries and row sums one. The series $p(t)=e^{-ct}\sum_{n=0}^\infty (ct)^n p(0)P^n/n!$ and its differentiated series converge uniformly on bounded time intervals; its coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one, so it is a probability vector, starts at $p(0)$, and differentiates to $\dot p=pQ$. Its $n=0$ term gives $p_i(t)\ge e^{-ct}p_i(0)>0$. For uniqueness, the difference $z$ of two solutions satisfies $z'=zQ$; with $C=\max_i\sum_j|q_{ij}|$ and $U(t)=\int_0^t\|z(s)\|_1ds$, one has $U'(t)=\|z(t)\|_1\le C U(t)$. Thus $(e^{-Ct}U(t))'\le0$ and $U(0)=0\le U(t)$ force $U=0$, hence $z=0$.

With $r_i=p_i/\pi_i$, detailed balance gives $\dot p_i=\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}(r_j-r_i)$. By [F4], differentiating the finite entropy sum gives $D'=\sum_i\dot p_i(\log r_i+1)=\sum_i\dot p_i\log r_i$, since $\sum_i\dot p_i=0$. Pairing the $i,j$ terms gives $D'=-\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}a_{ij}(r_i-r_j)(\log r_i-\log r_j)\le0$: if $r_i\ge r_j$, then $\log r_i-\log r_j=-\log(r_j/r_i)\ge0$ by [F3], and the reversed order gives the same product sign. The mean value theorem [F5] on each compact time interval makes $D$ nonincreasing.

Set $u_i=r_i-1$, so $\sum_i\pi_i u_i=0$, and $V(t)=\sum_i\pi_i u_i^2$. Since $\dot u_i=\pi_i^{-1}\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}(u_j-u_i)$, differentiating and pairing the two orientations of each edge gives $V'=2\sum_i u_i\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}(u_j-u_i)=-2\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}a_{ij}(u_i-u_j)^2$.

Let $a_*=\min_{\{i,j\}\in E}a_{ij}>0$. Fix a root state and choose one simple path from it to each state; this is only a finite family of choices, obtainable successively, and each path has length at most $N-1$. Telescoping and [F6] give $(u_i-u_r)^2\le(N-1)\sum_{\{j,k\}\in E}(u_j-u_k)^2$. The zero-mean identity gives $u_r=-\sum_i\pi_i(u_i-u_r)$; expanding $\sum_i\pi_i[(u_i-u_r)-\sum_j\pi_j(u_j-u_r)]^2\ge0$ yields $u_r^2\le\sum_i\pi_i(u_i-u_r)^2$. Since $(x+y)^2\le2x^2+2y^2$ and $\sum_i\pi_i=1$, it follows that $V\le4(N-1)\sum_E(u_i-u_j)^2\le4(N-1)a_*^{-1}\sum_Ea_{ij}(u_i-u_j)^2$.

Thus $V'\le-2\lambda V$ with $\lambda=a_*/[4(N-1)]>0$. By [F5], the derivative of $e^{2\lambda t}V(t)$ is nonpositive and that function is nonincreasing, so $V(t)\le e^{-2\lambda t}V(0)$. Since $\pi_i u_i(t)^2\le V(t)$ and $p_i-\pi_i=\pi_i u_i$, each $p_i(t)\to\pi_i$.

On a valid local energy-representation chart from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]], let $s,V,n_j,U,T,p,\mu_j$ and the potentials $H,F,G,\Omega$ be as defined in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. On every open neighborhood where the corresponding natural-coordinate maps have their stated $C^1$ inverses, the potentials are C2 and their differentials are

$$dU=T\,ds-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dH=T\,ds+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$dF=-s\,dT-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dG=-s\,dT+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$d\Omega=-s\,dT-p\,dV-\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j.$$

All differentials are local state-function differentials. They do not assert that heat or work is an exact differential on process space.

Fix a material constitution $c$ with finite species list $(1,\ldots,r)$ and a local energy representation $U_c=U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]]. Here $s$ is entropy in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, $V>0$ is volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, each $n_j>0$ is in $\mathrm{mol}$, $U_c$ is in joules, and the conjugates are $T=U_{c,s}$ in kelvins, $p=-U_{c,V}$ in pascals, and $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The derivatives hold every other listed natural coordinate fixed; the physical-coordinate and rest-frame conventions are those of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and [[def-td-si-quantities]].

For an open chart, a **local Legendre transformation** means the following partial transformation of $U_c$: select one or more of its extensive coordinates $q$, take their conjugate coordinates $x=D_qU_c$, and use only a neighborhood on which $(q,z)\mapsto(x,z)$, with $z$ the untransformed coordinates, has a $C^1$ inverse. Such a neighborhood is a valid local transform chart in the sense of [[def-td-response-functions]]. No inverse or potential as a function of the proposed natural coordinates is asserted outside that chart.

On their respective valid charts define the enthalpy, Helmholtz potential, Gibbs potential, and grand potential by

$$H_c:=U_c+pV,\qquad F_c:=U_c-Ts,\qquad G_c:=U_c-Ts+pV,\qquad \Omega_c:=U_c-Ts-\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j.$$

Their natural-coordinate charts are respectively $(s,p,n)$, $(T,V,n)$, $(T,p,n)$, and $(T,V,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r)$. In the volume transform the conjugate coordinate is $-p=U_{c,V}$, which accounts for the plus sign in $H_c$ and $G_c$; in the chemical transform the conjugates are $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$, which accounts for the minus signs in $\Omega_c$. All four potentials have units of joules. A displayed differential or global convex-duality characterization is not part of this definition; critical, coexistence, and other non-C2 boundaries are excluded.
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

derivations.claim: For $U(s,V,n)$ the coefficient of $ds$ is $T$, of $dV$ is $-p$, and of $dn_j$ is $\mu_j$ by [F1]. Apply [L1] to each unordered pair of its natural coordinates; the resulting equalities are exactly the four relations in the first bullet of the Statement.
For $H(s,p,n)$ the coefficients from [F1] are $T,V,\mu_j$. Equality of the mixed derivatives in [L1] for the pairs $(s,p)$, $(s,n_j)$, $(p,n_j)$, and $(n_i,n_j)$ gives the second bullet.
For $F(T,V,n)$ the coefficients are $-s,-p,\mu_j$. Applying [L1] to $(T,V)$, $(T,n_j)$, $(V,n_j)$, and $(n_i,n_j)$ yields the third bullet, including its minus signs.
For $G(T,p,n)$ the coefficients are $-s,V,\mu_j$. Applying [L1] to the same four types of coordinate pairs yields the fourth bullet.

For $\Omega(T,V,\mu)$ the coefficients are $-s,-p,-n_j$. Applying [L1] to $(T,V)$, $(T,\mu_j)$, $(V,\mu_j)$, and $(\mu_i,\mu_j)$ yields the fifth bullet. Each equality is confined to the same valid chart by [F2].

Assume each potential is C2 on its named open chart. Every pair of conjugate coefficients in its exact differential has equal cross derivatives. Explicitly, with all unlisted natural coordinates held fixed, for each species $i,j$:

- From $U(s,V,n)$: $T_V|_{s,n}=-p_s|_{V,n}$; $T_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,s}|_{V,n}$; $-p_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,V}|_{s,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{s,V}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{s,V}$.
- From $H(s,p,n)$: $T_p|_{s,n}=V_s|_{p,n}$; $T_{n_j}|_{s,p,n}=\mu_{j,s}|_{p,n}$; $V_{n_j}|_{s,p,n}=\mu_{j,p}|_{s,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{s,p}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{s,p}$.
- From $F(T,V,n)$: $s_V|_{T,n}=p_T|_{V,n}$; $s_{n_j}|_{T,V,n}=-\mu_{j,T}|_{V,n}$; $-p_{n_j}|_{T,V,n}=\mu_{j,V}|_{T,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{T,V}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{T,V}$.
- From $G(T,p,n)$: $-s_p|_{T,n}=V_T|_{p,n}$; $-s_{n_j}|_{T,p,n}=\mu_{j,T}|_{p,n}$; $V_{n_j}|_{T,p,n}=\mu_{j,p}|_{T,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{T,p}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{T,p}$.
- From $\Omega(T,V,\mu)$: $s_V|_{T,\mu}=p_T|_{V,\mu}$; $s_{\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,T}|_{V,\mu}$; $p_{\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,V}|_{T,\mu}$; and $n_{i,\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,\mu_i}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne i}}$.

For all $x,y\in\mathbb R$ and $0\le t\le1$,
$$\exp((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)\exp x+t\exp y.$$

Let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex. If $N\ge1$, $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in I$, and $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i=1$, then

$$f\left(\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i x_i\right)\le\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i f(x_i).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.
