For every admitted $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ with equilibrium endpoints $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$, fixed material constitution, zero change in center-of-mass kinetic energy, and zero change in separately tracked external-field potential energy in the fixed chart selected by the process model, the adopted model balance is
$$U_c(x_P^+)-U_c(x_P^-)=Q[P]+W_{\mathrm{on}}[P],$$
where $U_c$ is the dimensioned energy-coordinate map of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]].

Here the internal-energy coordinate is evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame as in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], while $Q[P]$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]$ are the protocol transfers defined by [[def-td-process-and-protocol]], in joules as in [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The sign convention is positive $Q$ into the system and positive $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ for work done on it. If $P$ is adiabatic, its defining condition is $Q[P]=0$, so the same adopted balance gives $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]=U_c(x_P^+)-U_c(x_P^-)$.

This equation is an adopted physical postulate of the stated framework. It is not deduced here from a mechanical model or from experimental observations. Records with matter exchange or nonzero changes in omitted kinetic or external-field energy require a separately specified balance and are outside this item.

For every admitted closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ of an isolated compound, assume its declared outer boundary is isolated throughout, its material constitution is fixed, its center-of-mass kinetic and separately tracked external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change, and both endpoint preparations are equilibrium macrostates. Include every named auxiliary and work device in the compound, and restrict to constituent splits for which [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] supplies the additive total entropy. The adopted macroscopic second law is

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^+)-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^-)\ge0,$$

where $S_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the sum of the constituent entropies in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. The process record and the zero-change conditions are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The process may pass through nonequilibrium configurations; this postulate compares endpoint entropies only and assigns no entropy function to those intermediate configurations.

For an admitted reversible operation in the sense of [[def-td-reversible-process]], adopt zero total entropy change. An admitted irreversible adiabatic operation may have a strictly positive entropy increase, but strict increase is not required for every irreversible operation. The postulate does not state monotonicity for an open compound, an externally driven process, a subsystem that exchanges energy with an omitted environment, or every microscopic trajectory.

Let $\mathcal F$ be the explicitly declared feasible endpoint set of an isolated compound whose constituents are independent separated macroscopic systems, as defined in [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. For this route, adopt the physical criterion that any endpoint tuple the model classifies as a stable equilibrium under these fixed totals, retained partitions, and permitted exchanges satisfies

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^{\mathrm{eq}})=\max_{x\in\mathcal F}S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x),\qquad S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}S_{c_i}(x_i),$$

Here $\max$ means that $x^{\mathrm{eq}}\in\mathcal F$ and $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^{\mathrm{eq}})\ge S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x)$ for every $x\in\mathcal F$, using maximum in the sense of [[def-max-min]]. The finite sum is as in [[def-finite-sum]], and the summands are those of the separated macroscopic constituents under [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Whenever the stable-equilibrium label is used, attainment is assumed: at least one maximizing endpoint lies in $\mathcal F$. If $\mathcal F$ is empty or the entropy supremum is not attained, this item supplies no equilibrium state.

“Global” refers to every endpoint in this exact $\mathcal F$, not just nearby states, states reachable by a restricted short-time dynamics, or states on a selected branch. A local maximum that is not global, or a long-lived preparation trapped by kinetic barriers, is not declared stable equilibrium by this postulate. No uniqueness or relaxation dynamics is assumed.

Fix a material constitution $c$ with finite species list $(1,\ldots,r)$ and a local energy representation $U_c=U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]]. Here $s$ is entropy in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, $V>0$ is volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, each $n_j>0$ is in $\mathrm{mol}$, $U_c$ is in joules, and the conjugates are $T=U_{c,s}$ in kelvins, $p=-U_{c,V}$ in pascals, and $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The derivatives hold every other listed natural coordinate fixed; the physical-coordinate and rest-frame conventions are those of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and [[def-td-si-quantities]].

For an open chart, a **local Legendre transformation** means the following partial transformation of $U_c$: select one or more of its extensive coordinates $q$, take their conjugate coordinates $x=D_qU_c$, and use only a neighborhood on which $(q,z)\mapsto(x,z)$, with $z$ the untransformed coordinates, has a $C^1$ inverse. Such a neighborhood is a valid local transform chart in the sense of [[def-td-response-functions]]. No inverse or potential as a function of the proposed natural coordinates is asserted outside that chart.

On their respective valid charts define the enthalpy, Helmholtz potential, Gibbs potential, and grand potential by

$$H_c:=U_c+pV,\qquad F_c:=U_c-Ts,\qquad G_c:=U_c-Ts+pV,\qquad \Omega_c:=U_c-Ts-\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j.$$

Their natural-coordinate charts are respectively $(s,p,n)$, $(T,V,n)$, $(T,p,n)$, and $(T,V,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r)$. In the volume transform the conjugate coordinate is $-p=U_{c,V}$, which accounts for the plus sign in $H_c$ and $G_c$; in the chemical transform the conjugates are $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$, which accounts for the minus signs in $\Omega_c$. All four potentials have units of joules. A displayed differential or global convex-duality characterization is not part of this definition; critical, coexistence, and other non-C2 boundaries are excluded.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

derivations.claim: In the fixed-volume case, the first-law balance [F1] has $W_{\mathrm{on}}=0$ by [A2], so $\Delta U=Q$. The bath relation [A1] gives $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}=\Delta S-Q/T_0$. By [F2], $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}\ge0$, and therefore $\Delta F_{T_0}=Q-T_0\Delta S=-T_0\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}\le0$.

In the fixed-pressure case, [A2] and [F1] give $\Delta U=Q-p_0\Delta V$, while [A1] gives $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}=\Delta S-Q/T_0$. Hence $\Delta G_{T_0,p_0}=\Delta U+p_0\Delta V-T_0\Delta S=Q-T_0\Delta S=-T_0\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}\le0$.

For fixed volume, [A1] and [A3] express total entropy on the feasible set as $S_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mathrm{constant}-F_{T_0}/T_0$. Since $T_0>0$, maximizing total entropy is equivalent to minimizing $F_{T_0}$; on the natural-variable chart the function is the Helmholtz potential by [F4].

For fixed pressure, [A1]–[A3] express total entropy as $S_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mathrm{constant}-G_{T_0,p_0}/T_0$. Again $T_0>0$, so every attained global entropy maximizer on that feasible set is a global minimizer of $G_{T_0,p_0}$; on the natural-variable chart it is the Gibbs potential by [F4]. Neither equivalence implies uniqueness or attainment beyond [F3].

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Fix a closed macroscopic system with composition fixed and two admitted equilibrium endpoints. In the fixed-volume model, couple it only to an ideal thermal reservoir at constant $T_0>0$. In the fixed-pressure model, also couple it to an ideal pressure store at constant $p_0>0$. Define the constrained potentials

$$F_{T_0}(x):=U(x)-T_0S(x),\qquad G_{T_0,p_0}(x):=U(x)+p_0V(x)-T_0S(x).$$

Assume the ideal-reservoir bookkeeping specified in [A1]–[A3] of Facts & Assumptions and the adopted isolated-compound second law [[post-td-macroscopic-second-law]]. Then along every admitted spontaneous endpoint change at fixed volume, $F_{T_0}$ does not increase; at fixed pressure, $G_{T_0,p_0}$ does not increase. If an endpoint is an attained global entropy maximum on the same feasible set, the corresponding constrained potential attains a global minimum there. If the system endpoint is on its $T=T_0$ or $(T,p)=(T_0,p_0)$ natural-variable chart, these constrained functions agree with the Helmholtz or Gibbs potentials of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]].

The statement is conditional on the ideal bath/load model and is not a claim that every physical process has such a reservoir or reaches the minimum.

Fix an integer spatial dimension $d\geq 1$, a reference length $\ell_0>0$, and a bounded measurable region $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$ with dimensionless volume $V=|\Lambda|$. Its physical region is $\ell_0\Lambda$. A finite positional configuration of $N$ classical point particles in $\Lambda$ is an unordered simple set $\omega=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subset\Lambda$; simple means that no point is repeated. Particle number $N$ is a dimensionless nonnegative integer and the physical number density corresponding to $N/V$ is $N/(\ell_0^dV)$.

A pair potential is an even measurable function $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where $\varphi(x)$ is the interaction energy in joules at physical displacement $\ell_0x$ and evenness means $\varphi(x)=\varphi(-x)$. For a labelled representative of $\omega$, define the positional pair energy
$$H_N(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\varphi(x_i-x_j),\qquad H_0=H_1=0.$$
If any pair is forbidden by the potential, its energy and hence $H_N$ are $+\infty$. This model contains no kinetic energy, internal molecular coordinates, quantum exchange terms, or external field.

The interaction is stable if there is a constant $B\geq0$, measured in joules, such that $H_N(\omega)\geq-BN$ for every finite simple configuration. It has a regular integrable tail if there are $R>0$ and a nonnegative nonincreasing measurable function $\psi:[R,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, measured in joules, such that $|\varphi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R$ and
$$\int_R^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)\,dr<\infty.$$
A stable potential with this tail condition is the stable regularly tempered class used for the free-cube results on this page. Superstability and a positive divergent core are stronger, separate hypotheses and are not implied by stability.

At temperature $T>0$, write $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in joules inverse. The activity $z>0$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity $\ell_0^{-d}$. A free-wall finite-volume model contains only positions in $\Lambda$ and uses $H_N$ above. A periodic model uses the declared periodic cell and sums its periodic-image pair interactions with each unordered pair counted once. These are distinct boundary preparations. The limits on this page are positional configurational limits and do not by themselves include a momentum integral or a full phase-space energy shell.

For a specified finite region and boundary preparation, take $T>0$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, and the positional energy in [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. For each fixed $N$, specialize the measurable-model canonical preparation of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] to the dimensionless positional configuration measure $\mu_{\Lambda,N}$; adopt the law
$$P_{\Lambda,N}^{\mathrm{can}}(d\omega)=Z_{\Lambda,N}^{-1}e^{-\beta H_N(\omega)}\mu_{\Lambda,N}(d\omega),\qquad Z_{\Lambda,N}=\int e^{-\beta H_N}\,d\mu_{\Lambda,N},$$
whenever $0<Z_{\Lambda,N}<\infty$. Separately adopt the grand-canonical law at activity $z>0$ to have weights $z^{N(\omega)}e^{-\beta H_{N(\omega)}(\omega)}$ relative to the same indistinguishable positional measures; its normalizer is $\Xi_\Lambda(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{\Lambda,N}$ when finite. Here $z$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity in [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]], and $\alpha=\log z$.

For the controlled positional shell of [[def-td-controlled-fixed-n-energy-shell]], adopt the conditional measure $M_n$ only when its shell has positive finite reference measure. These are probability-law preparations used to define the model. They are not derived from Hamiltonian trajectories, and they do not assert that a laboratory apparatus reaches any of them. The inverse-temperature-zero hard-core continuation is governed separately by [[def-td-retained-hard-core-zero-beta-preparation]].

Let $F_\beta$ be the finite concave canonical rate on the interior attainable-density interval from [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]]. Extend it by $F_\beta(0)=0$, by its interior upper-semicontinuous limit at any finite upper endpoint of its effective domain, and by $-\infty$ outside the closed effective domain; retain the value $-\infty$ if the endpoint limit is $-\infty$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, define
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(e^\alpha,\beta),$$
whose existence is [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. Then
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\bigl(F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho\bigr),\qquad F_\beta(\rho)=\inf_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\bigl(P(\alpha,\beta)-\alpha\rho\bigr)$$
for every $\rho$ in the closed effective domain of $F_\beta$. These are thermodynamic limits of positional partition functions. They do not assert local-observable equivalence, a finite-volume endpoint realization, or a thin energy-shell limit.

derivations.claim: By [A1], the physical positional partition sum is $\Xi_L(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{\Lambda_L,N}$. Set $\alpha=\log z$; then $z^N=e^{\alpha N}$. Translate the centered cube by $L/2$ in each coordinate to $[0,L)^d$; this preserves Lebesgue measure and every pair displacement, so the positional partition is exactly the free-cube sum of [L1]. The dimensionless energy conversion in [F1] matches its numerical $\widehat\beta$.

The conditional conclusion of [L1] gives a finite limit $P(\log z,\widehat\beta)$ for $|\Lambda_L|^{-1}\log\Xi_L$. Multiplying by $k_BT/\ell_0^d$, which is independent of $L$, converts the dimensionless reference-volume rate to pressure per physical volume.

Let $d\geq2$, $\varphi$ be stable with the regular integrable tail of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]], and assume its dimensionless representative $\widehat\varphi=\varphi/E_0$ is Borel measurable, as required by the current mathematical supplier. Take $E_0=1\,\mathrm J$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, and $\widehat\beta=E_0\beta>0$. For cubes $\Lambda_L=[-L/2,L/2)^d$, let $\Xi_L(z,\beta)$ be the free-wall grand partition function specified by [[post-td-equilibrium-ensemble-sampling]]. Then the positional grand pressure
$$p_L(z,T)=\frac{k_BT}{\ell_0^d|\Lambda_L|}\log\Xi_L(z,\beta)$$
has a finite limit as $L\to\infty$. In the dimensionless reference-volume convention of [[thm-tdmath-canonical-grand-duality]], let $P(\alpha,\widehat\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}|\Lambda_L|^{-1}\log\Xi_L(e^\alpha,\widehat\beta)$, where the supplier uses numerical energies in units of $E_0$. Then $p=(k_BT/\ell_0^d)P(\log z,\widehat\beta)$. This is a conditional model deduction, not a measurement or an assertion that every real gas realizes the preparation.

citations.quote:
For every admitted $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ with equilibrium endpoints $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$, fixed material constitution, zero change in center-of-mass kinetic energy, and zero change in separately tracked external-field potential energy in the fixed chart selected by the process model, the adopted model balance is
$$U_c(x_P^+)-U_c(x_P^-)=Q[P]+W_{\mathrm{on}}[P],$$
where $U_c$ is the dimensioned energy-coordinate map of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]].

Here the internal-energy coordinate is evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame as in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], while $Q[P]$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]$ are the protocol transfers defined by [[def-td-process-and-protocol]], in joules as in [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The sign convention is positive $Q$ into the system and positive $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ for work done on it. If $P$ is adiabatic, its defining condition is $Q[P]=0$, so the same adopted balance gives $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]=U_c(x_P^+)-U_c(x_P^-)$.

This equation is an adopted physical postulate of the stated framework. It is not deduced here from a mechanical model or from experimental observations. Records with matter exchange or nonzero changes in omitted kinetic or external-field energy require a separately specified balance and are outside this item.

For every admitted closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ of an isolated compound, assume its declared outer boundary is isolated throughout, its material constitution is fixed, its center-of-mass kinetic and separately tracked external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change, and both endpoint preparations are equilibrium macrostates. Include every named auxiliary and work device in the compound, and restrict to constituent splits for which [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] supplies the additive total entropy. The adopted macroscopic second law is

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^+)-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^-)\ge0,$$

where $S_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the sum of the constituent entropies in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. The process record and the zero-change conditions are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The process may pass through nonequilibrium configurations; this postulate compares endpoint entropies only and assigns no entropy function to those intermediate configurations.

For an admitted reversible operation in the sense of [[def-td-reversible-process]], adopt zero total entropy change. An admitted irreversible adiabatic operation may have a strictly positive entropy increase, but strict increase is not required for every irreversible operation. The postulate does not state monotonicity for an open compound, an externally driven process, a subsystem that exchanges energy with an omitted environment, or every microscopic trajectory.

For a system $s$ of constitution $c$, the process model fixes one Galilean inertial chart $g_s$ for kinetic-energy bookkeeping and transfer records and holds that chart fixed throughout each process. A process record is a tuple
$$P=(I_P,x_P^-,x_P^+,z_P,\kappa_P,r_P).$$
For each finite closed time interval $I_P=[t_0,t_1]\subseteq\mathbb R$ with $t_0<t_1$ as in [[def-interval]], measured in seconds, its component fields have these types: $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$ are equilibrium endpoint coordinates from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]; $Z_s$ is the model-declared configuration space of the system, its auxiliaries and devices; $Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}\subseteq Z_s$ is the model-declared set of equilibrium configurations and $\xi_s:Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}\to D_c$ assigns their state coordinates; $z_P:I_P\to Z_s$ is a function ([[def-function-space]]); $\mathcal K_s$ is the model-declared set of control/contact records and $\kappa_P\in\mathcal K_s$; and $\mathcal R_s$ is the model-declared set of signed transfer records and $r_P\in\mathcal R_s$. These fields form a finite Cartesian product ([[def-cartesian-product]]). The admitted records $\mathcal P_s$ are the model-specified subset of tuples with these types that additionally satisfy $z_P(t_0),z_P(t_1)\in Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}$, $\xi_s(z_P(t_0))=x_P^-$, and $\xi_s(z_P(t_1))=x_P^+$. No continuity or differentiability is imposed on $z_P$, and its values at interior times need not represent equilibrium states.

For an endpoint bookkeeping quantity $F$, write $\Delta F=F_P^+-F_P^-$. A closed record in the sense of [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]] has no matter crossing the chosen outer boundary. The core closed-record class $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\subseteq\mathcal P_s$ ([[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]) contains only records for which the system has a supplied total mass $M>0$ and defined center-of-mass velocities at both endpoints in the fixed chart $g_s$, so the kinetic energies $K_{\mathrm{cm}}^\pm=\tfrac12M\|\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}^\pm\|_2^2$ are defined as in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. It further requires $\Delta K_{\mathrm{cm}}=0$ and $\Delta U_{\mathrm{ext}}=0$, where $U_{\mathrm{ext}}$ denotes any model-specified external-field potential energy tracked separately from the internal-energy coordinate in $g_s$. Other process classes require an expanded energy bookkeeping rule.

For each $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$, the protocol supplies maps $Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}:\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\to\mathbb R$ whose values are interpreted in joules as in [[def-td-si-quantities]] and whose energy bookkeeping uses $g_s$. $Q[P]>0$ means energy enters the system through the declared thermal-transfer channel; $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]>0$ means mechanical work is done on the system. These are functionals of the process record, not state functions of $x_P^-$ and $x_P^+$. Heat is the protocol-assigned thermal mode of energy transfer, not a quantity stored in the equilibrium state. A record is adiabatic exactly when $Q[P]=0$. A closed record may still exchange energy; it is not thereby isolated.

A preparation is a model-specified rule selecting the particular initial equilibrium state $x_P^-$. A statistical extension may instead specify a normalized probability measure on a declared measurable space, as in [[def-probability-measure]]; such a statistical preparation is outside this deterministic process class. A preparation does not assert later equilibration. An admitted record may pass through nonequilibrium configurations even though both endpoints lie in $D_c$.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and the work-transfer model [A2], $\Delta U=Q-p_0\Delta V-W_{\mathrm{out}}$. By [A1] and [A3], $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}=\Delta S-Q/T_0$; [F2] gives $Q\le T_0\Delta S$. The signs of $Q$ and work transfers are those in [F3].

Rearranging the energy balance in step 1.1 gives $W_{\mathrm{out}}=Q-\Delta U-p_0\Delta V\le T_0\Delta S-\Delta U-p_0\Delta V=-\Delta G_{T_0,p_0}$. By [F4], all terms in this inequality have units of joules. This is the stated endpoint bound.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
For a fixed-composition closed system coupled to an ideal thermal reservoir at $T_0>0$ and ideal pressure store at $p_0>0$, let $Q$ be heat into the system and let $W_{\mathrm{out}}$ be net energy delivered by the system to an ideal work store whose entropy is constant. Assume the isolated-composite bookkeeping of [A1]–[A3] in Facts & Assumptions. Then for any admitted process between equilibrium endpoints $x_i,x_f$,

$$W_{\mathrm{out}}\le G_{T_0,p_0}(x_i)-G_{T_0,p_0}(x_f),\qquad G_{T_0,p_0}(x):=U(x)+p_0V(x)-T_0S(x).$$

If the endpoint states lie on the $(T,p)=(T_0,p_0)$ natural-variable chart, this is the decrease in the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Equality requires zero total entropy production; the theorem does not assert that a protocol realizing equality exists.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
The finite canonical, maximum-entropy, independent-factorization and finite-bath claims concern the exact finite state spaces and shell-weight assumptions stated in their items. Countable and measurable derivative identities require their local summable or integrable moment envelopes; a lower energy bound alone does not normalize the partition function. The lattice bulk-pressure and concentration claims apply only to the bounded finite-range lattice model and, for concentration, a differentiability point of the limiting log-partition density. The page-level continuum-pressure prerequisite is a distinct interaction model; no stable-tempered continuum limit is inferred from the lattice theorem.

The classical shell result applies only to a nonempty compact regular level with the coarea normalization and a globally defined invertible flow on the stated band. It does not imply ergodicity or equality of long-time averages with the shell law. The quantum trace identities require a semibounded self-adjoint generator, a positive finite Gibbs trace and the stated moment envelope; discrete dephasing is a trace-norm Cesaro limit with degenerate eigenspaces retained, not pointwise relaxation or a Gibbs limit.

Boltzmann microstate entropy, finite Gibbs entropy, von Neumann entropy and the macroscopic entropy function are distinct objects until a model supplies an explicit identification. The statistical value $-k_{\mathrm B}T\log Z$ is not silently identified with a macroscopic Helmholtz or grand potential. Canonical and microcanonical sampling are adopted preparation assumptions. None of the finite probability identities, continuum or lattice pressure limits, shell-invariance results or quantum trace calculations reports an experiment or establishes that nature follows the model.

Fix a nonempty set $X$ and the compounds of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. A **comparison relation** $\preceq$ is defined only for pairs $(A,B)$ with $m(A)=m(B)$. Write $A\sim B$ when both $A\preceq B$ and $B\preceq A$; this is equivalence, not equality of coefficient functions. The following are explicit hypotheses on $\preceq$:

1. **Preorder:** $A\preceq A$, and $A\preceq B\preceq C$ implies $A\preceq C$.
2. **Composition consistency:** $A\preceq B$ implies $A+C\preceq B+C$ for every compound $C$.
3. **Positive scaling:** $A\preceq B$ implies $tA\preceq tB$ for every real $t>0$.
4. **Splitting and recombination:** for $x\in X$, $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, the one-state compound $te_x$ is equivalent to $se_x+(t-s)e_x$.
5. **Stability:** for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive compounds $Z_0,Z_1$ with $m(Z_0)=m(Z_1)$, and a sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to $0$, if $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\preceq B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for every $n$, then $A\preceq B$.
6. **Comparison hypothesis (CH):** for every equal-mass pair $A,B$, either $A\preceq B$ or $B\preceq A$ (or both).

These are mathematical assumptions, not conclusions about a physical system. No antisymmetry, continuity, convexity, or strict comparison is included. Strict comparison means $A\preceq B$ and not $B\preceq A$.

Let $u,v:X\to\mathbb R$ be finite-support real coefficient maps with equal total coefficient $\sum_xu(x)=\sum_xv(x)$. These signed maps are formal comparison notation, not compounds. Put $d:=v-u$ and define $d^+(x):=\max\{d(x),0\}$ and $d^-(x):=\max\{-d(x),0\}$. Then $d^+,d^-$ are nonnegative finite-support compounds of equal mass, as verified in [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]. Define

$$u\preceq_s v\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d^-\preceq d^+,$$

using the compound comparison relation of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]. Thus positive coefficients of $v-u$ remain on the right and negative coefficients move to the left. Signed notation is never a claim that a negative amount of a physical system exists.

Under [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]], for equal-mass compounds $A,B,C$, $A+C\preceq B+C$ if and only if $A\preceq B$. The signed relation of [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] is well-defined; on nonnegative equal-mass maps it agrees with $\preceq$, is invariant under adding the same finite-support signed map to both sides, and is transitive and closed under adding two comparisons.

Assume [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] on compounds over a nonempty state set $X$, a strict reference pair $x_0\preceq x_1$ with not $x_1\preceq x_0$, and the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. For $x\in X$ define

$$L_x:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R:R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x\}.$$

Then $L_x$ is nonempty, bounded above, and downward closed. Its supremum $S(x):=\sup L_x$ is a real number and satisfies $R_{S(x)}\sim_s e_x$. Stability is used to prove attainment; no continuity of states or order is assumed.

Let $x_0,x_1\in X$ satisfy $x_0\preceq x_1$ and not $x_1\preceq x_0$. For every real $\lambda$, define the signed unit-mass reference map $R_\lambda:=(1-\lambda)e_{x_0}+\lambda e_{x_1}$. For all $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$,

$$R_\lambda\preceq_s R_\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda\le\mu.$$

The parameters need not lie in $[0,1]$; outside that interval $R_\lambda$ is signed notation, not a compound.

For every state label $x\in X$, the **unit-state compound** $e_x$ is the coefficient function with $e_x(y)=1$ if $y=x$ and $e_x(y)=0$ otherwise. Its support is $\{x\}$, so it is a tagged compound. In compound comparisons, a state label $x$ denotes $e_x$. Every compound has the canonical finite decomposition $c=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)e_x$, with an empty sum when $c=0$; coefficients on this support are strictly positive. The mass-one property $m(e_x)=1$ and the equivalence $m(c)=0\Longleftrightarrow c=0$ are proved in [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

For every tagged scalable compound $c$, the mass in [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] is independent of the finite summation set used. For any compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; $m(0)=0$. For every $x\in X$, the unit-state compound $e_x$ has $m(e_x)=1$. A compound has zero mass if and only if it is the empty compound.

derivations.claim: In the strict-reference case, [F3] gives $R_\lambda\preceq_s e_{x_0}$ exactly for $\lambda\le0$, and $R_\lambda\preceq_s e_{x_1}$ exactly for $\lambda\le1$. Their suprema are therefore $S(x_0)=0$ and $S(x_1)=1$.

Let $C=\sum_i a_i e_{x_i}$ have mass $M$ and set $q_C:=\sum_i a_iS(x_i)$. Discard any zero terms in this presentation using [F4]. If the support is empty, $C=0$, $M=q_C=0$ and $C_R=0$, so signed reflexivity gives the claimed equivalence. Otherwise each remaining coefficient is strictly positive. For each remaining constituent, [F2] gives $e_{x_i}\sim_sR_{S(x_i)}$; positive scaling and finite repeated use of composition combine these into $C\sim_s C_R$, where $C_R:=\sum_i a_iR_{S(x_i)}=(M-q_C)e_{x_0}+q_Ce_{x_1}$. This calculation is valid for signed coefficients because the signed relation is additive and translation-invariant by [F1].

Apply step 1.2 to both $A$ and $B$, and write $q_A,q_B$ for the resulting scalar sums. Since $A\sim_sA_R$ and $B\sim_sB_R$, transitivity gives $A\preceq B$ exactly when $A_R\preceq_sB_R$. Their masses agree, and $B_R-A_R=(q_B-q_A)(e_{x_1}-e_{x_0})$; [F3] therefore gives $A_R\preceq_sB_R$ exactly when $q_A\le q_B$. This proves the representation formula.

In the no-strict-pair case, take any $x,y\in X$. By [F4] their unit compounds have equal mass one, so CH gives one of $x\preceq y$ or $y\preceq x$; if exactly one held it would be a strict pair, so both hold. Fix $r\in X$. Let $C$ have mass $M$. If $M=0$, [F4] gives $C=0$, and reflexivity handles this empty compound without applying the positive-scaling axiom at zero. If $M>0$, use the canonical finite decomposition over the support from [F4]; every coefficient there is positive. Scale each constituent equivalence $e_x\sim e_r$ by its positive coefficient and compose the finitely many comparisons to obtain $C\sim M e_r$. Thus equal-mass $A,B$ are both empty when their common mass is zero, and otherwise each is equivalent to the same $M e_r$; hence they are equivalent in both cases. For a constant $S(x)=c$, both compound values equal $cM$, including zero for empty compounds, so the representation equivalence holds.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2$ be simple domains in a family of finite thermal joins satisfying A1–A7, S1–S3, T1–T5, and C1 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Then there are $x_0\prec\prec x_1$ in $\Gamma_1$ and $y_0\prec\prec y_1$ in $\Gamma_2$ such that

$$(x_0,y_1)\sim(x_1,y_0).$$

Moreover, for every fixed finite composition of scaled copies of $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$, any two equal-mass states of that same composition are comparable (CH). The conclusion is conditional on the explicitly stated join-coherence and universal-range assumptions C1 and T5.

Then $S:X\to\mathbb R$ is normalized by $S(x_0)=0$, $S(x_1)=1$, and for all equal-mass compounds $A=\sum_i a_i e_{x_i}$ and $B=\sum_j b_j e_{y_j}$,

$$A\preceq B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_i a_iS(x_i)\le\sum_j b_jS(y_j).$$

Thus $S$ is an additive extensive representation on finite compounds. If no strict pair exists, CH instead makes every equal-mass pair of compounds equivalent, and any constant state function gives a (degenerate) additive representation. No concavity, continuity, or physical law follows without additional hypotheses.

Let $u,v$ be finite-support real coefficient maps on the tagged state labels of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] with equal total coefficient. For a typed state $x$, compound notation uses the represented map $\mathsf{J}(x)$ from [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]; its raw unit point mass is $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. Signed maps still use the ordinary total of their raw coefficients, exactly the bookkeeping mass of the represented nonnegative maps. Put $d=v-u$, $d^+(x)=\max(d(x),0)$ and $d^-(x)=\max(-d(x),0)$. Define $u\preceq_s v$ to mean $d^-\prec d^+$ under the compound relation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Write $u\sim_s v$ when both $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s u$. These are formal signed comparison maps, not physical negative amounts. The positive and negative parts are finite-support compounds of equal mass. If $u\sim_s v$, then $cu\sim_s cv$ for every real $c$: positive $c$ uses scaling, $c=0$ is reflexivity, and negative $c$ swaps the positive and negative parts while equivalence supplies both comparison directions. This Definition introduces the signed notation; ordinary-order compatibility and the signed-order laws are proved separately.

Under A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for compounds $A,B$ with $m(A)=m(B)$ and every finite spectator compound $C$, $A+C\prec B+C$ if and only if $A\prec B$. Consequently, for finite-support signed maps $u,v$ of equal total coefficient, define $u\preceq_s v$ by $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$. For the meter label set $a_m=c_m=z_0$ and $b_m=d_m=z_1$; the two pairs $(z_0,z_1)$ and $(z_1,z_0)$ are the same two-copy meter compound up to permutation. Write $S_i^0$ for the selected entropy representative, with $S_m^0=S_m$, and put $\Delta_i=S_i^0(b_i)-S_i^0(a_i)>0$ and $\mu_i=S_m(d_i)-S_m(c_i)>0$. Define $S_i(x):=\frac{\mu_i}{\Delta_i}\bigl(S_i^0(x)-S_i^0(r_i)\bigr)$. Then $S_i(r_i)=0$ and $S_i(b_i)-S_i(a_i)=\mu_i$, matching the meter entropy increment across the chosen calibrator endpoints. For $i=m$, $\Delta_m=\mu_m=1$, so this agrees with the fixed meter normalization.

For a finite separated compound $A$ with factors $(t_\ell i_\ell,x_\ell)$, define $S(A):=\sum_\ell t_\ell S_{i_\ell}(x_\ell)$. The sum is finite and invariant under reordering; concatenating compounds adds the sums, and scaling every amount by $t>0$ multiplies it by $t$. The explicit-factor convention in the Statement therefore makes $S$ well-defined, additive, and extensive.

Fix a composition with amounts $M_i$ for finitely many labels and let $A,B$ be two states of that same composition. For a state $x$ of type $i$, put
$s_i(x):=\frac{S_i(x)-S_i(a_i)}{\mu_i}.$
The same-type entropy representation and the CH for type $i$ show
$\mathsf{J}(x)\sim_s(1-s_i(x))\mathsf{J}(a_i)+s_i(x)\mathsf{J}(b_i).$
Indeed, the signed difference has total coefficient zero and $S_i$-value zero, so its positive and negative parts have equal mass and entropy and therefore compare both ways by [F2]. The calibrator relation gives
$(\mathsf{J}(b_i)-\mathsf{J}(a_i))\sim_s(\mathsf{J}(d_i)-\mathsf{J}(c_i))$
by taking the signed difference of $(a_i,d_i)\sim(b_i,c_i)$ and canceling common terms with [F3]. Add and scale these identities over the finitely many factors of $A$. With
$q_i(A):=\sum_{\ell:\,i_\ell=i}t_\ell s_i(x_\ell),$
the resulting signed map is
$A\sim_s \sum_i M_i \mathsf{J}(a_i)+\sum_i q_i(A)(\mathsf{J}(d_i)-\mathsf{J}(c_i)),$
where the sums range over the finite support of the composition. The same holds for $B$. Since they have the same composition, the reference base cancels, and $B-A$ is signed-equivalent to the finite meter map
$D:=\sum_i\bigl(q_i(B)-q_i(A)\bigr)(\mathsf{J}(d_i)-\mathsf{J}(c_i)).$
Extend the meter entropy linearly to raw finite signed coefficient maps using density $S_m(z)/w_{\Gamma_m}$ at a meter raw tag $(\Gamma_m,z)$; in particular its value on $\mathsf{J}(z)$ is $S_m(z)$. Then
$S_m(D)=\sum_i\bigl(q_i(B)-q_i(A)\bigr)\mu_i=S(B)-S(A).$
The positive and negative parts of $D$ have equal mass. If $S(A)\le S(B)$, the same-type entropy representation [F2] for finite meter products gives $D^-\prec D^+$, hence $D$ compares in the forward signed direction. Translation, addition, and ordinary-order compatibility [F3] transfer this to $A\prec B$. Conversely, if $A\prec B$, the same signed equivalences and translation in [F3] give $D^-\prec D^+$. The meter representation in [F2] then forces $S_m(D)=S(B)-S(A)\ge0$. Reversing the entropy inequality gives the reverse comparison. Thus $S$ characterizes every same-composition comparison. Each particular comparison uses only finitely many labels; no infinite sum or uncountable product occurs.

The meter normalization fixes the multiplicative unit. Changing the chosen reference state for type $i$ changes only its additive constant; on a finite compound these constants contribute amount-weighted conserved-type offsets. This proves the stated freedom and completes the construction.

derivations.claim: Fix an interior attainable density $\rho>0$ and a sequence $N_L/L^d\to\rho$. The grand sum contains the nonnegative term $e^{\alpha N_L}Z(L,N_L;\beta)$, so $\liminf_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(e^\alpha,\beta)\geq F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho$ by [F1]. Taking the supremum over interior densities gives the lower bound. The vacuum term $Z(L,0)=1$ gives the value $0$ at density zero. Endpoint values are limits from the interior by their definition, so they do not enlarge the supremum.

Put $q=e^{\alpha+\beta B}$. For each $N\geq0$, stability and the box-volume formula give $e^{\alpha N}Z(L,N;\beta)\leq(qL^d)^N/N!$. Choose $K>eq+1$. For $N>KL^d$, $1\leq e^{N-KL^d}$, so the factorial bound gives $\sum_{N>KL^d}e^{\alpha N}Z(L,N;\beta) \leq e^{-KL^d}\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{(eqL^d)^N}{N!} \leq e^{-L^d}.$ The remaining at most $KL^d+2$ terms are bounded by their maximum times this number; its logarithm divided by $L^d$ tends to zero.

Choose maximizing retained particle numbers and a subsequence with $N_L/L^d\to\rho\in[0,K]$; nested-interval bisection on the compact interval $[0,K]$ supplies the subsequence. The canonical upper rate is at most $b(\rho)\leq F_\beta(\rho)$, since the one-term mixture in the definition of $F_\beta$ includes $b(\rho)$. At $\rho=0$, stability gives upper rate at most $0=F_\beta(0)$. If $u$ is a finite upper endpoint and $b(u)>-\infty$, mix a preparation approaching $b(u)$ with an interior preparation of density $r<u$, in slab fractions $1-\epsilon$ and $\epsilon$. The exact packing inequality in [F1] gives $F_\beta((1-\epsilon)u+\epsilon r)\geq(1-\epsilon)b(u)+\epsilon b(r).$ As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, the left side tends to the assigned interior endpoint limit; hence $b(u)\leq F_\beta(u)$. If $b(u)=-\infty$ this bound is automatic. Outside the closed effective domain, $b(\rho)=-\infty$, again because a finite $b(\rho)$ would make $F_\beta(\rho)\geq b(\rho)$. Thus the maximum retained term has limiting rate at most $\sup_{\rho\geq0}(F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho)$. The tail estimate in step 1.2 and the lower bound in step 1.1 prove the first equality.

The extension $F_\beta$ is proper, upper-semicontinuous and concave. It is finite and concave on its open effective interior by [F1], hence continuous there. At zero, stability and the concavity of $g(\rho)=\rho(1+\beta B-\log\rho)$ give $F_\beta(\rho)\leq g(\rho)\to0$. The sparse separated-cell lower bound in [F1] gives $F_\beta(\rho)\geq c\rho$ for a fixed finite $c$, so $F_\beta(\rho)\to0=F_\beta(0)$. At any finite upper endpoint use the assigned interior upper-semicontinuous limit; outside the closed effective domain set $F_\beta=-\infty$. Hence $G=-F_\beta$, with $G=+\infty$ on negative densities, is a proper closed convex extended-real function on $\mathbb R$. Its conjugate is $G^*(\alpha)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\{\alpha\rho+F_\beta(\rho)\}=P(\alpha,\beta)$ by steps 1.1–2.2. Applying [F3] gives $G(\rho)=\sup_\alpha\{\alpha\rho-P(\alpha,\beta)\}$, which is the second equality. The endpoint convention is needed for closedness; it asserts no finite-volume endpoint realization.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $F_\beta$ be the finite concave canonical rate on the interior attainable-density interval from [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]]. Extend it by $F_\beta(0)=0$, by its interior upper-semicontinuous limit at any finite upper endpoint of its effective domain, and by $-\infty$ outside the closed effective domain; retain the value $-\infty$ if the endpoint limit is $-\infty$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, define
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(e^\alpha,\beta),$$
whose existence is [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. Then
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\bigl(F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho\bigr),\qquad F_\beta(\rho)=\inf_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\bigl(P(\alpha,\beta)-\alpha\rho\bigr)$$
for every $\rho$ in the closed effective domain of $F_\beta$. These are thermodynamic limits of positional partition functions. They do not assert local-observable equivalence, a finite-volume endpoint realization, or a thin energy-shell limit.

derivations.claim: Stability and [F3] give $Z(L,N;\beta)\leq e^{\beta BN}L^{dN}/N!$. If $N/L^d\to\rho>0$, the factorial integral bounds [F4] imply $$ \limsup L^{-d}\log Z(L,N;\beta)\leq \rho(1+\beta B-\log\rho), $$ so $b(\rho)$ and $F(\rho)$ are bounded above on every compact positive-density interval. The vacuum term gives $b(0)=0$: $Z(L,0)=1$ is a lower bound, and the same stability estimate with $N/L^d\to0$ gives a nonpositive upper limit.

The effective domain of $F$ has nonempty interior. Fix a core cube of side $s>0$ and a gap $g>R_0$; place one particle in each selected core of a lattice of spacing $s+g$ inside a large box. The absolute interaction from any one occupied core to all others is bounded by $C\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg)<\infty$ by [F1]–[F2]. Restricting each particle to a subcube of volume $v_0>0$ therefore gives $Z(L,N;\beta)\geq v_0^N e^{-C_0N}$ for every density strictly below $(s+g)^{-d}$, after omitting unused lattice cells. Thus $F$ is finite on a nonempty interval of positive densities; by its definition as a finite-mixture envelope it is concave.

Fix a finite list of core preparations $(s_i,n_i)$ with $0<Z(s_i,n_i;\beta)<\infty$. For each $i$, choose a gap $g_i=g(s_i)$ from [F2] along a sequence $s_i\to\infty$ so that $g_i/s_i\to0$ and the positive interaction between distinct cores in the same lattice packing, divided by core volume, tends to zero. Set tile side $a_i=s_i+g_i$ and effective density $r_i=n_i/a_i^d$. If $M_i$ such tiles carry exactly $n_i$ particles in their central $s_i$-cubes, the same shell count as in the proof of [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]] gives cross-energy penalty per occupied volume at most $C (n_i/s_i^d)^2(s_i/g_i)^d\eta(g_i)$, which tends to zero by [F2]. Exact factorization over disjoint core cubes follows because assigning the labeled coordinates to their cores contributes $N!/\prod_i(n_i!)^{M_i}$, cancelling the global $N!$.

For any finite convex combination in the definition of $F(\rho)$, choose core preparations with densities tending to its $\rho_i$ and rates tending to $b(\rho_i)$. If their effective densities do not strictly bracket the target $\rho$, add arbitrarily small weights at one attainable density below and one above $\rho$; such densities exist because $\rho$ is interior. Their mixture coefficients can then be perturbed by quantities tending to zero so the effective mean is exactly $\rho$. Place the fixed core types in finitely many macroscopic slabs with these volume fractions, inserting fixed empty layers wider than $R_0$ between slabs. For fixed core sizes and gaps, the distinct-slab cross energy divided by total volume tends to zero: for interaction distances at most $R$, only $O(RL^{d-1})$ particles lie in the interface strips, while the remaining contribution is bounded by a constant times $L^d\sum_{|j|_\infty>R}\Psi_j$; take $L\to\infty$ and then $R\to\infty$.

First reserve an outer layer of fixed width $W$ and adjust slab fractions in the remaining volume to match the target density; the strict bracketing in step 3.1 absorbs the reserved layer's $O(WL^{d-1})$ volume without assuming its one-particle capacity replaces a bulk density. Rounding the finitely many core counts then changes particle number by at most $C_1L^{d-1}$ with $C_1$ depending on the fixed preparations, not on $W$, because only boundary tiles are incomplete. Choose $W$ large enough to contain at least $C_1L^{d-1}$ small cells separated from each other and every core by more than $R_0$. Put each missing particle in one such cell. Its interaction with the fixed preparations is bounded by the same summable tail, so the correction changes log weight by only $O(L^{d-1})$. This constructs exactly $N_L$ particles for every sequence $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, and gives $$ \liminf_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log Z(L,N_L;\beta)\geq\sum_i\theta_i\frac{\log Z(s_i,n_i;\beta)-\mathrm{cross}_i}{a_i^d}, $$ where $\mathrm{cross}_i/a_i^d\to0$ by step 2.1. Taking preparations approaching the selected convex combination and then the supremum gives $\liminf\geq F(\rho)$.

By the definition of $b$, every sequence with density tending $\rho$ has limsup rate at most $b(\rho)\leq F(\rho)$. Together with step 4.1 this proves the asserted limit. A finite concave function on an open interval is continuous: fix $a<\rho<b$ in the interval; the chord slopes from $a$ and $b$ bound the difference quotients on a smaller interval around $\rho$, yielding a finite local Lipschitz bound. This establishes finiteness and continuity of $F$ on its effective interior while leaving excluded endpoints undecided.

Let $\phi$ be stable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], fix $\beta>0$, and define $Z(L,N;\beta)$ as in that definition. For sequences $L_j\to\infty$ and integers $N_j\geq0$ with $N_j/L_j^d\to\rho$, define
$$b(\rho)=\sup\left\{\limsup_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta):\frac{N_j}{L_j^d}\to\rho\right\}.$$
Let $F$ be the concave envelope of $b$ on $[0,\infty)$, namely the supremum of $\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i b(\rho_i)$ over finite lists with $\theta_i\geq0$, $\sum_i\theta_i=1$, $\rho_i\geq0$, and $\sum_i\theta_i\rho_i=\rho$; the empty supremum is $-\infty$. On the interior of $\{\rho:F(\rho)>-\infty\}$, $F$ is finite and continuous. For every $\rho>0$ in that interior and every such sequence $(L_j,N_j)$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta)=F(\rho).$$
No claim is made at a close-packing endpoint or at any other excluded endpoint.

citations.quote:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open, $n\ge1$, with coordinates $(x_1,\ldots,x_n,z)$. A $C^2$ one-form on $U$ is a field of linear functionals on tangent vectors of the form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i(x,z)\,dx_i+b(x,z)\,dz$, where every coefficient is twice continuously differentiable. At $q\in U$, it acts by $\omega_q(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)=\sum_i a_i(q)u_i+b(q)w$. It is nonsingular on $U$ when $\omega_q\ne0$ for every $q$; then $H_q:=\ker\omega_q$ is an $n$-dimensional subspace of $T_qU\cong\mathbb R^{n+1}$.

For one-forms $\alpha,\beta$, their exterior product is the alternating two-form $(\alpha\wedge\beta)(u,v)=\alpha(u)\beta(v)-\alpha(v)\beta(u)$. For a one-form $\alpha$ and a two-form $\sigma$, $(\alpha\wedge\sigma)(u,v,w)=\alpha(u)\sigma(v,w)-\alpha(v)\sigma(u,w)+\alpha(w)\sigma(u,v)$. The exterior derivative of the displayed $C^2$ form is the $C^1$ two-form

$$d\omega=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dx_j+\sum_{i=1}^n(\partial_i b-\partial_z a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dz.$$

A piecewise-$C^1$ path is a continuous $\gamma:[s_0,s_1]\to U$ with $s_0\le s_1$ and admitting a finite partition on each closed subinterval of which it is $C^1$. It is $\omega$-horizontal when $\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))=0$ on the interior of each such subinterval. Endpoints where a derivative is one-sided are included by continuity. For an open $V\subseteq U$, $p$ is horizontally reachable from $q$ within $V$ if a horizontal path in $V$ joins $q$ to $p$. Both signs of time and finite concatenations are allowed by this definition.

On a neighborhood $W$, an integrating factor for $\omega$ is a nowhere-zero $\mu\in C^1(W)$ for which $\mu\omega=dS$ for some $S\in C^2(W)$ with $dS$ nowhere zero. This definition is local; it asserts neither a global potential on $U$ nor a physical identification or calibration of $S$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, $m\ge1$, let $X:U\to\mathbb R^m$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and fix $q_0\in U$. There are $r,\delta>0$ and a map $\phi:[-\delta,\delta]\times\overline B(q_0,r/2)\to\overline B(q_0,r)$ such that for each $p\in\overline B(q_0,r/2)$, $t\mapsto\phi(t,p)$ is $C^1$, satisfies $\phi(0,p)=p$ and $\partial_t\phi(t,p)=X(\phi(t,p))$ on $(-\delta,\delta)$, and is the unique such solution that stays in $\overline B(q_0,r)$. The dependence on the initial point is locally Lipschitz, and the local flow law $\phi(t,\phi(s,p))=\phi(t+s,p)$ holds whenever the displayed maps are defined in the chosen neighborhood.

Let $X$ be a $C^2$ vector field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, where $C^2$ means that total derivatives through order two exist and are continuous. Its local flow $\phi_X^t(q)$ from [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]] is $C^2$ jointly in $(t,q)$, and $J(t,q):=D_q\phi_X^t(q)$ satisfies $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X^t(q))J$ and $J(0,q)=I$. For two such fields define their bracket by $[X,Y](q):=DY(q)X(q)-DX(q)Y(q)$. If $[X,Y]=0$ on a neighborhood and all local maps stay there, then $D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$ and their local flows commute: $\phi_X^t\circ\phi_Y^s=\phi_Y^s\circ\phi_X^t$ whenever both sides are defined.
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open. Let $\omega$ be a $C^1$ one-form on $U$, $\mu\in C^1(U)$ nowhere zero, and $S\in C^2(U)$ with $dS=\mu\omega$. Then $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$ on $U$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $1\le q\le n$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Suppose $F(x_*)=0$ and some $q\times q$ minor of the derivative matrix $DF(x_*)$ is invertible. This nonsingular-minor hypothesis is the explicit full-row-rank condition used here. If $q<n$, then after permuting coordinates $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\mathbb R^q$, there are open neighborhoods $P$ of $u_*$ and $Q$ of $v_*$ and a unique $C^1$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$ such that

$$F(u,v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=\varphi(u)\qquad((u,v)\in P\times Q).$$

Its derivative is

$$D\varphi(u)=-D_vF(u,\varphi(u))^{-1}D_uF(u,\varphi(u)).$$

Thus the local zero set is a graph over $n-q$ free coordinates. If $q=n$, the zero is locally isolated, so the local graph dimension is zero. Here “local graph dimension $k$” means a local graph parameterized by an open subset of $\mathbb R^k$, with a singleton counted as dimension zero.

derivations.claim: Since $\omega_{q_0}\ne0$, one coordinate coefficient is nonzero at $q_0$; relabel that coordinate as $z$ and shrink the neighborhood so $b\ne0$. Put $c_i:=-a_i/b$ and $X_i:=\partial_{x_i}+c_i\partial_z$. Then $X_i\in C^2$, $\omega(X_i)=a_i+bc_i=0$, and the $X_i$ are a basis of $\ker\omega$ because their first $n$ components form the standard basis.

Define $[X,Y]:=DY\,X-DX\,Y$. Coordinate expansion of the displayed formula for $d\omega$ gives $d\omega(X,Y)=X[\omega(Y)]-Y[\omega(X)]-\omega([X,Y])$. Thus for horizontal fields $d\omega(X_i,X_j)=-\omega([X_i,X_j])$. Also $[X_i,X_j]$ has zero $x$-components, hence is vertical. Evaluating the three-form on $(\partial_z,X_i,X_j)$ gives $(\omega\wedge d\omega)(\partial_z,X_i,X_j)=b\,d\omega(X_i,X_j)$. Under (i), $d\omega(X_i,X_j)=0$; then $\omega([X_i,X_j])=0$, and a vertical vector $v\partial_z$ has $\omega(v\partial_z)=vb$, so $[X_i,X_j]=0$.

By [F2]–[F3] and step 1.2, the fields $X_i$ have commuting local $C^2$ flows $\phi_i^t$. Define $\Phi(x,\eta):=\phi_n^{x_n}\circ\cdots\circ\phi_1^{x_1}(0,\eta)$ for $(x,\eta)$ near $(0,z_0)$. Each $X_i$ changes only $x_i$, at rate one, so the first $n$ coordinates of $\Phi(x,\eta)$ are exactly $x$. Commutation and the transported-field identity in [F3] give $\partial_{x_i}\Phi=X_i(\Phi)$. At $(0,z_0)$ the columns of $D\Phi$ are $X_1,\ldots,X_n,\partial_z$; their first $n$ components form $I_n$ and the last column is $\partial_z$, so $D\Phi$ is invertible.

Let $N=n+1$. On an open product neighborhood of $(u_0,y_0)=((0,z_0),(0,z_0))$ where $\Phi$ is defined, set $H(u,y):=\Phi(u)-y$. Then $H(u_0,y_0)=0$ and its $u$-derivative $D_uH=D\Phi(u_0)$ is invertible. Apply [L1] with ambient dimension $2N$ and target dimension $N$, permuting the input coordinates to $(y,u)$ so the $y$ block is free and the solved $u$ block has the invertible minor: conditionally, the zero set is the graph of a unique local $C^1$ map $G(y)$, so $\Phi(G(y))=y$. Since $\Phi$ is $C^2$, differentiating this identity by [F5] gives $D\Phi(G(y))DG(y)=I$ and hence $DG(y)=(D\Phi(G(y)))^{-1}$. The right side is $C^1$ (matrix inverse entries are cofactors divided by the nonzero determinant), so $G$ is $C^2$.

Let $S(x,z)$ be the last coordinate $\eta$ of $G(x,z)$. Then $S\in C^2$, $S(\Phi(x,\eta))=\eta$, and $S_z(0,z_0)=1$; after shrinking, $S_z\ne0$. Differentiating along $X_i$ gives $S_{x_i}+c_iS_z=0$, so $dS=S_z(dz-\sum_i c_i dx_i)=(S_z/b)\omega$. Thus $\mu:=S_z/b$ is $C^1$ and nowhere zero. This proves (ii), conditionally on [L1].
Conversely, if (ii) holds, [F4] gives $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$ on that neighborhood, proving (i).

boundaries.evidence: Statement fixes q_0 in the open neighborhood and n>=1, with a nonzero one-form there. Thus its local integration argument does not start from an empty neighborhood or a missing base point.

case_scope.source_excerpt: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\ge1$, be open and let $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i dx_i+b dz$ be a $C^2$ one-form with $\omega_q\ne0$ near $q_0\in U$. After shrinking to a neighborhood on which one coefficient $b$ is nonzero, the following are equivalent: (i) $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$ throughout that neighborhood; (ii) on a possibly smaller neighborhood there are $\mu\in C^1$ nowhere zero and $S\in C^2$ with $dS=\mu\omega$. The theorem is local; it gives no global exactness or thermodynamic calibration.

boundaries.reason: Nonsingularity excludes the zero covector near q0.

boundaries.evidence: For n=1 the rank-one horizontal field has zero self-bracket in step 1.2, and the conditional local construction proceeds in steps 2.1–4.1.
If the initially named coefficient b(q0) vanishes, a finite coordinate relabel selects a nonzero component; if omega(q0)=0 the theorem excludes the point, step 1.1.
All constructions occur on open neighborhoods shrunk so flows remain interior, in steps 2.1, 3.1, and 4.1.
Only finite coordinate choices and a deterministic flow composition are used in steps 1.1 and 2.1; the separate local-rank input is conditional at step 3.1.
The Pfaff condition constructs mu and S conditionally on the rank carrier through steps 1.1–4.1.
An exact nonzero multiple implies the Pfaff condition by the local exactness lemma in step 5.1.

Let $X$ be nonempty and suppose its finite-support compounds carry the comparison structure of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] over the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. If there are $x_0,x_1\in X$ with $x_0\preceq x_1$ and not $x_1\preceq x_0$, define $S(x):=\sup L_x$ using [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]]. Then $S:X\to\mathbb R$ is normalized by $S(x_0)=0$, $S(x_1)=1$, and for all equal-mass compounds $A=\sum_i a_i e_{x_i}$ and $B=\sum_j b_j e_{y_j}$,

$$A\preceq B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_i a_iS(x_i)\le\sum_j b_jS(y_j).$$

Thus $S$ is an additive extensive representation on finite compounds. If no strict pair exists, CH instead makes every equal-mass pair of compounds equivalent, and any constant state function gives a (degenerate) additive representation. No concavity, continuity, or physical law follows without additional hypotheses.

Assume [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] on compounds over a nonempty state set $X$, a strict reference pair $x_0\preceq x_1$ with not $x_1\preceq x_0$, and the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. For $x\in X$ define

$$L_x:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R:R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x\}.$$

Then $L_x$ is nonempty, bounded above, and downward closed. Its supremum $S(x):=\sup L_x$ is a real number and satisfies $R_{S(x)}\sim_s e_x$. Stability is used to prove attainment; no continuity of states or order is assumed.

Under [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]], for equal-mass compounds $A,B,C$, $A+C\preceq B+C$ if and only if $A\preceq B$. The signed relation of [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] is well-defined; on nonnegative equal-mass maps it agrees with $\preceq$, is invariant under adding the same finite-support signed map to both sides, and is transitive and closed under adding two comparisons.

Let $u,v:X\to\mathbb R$ be finite-support real coefficient maps with equal total coefficient $\sum_xu(x)=\sum_xv(x)$. These signed maps are formal comparison notation, not compounds. Put $d:=v-u$ and define $d^+(x):=\max\{d(x),0\}$ and $d^-(x):=\max\{-d(x),0\}$. Then $d^+,d^-$ are nonnegative finite-support compounds of equal mass, as verified in [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]. Define

$$u\preceq_s v\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d^-\preceq d^+,$$

using the compound comparison relation of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]. Thus positive coefficients of $v-u$ remain on the right and negative coefficients move to the left. Signed notation is never a claim that a negative amount of a physical system exists.

Fix a nonempty set $X$ and the compounds of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. A **comparison relation** $\preceq$ is defined only for pairs $(A,B)$ with $m(A)=m(B)$. Write $A\sim B$ when both $A\preceq B$ and $B\preceq A$; this is equivalence, not equality of coefficient functions. The following are explicit hypotheses on $\preceq$:

1. **Preorder:** $A\preceq A$, and $A\preceq B\preceq C$ implies $A\preceq C$.
2. **Composition consistency:** $A\preceq B$ implies $A+C\preceq B+C$ for every compound $C$.
3. **Positive scaling:** $A\preceq B$ implies $tA\preceq tB$ for every real $t>0$.
4. **Splitting and recombination:** for $x\in X$, $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, the one-state compound $te_x$ is equivalent to $se_x+(t-s)e_x$.
5. **Stability:** for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive compounds $Z_0,Z_1$ with $m(Z_0)=m(Z_1)$, and a sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to $0$, if $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\preceq B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for every $n$, then $A\preceq B$.
6. **Comparison hypothesis (CH):** for every equal-mass pair $A,B$, either $A\preceq B$ or $B\preceq A$ (or both).

These are mathematical assumptions, not conclusions about a physical system. No antisymmetry, continuity, convexity, or strict comparison is included. Strict comparison means $A\preceq B$ and not $B\preceq A$.

Let $x_0,x_1\in X$ satisfy $x_0\preceq x_1$ and not $x_1\preceq x_0$. For every real $\lambda$, define the signed unit-mass reference map $R_\lambda:=(1-\lambda)e_{x_0}+\lambda e_{x_1}$. For all $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$,

$$R_\lambda\preceq_s R_\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda\le\mu.$$

The parameters need not lie in $[0,1]$; outside that interval $R_\lambda$ is signed notation, not a compound.

derivations.claim: For each constituent $(i,x_{ik},z_0)$ of $C$, its mass-two shared compound $u_{i,x_{ik}}$ is equivalent by the exact substitution in [A1] to $e_{r_i}+(1-\sigma_i(x_{ik}))e_{z_0}+\sigma_i(x_{ik})e_{z_1}$. Each side has total coefficient two, so this signed substitution is defined. Scale by $t_{ik}>0$ and combine the finitely many comparisons using [A1] and [F2]. The resulting reference-system part is $\sum_iT_i e_{r_i}$, independent of the chosen states. The meter part has coefficients $T-\Sigma(C)$ on $e_{z_0}$ and $\Sigma(C)$ on $e_{z_1}$, where $T:=\sum_iT_i$. Hence $C$ is equivalent to that fixed reference-system compound plus $(T-\Sigma(C))e_{z_0}+\Sigma(C)e_{z_1}$, whose total coefficient is $T+T=2T$. If the collection is empty, both expressions are zero and the equivalence is reflexivity, requiring no order scaling at zero.

The same substitution for $D$ gives the same reference-system compound because its type totals are the same, and the same total meter mass $T$. Cancel the common reference-system terms by [A1] and [F2]. If $T>0$, the remaining meter expressions have total coefficient $T$; positive scaling by $1/T$ turns them into the unit reference maps $R_{\Sigma(C)/T}$ and $R_{\Sigma(D)/T}$. By [F3] these compare exactly when $\Sigma(C)/T\le\Sigma(D)/T$, which is equivalent to $\Sigma(C)\le\Sigma(D)$. Scaling back by $T>0$ proves the reverse comparison equivalence, so no unit-mass reference theorem is applied directly at mass $T$. Reversing the same equivalences proves the converse implication as well. Since $C=C_0+T e_{z_0}$ and $D=D_0+T e_{z_0}$, [F2] also gives $C\preceq D$ exactly when $C_0\preceq D_0$; for $T=0$ all these compounds are empty and the criterion is $0\le0$.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $I$ be a finite nonempty set of system types, $X_i$ a nonempty state set with chosen reference $r_i\in X_i$ for each $i\in I$, and $M$ a common meter state set with $z_0,z_1\in M$. Assume for every $i$ that the product state set $X_i\times M$ satisfies the hypotheses of [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]], with strict reference pair $(r_i,z_0)\prec\prec(r_i,z_1)$. Let $S_i$ be its normalized representation and put $\sigma_i(x):=S_i(x,z_0)$. In that product comparison, the unit product-state point mass satisfies $e_{(x,z_0)}\sim_s(1-\sigma_i(x))e_{(r_i,z_0)}+\sigma_i(x)e_{(r_i,z_1)}$, by [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]]. These product-state point masses are distinct from the shared state-and-meter compounds defined next.

Assume in addition a **common-meter compatibility interface**. Let $\mathcal Y$ contain disjoint families of raw state tags $a_{i,x}$, raw type-reference tags $\rho_i$, and two distinct raw meter tags $\zeta_0,\zeta_1$. Using the unit point masses on these tags, write $e_{r_i}:=e_{\rho_i}$ and $e_{z_j}:=e_{\zeta_j}$, and define $u_{i,x}:=e_{a_{i,x}}+e_{z_0}$. Thus $u_{i,x}$ is an explicit mass-two state-and-fixed-meter compound; it is not a unit tag. Compounds over $\mathcal Y$ use the finite-support convention of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]], and their signed comparison is the one in [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]]. Require the exact substitution

$$u_{i,x}\sim_s e_{r_i}+(1-\sigma_i(x))e_{z_0}+\sigma_i(x)e_{z_1}\qquad(i\in I,\ x\in X_i),$$

finite substitutions to compose, and the fixed reference sum $\sum_iT_ie_{r_i}$ to cancel when type totals agree. Both sides of this signed substitution have total coefficient two, even when $\sigma_i(x)$ lies outside $[0,1]$. Require the common meter point masses to satisfy $e_{z_0}\preceq e_{z_1}$ and not $e_{z_1}\preceq e_{z_0}$. These are hypotheses on the comparison algebra, not consequences of separate numerical meter readings.

For positive coefficients $t_{ik}$ on a finite collection of type-$i$ states $x_{ik}$, define $T_i:=\sum_k t_{ik}$ and $T:=\sum_iT_i$. Put $C_0:=\sum_{i,k}t_{ik}e_{a_{i,x_{ik}}}$ and $C:=\sum_{i,k}t_{ik}u_{i,x_{ik}}=C_0+T e_{z_0}$. Thus $C_0$ is the state compound of mass $T$ and $C$ is its fixed-meter encoding of mass $2T$. Empty collections give $T=0$ and $C_0=C=0$. Define

$$\Sigma(C):=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_k t_{ik}\sigma_i(x_{ik}).$$

For two such compounds $C,D$ with the same type-total vector $(T_i)_{i\in I}$, the common comparison satisfies $C\preceq D$ exactly when $\Sigma(C)\le\Sigma(D)$. Equivalently, the same order criterion holds for the state compounds $C_0,D_0$ after canceling their common $T e_{z_0}$. The index family is finite; no arbitrary-index choice or infinite decomposition is asserted.
