citations.quote:
Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with finite slope $P_i(x)$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

For two simple domains $\Gamma_i\subset\mathbb R^{n_i+1}$ and $\Gamma_j\subset\mathbb R^{n_j+1}$, write their coordinates $(u_i,v_i)$ and $(u_j,v_j)$. Their thermal-join domain is

$$\Delta_{ij}:=\{(u,v_i,v_j):\exists u_i,u_j,\ (u_i,v_i)\in\Gamma_i,\ (u_j,v_j)\in\Gamma_j,\ u=u_i+u_j\}.$$

The joined simple type is a distinct formal tag with amount function $\nu_{\Delta_{ij}}=\nu_{\Gamma_i}+\nu_{\Gamma_j}$ and weight $w_{\Delta_{ij}}=w_{\Gamma_i}+w_{\Gamma_j}$, as defined in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Encode the separated pair by $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and a joined coordinate $Z$ by $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(Z)$. Their bookkeeping masses agree, and their aggregate composition functions agree. These encoded maps and their raw tags remain distinct. Positive coordinate-scaled copies use the reversible preparation transport of that definition; nested joins preserve their finite primitive amount function under reassociation and permutation. The empty type contributes the zero map.

Write $J_{ij}(x,y)$ for the join state with the summed energy coordinate and the unchanged work coordinates. A compound pair $(x,y)$ and $J_{ij}(x,y)$ have the same total energy and work coordinates but are distinct tagged objects. Define $x\sim_T y$ exactly when $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(J_{ij}(x,y))$ are accessible in both directions. Nested joins use the declared reassociation and permutation identifications.

Assume every finite join is itself a simple domain satisfying [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. The contact hypotheses are mathematical assumptions on the common relation: (T1) $(x,y)\prec J_{ij}(x,y)$; (T2) every join state has at least one reversible split into component states at its stated coordinates, and the equal-state split of any state into positive scaled copies of itself is reversible; (T3) $\sim_T$ is transitive; (T4) for every simple state $x$ there are states $x_0,x_1$ in its domain with $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ and $x_0\sim_T x_1$; (T5) for every ordered pair of simple systems, every $x$ in the first and every work coordinate $v$ in the second's projection $\rho(\Gamma_j):=\{v:\exists u,(u,v)\in\Gamma_j\}$, there is a state $y$ with work coordinate $v$ and $x\sim_T y$.

For the completed calibrator branch, add (C1) **join coherence**: whenever $x\sim_T y$, the join state $J_{ij}(x,y)$ is thermally equivalent to each of $x$ and $y$ under the nested-join identifications. The coordinate sum in the definition alone does not assert C1. In later theorem statements, T1–T5 and C1 are explicitly listed as hypotheses; they are not treated as established physical laws.

Assume [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and T1–T4 of [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]] for every finite join. For any one simple type $\Gamma_i$, every two finite compounds of its scaled copies with the same total coefficient mass are comparable. Thus CH holds on all multiple scaled products of that type. No entropy across different material types is asserted here.

Let $X$ be nonempty and suppose its finite-support compounds carry the comparison structure of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] over the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. If there are $x_0,x_1\in X$ with $x_0\preceq x_1$ and not $x_1\preceq x_0$, define $S(x):=\sup L_x$ using [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]]. Then $S:X\to\mathbb R$ is normalized by $S(x_0)=0$, $S(x_1)=1$, and for all equal-mass compounds $A=\sum_i a_i e_{x_i}$ and $B=\sum_j b_j e_{y_j}$,

$$A\preceq B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_i a_iS(x_i)\le\sum_j b_jS(y_j).$$

Thus $S$ is an additive extensive representation on finite compounds. If no strict pair exists, CH instead makes every equal-mass pair of compounds equivalent, and any constant state function gives a (degenerate) additive representation. No concavity, continuity, or physical law follows without additional hypotheses.

Let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be a simple domain satisfying the forward-sector hypotheses and T1–T4. Let $S$ be the additive extensive entropy supplied by [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]] after CH for its finite scaled products is proved by [[thm-tdmath-reference-strip-gluing]]. Then either all pairs of states in $\Gamma$ are thermally equivalent, or there are $x,y$ on one entropy level (equivalently, one adiabat $\partial A_x$ by [[thm-tdmath-sector-nesting]]) with $x\not\sim_T y$.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], the sectors are nested: if $y\in A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$; equality holds when $y\in\partial A_x$, and $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ when $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$. For every $x,y\in\Gamma_i$, either $x\prec y$ or $y\prec x$ (possibly both). Strict comparison is exactly interior membership: $x\prec\prec y$ if and only if $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], each simple domain has one orientation sign $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$, constant across the domain, such that at fixed work coordinate $v$, $x\prec y$ exactly when $\varepsilon_i(u_y-u_x)\ge0$. In coordinates oriented so $\varepsilon_i=1$, for each $x\in\Gamma_i$ the projection $\rho_x$ of $\partial_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ onto work coordinates is open and connected; the boundary is the graph $(u_x(v),v)$ of a $C^1$ function with locally Lipschitz derivative

$$Du_x(v)=-P_i(u_x(v),v).$$

If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y=A_x$ and their boundary graphs agree.

Under A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for compounds $A,B$ with $m(A)=m(B)$ and every finite spectator compound $C$, $A+C\prec B+C$ if and only if $A\prec B$. Consequently, for finite-support signed maps $u,v$ of equal total coefficient, define $u\preceq_s v$ by $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$. This relation is well-defined, agrees with $\prec$ on nonnegative maps, is invariant under adding a common signed map, is transitive, and is closed under addition of two comparisons. No comparison hypothesis is used.

Let $u,v$ be finite-support real coefficient maps on the tagged state labels of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] with equal total coefficient. For a typed state $x$, compound notation uses the represented map $\mathsf{J}(x)$ from [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]; its raw unit point mass is $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. Signed maps still use the ordinary total of their raw coefficients, exactly the bookkeeping mass of the represented nonnegative maps. Put $d=v-u$, $d^+(x)=\max(d(x),0)$ and $d^-(x)=\max(-d(x),0)$. Define $u\preceq_s v$ to mean $d^-\prec d^+$ under the compound relation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Write $u\sim_s v$ when both $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s u$. These are formal signed comparison maps, not physical negative amounts. The positive and negative parts are finite-support compounds of equal mass. If $u\sim_s v$, then $cu\sim_s cv$ for every real $c$: positive $c$ uses scaling, $c=0$ is reflexivity, and negative $c$ swaps the positive and negative parts while equivalence supplies both comparison directions. This Definition introduces the signed notation; ordinary-order compatibility and the signed-order laws are proved separately.

Let a family of simple domains satisfy [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], and suppose every pair has an admitted simple thermal join satisfying T1 and T2 of [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Then the fixed-work orientation signs from [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]] agree throughout the family. One common affine proof-coordinate convention $u'=\varepsilon u$, $\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, therefore makes each fixed-work accessibility order increase with $u'$ and preserves the energy-sum formula for joins. This is a mathematical coordinate convention; it does not change a physical energy quantity or assert a sign of a measured temperature.

derivations.claim: Work in [F8]'s common affine mathematical energy orientation, without redefining any physical energy or calibration. Apply [F1] and [F2] to each simple type, including every finite join, using the positive normalization by its fixed weight in [A1]. Throughout, entropy at a state means its represented-state value: $w_\Gamma$ times its unit-point-mass representation. This normalization preserves order and finite scalar amounts. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] makes each resulting entropy concave, since the comparison of a scaled pair with its convex-combination state translates under the representation to the concavity inequality. By [F4], each entropy is strictly increasing with energy at fixed work coordinates.

Use T5 to choose $\bar x\in\Gamma_1$ and $\bar y\in\Gamma_2$ with $\bar x\sim_T\bar y$. Let $\phi=J_{12}(\bar x,\bar y)$ and consider its adiabat $\partial A_\phi$. T2 gives every $Z$ on that adiabat at least one split $Z=J_{12}(x_Z,y_Z)$ with $x_Z\sim_T y_Z$.

Suppose a join state $Z$ on $\partial A_\phi$ has two distinct equilibrium splits $(x^{(1)},y^{(1)})$ and $(x^{(2)},y^{(2)})$. By the definition of $\sim_T$, both pairs are reversible with $Z$, hence mutually accessible compounds. Their work coordinates are fixed by $Z$ and their total energies equal its energy. If the first-component energies agreed, both component states in the splits would agree, so distinctness forces unequal first-component energies. If $u_{x^{(1)}}<u_{x^{(2)}}$, fixed-work comparison [F4] gives $x^{(1)}\prec\prec x^{(2)}$; conservation of total energy gives $u_{y^{(2)}}<u_{y^{(1)}}$, hence $y^{(2)}\prec\prec y^{(1)}$. Taking $(x_0,x_1,y_0,y_1)=(x^{(1)},x^{(2)},y^{(2)},y^{(1)})$ gives $(x_0,y_1)\sim(x_1,y_0)$ because both split compounds are reversible with $Z$. If the first energies occur in the opposite order, swap the two splits and obtain the same calibrator form. Therefore, if no calibrator exists, every $Z\in\partial A_\phi$ has a unique equilibrium split.

Assume no calibrator exists. For any equilibrium split $(x_Z,y_Z)$ of $Z\in\partial A_\phi$, reversibility with $Z$ and the common adiabat give $(x_Z,y_Z)\sim(\bar x,\bar y)$ as compounds. By [F1], $x_Z$ and $\bar x$ are comparable; [F4] says their sectors coincide exactly when they are equivalent. If $x_Z\prec\prec\bar x$, pair reversibility gives $(\bar x,\bar y)\prec(x_Z,y_Z)$. Consistency adds $\bar y$ to $x_Z\prec\bar x$, and cancellation [F5] gives $\bar y\prec y_Z$. If $y_Z\prec\bar y$, consistency and the pair comparison instead cancel to give $\bar x\prec x_Z$, a contradiction. Thus $\bar y\prec\prec y_Z$, making a calibrator. The case $\bar x\prec\prec x_Z$ is symmetric: it gives $y_Z\prec\prec\bar y$, again a calibrator. Since neither is allowed under the assumption, $x_Z\sim\bar x$. Adding spectators to the two directions and cancelling by [F5] then gives both $\bar y\prec y_Z$ and $y_Z\prec\bar y$, so $y_Z\sim\bar y$. Thus every split on this adiabat has components in the corresponding component adiabats.

Under the no-calibrator assumption, fix a first-component work coordinate $v_1$ in the projection of $\partial A_{\bar x}$. The boundary-graph result [F4] gives exactly one state $x_*$ on that component adiabat at $v_1$. Every split of a join state on $\partial A_\phi$ with first work coordinate $v_1$ therefore has first component $x_*$. Each split is thermal, so $x_*\sim_T y_Z$ for its second component. T3 makes all such $y_Z$ thermally equivalent, and C1 makes each joined state $J(x_*,y_Z)=Z$ thermally equivalent to $x_*$. Hence all join states on this adiabat over fixed $v_1$ lie in one thermal class. Fixing a second-component work coordinate instead gives the corresponding conclusion for first components.

Let $\Omega$ be the open connected work-coordinate projection of $\partial A_\phi$ from [F4]. From any point of $\Omega$, the set reachable by finitely many coordinate-axis segments contained in open boxes in $\Omega$ is relatively open, and its complement is also relatively open; connectedness makes the reachable set all of $\Omega$. Along each such segment, step 4.1 gives equivalence of the corresponding join states; T3 composes these finitely many equivalences. Thus the whole adiabat $\partial A_\phi$ is one thermal class. Since the argument works for every starting join state, every join adiabat is one thermal class.

Still assuming no calibrator, apply [F3] to each join system. Its alternative with two thermally inequivalent states on one adiabat is excluded by step 5.1, so all states of each join system are thermally equivalent. For any $x,x'\in\Gamma_1$, use T5 with one allowed second work coordinate to choose $y,y'$ with $x\sim_T y$ and $x'\sim_T y'$. C1 relates each component to its joined state, and all join states are in one thermal class; T3 therefore gives $x\sim_T x'$. The same argument gives one thermal class in $\Gamma_2$. Now take $Z=\phi\in\partial A_\phi$ and a split $(x,y)$ supplied by T2. Choose nonzero sufficiently small $\delta$ so $(u_x+\delta,v_1)\in\Gamma_1$ and $(u_y-\delta,v_2)\in\Gamma_2$, possible because the domains are open. These states form a distinct split of the same $Z$. Since the original split has $x\sim_T y$ and each component type is one thermal class, T3 gives thermal equivalence of the changed pair as well. This contradicts uniqueness of the split from step 2.1. Therefore a calibrator exists.

Fix a calibrator $x_0\prec\prec x_1$, $y_0\prec\prec y_1$, whose existence is step 6.1. Choose same-type entropy representatives $S_1,S_2$ from [F2], with positive gaps $h_1=S_1(x_1)-S_1(x_0)$ and $h_2=S_2(y_1)-S_2(y_0)$. Normalize $\widetilde S_i=S_i/h_i$, so both calibrator increments are one, and put $s(x)=\widetilde S_1(x)-\widetilde S_1(x_0)$ and $t(y)=\widetilde S_2(y)-\widetilde S_2(y_0)$. Write $u=\mathsf{J}(x_0)+\mathsf{J}(y_1)$ and $v=\mathsf{J}(x_1)+\mathsf{J}(y_0)$. The calibrator says $u\sim v$, so $v-u=(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))-(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))$ is equivalent to zero; translation and cancellation [F5] give $(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))\sim_s(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))$. For any state $x$, the signed map $d_x=\mathsf{J}(x)-(1-s(x))\mathsf{J}(x_0)-s(x)\mathsf{J}(x_1)$ has total mass and $\widetilde S_1$-value zero. Its positive and negative parts have equal mass and entropy, so [F2] makes them equivalent. Hence $\mathsf{J}(x)\sim_s(1-s(x))\mathsf{J}(x_0)+s(x)\mathsf{J}(x_1)$; the same argument applies to states of the second type. These are formal signed maps when a coefficient lies outside $[0,1]$.

For a state pair $(x,y)$, put $\lambda=(s(x)+t(y))/2$ and $\delta=(s(x)-t(y))/2$. Adding the signed reductions from step 7.1 makes the pair equivalent to $(1-\lambda)(\mathsf{J}(x_0)+\mathsf{J}(y_0))+\lambda(\mathsf{J}(x_1)+\mathsf{J}(y_1))$ plus $\delta[(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))-(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))]$. The calibrator increment equivalence from step 7.1 makes the latter term equivalent to zero for either sign of $\delta$. Thus each pair reduces to its reference map at parameter $\lambda$. For any finite compound $A$ with amounts $M_1,M_2$ of the two types, add and scale these single-state reductions. Writing $q_1(A),q_2(A)$ for the amount-weighted sums of $s(x),t(y)$, respectively, gives $A\sim_s(M_1-q_1(A))\mathsf{J}(x_0)+q_1(A)\mathsf{J}(x_1)+(M_2-q_2(A))\mathsf{J}(y_0)+q_2(A)\mathsf{J}(y_1)$. Using $(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))\sim_s(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))$, this is equivalent to $M_1\mathsf{J}(x_0)+M_2\mathsf{J}(y_0)+Q(A)(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))$, where $Q(A)=q_1(A)+q_2(A)$. If the total mass is zero, both compounds are empty and reflexivity compares them. Otherwise, for same-composition $A,B$, their base terms agree. If $Q(A)<Q(B)$, the positive and negative parts of the reference-map difference are $(Q(B)-Q(A))\mathsf{J}(x_1)$ and $(Q(B)-Q(A))\mathsf{J}(x_0)$, so $x_0\prec x_1$ and positive scaling compares the maps forward. If the Q values agree the maps coincide; if $Q(A)>Q(B)$ the reverse comparison holds. Translation, addition, and ordinary-order compatibility [F5] transfer the result to $A,B$. This proves CH for every fixed finite composition of the two types and their scaled copies.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$
The function $L:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

derivations.claim: The integrand is nonnegative, so [F3] factors the position and momentum integrals: $$Z_N=\frac1{N!h^{dN}}\int_{\Lambda_N^N}\int_{\mathbb R^{dN}} e^{-\beta\sum_i|p_i|^2/(2m)}\,dp\,dq =\frac{V_N^N}{N!h^{dN}}\left(\int_\mathbb R e^{-\beta p^2/(2m)}\,dp\right)^{dN}.$$ By [F4]–[F5] the one-coordinate integral is $\sqrt{2\pi m/\beta}$, proving the stated exact formula with $\lambda_\beta=h\sqrt{\beta/(2\pi m)}$. The dimensions are consistent: $\lambda_\beta$ is a length, so $V_N^N/\lambda_\beta^{dN}$ and $Z_N$ are dimensionless. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5]

Let $G$ have the density in [A2]. By [F4]–[F5], it is normalized. Apply [F7] on $[-R,R]$ first with $u(x)=x$, $v'(x)=xe^{-x^2/2}$, and then with $u(x)=x^3$, $v'(x)=xe^{-x^2/2}$. In each case $v(x)=-e^{-x^2/2}$. Letting $R\to\infty$, the endpoint terms vanish by [F8], giving $\mathbb E G^2=1$ and $\mathbb E G^4=3$. Thus $\mathbb E(G^2-1)=0$ and $\mathbb E(G^2-1)^2=2$. Product measure and [F3] make distinct coordinates independent, so expanding the square and factoring cross integrals gives $$\mathbb E(A_N-1)^2=M^{-2}\sum_{a=1}^M2=2/M.$$ For any $\eta>0$, $\eta^2\mathbf1_{\{|A_N-1|>\eta\}}\le(A_N-1)^2$, so integration proves $P(|A_N-1|>\eta)\le2/(M\eta^2)\to0$. Hence $A_N\to1$ in probability. [A2, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F7, F8, algebra]

Monotonicity of $\log$ from [F6] gives $\int_1^N\log x\,dx\le\log N!\le\int_1^{N+1}\log x\,dx$, hence $\log N!=N\log N-N+O(\log(N+1))$. Substituting the exact $Z_N$ yields $$N^{-1}\log Z_N=\log(V_N/N)+1-d\log\lambda_\beta+o(1)\to-\log\rho+1-d\log\lambda_\beta.$$ Multiplication by $-\beta^{-1}$ proves the per-particle limit; multiplying by $N/V_N\to\rho$ proves the per-volume limit. [A1, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

Since $A_N>0$ almost surely, the shell-prepared variables are defined. Algebra gives $$\sum_{a=1}^{dN}\frac{(P_a^{\rm sh})^2}{2m} =\frac1{2\beta A_N}\sum_aG_a^2=\frac{M}{2\beta}=\frac{dN}{2\beta}.$$ This exact energy constraint holds on every outcome where $A_N>0$, an event of probability one since the joint Gaussian density assigns zero mass to the origin. [A2, step 1.2]

For fixed $r$, the scalar multiplier $A_N^{-1/2}$ tends to $1$ in probability by continuity at $1$ and step 1.2. Therefore $(P_1^{\rm sh},\ldots,P_r^{\rm sh})-(P_1^{\rm can},\ldots,P_r^{\rm can})$ tends to zero in probability: restrict first to the event $\sum_{a=1}^rG_a^2\le R^2$, where its norm is at most $\sqrt{m/\beta}R|A_N^{-1/2}-1|$, and then bound the complement by $P(\sum_{a=1}^rG_a^2>R^2)\le r/R^2$ using the second moment. For bounded continuous $\psi$, choose $R$ so this tail is small, use uniform continuity of $\psi$ on the compact ball of radius $2\sqrt{m/\beta}R$, and then use convergence in probability of the difference. On the complement the expectation difference is at most $2\|\psi\|_\infty$. Sending first $N\to\infty$ and then $R\to\infty$ proves the claimed expectation limit. [A2, F1, F3, step 1.2]

If positions are included, choose them independently and uniformly in the same cube under both preparations. After coordinatewise rescaling by the side length, every fixed position block already has the same uniform law in both models and is independent of the momentum vector. The same bounded-continuous test argument as in 2.3, first on compact sets and then on their small tails, proves the joint fixed-block limit. This does not change the energy computation because the Hamiltonian has no position dependence. [A1, A2, F1, step 2.3] ∎

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Fix dimension $d\ge1$, particle mass $m>0$, action reference $h>0$, inverse energy $\beta>0$, and positive cube volumes $V_N$ with $N/V_N\to\rho\in(0,\infty)$. For $N$ indistinguishable classical noninteracting particles in a cube of volume $V_N$, use the phase-space reference $dq\,dp/(N!h^{dN})$ and Hamiltonian $H_N(q,p)=\sum_{i=1}^N|p_i|^2/(2m)$. Define $\lambda_\beta=h\sqrt{\beta/(2\pi m)}$. Then the dimensionless partition integral and free-energy limits are
$$Z_N=\frac{V_N^N}{N!\lambda_\beta^{dN}},\quad\frac{-\beta^{-1}\log Z_N}{N}\longrightarrow\beta^{-1}[\log(\rho\lambda_\beta^d)-1],\quad\frac{-\beta^{-1}\log Z_N}{V_N}\longrightarrow\beta^{-1}\rho[\log(\rho\lambda_\beta^d)-1].$$
There is also the following finite-momentum-block limit. Let $M=dN$, let $G_1,\ldots,G_M$ be independent standard normal variables, set $A_N=M^{-1}\sum_{a=1}^MG_a^2$, and define canonical momenta $P_a^{\rm can}=\sqrt{m/\beta}\,G_a$ and shell-prepared momenta $P_a^{\rm sh}=\sqrt{m/\beta}\,G_a/\sqrt{A_N}$. The shell-prepared vector has exactly energy $dN/(2\beta)$, and for every fixed $r$ and bounded continuous $\psi:\mathbb R^r\to\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb E\psi(P_1^{\rm sh},\ldots,P_r^{\rm sh})\longrightarrow\mathbb E\psi(P_1^{\rm can},\ldots,P_r^{\rm can}).$$
This is weak convergence for each fixed block in this free-particle model. The shell preparation is the stated normalized-Gaussian construction, and no finite-width shell or interacting-gas equivalence is asserted.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

The normalized unit-intensity Poisson version is $Z_Q(L;z,\beta)=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,\mathrm{free}}}]$; since the Poisson density contributes $e^{-V_L}$, $\Xi(L;z,\beta)=e^{V_L}Z_Q(L;z,\beta)$.

For the unit cells $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$, there are constants $A>0$ and $B\geq0$ such that every finite configuration satisfies
$$H_\phi(\omega)\geq A\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}N_{C_i}(\omega)^2-BN(\omega).$$
Only finitely many summands are nonzero.
Then $\mathcal H_c$ is compact and sequentially compact in $\tau_L$.

Let $d\geq1$, let $P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$, with this class defined in [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], be ergodic under the full translation group $\mathbb R^d$, and suppose its specific relative entropy $I(P)=\gamma$ relative to the unit-intensity Poisson law $Q$ is finite.
A real measurable function $f$ on $\Omega$ is local if there is a bounded Borel set $A$ such that $f$ is measurable with respect to the restriction $\omega\mapsto\omega|_A$.
Let $\phi$ be stable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], with stability constant $B$, and fix $a,\beta>0$.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$.

Then
$$D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)=D(P_X\Vert Q_X)+\int_X D(P_{Y|X=x}\Vert Q_Y)\,P_X(dx).$$
More generally, for nested standard-Borel observations $R$ and $S$ with $R$ a measurable function of $S$, and a fixed probability reference $Q_Y$ for a further variable $Y$, the conditional increments
$$G(R):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|R}\Vert Q_Y)\right],\qquad G(S):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|S}\Vert Q_Y)\right]$$
satisfy $0\leq G(R)\leq G(S)$ whenever the joint relative entropy is finite.

If $P$ and $Q$ are probability measures on the same measurable space, define
$$D(P\Vert Q)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int h\log h\,dQ,&P\ll Q\text{ and }h=dP/dQ,\\+\infty,&P\not\ll Q.\end{cases}$$
Use $0\log0=0$.

derivations.claim: Georgii's Theorem 1 [L1] gives existence of $\Phi(P)$ and lower semicontinuity for every stationary finite-intensity law. Its Euclidean radial tail hypothesis follows from ours: $|x|_\infty\leq|x|_2\leq\sqrt d\,|x|_\infty$, so replacing $\psi(r)$ by $\psi(r/\sqrt d)$ preserves monotonicity and finite weighted integral by a change of variables. The stable-plus-positive-core definition matches the source's superstable condition after choosing a smaller Euclidean core ball. Thus $\Phi$ has exactly the domain and convention in the Statement.

The cell estimate [F2] and $\beta>0$ imply $J=I+\beta\Phi-\rho\log z$ is lower semicontinuous and coercive on bounded-$J$ sets: the Poisson entropy variational inequality with bounded truncations of $aN_{C_0}$ gives $I(P)\geq a\rho(P)-(e^a-1)$; the pointwise square inequality gives $E_PN_{C_0}^2\geq\rho(P)^2$. Hence bounded $J$ bounds $\rho$, $I$, and $\Phi$ from above. A finite candidate exists: take independent Bernoulli occupancy of widely separated small cubes, at most one absolutely continuously distributed point per cube, and a uniform random lattice phase. Each tile has finite relative entropy to Poisson, and the summable regular tail bounds its absolute intertile energy per volume. Thus $J$ is proper. By [F3] and the choice assumptions [A1], its bounded sublevels are compact in $\tau_L$.

For the finite-volume Gibbs tilt $G_{L,z,\beta,bc}$, direct integration gives $$ L^{-d}\log Z_{L,z,\beta,bc} =-L^{-d}D(G_{L,z,\beta,bc}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L}) -\beta L^{-d}E_GH_{L,bc} +L^{-d}\log z\,E_GN. $$ Georgii's Theorem 2 [L2], applied with the present superstable regular interaction and $F=0$, supplies the matching upper and lower empirical-field bounds and the free/periodic pressure limit. Its upper proof uses this entropy identity, block stationarization, and the superstable cell cutoff; its lower proof conditions finite blocks on bounded finite-energy events, inserts empty corridors, and applies the spatial likelihood limit. The inspected source hypotheses match [F1]–[F8]: the Poisson reference is independent unit intensity, $\tau_L$ is the local-tame topology [F5], entropy compactness is [F3], and the energy-density interface is [L1]. The theorem therefore yields $$ p_Q(z,\beta)=-\min_P\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\} $$ for both boundary conditions, with compact variational sublevels.

The minimum is attained: a minimizing sequence lies in a finite sublevel by the sparse finite candidate in step 1.2; compactness [F3] gives a convergent subsequence and lower semicontinuity from step 1.1 gives a minimizer. The set of minimizers is the closed minimum level within that compact sublevel, hence nonempty and compact. This agrees with the compact-sublevel conclusion in [L2].

The unit-intensity Poisson law on $\Lambda_L$ has density $e^{-L^d}/N!$ relative to Lebesgue measure on the $N$-point sector. Therefore the physical partition $\Xi_{L,z,\beta}=e^{L^d}Z_{L,z,\beta,\mathrm{free}}$; its log rate is $p_Q+1$. This is only a positional normalization conversion.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Assume AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, and HB. Let $\phi$ be superstable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], and fix $z,\beta>0$. For stationary finite-intensity configuration laws, let $I(P)$ be relative entropy density with respect to the independent unit-intensity Poisson law, $\rho(P)=E_PN_{[0,1)^d}$, and $\Phi(P)$ the limiting positional energy density. The existence and lower semicontinuity of $\Phi$ under these hypotheses are part of the proof below. For free and periodic cubes define
$$Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}\!\left[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,bc}}\right],\qquad bc\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{per}\}.$$
Then the limit $p_Q(z,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}$ exists, is independent of $bc$, and
$$p_Q(z,\beta)=-\min_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
The minimizer set is nonempty and compact in the local-tame topology $\tau_L$. This theorem concerns positional configurations only. If $\Xi_{L,z,\beta}$ is instead normalized against Lebesgue measure with $1/N!$, then $\Xi_{L,z,\beta}=e^{L^d}Z_{L,z,\beta,\mathrm{free}}$, so its logarithmic rate is $p_Q+1$.

citations.quote: For any finite supporting activity $z>0$ of $F_\beta$ at $\rho$, these empirical fields concentrate in every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood of the minimizer set of $I+\beta\Phi-\rho\log z$.

Let $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, let $C_{L,N_L}$ be the free-boundary positional canonical law with exactly $N_L$ particles, and let $R_{L,\omega}$ be its periodized empirical field from [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]].

For free and periodic cubes define
$$Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}\!\left[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,bc}}\right],\qquad bc\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{per}\}.$$
Then the limit $p_Q(z,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}$ exists, is independent of $bc$, and
$$p_Q(z,\beta)=-\min_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
The minimizer set is nonempty and compact in the local-tame topology $\tau_L$.

Define its **periodized empirical field**
$$R_{L,\omega}:=\frac1{L^d}\int_{\Lambda_L}\delta_{T_x\omega^{(L)}}\,dx.$$
The integral is the push-forward of normalized Lebesgue measure on $\Lambda_L$ under $x\mapsto T_x\omega^{(L)}$.

For $L>0$ and a finite configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$ with $N(\omega)=N$, the measure $R_{L,\omega}$ of [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]] is a stationary probability law of finite intensity and
$$\rho(R_{L,\omega})=\frac{N}{L^d}.$$
For any probability law $C_L$ on finite configurations in $\Lambda_L$ with $E_{C_L}N<\infty$, its empirical-field barycenter $\bar C_L$ is also a stationary probability law of finite intensity and $\rho(\bar C_L)=E_{C_L}N/L^d$.

derivations.claim: Let $C_L$ be the periodic exact-$N_L$ canonical law. For $|t|<\beta$, $$ E_{C_L}e^{tH_{\mathrm{per}}} =Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta-t)/Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta). $$ By [F1], the normalized log moment generating function converges to $F_{\beta-t}(\rho)-F_\beta(\rho)$, whose derivative at zero is $e$. For any fixed $\epsilon>0$, choose small positive and negative $t$ so the Chernoff exponents for $H/L^d\geq e+\epsilon$ and $H/L^d\leq e-\epsilon$ are strictly negative. Hence the canonical probability outside the fixed $\epsilon$-window tends to zero.

Choose increasing thresholds $L_k$ so that for every $L\geq L_k$ the probability outside the $1/k$ window is at most $1/k$. Set $k(L)=\max\{k:L_k\leq L\}$ and $\delta_L=1/k(L)$. Then $\delta_L\downarrow0$ and the canonical probability of the selected shell tends to one. Positivity of the canonical weight on the shell implies positive Poisson reference measure, so the shell law is defined eventually.

Let $U$ be any open $\tau_L$ neighborhood of $P_*$ and let $S_L$ be the selected shell event. On $S_L$, the periodic canonical density relative to the uniform positional law lies between $e^{-\beta L^d(e+\delta_L)}$ and $e^{-\beta L^d(e-\delta_L)}$. Hence
$$Q_{\Lambda_L}(R_{L,\omega}\notin U\mid S_L)\leq\frac{e^{2\beta\delta_L L^d}}{C_L^{\mathrm{per}}(S_L)}\,C_L^{\mathrm{per}}(R_{L,\omega}\notin U).$$
By step 2.1, $C_L^{\mathrm{per}}(S_L)\to1$. By [F1], the last probability has a strictly negative exponential rate. Since $\delta_L\to0$, the right side tends to zero. Thus the uniform shell empirical field converges in probability to $P_*$.

The free exact-$N$ empirical field converges in probability by [F2]. The periodic grand empirical fields obey the good LDP [L1]; its unique zero is $P_*$ by [F3], so the probability outside each neighborhood of $P_*$ tends to zero. derivations.claim: Put $q=ae^{\beta B}$. For every $N$-point configuration, $0\leq e^{-\beta H_\phi}\leq e^{\beta BN}$ by [A1]. Applying [F3] to the finite-volume integral gives $Z(L,N;\beta)\leq(qL^d)^N/N!$. Summing by [F4] yields $\Xi_L\leq e^{qL^d}$; the empty configuration contributes exactly $1$, so $\Xi_L\geq1$.

Choose $K>eq+1$ and an integer cutoff $n_\ell$ with $K\ell^d<n_\ell\leq K\ell^d+1$. For $N>n_\ell$, $1\leq e^{N-K\ell^d}$, so $$ \sum_{N>n_\ell}Z(\ell,N;\beta)\leq e^{-K\ell^d}\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{(eq\ell^d)^N}{N!}=e^{(eq-K)\ell^d}\leq e^{-\ell^d}. $$ Because $\Xi_\ell\geq1$, the truncated sum $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}=\sum_{N=0}^{n_\ell}Z(\ell,N;\beta)$ satisfies $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}\geq(1-e^{-\ell^d})\Xi_\ell$.

Fix a core side $\ell$ and a gap $g>2R_0$. Place $M=\lfloor L/(\ell+g)\rfloor^d$ disjoint core cubes of side $\ell$ in $[0,L)^d$ on the lattice of spacing $\ell+g$. Restrict every core to at most $n_\ell$ particles. If two core indices differ by maximum norm $m\geq1$, every pair between them has separation at least $mg$ in maximum norm. The number of offsets in shell $m$ is $(2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d\leq c_dm^{d-1}$. By [F1], the sum of positive cross-core pair energies is therefore at most $$ D_{L,\ell,g}\leq c_dM n_\ell^2\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg). $$ Negative cross-core energies only increase the Boltzmann weight. Splitting the grand sum by the particle counts in these disjoint cores, Tonelli [F5] and the multinomial coefficient show that the global $N!$ cancels the assignments of labeled coordinates to cores. Thus $$ \Xi_L\geq e^{-\beta D_{L,\ell,g}}(\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut})^M. $$

Divide the last inequality by $L^d$ and let $L\to\infty$ with $\ell,g$ fixed. Since $M/L^d\to(\ell+g)^{-d}$, [F2] gives $$ \liminf_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L\geq\left(\frac{\ell}{\ell+g}\right)^d\left[\ell^{-d}\log\Xi_\ell+\ell^{-d}\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})-C_dK_1^2\left(\frac{\ell}{g}\right)^d\eta(g)\right], $$ where $K_1=K+1$ bounds $n_\ell/\ell^d$ for $\ell\geq1$ and $C_d$ absorbs the fixed shell-count constant and $\beta$.

The numbers $p_\ell=\ell^{-d}\log\Xi_\ell$ lie in $[0,q]$ by step 1.1, so choose $\ell_j\to\infty$ with $p_{\ell_j}\to\limsup_{\ell\to\infty}p_\ell$. Set $g=g(\ell_j)$ from [F2]. Then $g/\ell_j\to0$, the volume fraction tends to $1$, the cutoff logarithm divided by $\ell_j^d$ tends to zero, and the cross-core error tends to zero. Step 4.1 therefore yields $\liminf_{L\to\infty}p_L\geq\limsup_{L\to\infty}p_L$. The reverse inequality is automatic for every real sequence, so the limit exists; step 1.1 makes it finite.

Let $\phi$ be stable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], with stability constant $B$, and fix $a,\beta>0$. For free-boundary cubes define $\Xi_L(a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$. Then

citations.quote: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.
Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable. Then $\int\liminf_{n\to\infty} f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu$.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable with $f_n\le f_{n+1}$ and $f_n\to f$ pointwise. Then $\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu$, including infinite values. Also, for measurable $f,g\ge0$, $\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu$. For every $c\ge0$, $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$; the integral is also linear on real integrable functions.

derivations.claim: The exceptional convergence and domination sets have a common measurable null superset $N$, by countable subadditivity: disjointifying $N_1,N_2,\ldots$ into successive differences and applying countable additivity gives $\mu(\bigcup_jN_j)\le\sum_j\mu(N_j)=0$. A nonnegative measurable function supported on $N$ has integral zero, since every simple minorant is supported there. Redefine all $f_n$ and $f$ to be zero on $N$; this preserves measurability and their integrals, and now convergence and domination hold everywhere. Also $|f|\le g$ pointwise, hence $f$ is integrable.

First take all functions real. The nonnegative functions $f_n+g$ converge pointwise to $f+g$. Fatou gives $\int(f+g)\le\liminf_n\int(f_n+g)=\int g+\liminf_n\int f_n$, so $\int f\le\liminf_n\int f_n$. Applying Fatou to $g-f_n\ge0$ gives $\int(g-f)\le\liminf_n\int(g-f_n)=\int g-\limsup_n\int f_n$, hence $\limsup_n\int f_n\le\int f$. Additivity of integrable signed integrals follows by writing each as a difference of its positive and negative parts and using [F3]. The inequalities imply convergence of integrals.

For complex $f_n$, apply step 2.1 separately to their real and imaginary parts, each dominated by $g$; their integral limits combine to $\int f$. To prove $L^1$ convergence, apply Fatou to the nonnegative functions $2g-|f_n-f|$, which converge to $2g$; it gives $2\int g\le2\int g-\limsup_n\int|f_n-f|$, so the latter limsup is zero. Therefore $\int|f_n-f|\to0$ as claimed.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

citations.quote: Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$; then $(p_i)$ is a countable probability law. For any real observable $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, and suppose $f$ has derivatives through order $n+1$ on the closed interval between $a$ and $x$, with the usual endpoint continuity. If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ throughout that interval, then
$$|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le \frac{M}{\iota((n+1)!)}|x-a|^{n+1}.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] to $s_B$ at $u_0$ with increment $-E_i$. It gives $s_B(u_0-E_i)=s_B(u_0)-\beta E_i+r_i$ where $|r_i|\le M E_i^2/2\le\delta$.

The marginal is therefore $p_i=q_i e^{r_i}/C$, where $C:=\sum_jq_je^{r_j}$. The bounds $e^{-\delta}\le e^{r_j}\le e^\delta$ and $\sum_jq_j=1$ imply $e^{-\delta}\le C\le e^\delta$, so $e^{-2\delta}\le p_i/q_i\le e^{2\delta}$.

For $x\in[e^{-2\delta},e^{2\delta}]$, $|x-1|\le e^{2\delta}-1$. Thus $\sum_i|p_i-q_i|=\sum_iq_i|p_i/q_i-1|\le(e^{2\delta}-1)\sum_iq_i=e^{2\delta}-1$. The case $\delta=0$ is included and gives equality of the laws.

case_scope.source_excerpt: Let $I$ be a finite nonempty subsystem state set, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $|E_i|\le L$ for $L\ge0$, and let the dimensionless bath entropy $s_B$ be $C^2$ on an open interval $U$ containing $[u_0-L,u_0+L]$, with $|s_B''(u)|\le M$ on that closed interval for $M\ge0$. Use one energy unit for $E_i,u_0,L$, so $\beta=s_B'(u_0)$ has inverse-energy units and $M$ has inverse-energy-squared units; $\delta=ML^2/2$ is dimensionless. Put $Z:=\sum_{j\in I}e^{-\beta E_j}$ and $q_i:=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$. Suppose the joint shell weights induce the normalized subsystem law $p_i:=e^{s_B(u_0-E_i)}/\sum_{j\in I}e^{s_B(u_0-E_j)}$. Then $|s_B(u_0-E_i)-s_B(u_0)+\beta E_i|\le\delta$ for every $i$, and $\sum_i|p_i-q_i|\le e^{2\delta}-1$.

boundaries.evidence: For M=0, delta=0 and the ratio bound in step 3.1 gives p=q exactly.

citations.quote: Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), with additive identity $0_F$, multiplicative
identity $1_F$, and the field axioms as stated there. A **vector space over $F$**,
also called an **$F$-vector space**, consists of

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).

A natural number is a von Neumann natural ([[def-natural-numbers]]), that is a
set, and $n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$
([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). Taking $X = n$ therefore gives

$$F^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to F \,\},$$

whose elements are written $x = (x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})$ with $x_i := x(i)$ for
$i < n$. **The coordinates are indexed from $0$**, because $0 \in n$ whenever
$n \ne 0$ and $n \notin n$ always. The operations read

$$(x + y)_i = x_i + y_i, \qquad (\lambda x)_i = \lambda x_i \qquad (i < n),$$

and the zero of $F^{n}$ is the tuple all of whose coordinates are $0_F$.

derivations.claim: If $b$ solves the system and $\lambda_j\ge0$ with $\sum_j\lambda_jc_j=0$, multiply row $j$ by $\lambda_j$ and add the finitely many inequalities. The left side is $(\sum_j\lambda_jc_j)\cdot b=0$ by [F2]; hence $0\ge\sum_j\lambda_jh_j$. This proves necessity.

For sufficiency, prove by induction on $n$ the alternative: if the finite system has no solution, there is a nonnegative combination of its rows whose coefficient vector is zero and whose right side is positive. If $n=0$, every row has zero left side; infeasibility means some $h_j>0$, and that single row is the certificate. If $m=0$, the system is feasible, so this case cannot occur under the induction claim's antecedent.

Let $n>0$ and assume the alternative for $n-1$ variables. Write $c_j=(a_j,\alpha_j)$ with $a_j\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and split the row indices into $P=\{j:\alpha_j>0\}$, $N=\{j:\alpha_j<0\}$, and $Z=\{j:\alpha_j=0\}$. Retain each row $(a_j,h_j)$ for $j\in Z$. For every $p\in P$ and $q\in N$, add the reduced row $((-\alpha_q)a_p+\alpha_p a_q,\;(-\alpha_q)h_p+\alpha_p h_q)$. Every multiplier used is positive.

The reduced system in $u\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ is feasible exactly when the original is. Indeed, a solution $(u,t)$ implies every retained inequality; adding row $p$ multiplied by $-\alpha_q>0$ to row $q$ multiplied by $\alpha_p>0$ cancels $t$ and gives each pair row. Conversely, if $u$ satisfies the reduced system, rows in $P$ impose finitely many lower bounds $t\ge(h_p-a_p\cdot u)/\alpha_p$, and rows in $N$ impose finitely many upper bounds $t\le(h_q-a_q\cdot u)/\alpha_q$. Each pair row is exactly the inequality that its lower bound is no greater than its upper bound. If both sets are nonempty, their finite maximum lower bound is at most their finite minimum upper bound, so choose $t$ between them. If only lower bounds occur choose their maximum; if only upper bounds occur choose their minimum; if neither occurs choose $t=0$. Thus the original system has a solution.

If the original system is infeasible, step 1.4 makes the reduced system infeasible. By induction there are nonnegative multipliers on reduced rows with zero combined first $n-1$ coordinates and positive combined right side. Lift each retained zero-row multiplier to its original row; lift each pair-row multiplier $\mu_{pq}$ to coefficients $-\alpha_q\mu_{pq}$ on row $p$ and $\alpha_p\mu_{pq}$ on row $q$. All lifted coefficients are nonnegative. Every pair lift has last coordinate $(-\alpha_q)\alpha_p+\alpha_p\alpha_q=0$; the total first coordinates vanish by the reduced certificate, and its right side remains positive. This is the required certificate for the original system and completes the induction.

If the stated multiplier condition holds, the certificate from step 2.1 cannot exist, because it would have zero combined left coefficient and positive combined right side. Therefore the system is feasible. Together with step 1.1 this proves both directions, including the empty-variable base case in step 1.2, the zero/positive/negative sign partition and bound reconstruction in steps 1.3–1.4, and the lifted certificate in step 2.1.

citations.quote: Fix integers $d\ge1$, $L\ge1$, a finite alphabet $\mathcal A$ of cardinality $q\ge1$, and a finite, possibly empty, list of interaction shapes $S_a\subset\mathbb Z^d$, each nonempty and contained in $[-R,R]^d$ for some integer $R\ge0$. $\|\Phi_a\|_\infty$ is finite because its domain is finite. For each shape let $\Phi_a:\mathcal A^{S_a}\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded interaction function. Set $J_0:=\sum_a\|\Phi_a\|_\infty$. On $\Lambda_L:=\{1,\ldots,L\}^d$, define the free-boundary energy $H_L(s):=\sum_a\sum_{x:x+S_a\subseteq\Lambda_L}\Phi_a((s_{x+u})_{u\in S_a})$, for configurations $s\in\mathcal A^{\Lambda_L}$. For $\beta>0$, define the finite partition sum $Z_L(\beta):=\sum_{s\in\mathcal A^{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_L(s)}$ and normalized log-partition density $p_L(\beta):=L^{-d}\log Z_L(\beta)$.

For each shape let $\Phi_a:\mathcal A^{S_a}\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded interaction function. Set $J_0:=\sum_a\|\Phi_a\|_\infty$. On $\Lambda_L:=\{1,\ldots,L\}^d$, define the free-boundary energy $H_L(s):=\sum_a\sum_{x:x+S_a\subseteq\Lambda_L}\Phi_a((s_{x+u})_{u\in S_a})$, for configurations $s\in\mathcal A^{\Lambda_L}$. For $\beta>0$, define the finite partition sum $Z_L(\beta):=\sum_{s\in\mathcal A^{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_L(s)}$ and normalized log-partition density $p_L(\beta):=L^{-d}\log Z_L(\beta)$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-integers]]) with $b > 0$. Then there exist
integers $q$ and $r$ with

$$a \;=\; qb + r, \qquad 0 \le r < b,$$

and the pair $(q,r)$ with these two properties is unique.

We say $b$ **divides** $a$, written $b \mid a$, when $a = qb$ for some
$q \in \mathbb{Z}$; by the above, for $b > 0$ this holds exactly when the
remainder $r$ is $0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: Write $V=L^d$ and $J_0=\sum_a\|\Phi_a\|_\infty$. Each configuration satisfies $|H_L(s)|\le J_0V$, so $q^Ve^{-\beta J_0V}\le Z_L\le q^Ve^{\beta J_0V}$. Hence $p_L$ is bounded above and below uniformly in $L$.

Fix an integer block length $\ell>2R$ and write $L=k\ell+r$ with $0\le r<\ell$ using [F3]. Partition $\Lambda_L$ into $k^d$ disjoint $\ell$-cubes and an outer remainder. Form $H_{L,\ell}^{\rm cut}$ by retaining only interactions whose entire support lies in one full cube and assigning zero energy to remainder sites. For a fixed shape, every eligible anchor lies in $[1-R,L+R]^d$. If its support crosses an internal block seam, its coordinate normal to that seam lies in at most $2R+1$ integer positions; the other coordinates have at most $(L+2R)^{d-1}$ choices. If it is not in such a seam strip but the interaction is omitted, its support meets the outer remainder, so its anchor lies within $\ell+2R+1$ layers of one of the $d$ outer faces. Counting at most $d(k-1)$ internal seams and $d$ outer faces bounds the omitted anchors per shape by $d(2R+1)(L/\ell)(L+2R)^{d-1}+d(\ell+2R+1)(L+2R)^{d-1}$. Therefore $\sup_s|H_L(s)-H_{L,\ell}^{\rm cut}(s)|\le J_0d[(2R+1)(L/\ell)+\ell+2R+1](L+2R)^{d-1}$.

If two energies on a finite state set differ pointwise by at most $D$, their partition sums satisfy $e^{-\beta D}Z'\le Z\le e^{\beta D}Z'$, so their log partition sums differ by at most $\beta D$ using [F2]. The cut energy factorizes over the cubes and has zero-energy remainder, hence $Z_{L,\ell}^{\rm cut}=Z_\ell^{k^d}q^{L^d-k^d\ell^d}$. Divide the comparison by $L^d$ and let $L\to\infty$ with $\ell$ fixed; the remainder fraction tends to zero, $k^d/L^d\to\ell^{-d}$, and the energy error has limsup at most $2^{d-1}\beta J_0d(2R+1)/\ell$.

It follows for every $\ell>2R$ that $\limsup_L p_L\le p_\ell+2^{d-1}\beta J_0d(2R+1)/\ell$ and $\liminf_L p_L\ge p_\ell-2^{d-1}\beta J_0d(2R+1)/\ell$. Thus $0\le\limsup_Lp_L-\liminf_Lp_L\le2^d\beta J_0d(2R+1)/\ell$ for every such $\ell$. Letting $\ell\to\infty$ makes the difference zero; boundedness from step 1.1 then gives a finite limit.
For $\widetilde H_L$, the finite-state comparison of step 2.1 gives $|L^{-d}\log\widetilde Z_L-p_L|\le\beta C_b/L$, which tends to zero. Its limit is therefore the same.

Assume the superstable regular model of [[thm-tdmath-continuum-variational-pressure]], $\beta>0$, and an interior attainable density $\rho>0$. Let $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, let $C_{L,N_L}$ be the free-boundary positional canonical law with exactly $N_L$ particles, and let $R_{L,\omega}$ be its periodized empirical field from [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]]. Choose any finite supporting activity $z>0$ of $F_\beta$ at $\rho$ and set
$$\mathcal M_{z,\beta}:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
For every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$,
$$C_{L,N_L}\{\omega:R_{L,\omega}\in U\}\longrightarrow1.$$
If $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}=\{P_*\}$, then $R_{L,\omega}\to P_*$ in probability in $\tau_L$. This is local observable equivalence for a uniformly sampled bulk location; it makes no claim about the raw finite-box law at a fixed origin or about uniqueness for every interaction.

Assume the superstable regular model of [[thm-tdmath-continuum-variational-pressure]], $\beta>0$, and an interior attainable density $\rho>0$. Let $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, let $C_{L,N_L}$ be the free-boundary positional canonical law with exactly $N_L$ particles, and let $R_{L,\omega}$ be its periodized empirical field from [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]]. Choose any finite supporting activity $z>0$ of $F_\beta$ at $\rho$ and set
$$\mathcal M_{z,\beta}:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
For every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$,
$$C_{L,N_L}\{\omega:R_{L,\omega}\in U\}\longrightarrow1.$$
If $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}=\{P_*\}$, then $R_{L,\omega}\to P_*$ in probability in $\tau_L$. This is local observable equivalence for a uniformly sampled bulk location; it makes no claim about the raw finite-box law at a fixed origin or about uniqueness for every interaction.
