citations.quote:
Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with finite slope $P_i(x)$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for every simple state $x$, the forward sector $A_x=\{y\in\Gamma_i:x\prec y\}$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$. For collinear $y=tx+(1-t)z$, $0<t<1$, $y\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$, and $x\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$.
Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], every forward sector $A_x$ has nonempty interior in its ambient simple domain $\Gamma_i$.

Let $C$ be a nonempty convex set in a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$ of dimension $k\ge1$, let $\operatorname{aff}C=H$, and put $K=\overline{C}^{\,H}$. If $z\in\partial_H K$ (that is, $z\in K$ and every relative neighborhood of $z$ meets $H\setminus K$), then there is a nonzero linear functional $\ell$ on the translation space of $H$ such that $\ell(q-z)\le0$ for all $q\in C$. If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine dimension at most $d-2$, then every $z\in C$ has at least two distinct ambient supporting hyperplanes containing $\operatorname{aff}C$.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be closed and convex with nonempty interior, $d\ge1$, and let $x\in\partial K$. Suppose $K$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$. Choose its inward unit normal $n$, so $n\cdot(q-x)\ge0$ for every $q\in K$. Then for every $v$ with $n\cdot v>0$, there is $\delta>0$ such that $x+tv\in\operatorname{int}K$ for every $0<t<\delta$.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be finite and convex. For every $x_0\in U$, there are a neighborhood $V$ of $x_0$ and $L<\infty$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|$ for all $x,y\in V$. The same conclusion holds for finite concave functions by applying the result to $-f$.
Let $L\ge0$, $T>0$, and let $f:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous. If $f(t)\le L\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$ for every $t\in[0,T]$, then $f(t)=0$ for every $t\in[0,T]$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

derivations.claim: For fixed $x=(u_x,v_x)$, the vertical section $I_x:=\{u:(u,v_x)\in A_x\}$ is a relatively closed convex interval by [F1]. The support plane at $x$ confines it to one side of $u_x$. Its inward normal has nonzero energy component, so [F4] gives a nontrivial interior vertical segment on that side.

The fiber orientation is locally constant in $v$. At any $x$, choose one vertical point just inside the supported half-space and one just outside; by [F4] the inside point can be chosen in $\operatorname{int}A_x$. Openness of $\Gamma_i$ and of the interior and exterior regions preserves these memberships on nearby fibers. Each such fiber therefore meets $\partial A_x$ between these two energy values. A support of $A_x$ at that boundary point also supports the point's own sector and so has its S2 orientation; the inside/outside placement fixes that orientation. Thus nearby fibers have the same sign as the fiber through $x$. Since $\Gamma_i$ is convex, it is connected; a locally constant two-valued sign is constant.

Let $u,w$ be two $C^1$ graph solutions of $Dq=-P_i(q,v)$ on a common open domain, and suppose $u(v_0)=w(v_0)$. Since $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz, choose a convex neighborhood of $(u(v_0),v_0)$ on which one Lipschitz constant $L$ works. Continuity of $u,w$ lets us choose a convex ball about $v_0$ whose closure lies in the common domain and whose two graph images stay in that neighborhood; take any $v$ in a smaller concentric ball. Put $d=v-v_0$ and $\gamma(t)=v_0+td$ for $0\le t\le1$. By [F8], $r(t)=u(\gamma(t))-w(\gamma(t))$ is $C^1$ and
$r'(t)=[-P_i(u(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))+P_i(w(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))]\cdot d.$
The local Lipschitz bound for $P_i$ gives $|r'(t)|\le L\|d\||r(t)|$. The derivative is continuous, hence integrable by [F10]; [F9] gives $r(t)=\int_0^t r'(s)\,ds$; hence $h(t):=|r(t)|\le L\|d\|\int_0^t h(s)\,ds$. Apply [F6] on $[0,1]$ to obtain $h=0$. Thus $u=w$ near $v_0$. Along any polygonal path in the common open domain, the set of path parameters at which equality holds is closed by continuity and open by this local result; since the path interval is connected and the set is nonempty, equality holds along the whole path. Every open connected subset of Euclidean space is polygonally connected: points reachable from a fixed point by finitely many segments in small balls form a nonempty relatively open and relatively closed set. Therefore equality extends throughout each common connected domain.

The convex, relatively closed interval $I_x$ contains a nontrivial segment on the inward side by step 1.1 and [F4]. Suppose it does not contain the whole open $\Gamma_i$-fiber on that side. Its endpoint $b$ toward that side then lies inside $\Gamma_i$; relative closedness puts $b$ in $I_x$, so the interval from $x$ to $b$ is a compact nondegenerate interval by [F7]. Let $x_1$ be its midpoint. Since $x_1\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_{x_1}\subseteq A_x$. The supporting plane of $A_{x_1}$ has nonzero energy coefficient, so its vertical section lies wholly on one side of $x_1$; being contained in $I_x$, it lies in one half of $[x,b]$ and has at most half its length. It is nonempty and closed relative to $[x,b]$, hence compact. Repeat: take the midpoint $x_{k+1}$ of the current compact interval $I_{x_k}$; then $x_k\prec x_{k+1}$, so the next section is nested inside the current one and again has at most half its length. The nested compact intervals have a common limit point $x_\infty\in\Gamma_i$ by [F7], and their lengths tend to zero. Relative closedness puts $x_\infty$ in every $A_{x_k}$, hence $A_{x_\infty}\subseteq A_{x_k}$ by transitivity. Its vertical section is therefore only $\{x_\infty\}$, contradicting the nontrivial interior vertical segment at $x_\infty$ supplied by [F4]. Thus $I_x$ contains the whole open fiber on its inward side.

All states on a fixed work-coordinate fiber have the same orientation. If $x$ is oriented upward and a state $z$ above it were oriented downward, the full upward section from step 2.1 gives $x\prec z$, and the full downward section from $z$ gives $z\prec w$ for a state $w$ below $x$, contradicting the support at $x$. If a state $y$ below an upward $x$ were oriented downward, choose $z$ above $x$ with $x\prec z$; the first collinear implication in [F1], applied to $x$ between $y$ and $z$, gives $y\prec x$, contradicting the downward support at $y$. The reversed argument handles a downward $x$.
Adopt the coordinate convention $\varepsilon_i=1$. Step 2.1 and the common orientation give $x\prec y$ exactly for $u_y\ge u_x$ at fixed $v$, with strict comparison for $u_y>u_x$.

Put $\rho_x=\pi_v(\partial A_x)$. At a boundary point $z\in\partial A_x$, [F3] supplies a support to $A_x$. Because $A_z\subseteq A_x$, that plane also supports $A_z$ and equals its unique S2 plane. Its finite slope gives a nonvertical inward direction; [F4] supplies nearby vertical points inside $A_x$, while the opposite side is outside by the support. Neighborhoods of one inside and one outside point show every nearby work fiber meets $\partial A_x$. Hence $\rho_x$ is open. It is connected because S3 makes $\partial A_x$ arcwise connected and projection is continuous. By step 4.1, every vertical fiber over $\rho_x$ has exactly one boundary energy; call it $u_x(v)$.

For $v,v'\in\rho_x$, convexity of $A_x$ puts every convex combination of their boundary states in $A_x$. On any sufficiently small convex ball in $\rho_x$, the unique-boundary property and upward orientation make $u_x$ the least energy in each fiber. Therefore $u_x(tv+(1-t)v')\le t u_x(v)+(1-t)u_x(v')$, so $u_x$ is finite and convex there. It is locally Lipschitz by [F5]. The inward support at $(u_x(v),v)$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\ge -P_i(u_x(v),v)\cdot(v'-v).$
The support at $(u_x(v'),v')$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\le -P_i(u_x(v'),v')\cdot(v'-v).$
Local Lipschitz continuity of $u_x$ and $P_i$ makes the difference between these linear bounds $O(\|v'-v\|^2)$. Thus $u_x$ is differentiable with derivative $-P_i(u_x(v),v)$, and that derivative is locally Lipschitz. Hence $u_x\in C^1$ with locally Lipschitz derivative.

If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$. The boundary graphs agree at $v_y$ and solve the same differential equation. The set of $v\in\rho_y$ where $v\in\rho_x$ and $u_y(v)=u_x(v)$ is nonempty, open by step 1.3, and closed by continuity and relative closedness of $\partial A_x$. Connectedness of $\rho_y$ makes it all of $\rho_y$. This shows $\rho_y\subseteq\rho_x$. The same argument, using relative closedness of $\partial A_y$, shows $\rho_y$ is relatively closed in connected $\rho_x$; it is relatively open because both projections are open. Hence $\rho_x=\rho_y$ and the boundary graphs agree. In particular $x\in\partial A_y$, so $y\prec x$; together with $y\in A_x$ and transitivity this gives $A_x=A_y$.

boundaries.reason: Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], each simple domain has one orientation sign $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$, constant across the domain, such that at fixed work coordinate $v$, $x\prec y$ exactly when $\varepsilon_i(u_y-u_x)\ge0$. Boundary empty: The item makes no empty boundary claim; this case does not apply to its stated result.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], each simple domain has one orientation sign $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$, constant across the domain, such that at fixed work coordinate $v$, $x\prec y$ exactly when $\varepsilon_i(u_y-u_x)\ge0$. In coordinates oriented so $\varepsilon_i=1$, for each $x\in\Gamma_i$ the projection $\rho_x$ of $\partial_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ onto work coordinates is open and connected; the boundary is the graph $(u_x(v),v)$ of a $C^1$ function with locally Lipschitz derivative

$$Du_x(v)=-P_i(u_x(v),v).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and $\Sigma$-measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). Then:

1. there is a unique operator $\Phi_E(f)\in\mathcal B(H)$ with
   $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,y\rangle=\int f\,dE_{x,y}\qquad(x,y\in H),$$
   and for every sequence $(s_n)$ of complex simple functions with
   $\|f-s_n\|_\infty\to0$ one has $\|\Phi_E(f)-\int s_n\,dE\|\to0$: the integral
   is obtained from uniform simple approximations and is independent of the
   approximating sequence;
2. $\|\Phi_E(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, and for every $x\in H$
$$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,x\rangle=\int f\,dE_x,\qquad \|\Phi_E(f)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x ;$$
3. the exact norm is the **$E$-essential supremum**
$$\|f\|_{E,\infty}:=\sup\bigl\{\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}:\ x\in H,\ \|x\|=1\bigr\}, \qquad \|\Phi_E(f)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty},$$
   where $\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}$ denotes the essential supremum of the real measurable function $|f|$ with respect to
   the finite measure $E_x$ ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a
compact self-adjoint operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). Then $T$ has a
Hilbert basis ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]])
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]): one may take the union
of orthonormal bases of the finitely many-dimensional nonzero eigenspaces with a
Hilbert basis of $\ker T$. If $\ker T=\{0\}$ no vectors from the kernel are
needed, and if all nonzero eigenspaces are absent (that is $T=0$) the union is a
Hilbert basis of $H=\ker T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$; then $(p_i)$ is a countable probability law. For any real observable $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

Let $I,E_i,g_i,J,Z$ be as in [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]. Suppose that for every compact interval $K\subset J$ there is a summable sequence $a_i\ge0$ such that $g_i(1+|E_i|^2)\exp(-\beta E_i)\le a_i$ for every $i\in I$ and $\beta\in K$. Then $Z$ is positive, finite, and $C^2$ on $J$, with $Z'(\beta)=-\sum_i g_iE_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ and $Z''(\beta)=\sum_i g_iE_i^2\exp(-\beta E_i)$. The probabilities $p_i$ are normalized; their mean $\bar E$ and variance are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. Moreover $H_g(p)=\log Z+\beta\bar E$, and its defining series is absolutely convergent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let
$S\in\mathcal B(H)$ be bounded. Then $ST$ and $TS$ are trace class and
$$\operatorname{tr}(ST)=\operatorname{tr}(TS) .$$
If $A,B\in\mathcal B(H)$ are Hilbert–Schmidt relative to a supplied Hilbert
basis $E$ of $H$ ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]), then the products $AB$ and
$BA$ are trace class and
$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), with Hilbert adjoint $T^*\in\mathcal B(K,H)$
([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]], [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]).

**The absolute value.** The operator $T^*T\in\mathcal B(H)$ is compact, since it
is the composite of the compact $T$ with the bounded $T^*$
([[lem-compositions-with-a-compact-operator-are-compact]]); it is self-adjoint,
because $(T^*T)^*=T^*T^{**}=T^*T$ ([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]); and it
is positive, because
$$\langle T^*Tx,x\rangle=\langle Tx,Tx\rangle=\|Tx\|^{2}\ge0$$
for every $x\in H$ ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]).
The **absolute value** of $T$ is the unique compact self-adjoint positive
operator
$$|T|:=(T^*T)^{1/2}$$
with $|T|^{2}=T^*T$, whose existence and uniqueness are the preceding square-root
lemma ([[lem-positive-square-root-of-a-compact-positive-operator]]). It satisfies
$$\||T|x\|^{2}=\langle|T|^{2}x,x\rangle=\langle T^*Tx,x\rangle=\|Tx\|^{2}\qquad(x\in H),$$
so in particular $\bigl\||T|\bigr\|=\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]) and
$\ker|T|=\ker T$, since $\||T|x\|=\|Tx\|$ for every $x$.

**The singular values.** By the spectral theorem for $|T|$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators]]) the nonzero
eigenvalues of $|T|$ form a finite or countably infinite set of positive reals,
each with finite multiplicity, and for every real $\varepsilon>0$ only finitely
many of them exceed $\varepsilon$; positivity rules out negative eigenvalues and
$0$ already corresponds to the kernel. The **multiset of positive singular
values of $T$** is the multiset of positive eigenvalues of $|T|$, counted with
multiplicity ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]).

**The ordered singular-value sequence.** The **distinct** positive singular
values are listed with positive labels in *decreasing* order $\mu_1>\mu_2>\cdots$ as follows:
if the multiset of positive eigenvalues is empty (equivalently $|T|=0$,
equivalently $T=0$), the list is empty; otherwise $\mu_1:=\max\{\lambda>0:\lambda$
is an eigenvalue of $|T|\}$, a maximum and not merely a supremum, because a
supremum value not attained would be an accumulation point different from $0$;
having chosen $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_k$, put $\mu_{k+1}:=\max\{\lambda>0:\lambda$ is an
eigenvalue of $|T|$ and $\lambda<\mu_k\}$ whenever that set is nonempty, and stop
otherwise. Each step is legitimate by the finiteness-above-thresholds property
above, and an infinite list satisfies $\mu_k\to0$ (otherwise its decreasing
limit would be a nonzero accumulation point). Writing $d_k$ for the multiplicity
of $\mu_k$ (a positive integer), the **zero-padded singular-value sequence** is
$$s_1\ge s_2\ge s_3\ge\cdots$$
where $s_1=\cdots=s_{d_1}=\mu_1$, $s_{d_1+1}=\cdots=s_{d_1+d_2}=\mu_2$, and so
on; if the multiset is finite with total multiplicity $r=d_1+\cdots+d_m$, one
sets $s_n:=0$ for every $n>r$, and if $T=0$ one sets $s_n:=0$ for every
$n\ge1$. The number $s_n$ is written $s_n(T)$ and called the $n$-th **singular
value** of $T$.

**Zero-based domain and positive labels.** Set $s_0(T):=\|T\|=s_1(T)$.
Thus the numerical sequence is the function $n\mapsto s_n(T)$ on all of
$\mathbb N$, including zero. The positive-labelled tail $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$
is the multiplicity-counting list constructed above. The auxiliary initial
value $s_0$ is not an additional entry of the eigenvalue multiset, does not index
a singular vector, and is excluded from multiplicity counts and singular-value
sums, which use $n\ge1$. The full sequence satisfies
$s_0\ge s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots$ and tends to zero. This preserves the page's
positive rank labels while giving convergence statements a zero-based domain.

**Rank and the finiteness of the list.** The map $\Phi:\operatorname{ran}|T|\to\operatorname{ran}T$
given by $\Phi(|T|x):=Tx$ is well defined and linear, because $|T|x=|T|x'$ forces
$x-x'\in\ker|T|=\ker T$ and hence $Tx=Tx'$; it is injective, because $Tx=0$ gives
$x\in\ker T=\ker|T|$ and $|T|x=0$; it is surjective onto $\operatorname{ran}T$
because $T=\Phi\circ|T|$; and it is isometric, $\|Tx\|=\||T|x\|$. Hence
$\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite-dimensional if and only if
$\operatorname{ran}|T|$ is finite-dimensional; in that case the linear
bijection $\Phi$ gives
$\dim\operatorname{ran}T=\dim\operatorname{ran}|T|$
([[def-dimension]]). Consequently, whenever $T$ has finite rank, the positive
singular values with multiplicity number exactly
$\dim\operatorname{ran}T$, the rank of $T$, and all later $s_n$ vanish, so the
sequence is **zero-padded**. If $T$ does not have finite rank, the multiset of
positive singular values is infinite and countable
([[def-countable]]) and $s_n>0$ for every $n$, with $s_n\downarrow0$; in
particular finite rank of $T$ is characterised by the eventual vanishing $s_n=0$ for all sufficiently large
$n$, and conversely such eventual vanishing forces finite rank. The sequence $(s_n)$ is numerical data only: no orthonormal system is
selected here, and the zero padding is *not* an indexing of any family of
vectors. The unordered multiset determines $(s_n)$ uniquely, so $(s_n)$ is well
defined, and $s_1(T)=\||T|\|=\|T\|$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

$$\exp:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(0,\infty)$$
is a bijection.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$,
and let $s:X\to\mathbb C$ be a complex simple function
([[def-complex-simple-function]], [[def-measurable-space]]). Present $s$ in
**disjoint normal form with a zero-coefficient complement**, that is

$$s=\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_j\mathbf 1_{B_j},$$

where $m\ge1$, and $B_1,\dots,B_m\in\Sigma$ are pairwise disjoint with
$B_1\cup\dots\cup B_m=X$ and $a_1,\dots,a_m\in\mathbb C$; a representation over
a disjoint family whose union misses some measurable set is completed by adding
that set with the coefficient $0$, and any coefficient is allowed to vanish.
In particular the zero function on the empty space uses $m=1$, $B_1=\varnothing$
and $a_1=0$; an empty presentation is not used.
Then define

$$\int s\,dE:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_jE(B_j)\in\mathcal B(H).$$

Here $\mathbf 1_{B}$ is the indicator of $B$ and $E(B_j)$ is the value of the
projection valued measure on $B_j$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]).

**Well-definedness.** Because the $B_j$ are pairwise disjoint and cover $X$,
the operator $\sum_ja_jE(B_j)$ is a finite sum of bounded operators and hence a
bounded operator; the sum is meaningful in $\mathcal B(H)$ with the operator
norm, and $\|\sum_ja_jE(B_j)\|\le\max_j|a_j|$, since the projection values are
contractive and pairwise orthogonal. The value displayed a priori depends on
the chosen disjoint presentation of $s$; that it does not,
$\int s\,dE$ is independent of the disjoint presentation of $s$, is proved as
[[lem-simple-pvm-integral-is-representation-independent]] immediately below,
before the symbol is used. The normal-form convention $s=\sum_ja_j\mathbf 1_{B_j}$
with $B_1\cup\dots\cup B_m=X$ is the one used throughout this page, and the
identity $\int\mathbf 1_B\,dE=E(B)$ holds for every $B\in\Sigma$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$,
and for $x,y\in H$ define

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad E_{x,y}(B):=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle \qquad(B\in\Sigma).$$

Then:

1. $E_x$ is a positive measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ with $E_x(X)=\|x\|^2$ and
   $0\le E_x(B)\le\|x\|^2$ for every $B$;
2. $E_{x,y}$ is a finite complex measure on $(X,\Sigma)$, the map
   $(x,y)\mapsto E_{x,y}$ is linear in $x$ and conjugate-linear in $y$, and
   $E_{y,x}=\overline{E_{x,y}}$, meaning $E_{y,x}(B)=\overline{E_{x,y}(B)}$ for
   every $B$;
3. $|E_{x,y}|(X)\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$, so $|E_{x,y}(B)|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$ for every
   $B$, and the polarization identity
   $$E_{x,y}=\frac14\sum_{k=0}^{3}i^kE_{x+i^ky}$$
   holds as an identity of complex measures, where $i^k$ are the fourth roots
   of unity $1,i,-1,-i$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field and let
$T:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) whose range $T(X)$ admits an ordered basis of
finite length ([[def-linear-basis]]). Then $T$ is compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space, let $Y$ be a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]), and let
$T_n:X\to Y$, $n\in\mathbb N$, be compact operators
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) with $\|T_n-T\|\to0$ for a bounded linear
operator $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
[[def-operator-norm]], [[def-metric-convergence]]). Then $T$ is compact.

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

derivations.claim: Since $\beta>0$, $-\beta\lambda\le-\beta a$ for $\lambda\ge a$; strict increase and positivity from [F11] show that $f_\beta$ is bounded and strictly positive. Each branch is continuous and their values agree at $a$, so $f_\beta$ is Borel. For each $n$, partition its bounded range into finitely many intervals of length at most $1/n$ and take their Borel preimages; choosing a nonnegative value in each interval gives a nonnegative real simple $s_n$ converging uniformly to $f_\beta$. By [F13], $T_n:=\int s_n\,dE$ is a finite real linear combination of self-adjoint projections, hence self-adjoint and has nonnegative quadratic form. By [F2], $T_n\to K_\beta$ in operator norm. Therefore $\langle K_\beta x,y\rangle=\langle x,K_\beta y\rangle$ and $\langle K_\beta x,x\rangle\ge0$ by [F14] and passage to the limit, so $K_\beta$ is self-adjoint and positive. If $K_\beta x=0$, [F2] gives $\int f_\beta^2dE_x=0$. For each $n\ge1$, $f_\beta\ge1/n$ on $C_n:=\{\lambda:f_\beta(\lambda)\ge1/n\}$; [F16] gives $0=\int f_\beta^2dE_x\ge n^{-2}E_x(C_n)$, so $E_x(C_n)=0$. The sets $C_n$ increase to $\mathbb R$; set $D_1=C_1$ and $D_n=C_n\setminus C_{n-1}$ for $n>1$. They are disjoint, cover $\mathbb R$, and satisfy $E_x(D_n)\le E_x(C_n)=0$. Countable additivity in [F13] gives $E_x(\mathbb R)=\sum_nE_x(D_n)=0$, hence $\|x\|=0$ and $K_\beta$ is injective.

By the trace-class definition [F4], $K_\beta$ is compact; together with step 1.1 it is compact self-adjoint and positive. Apply [F3]: its nonzero eigenspaces have finite multiplicity and span $(\ker K_\beta)^\perp=\mathcal H$, so AC supplies a finite or countable complete orthonormal family $(u_j)$ of eigenvectors with eigenvalues $\kappa_j>0$. By [F4], $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=\sum_j\kappa_j<\infty$; because $\mathcal H\ne0$ and $K_\beta$ is injective, this sum is positive.

Fix $j$. To justify the constant shift in the calculus, choose bounded simple $s_n\to f_\beta$ uniformly. By [F13], $\int(s_n-\kappa_j)\,dE=\int s_n\,dE-\kappa_jI$; [F2] passes both uniform limits, so $\Phi_E(f_\beta-\kappa_j)=K_\beta-\kappa_jI$. Applying the norm identity in [F2] to this difference and the eigenvector gives $\int|f_\beta-\kappa_j|^2dE_{u_j}=\|(K_\beta-\kappa_jI)u_j\|^2=0$. For every $n$, [F16] shows that the set where $|f_\beta-\kappa_j|\ge1/n$ has zero $E_{u_j}$-measure; their union is the complement of the level set. Hence $E_{u_j}$ is supported on $f_\beta^{-1}(\kappa_j)\cap[a,\infty)=\{E_j\}$: injectivity of the exponential gives uniqueness, and [F12] gives $E_j=-\beta^{-1}\log\kappa_j\ge a$. Thus $\int\lambda^2dE_{u_j}=E_j^2<\infty$ and [F1] yields $u_j\in D(A)$ and $Au_j=E_ju_j$.

The spectral measure of each $u_j$ is the unit mass at $E_j$ by step 3.1. Hence $\|(I-E(\{E_j\}))u_j\|^2=E_{u_j}(\mathbb R\setminus\{E_j\})=0$, so $E(\{E_j\})u_j=u_j$; for Borel $D$ not containing $E_j$, $E(D)u_j=E(D)E(\{E_j\})u_j=E(\varnothing)u_j=0$ by [F13]. For every $\gamma>0$, choose nonnegative simple $s_n\to f_\gamma$ uniformly as in step 1.1. In each disjoint normal form, [F13] then gives $(\int s_n\,dE)u_j=s_n(E_j)u_j$; the uniform-limit clause of [F2] yields $K_\gamma u_j=f_\gamma(E_j)u_j=e^{-\gamma E_j}u_j$. Fix $\gamma\in J$ and enumerate that basis; let $P_N$ project onto its first $N$ vectors, taking $P_N=I$ once a finite basis is exhausted. Parseval gives $\|P_Nx\|\le\|x\|$, so $K_\gamma P_N$ is bounded and finite rank. Fix the summable envelope $a_j$ for $\{\gamma\}\subset J$; every finite subsum of $t_j:=e^{-\gamma E_j}$ is at most the corresponding sum of $a_j$, hence $S:=\sum_jt_j<\infty$ by the finite-subsum definition [F6]. This sum is positive because the basis is nonempty and every term is positive. For $\varepsilon>0$, choose a finite set $F$ with $S-\varepsilon<\sum_{j\in F}t_j$; once $N$ contains $F$, every finite tail subsum is at most $S-\sum_{j\in F}t_j<\varepsilon$, so $\sum_{j>N}t_j\to0$. Again by Parseval, $$\|(K_\gamma-K_\gamma P_N)x\|^2=\sum_{j>N}e^{-2\gamma E_j}|\langle x,u_j\rangle|^2\le\Bigl(\sum_{j>N}e^{-\gamma E_j}\Bigr)^2\|x\|^2,$$ so $K_\gamma P_N$ converges to $K_\gamma$ in operator norm. For $t_j=e^{-\gamma E_j}$ its finite diagonal expansion is $K_\gamma P_Nx=\sum_{j\le N}t_j\langle x,u_j\rangle u_j$; orthonormality and [F8] give $\langle K_\gamma P_Nx,y\rangle=\langle x,K_\gamma P_Ny\rangle$ and $\langle K_\gamma P_Nx,x\rangle=\sum_{j\le N}t_j|\langle x,u_j\rangle|^2\ge0$. Thus each truncation is self-adjoint and positive, and [F14] plus operator-norm convergence preserves both properties. It is compact by [F15], since the truncations are bounded finite-rank operators and $\mathcal H$ is Banach. Thus $K_\gamma$ is compact self-adjoint and positive. Its absolute value is $K_\gamma$, by the unique positive square-root definition in [F9]. If $K_\gamma x=\lambda x$, taking coordinates in the complete basis gives $(t_j-\lambda)\langle x,u_j\rangle=0$ for every $j$; thus its eigenvalues and their multiplicities are exactly the diagonal values $t_j$. Hence [F9] identifies its positive singular values, with multiplicity, as the list $(t_j)$. Their finite subsums are bounded by $\sum_j a_j$, so the trace-class definition [F4] applies and gives $\operatorname{Tr}K_\gamma=\sum_j t_j$.

At the fixed $\beta$, $\rho_\beta=K_\beta/Z_\beta$ is positive trace class and [F5] gives $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_\beta=Z_\beta^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=1$. For each $\gamma\in J$, $\rho_\gamma=K_\gamma/Z_\gamma$ likewise has trace one; its eigenvalues $p_j=e^{-\gamma E_j}/Z_\gamma$ form the canonical law, so [F6] gives the finite mean, variance, and identity $-\sum_jp_j\log p_j=\log Z_\gamma+\gamma\sum_jp_jE_j$.

For bounded $B$, [F5] makes $\rho_\beta B$ and $B\rho_\beta$ trace class and [F7] gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta B)=\operatorname{Tr}(B\rho_\beta)$. Evaluate the second trace in the complete basis $(u_j)$: $\operatorname{Tr}(B\rho_\beta)=\sum_j\langle B\rho_\beta u_j,u_j\rangle=\sum_jp_j\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle$, where [F8] and real $p_j$ justify pulling the scalar out. This series is absolutely convergent since $|\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle|\le\|B\|$ and $\sum_jp_j=1$.

boundaries.evidence: The theorem assumes a nonzero Hilbert space; the zero-space boundary is explicitly excluded in the statement.
Strict positivity of f_beta gives injectivity and excludes zero eigenvalues in steps 1.1–2.1.

The one-dimensional case is covered by steps 1.1–5.1 and verified by the finite check below: for A=0 on C, the sole Gibbs weight is 1, Z=1, rho=I, and the canonical mean, variance, and entropy vanish.
Repeated eigenvalues are counted with multiplicity in the complete eigenbasis in step 2.1.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$

the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and $\Sigma$-measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). Then:

   $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,y\rangle=\int f\,dE_{x,y}\qquad(x,y\in H),$$

   $\|f-s_n\|_\infty\to0$ one has $\|\Phi_E(f)-\int s_n\,dE\|\to0$: the integral
   is obtained from uniform simple approximations and is independent of the
   approximating sequence;
2. $\|\Phi_E(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, and for every $x\in H$
$$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,x\rangle=\int f\,dE_x,\qquad \|\Phi_E(f)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x ;$$
3. the exact norm is the **$E$-essential supremum**
$$\|f\|_{E,\infty}:=\sup\bigl\{\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}:\ x\in H,\ \|x\|=1\bigr\}, \qquad \|\Phi_E(f)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty},$$
   where $\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}$ denotes the essential supremum of the real measurable function $|f|$ with respect to
   the finite measure $E_x$ ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a

   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$

   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);

   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), with Hilbert adjoint $T^*\in\mathcal B(K,H)$
([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]], [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]).

**The absolute value.** The operator $T^*T\in\mathcal B(H)$ is compact, since it
is the composite of the compact $T$ with the bounded $T^*$
([[lem-compositions-with-a-compact-operator-are-compact]]); it is self-adjoint,
because $(T^*T)^*=T^*T^{**}=T^*T$ ([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]); and it
is positive, because
$$\langle T^*Tx,x\rangle=\langle Tx,Tx\rangle=\|Tx\|^{2}\ge0$$
for every $x\in H$ ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]).
The **absolute value** of $T$ is the unique compact self-adjoint positive
operator
$$|T|:=(T^*T)^{1/2}$$
with $|T|^{2}=T^*T$, whose existence and uniqueness are the preceding square-root
lemma ([[lem-positive-square-root-of-a-compact-positive-operator]]). It satisfies
$$\||T|x\|^{2}=\langle|T|^{2}x,x\rangle=\langle T^*Tx,x\rangle=\|Tx\|^{2}\qquad(x\in H),$$
so in particular $\bigl\||T|\bigr\|=\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]) and
$\ker|T|=\ker T$, since $\||T|x\|=\|Tx\|$ for every $x$.

**The singular values.** By the spectral theorem for $|T|$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators]]) the nonzero
eigenvalues of $|T|$ form a finite or countably infinite set of positive reals,
each with finite multiplicity, and for every real $\varepsilon>0$ only finitely
many of them exceed $\varepsilon$; positivity rules out negative eigenvalues and
$0$ already corresponds to the kernel. The **multiset of positive singular
values of $T$** is the multiset of positive eigenvalues of $|T|$, counted with
multiplicity ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]).

**The ordered singular-value sequence.** The **distinct** positive singular
values are listed with positive labels in *decreasing* order $\mu_1>\mu_2>\cdots$ as follows:
if the multiset of positive eigenvalues is empty (equivalently $|T|=0$,
equivalently $T=0$), the list is empty; otherwise $\mu_1:=\max\{\lambda>0:\lambda$
is an eigenvalue of $|T|\}$, a maximum and not merely a supremum, because a
supremum value not attained would be an accumulation point different from $0$;
having chosen $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_k$, put $\mu_{k+1}:=\max\{\lambda>0:\lambda$ is an
eigenvalue of $|T|$ and $\lambda<\mu_k\}$ whenever that set is nonempty, and stop
otherwise. Each step is legitimate by the finiteness-above-thresholds property
above, and an infinite list satisfies $\mu_k\to0$ (otherwise its decreasing
limit would be a nonzero accumulation point). Writing $d_k$ for the multiplicity
of $\mu_k$ (a positive integer), the **zero-padded singular-value sequence** is
$$s_1\ge s_2\ge s_3\ge\cdots$$
where $s_1=\cdots=s_{d_1}=\mu_1$, $s_{d_1+1}=\cdots=s_{d_1+d_2}=\mu_2$, and so
on; if the multiset is finite with total multiplicity $r=d_1+\cdots+d_m$, one
sets $s_n:=0$ for every $n>r$, and if $T=0$ one sets $s_n:=0$ for every
$n\ge1$. The number $s_n$ is written $s_n(T)$ and called the $n$-th **singular
value** of $T$.

**Zero-based domain and positive labels.** Set $s_0(T):=\|T\|=s_1(T)$.
Thus the numerical sequence is the function $n\mapsto s_n(T)$ on all of
$\mathbb N$, including zero. The positive-labelled tail $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$
is the multiplicity-counting list constructed above. The auxiliary initial
value $s_0$ is not an additional entry of the eigenvalue multiset, does not index
a singular vector, and is excluded from multiplicity counts and singular-value
sums, which use $n\ge1$. The full sequence satisfies
$s_0\ge s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots$ and tends to zero. This preserves the page's
positive rank labels while giving convergence statements a zero-based domain.

**Rank and the finiteness of the list.** The map $\Phi:\operatorname{ran}|T|\to\operatorname{ran}T$
given by $\Phi(|T|x):=Tx$ is well defined and linear, because $|T|x=|T|x'$ forces
$x-x'\in\ker|T|=\ker T$ and hence $Tx=Tx'$; it is injective, because $Tx=0$ gives
$x\in\ker T=\ker|T|$ and $|T|x=0$; it is surjective onto $\operatorname{ran}T$
because $T=\Phi\circ|T|$; and it is isometric, $\|Tx\|=\||T|x\|$. Hence
$\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite-dimensional if and only if
$\operatorname{ran}|T|$ is finite-dimensional; in that case the linear
bijection $\Phi$ gives
$\dim\operatorname{ran}T=\dim\operatorname{ran}|T|$
([[def-dimension]]). Consequently, whenever $T$ has finite rank, the positive
singular values with multiplicity number exactly
$\dim\operatorname{ran}T$, the rank of $T$, and all later $s_n$ vanish, so the
sequence is **zero-padded**. If $T$ does not have finite rank, the multiset of
positive singular values is infinite and countable
([[def-countable]]) and $s_n>0$ for every $n$, with $s_n\downarrow0$; in
particular finite rank of $T$ is characterised by the eventual vanishing $s_n=0$ for all sufficiently large
$n$, and conversely such eventual vanishing forces finite rank. The sequence $(s_n)$ is numerical data only: no orthonormal system is

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$,
and let $s:X\to\mathbb C$ be a complex simple function
([[def-complex-simple-function]], [[def-measurable-space]]). Present $s$ in
**disjoint normal form with a zero-coefficient complement**, that is

$$s=\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_j\mathbf 1_{B_j},$$

where $m\ge1$, and $B_1,\dots,B_m\in\Sigma$ are pairwise disjoint with
$B_1\cup\dots\cup B_m=X$ and $a_1,\dots,a_m\in\mathbb C$; a representation over
a disjoint family whose union misses some measurable set is completed by adding
that set with the coefficient $0$, and any coefficient is allowed to vanish.
In particular the zero function on the empty space uses $m=1$, $B_1=\varnothing$
and $a_1=0$; an empty presentation is not used.
Then define

$$\int s\,dE:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_jE(B_j)\in\mathcal B(H).$$

Here $\mathbf 1_{B}$ is the indicator of $B$ and $E(B_j)$ is the value of the
projection valued measure on $B_j$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]).

**Well-definedness.** Because the $B_j$ are pairwise disjoint and cover $X$,
the operator $\sum_ja_jE(B_j)$ is a finite sum of bounded operators and hence a
bounded operator; the sum is meaningful in $\mathcal B(H)$ with the operator
norm, and $\|\sum_ja_jE(B_j)\|\le\max_j|a_j|$, since the projection values are
contractive and pairwise orthogonal. The value displayed a priori depends on
the chosen disjoint presentation of $s$; that it does not,
$\int s\,dE$ is independent of the disjoint presentation of $s$, is proved as
[[lem-simple-pvm-integral-is-representation-independent]] immediately below,
before the symbol is used. The normal-form convention $s=\sum_ja_j\mathbf 1_{B_j}$
with $B_1\cup\dots\cup B_m=X$ is the one used throughout this page, and the
identity $\int\mathbf 1_B\,dE=E(B)$ holds for every $B\in\Sigma$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.
