citations.quote: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to\mathbb C$ be measurable with $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere. Suppose $g\ge0$ is measurable and $\int g\,d\mu<\infty$, and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for every $n$. Then $f$ is integrable, $\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu$, and $\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\to0$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

derivations.claim: For $\beta$ in the interior of a compact interval $K\subset J$, the difference quotient of $e^{-\beta E(x)}$ tends pointwise to $-E(x)e^{-\beta E(x)}$. The mean-value theorem [F5] bounds its absolute value, for small $h$, by $|E|e^{-\theta E}$ for an intermediate $\theta\in K$; this is at most $G_K$ because $|E|\le1+|E|^2$. Dominated convergence [F2] therefore gives $Z'=-\int E e^{-\beta E}d\mu$. Applying the same argument to $-E e^{-\beta E}$, dominated by $G_K$, gives $Z''=\int E^2e^{-\beta E}d\mu$; dominated convergence also gives continuity of both derivatives.

The density $p_\beta$ is nonnegative and integrates to one. The envelope makes its first and second energy moments finite. Differentiating $\log Z$ using [F4] gives $-Z'/Z=\int E p_\beta d\mu$ and $Z''/Z-(Z'/Z)^2=\int E^2p_\beta d\mu-(\int Ep_\beta d\mu)^2$. The latter is the variance by expanding its defining square.

Since $\log p_\beta=-\beta E-\log Z$ almost everywhere and $\int |E|p_\beta d\mu<\infty$, the entropy integrand is absolutely integrable. Substitution and normalization yield $-\int p_\beta\log p_\beta d\mu=\beta\langle E\rangle_\beta+\log Z$. This entropy depends on the chosen reference measure $\mu$.

case_scope.source_excerpt: Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $E:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable, and let $J\subset\mathbb R$ be open. Suppose $Z(\beta):=\int e^{-\beta E}\,d\mu$ satisfies $0<Z(\beta)<\infty$ on $J$, and for every compact interval $K\subset J$ there is $G_K\in L^1(\mu)$ with $(1+|E|^2)e^{-\beta E}\le G_K$ pointwise for every $\beta\in K$. Define $p_\beta=e^{-\beta E}/Z(\beta)$, $\langle Y\rangle_\beta:=\int Yp_\beta\,d\mu$ for integrable $Y$, and $\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E):=\int(E-\langle E\rangle_\beta)^2p_\beta\,d\mu$. Then $Z\in C^2(J)$, $Z'=-\int E e^{-\beta E}d\mu$, $Z''=\int E^2e^{-\beta E}d\mu$, and $-\partial_\beta\log Z=\langle E\rangle_\beta$, $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. The reference-relative entropy $-\int p_\beta\log p_\beta\,d\mu$ is finite and equals $\log Z+\beta\langle E\rangle_\beta$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

citations.quote: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, writing $d = n + 1 - m$
for the number of terms,

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.

derivations.claim: The simple minorants of $f_n$ are also minorants of $f_{n+1}$, so their integral suprema increase. Each is at most $\int f$; hence $L:=\lim_n\int f_n$ exists in $[0,\infty]$ and $L\le\int f$.

Fix a nonnegative simple $s\le f$ and $0<t<1$. The measurable sets $A_n:=\{f_n\ge ts\}$ increase and cover $\{s>0\}$, since $f_n(x)\to f(x)\ge s(x)>ts(x)$ there. Write $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{B_j}$ in disjoint level form. For each $c_j>0$, $A_n\cap B_j\uparrow B_j$; countable additivity, applied to successive disjoint differences, gives $\mu(A_n\cap B_j)\uparrow\mu(B_j)$. The finite-sum definition [F2] then gives $\int s\mathbf1_{A_n}\uparrow\int s$. As $f_n\ge ts\mathbf1_{A_n}$, monotonicity and homogeneity of the simple integral imply $L\ge t\int s$. Let $t\uparrow1$ and take the supremum over $s\le f$; [F1, F3] give $L\ge\int f$. Together with step 1.1 this proves monotone convergence.

For nonnegative measurable $f$, define $s_n:=2^{-n}\sum_{k=1}^{n2^n}\mathbf1_{\{f\ge k2^{-n}\}}$. Each $s_n$ is a finite-valued measurable simple function. Every threshold counted in $s_n$ is also counted at the even-index threshold in $s_{n+1}$, so $s_n\le s_{n+1}$. If $f(x)<\infty$, once $n>f(x)$ the mesh gives $0\le f(x)-s_n(x)<2^{-n}$; if $f(x)=\infty$, then $s_n(x)=n$. Thus $s_n\uparrow f$. Define $t_n:=2^{-n}\sum_{k=1}^{n2^n}\mathbf1_{\{g\ge k2^{-n}\}}$; the same threshold and mesh argument shows $t_n\uparrow g$. Apply step 1.1 to $s_n$, $t_n$, and $s_n+t_n$. Refine their finitely many level sets to the finite partition of intersections $B_j\cap C_k$; regrouping the resulting sums by [F2] gives $\int(s_n+t_n)=\int s_n+\int t_n$. Passing to the three monotone limits proves $\int(f+g)=\int f+\int g$.

For $c>0$, simple minorants of $cf$ are exactly $c$ times simple minorants of $f$, so the supremum definition gives $\int cf=c\int f$; for $c=0$ both sides are zero. If an integrable real function is expressed as $u-v$ with $u,v\ge0$ integrable, the value $\int u-\int v$ is independent of the expression: $u-v=u'-v'$ implies $u+v'=u'+v$, and step 2.2 equates the finite sums of integrals. The definition using positive and negative parts is one such expression, so signed integrals are linear.

The tail of the cell envelope $\psi(|j|_\infty-1)$ over all sufficiently large integer offsets is summable.

For the unit cells $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$, there are constants $A>0$ and $B\geq0$ such that every finite configuration satisfies
$$H_\phi(\omega)\geq A\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}N_{C_i}(\omega)^2-BN(\omega).$$
Only finitely many summands are nonzero.

For every $\rho>0$ in that interior and every such sequence $(L_j,N_j)$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta)=F(\rho).$$
No claim is made at a close-packing endpoint or at any other excluded endpoint.
Let $F_\beta$ be the finite concave canonical rate on the interior attainable-density interval from [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]].

For free and periodic cubes define
$$Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}\!\left[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,bc}}\right],\qquad bc\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{per}\}.$$
Then the limit $p_Q(z,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}$ exists, is independent of $bc$, and
$$p_Q(z,\beta)=-\min_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
The minimizer set is nonempty and compact in the local-tame topology $\tau_L$.

For either free or periodic boundary condition $b$, let $C^b_{L,N_L}$ be the exact-$N_L$ canonical law and $G^b_{L,z,\beta}$ the grand-canonical law using the same finite-volume energy, where $N_L/L^d\to\rho$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

Define its **periodized empirical field**
$$R_{L,\omega}:=\frac1{L^d}\int_{\Lambda_L}\delta_{T_x\omega^{(L)}}\,dx.$$
The integral is the push-forward of normalized Lebesgue measure on $\Lambda_L$ under $x\mapsto T_x\omega^{(L)}$.

For $L>0$ and a finite configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$ with $N(\omega)=N$, the measure $R_{L,\omega}$ of [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]] is a stationary probability law of finite intensity and
$$\rho(R_{L,\omega})=\frac{N}{L^d}.$$
For any probability law $C_L$ on finite configurations in $\Lambda_L$ with $E_{C_L}N<\infty$, its empirical-field barycenter $\bar C_L$ is also a stationary probability law of finite intensity and $\rho(\bar C_L)=E_{C_L}N/L^d$.

The canonical-grand duality [F5] gives $\limsup L^{-d}\log Z_{\mathrm{per}}\leq F_\beta(\rho)$.

Fix corridor width $k$ larger than the tail cutoff. Restrict the $N_L$ particles to the inner cube of side $L-k$, leaving the corridor empty. The exact-$N_L$ density is still $\rho$. The diagonal-gap supplier [F2] gives the vanishing regular-tail cutoff used here. By [L1], the periodized energy differs from the free inner-cube energy by at most $c_d\delta_kT_{L-k}$. The cell bound [F3] implies $T_{L-k}\leq A^{-1}(H_{L-k}+BN_L)$. Consequently $$ Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta)\geq e^{-\beta c_d\delta_k BN_L/A}\, Z(L-k,N_L;\beta(1+c_d\delta_k/A)). $$ The canonical theorem [F4] applies at the perturbed inverse temperature, giving the corresponding lower rate.

At fixed interior $\rho$, $F_\beta(\rho)$ is finite and convex as a function of $\beta>0$, by Hölder’s inequality [F8], since each finite-volume log partition is convex and the pointwise limit is finite. A finite convex function is continuous on the open interval: on a compact subinterval, its secant slopes are bounded by the slopes to fixed exterior endpoints. Let $L\to\infty$ in step 1.2 and then $k\to\infty$, so $\delta_k\to0$; continuity yields $\liminf\geq F_\beta(\rho)$.

Step 2.1 established the periodic exact-$N_L$ rate $F_\beta(\rho)$, and [F5] supplies a finite supporting activity. The grand rate in [F6] and the periodized empirical field in [F9] satisfy the hypotheses of [F7] with periodic boundary condition. Hence the periodic empirical fields concentrate near the minimizer set, and concentrate at its singleton when it is unique.

citations.quote:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

Let $1\le q\le n$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Suppose $F(x_*)=0$ and some $q\times q$ minor of the derivative matrix $DF(x_*)$ is invertible. This nonsingular-minor hypothesis is the explicit full-row-rank condition used here. If $q<n$, then after permuting coordinates $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\mathbb R^q$, there are open neighborhoods $P$ of $u_*$ and $Q$ of $v_*$ and a unique $C^1$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$ such that

$$F(u,v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=\varphi(u)\qquad((u,v)\in P\times Q).$$

Its derivative is

$$D\varphi(u)=-D_vF(u,\varphi(u))^{-1}D_uF(u,\varphi(u)).$$

Thus the local zero set is a graph over $n-q$ free coordinates. If $q=n$, the zero is locally isolated, so the local graph dimension is zero. Here “local graph dimension $k$” means a local graph parameterized by an open subset of $\mathbb R^k$, with a singleton counted as dimension zero.

If $f,g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ are totally differentiable at $a$ and $c\in\mathbb R$, then $f+g$ and $cf$ are totally differentiable at $a$, with

$$D(f+g)(a)=Df(a)+Dg(a),\qquad D(cf)(a)=cDf(a).$$

derivations.claim: For $P\ge2$, $F$ has one scalar component for each pair $(i,\alpha)$ with $1\le i\le C$ and $2\le\alpha\le P$, so it has $q=C(P-1)$ components. Each is a difference of $C^1$ maps and therefore $F$ is $C^1$ on the open set $U$ by [F1, L2]. The assumed minor lets [L1] apply, giving local graph dimension $n-q$. Expanding $n=2+P(C-1)$ gives $n-q=2+PC-P-CP+C=C-P+2$.
If $P=1$, no phase-equality equations are indexed because there is no $\alpha\ge2$. The local solution set is all of the open domain $U$, which has $n=2+(C-1)=C+1=C-P+2$ coordinates.

In the reactive variant, each added affinity is a finite linear combination of $C^1$ coordinate functions and is therefore $C^1$ by [F1, L2]; the combined map has $q+R$ scalar equations. Its stated minor satisfies [L1], so the graph dimension is $n-q-R=2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)-R=C-P+2-R$. Linear independence of the $\nu^r$ identifies $R$ distinct reaction directions, while the full-rank minor remains a separate necessary assumption on the equation derivatives.

Let $C\ge1$ be the number of components and $P\ge1$ the number of phases. Use common positive real coordinates $T,p$, expressed in fixed units if they are given a physical interpretation, and, for each phase $\alpha$, an interior composition vector

$$x^\alpha\in\Omega_C:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},$$

with the convention $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $\Omega_1=\{0\}$. The final component fraction is $1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$. The ambient coordinate domain $U=(0,\infty)^2\times\Omega_C^P$ is open in $\mathbb R^n$, where $n=2+P(C-1)$. For each phase $\alpha$ and component $i$, let $\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)$ be a real-valued $C^1$ coordinate function; these are mathematical maps and no thermodynamic potential or physical realization is assumed.

For $P\ge2$, define the $q=C(P-1)$ coexistence equations

$$F_{i,\alpha}(T,p,x^1,\ldots,x^P)=\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)-\mu_i^1(T,p,x^1)=0\quad(1\le i\le C,\ 2\le\alpha\le P).$$

At a solution $z_*\in U$, assume some $q\times q$ derivative minor of $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is invertible. Then the local solution set is a graph of dimension

$$n-q=2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)=C-P+2.$$

For $P=1$ there are no coexistence equations and the coordinate domain itself has dimension $n=C+1=C-P+2$. In a specified reactive variant with $R\ge1$, let $\nu^1,\ldots,\nu^R\in\mathbb R^C$ be linearly independent dimensionless stoichiometric vectors and add the $R$ affinity equations $A_r=\sum_{i=1}^C\nu_i^r\mu_i^1=0$. If the combined equation map has an invertible $(q+R)\times(q+R)$ derivative minor at a solution and $q+R\le n$, its local zero set has dimension

$$n-q-R=C-P+2-R.$$

These are conditional local dimensions under the displayed nonsingular-minor assumptions. No dimension formula follows at singular solutions, on composition boundaries, or from equation counting alone; no empirical or general physical phase rule is asserted.

derivations.claim: Fix one unit cell $C_i$ and a finite Borel partition $B_0,\ldots,B_s$ of it. Put $v_j=|B_j|$, so $\sum_jv_j=1$. Conditional on the cell count $N=n$, the $n$ independent uniform points give category-count probability $n!\prod_jv_j^{n_j}/\prod_jn_j!$ for $\sum_jn_j=n$. Multiplying by the Poisson count probability $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ gives $e^{-\lambda}\prod_j(\lambda v_j)^{n_j}/n_j!=\prod_je^{-\lambda v_j}(\lambda v_j)^{n_j}/n_j!$, by [F3]. This factors into the Poisson probabilities of the disjoint cell pieces, including the complement $B_0$; hence their counts are independent Poisson variables with respective means $\lambda v_j$. Zero-volume pieces have count zero almost surely by the same formula.

Each bounded $A_j$ intersects only finitely many unit cells. Apply step 1.1 to the partition formed by the sets $A_j\cap C_i$ and their complement in each such cell. Independence within each cell and independence between cell configurations show that all component counts, indexed by both $j$ and $i$, are independent Poisson variables.

For fixed $j$, sum the component counts over its finitely many cells. The sum of independent Poisson variables of means $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_q$ has mass at $n$ equal to $e^{-\sum\mu_i}(\sum\mu_i)^n/n!$: expand $(\sum_i\mu_i)^n$ by [F2], then use the product of the component masses. Thus $N_{A_j}$ is Poisson with mean $\lambda\sum_i|A_j\cap C_i|=\lambda|A_j|$. The groups of components for different $j$ are disjoint independent families, so their sums remain independent.

Let $A_1,\ldots,A_r$ be pairwise disjoint and, for each $j$, consider a finite count-cylinder event in the restriction to $A_j$. Refine the finitely many counting sets in each event into their disjoint atoms inside $A_j$. Step 3.1 gives independent Poisson counts on all these atoms across every $j$; the event for each restricted configuration is a measurable function only of its own atom counts. Thus finite cylinder events factor across $j$. The restriction sigma-fields are generated by these cylinders, so repeated pi-lambda extension proves independence of the restrictions themselves.

For a finite family of bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_s$, partition their union into the finitely many disjoint Boolean atoms formed by the sets and their complements. Every $N_{A_j}$ is a sum of the counts on these atoms. Translation preserves each atom's volume, so step 3.1 gives the same joint distribution of this whole count vector under $Q_\lambda$ and its translate. Thus the laws agree on every finite count cylinder. These cylinders generate the configuration sigma-algebra by [F4], and pi-lambda uniqueness identifies the laws. The one-set case gives $E_{Q_\lambda}N_A=\lambda|A|$, which is the asserted intensity measure.

case_scope.source_excerpt: Assume AC, fix $d\geq1$ and $\lambda>0$, and let $Q_\lambda$ be the configuration law of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. For pairwise disjoint bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_r\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, the restrictions $\omega|_{A_1},\ldots,\omega|_{A_r}$ are independent, each count $N_{A_j}$ has Poisson law with mean $\lambda|A_j|$, and the joint law of counts on any finite disjoint family is the product of those Poisson laws. In particular, $Q_\lambda$ is invariant under every translation $T_x$, and its intensity measure is $\lambda$ times Lebesgue measure.

Let $I$ be a finite nonempty set of system types, $X_i$ a nonempty state set with chosen reference $r_i\in X_i$ for each $i\in I$, and $M$ a common meter state set with $z_0,z_1\in M$. Assume for every $i$ that the product state set $X_i\times M$ satisfies the hypotheses of [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]], with strict reference pair $(r_i,z_0)\prec\prec(r_i,z_1)$. Let $S_i$ be its normalized representation and put $\sigma_i(x):=S_i(x,z_0)$. In that product comparison, the unit product-state point mass satisfies $e_{(x,z_0)}\sim_s(1-\sigma_i(x))e_{(r_i,z_0)}+\sigma_i(x)e_{(r_i,z_1)}$, by [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]]. These product-state point masses are distinct from the shared state-and-meter compounds defined next.

Assume in addition a **common-meter compatibility interface**. Let $\mathcal Y$ contain disjoint families of raw state tags $a_{i,x}$, raw type-reference tags $\rho_i$, and two distinct raw meter tags $\zeta_0,\zeta_1$. Using the unit point masses on these tags, write $e_{r_i}:=e_{\rho_i}$ and $e_{z_j}:=e_{\zeta_j}$, and define $u_{i,x}:=e_{a_{i,x}}+e_{z_0}$. Thus $u_{i,x}$ is an explicit mass-two state-and-fixed-meter compound; it is not a unit tag. Compounds over $\mathcal Y$ use the finite-support convention of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]], and their signed comparison is the one in [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]]. Require the exact substitution

$$u_{i,x}\sim_s e_{r_i}+(1-\sigma_i(x))e_{z_0}+\sigma_i(x)e_{z_1}\qquad(i\in I,\ x\in X_i),$$

finite substitutions to compose, and the fixed reference sum $\sum_iT_ie_{r_i}$ to cancel when type totals agree. Both sides of this signed substitution have total coefficient two, even when $\sigma_i(x)$ lies outside $[0,1]$. Require the common meter point masses to satisfy $e_{z_0}\preceq e_{z_1}$ and not $e_{z_1}\preceq e_{z_0}$. These are hypotheses on the comparison algebra, not consequences of separate numerical meter readings.

For positive coefficients $t_{ik}$ on a finite collection of type-$i$ states $x_{ik}$, define $T_i:=\sum_k t_{ik}$ and $T:=\sum_iT_i$. Put $C_0:=\sum_{i,k}t_{ik}e_{a_{i,x_{ik}}}$ and $C:=\sum_{i,k}t_{ik}u_{i,x_{ik}}=C_0+T e_{z_0}$. Thus $C_0$ is the state compound of mass $T$ and $C$ is its fixed-meter encoding of mass $2T$. Empty collections give $T=0$ and $C_0=C=0$. Define

$$\Sigma(C):=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_k t_{ik}\sigma_i(x_{ik}).$$

For two such compounds $C,D$ with the same type-total vector $(T_i)_{i\in I}$, the common comparison satisfies $C\preceq D$ exactly when $\Sigma(C)\le\Sigma(D)$. Equivalently, the same order criterion holds for the state compounds $C_0,D_0$ after canceling their common $T e_{z_0}$. The index family is finite; no arbitrary-index choice or infinite decomposition is asserted.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb N$ be finite, let $c_j\in\mathbb R^n$ and $h_j\in\mathbb R$ for $0\le j<m$. The finite system

$$c_j\cdot b\ge h_j\qquad(0\le j<m)$$

has a solution $b\in\mathbb R^n$ if and only if every $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$ with $\lambda_j\ge0$ and $\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jc_j=0$ satisfies $\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jh_j\le0$. Dot products and sums are finite. This includes empty rows, empty variables, and an empty inequality family.

Let $A$ be a finite set of reaction channels, let $r\in\mathbb N$, let $\nu_a\in\mathbb R^r$ be the output-minus-input type vector of channel $a$, and let $d_a\in\mathbb R$ be a finite lower bound on its already calibrated entropy change. There exists an offset vector $b\in\mathbb R^r$ satisfying

$$b\cdot\nu_a+d_a\ge0\qquad(a\in A)$$

if and only if every $\lambda\in\mathbb R^A$ with $\lambda_a\ge0$ and $\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_a\nu_a=0$ satisfies $\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_ad_a\ge0$. If an actual transition has entropy change $\Delta\sigma_a\ge d_a$, such a vector guarantees $\Delta\sigma_a+b\cdot\nu_a\ge0$. The criterion is exact for the finite lower-bound inequalities; it does not claim necessity for actual transitions when $d_a$ is only a loose bound.

Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with finite slope $P_i(x)$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

For two simple domains $\Gamma_i\subset\mathbb R^{n_i+1}$ and $\Gamma_j\subset\mathbb R^{n_j+1}$, write their coordinates $(u_i,v_i)$ and $(u_j,v_j)$. Their thermal-join domain is

$$\Delta_{ij}:=\{(u,v_i,v_j):\exists u_i,u_j,\ (u_i,v_i)\in\Gamma_i,\ (u_j,v_j)\in\Gamma_j,\ u=u_i+u_j\}.$$

The joined simple type is a distinct formal tag with amount function $\nu_{\Delta_{ij}}=\nu_{\Gamma_i}+\nu_{\Gamma_j}$ and weight $w_{\Delta_{ij}}=w_{\Gamma_i}+w_{\Gamma_j}$, as defined in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Encode the separated pair by $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and a joined coordinate $Z$ by $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(Z)$. Their bookkeeping masses agree, and their aggregate composition functions agree. These encoded maps and their raw tags remain distinct. Positive coordinate-scaled copies use the reversible preparation transport of that definition; nested joins preserve their finite primitive amount function under reassociation and permutation. The empty type contributes the zero map.

Write $J_{ij}(x,y)$ for the join state with the summed energy coordinate and the unchanged work coordinates. A compound pair $(x,y)$ and $J_{ij}(x,y)$ have the same total energy and work coordinates but are distinct tagged objects. Define $x\sim_T y$ exactly when $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(J_{ij}(x,y))$ are accessible in both directions. Nested joins use the declared reassociation and permutation identifications.

Assume every finite join is itself a simple domain satisfying [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. The contact hypotheses are mathematical assumptions on the common relation: (T1) $(x,y)\prec J_{ij}(x,y)$; (T2) every join state has at least one reversible split into component states at its stated coordinates, and the equal-state split of any state into positive scaled copies of itself is reversible; (T3) $\sim_T$ is transitive; (T4) for every simple state $x$ there are states $x_0,x_1$ in its domain with $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ and $x_0\sim_T x_1$; (T5) for every ordered pair of simple systems, every $x$ in the first and every work coordinate $v$ in the second's projection $\rho(\Gamma_j):=\{v:\exists u,(u,v)\in\Gamma_j\}$, there is a state $y$ with work coordinate $v$ and $x\sim_T y$.

For the completed calibrator branch, add (C1) **join coherence**: whenever $x\sim_T y$, the join state $J_{ij}(x,y)$ is thermally equivalent to each of $x$ and $y$ under the nested-join identifications. The coordinate sum in the definition alone does not assert C1. In later theorem statements, T1–T5 and C1 are explicitly listed as hypotheses; they are not treated as established physical laws.

Let a simple domain and its finite thermal joins satisfy [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Let $x_0\prec\prec x_1$ with $x_0\sim_T x_1$, and let $x$ satisfy $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$. For $0\le\lambda\le1$, write $R_\lambda$ for the compound state $((1-\lambda)x_0,\lambda x_1)$, omitting a zero coefficient at the endpoints. Then there is a unique $\lambda\in(0,1)$ with $R_\lambda\sim x$ in the common accessibility relation.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], the sectors are nested: if $y\in A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$; equality holds when $y\in\partial A_x$, and $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ when $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$. For every $x,y\in\Gamma_i$, either $x\prec y$ or $y\prec x$ (possibly both). Strict comparison is exactly interior membership: $x\prec\prec y$ if and only if $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$.

Let $u,v$ be finite-support real coefficient maps on the tagged state labels of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] with equal total coefficient. For a typed state $x$, compound notation uses the represented map $\mathsf{J}(x)$ from [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]; its raw unit point mass is $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. Signed maps still use the ordinary total of their raw coefficients, exactly the bookkeeping mass of the represented nonnegative maps. Put $d=v-u$, $d^+(x)=\max(d(x),0)$ and $d^-(x)=\max(-d(x),0)$. Define $u\preceq_s v$ to mean $d^-\prec d^+$ under the compound relation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Write $u\sim_s v$ when both $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s u$. These are formal signed comparison maps, not physical negative amounts. The positive and negative parts are finite-support compounds of equal mass. If $u\sim_s v$, then $cu\sim_s cv$ for every real $c$: positive $c$ uses scaling, $c=0$ is reflexivity, and negative $c$ swaps the positive and negative parts while equivalence supplies both comparison directions. This Definition introduces the signed notation; ordinary-order compatibility and the signed-order laws are proved separately.

Under A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for compounds $A,B$ with $m(A)=m(B)$ and every finite spectator compound $C$, $A+C\prec B+C$ if and only if $A\prec B$. Consequently, for finite-support signed maps $u,v$ of equal total coefficient, define $u\preceq_s v$ by $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$. This relation is well-defined, agrees with $\prec$ on nonnegative maps, is invariant under adding a common signed map, is transitive, and is closed under addition of two comparisons. No comparison hypothesis is used.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], each simple domain has one orientation sign $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$, constant across the domain, such that at fixed work coordinate $v$, $x\prec y$ exactly when $\varepsilon_i(u_y-u_x)\ge0$. In coordinates oriented so $\varepsilon_i=1$, for each $x\in\Gamma_i$ the projection $\rho_x$ of $\partial_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ onto work coordinates is open and connected; the boundary is the graph $(u_x(v),v)$ of a $C^1$ function with locally Lipschitz derivative

$$Du_x(v)=-P_i(u_x(v),v).$$

If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y=A_x$ and their boundary graphs agree.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

derivations.claim: By T4, the open strips $\Sigma(a,b):=\{x:a\prec\prec x\prec\prec b\}$ with $a\prec\prec b$ and $a\sim_T b$ cover $\Gamma_i$. They are open: by [F2], $a\prec\prec x$ is $x\in\operatorname{int}A_a$, and $x\prec\prec b$ is $x\notin A_b$; the latter set is open because $A_b$ is relatively closed.

Let $\Sigma(a,b)$ and $\Sigma(c,d)$ overlap. Their intersection is open. Choose two states $e\prec\prec f$ in a small vertical segment contained in the overlap, using [F4]. Let $s_e,s_f$ be their coordinates in the first strip and $t_e,t_f$ in the second, supplied by [F1]. If $s_f<s_e$, the signed difference $R_{s_e}-R_{s_f}=(s_e-s_f)(\mathsf{J}(b)-\mathsf{J}(a))$ and positive scaling and signed compatibility [A1, F3] give $R_{s_f}\prec R_{s_e}$, so $f\prec e$ by the two reference equivalences; if $s_f=s_e$, those references coincide and give $f\sim e$. Both contradict $e\prec\prec f$. Hence $s_f>s_e$, and the same argument gives $t_f>t_e$.

The four reference equivalences give, in signed comparison,
$f-e\sim_s(s_f-s_e)(b-a),\qquad f-e\sim_s(t_f-t_e)(d-c).$
Put $r=(s_f-s_e)/(t_f-t_e)>0$. Additivity and positive scaling in [F3] give $d-c\sim_s r(b-a)$. Applying the same algebra to the equivalences for $e$ gives $c\sim_s a+(s_e-r t_e)(b-a)$. Consequently a state in the second strip with coordinate $t$ has first-chart coordinate $s_e+r(t-t_e)$. The change of chart is affine with strictly positive slope.

The same calculation covers a finite chain of overlapping strips: after each overlap, express the new strip's endpoint states as signed-equivalent affine maps in the existing reference pair. The local strip lemma gives every state $z$ of the added strip a coordinate $s_z\in\mathbb R$ with $\mathsf{J}(z)\sim_s(1-s_z)\mathsf{J}(a)+s_z\mathsf{J}(b)$ in the existing chart. Signed addition, positive scaling, translation, and equivalence under negative scaling are valid by [F3]; hence induction along a finite overlap chain gives one such common chart for every state in the union.

Take any finite list of target states in $\Gamma_i$ and join them in order by finitely many straight segments, which lie in $\Gamma_i$ by convexity. The resulting connected path is a finite union of closed bounded segments, hence compact by [F5]. The open strips from step 1.1 cover it, so compactness gives a finite subcover. The intersection graph of those strips meeting the path is connected: otherwise their unions would partition the connected path into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets. Order a spanning tree from one root strip; each later strip overlaps an earlier one in an open set and can be glued by step 3.1. Thus every target state has a common signed chart $\mathsf{J}(z)\sim_s(1-s_z)\mathsf{J}(a)+s_z\mathsf{J}(b)$ with $a\prec\prec b$.

Let $A=\sum_j\alpha_j \mathsf{J}(x_j)$ and $B=\sum_k\beta_k \mathsf{J}(y_k)$ have equal total mass $M$, and let $s_j,t_k$ be their common-chart coordinates. If $M=0$, nonnegativity makes both maps empty and reflexivity compares them. Assume $M>0$ and put $L:=M/w_{\Gamma_i}$; both sums of scalar amounts are $L$, since each represented state has mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$. Each state has signed equivalence $\mathsf{J}(x_j)\sim_s(1-s_j)\mathsf{J}(a)+s_j\mathsf{J}(b)$ in the common chart; signed addition, scaling, and splitting [F3] therefore make $A$ and $B$ each signed-equivalent to reference maps $R_{q_A}=(L-q_A)\mathsf{J}(a)+q_A\mathsf{J}(b)$ and $R_{q_B}=(L-q_B)\mathsf{J}(a)+q_B\mathsf{J}(b)$, where $q_A=\sum_j\alpha_js_j$ and $q_B=\sum_k\beta_kt_k$. If $q_A<q_B$, the signed difference has positive part $(q_B-q_A)\mathsf{J}(b)$ and negative part $(q_B-q_A)\mathsf{J}(a)$, so $a\prec b$ and positive scaling compare $R_{q_A}\prec R_{q_B}$ by [F3]. If $q_A=q_B$, the reference maps coincide and reflexivity applies; if $q_B<q_A$, the same argument compares in the reverse direction. Transitivity transfers that comparison to $A,B$. Hence any equal-mass pair is comparable, proving CH.

Let $d\geq1$, let $P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$, with this class defined in [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], be ergodic under the full translation group $\mathbb R^d$, and suppose its specific relative entropy $I(P)=\gamma$ relative to the unit-intensity Poisson law $Q$ is finite.

Then
$$D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)=D(P_X\Vert Q_X)+\int_X D(P_{Y|X=x}\Vert Q_Y)\,P_X(dx).$$
More generally, for nested standard-Borel observations $R$ and $S$ with $R$ a measurable function of $S$, and a fixed probability reference $Q_Y$ for a further variable $Y$, the conditional increments
$$G(R):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|R}\Vert Q_Y)\right],\qquad G(S):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|S}\Vert Q_Y)\right]$$
satisfy $0\leq G(R)\leq G(S)$ whenever the joint relative entropy is finite.

For free and periodic cubes define
$$Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}\!\left[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,bc}}\right],\qquad bc\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{per}\}.$$
Then the limit $p_Q(z,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}$ exists, is independent of $bc$, and
$$p_Q(z,\beta)=-\min_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
The minimizer set is nonempty and compact in the local-tame topology $\tau_L$.
Equivalently, a net $(P_\alpha)$ converges to $P$ in $\tau_L$ exactly when $E_{P_\alpha}f\to E_Pf$ for every measurable local $f$ with at most linear growth in the count of a bounded support.

For pairwise disjoint bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_r\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, the restrictions $\omega|_{A_1},\ldots,\omega|_{A_r}$ are independent, each count $N_{A_j}$ has Poisson law with mean $\lambda|A_j|$, and the joint law of counts on any finite disjoint family is the product of those Poisson laws.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$.

Assume AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, and HB as in [[thm-tdmath-local-tame-entropy-compactness]]. Let $L\to\infty$ and let $C_L$ be probability laws on finite configurations in $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, invariant under every translation modulo $L\mathbb Z^d$. Write $Q_L$ for unit-intensity Poisson measure and suppose
$$c_L=L^{-d}D(C_L\Vert Q_L),\qquad \sup_L c_L<\infty.$$
Let $\widetilde C_L$ be the law of the periodic continuation. Then $\widetilde C_L=E_{C_L}R_{L,\omega}$; these laws are stationary and are relatively sequentially compact in $\tau_L$ as $L\to\infty$. Their local counts are uniformly integrable. Along any convergent subsequence with limit $P$,
$$I(P)\leq\liminf_L c_L.$$
If the empirical fields $R_{L,\omega}$ converge in probability in $\tau_L$ to a fixed $P_*$, then $\widetilde C_L\to P_*$ in $\tau_L$, including expectations of every measurable local $f$ with $|f|\leq b(1+N_A)$ for bounded $A$. This concerns periodic continuation, not the zero extension of a configuration outside its fundamental cube.

derivations.claim: Regularity bounds $\phi$ above outside a bounded set, so $B$ is bounded. Define $\chi=+\infty$ on $B$ and $0$ elsewhere. Then $\chi$ is even, stable with constant $0$, and has zero far tail. Its finite-volume beta-zero partition is exactly the specified hard-admissibility partition.

For each bounded region $A$, the event that $A$ contains a forbidden pair is a bounded measurable local event. Its probability is continuous under $\tau_L$ by [F6]. Exhausting space by countably many bounded cubes shows that $\mathcal K_B$ is $\tau_L$-closed. Apply [F4] to the bounded tests $f_M=a\min(N_C,M)$ and let $M\to\infty$. Monotone convergence and [F7] give $I(P)\geq a\rho(P)-(e^a-1)$, hence $\rho(P)\leq(I(P)+e^a-1)/a$. Choosing $a>2\max(\log z,0)$ makes $I(P)-\rho(P)\log z$ coercive in $I(P)$. By [F2], every finite sublevel is compact and lower semicontinuous, so the infimum on $\mathcal K_B$ is attained whenever the admissible class is nonempty. The empty configuration law gives a finite candidate.

Fix $P\in\mathcal K_B$ with $I(P)<\infty$. Condition its restriction to a cube of side $n$ on configurations whose distinct points have separation at least $1/q$ and whose finite pair energies are at most $q$. As $q\to\infty$, these events increase to probability one because configurations are locally finite, simple, and hard-admissible. Choose $q=q(n)$ so the conditioning probability tends to one. Tile space by these conditioned blocks separated by an empty corridor wider than the range of $B$ and the fixed tail cutoff, take independent copies, then average the lattice phase uniformly. No cross-block pair is forbidden. The conditional entropy inequality $$ D(P(\cdot\mid E)\Vert Q)\leq [D(P\Vert Q)+1]/P(E)-\log P(E) $$ follows by expanding the conditional density $1_E(dP/dQ)/P(E)$ and using $-u\log u\leq1/e$. Additivity on independent blocks and the vanishing corridor fraction give $\limsup I(P_n)\leq I(P)$; local count truncation and finite first moments give $P_n\to P$ in $\tau_L$. Each $P_n$ has finite original energy density.

For a finite-volume beta-zero Gibbs law $G_L^b$, direct integration of its density gives $$ -\log Z_{Q,L}=D(G_L^b\Vert Q_L)-(\log z)E_{G_L^b}N_L. $$ Stationarize independent blocks and average their phase. The entropy chain rule bounds the resulting specific entropy by the displayed finite-volume entropy per volume; hard admissibility passes to every local limit. Compactness [F2], lower semicontinuity, and the entropy identity therefore give the pressure upper bound by the negative minimum in the statement. For the reverse bound, use the approximating finite-energy laws from step 1.3. Their independent separated blocks are admissible; the spatial likelihood theorem [F3] supplies typical blocks with likelihood cost $I(P_n)$, while empirical counts converge to $\rho(P_n)$. Changing from Poisson measure to the beta-zero weight gives the lower rate $-I(P_n)+\rho(P_n)\log z$. Let $n\to\infty$ and optimize over $P$. Corridors change the normalized log weight by their vanishing volume fraction, so free and periodic rates agree.

Put $\alpha=\log z$, $p_L=L^{-d}\log Z_{Q,L}$, and $d_L=L^{-d}D(G_L^{\rm per}\Vert Q_L)$. The exact identity in step 2.1 reads $d_L=\alpha\rho_L-p_L$. For $a>\max(\alpha,0)$, the entropy count inequality gives $d_L\geq a\rho_L-(e^a-1)$; the convergent pressure rates therefore bound both $\rho_L$ and $d_L$. The grand density and periodic hard-admissibility condition are invariant under translations modulo the box, so [F8] gives relatively compact continued laws. Every limit $P$ lies in $\mathcal K_B$ by the bounded local forbidden-pair tests from step 1.2. Along a subsequence realizing the entropy liminf, [F8] and count-tail uniformity give
$$I(P)-\alpha\rho(P)\leq\liminf(d_L-\alpha\rho_L)=-\lim p_L=\min_{\mathcal K_B}(I-\alpha\rho).$$
The opposite inequality is the definition of the minimum. Thus every accumulation point is a minimizer. If there is just one, relative compactness forces convergence of the entire sequence in $\tau_L$, including every stated tame test.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $\phi$ be superstable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], and let $B=\{x:\phi(x)=+\infty\}$. For a finite configuration $\omega$, call it admissible when no pair displacement belongs to $B$; for periodic boxes require this also for every periodic image pair. Define the zero-inverse-temperature-parameter continuation (the mathematical $\beta=0$ branch) to be $z^{N(\omega)}\mathbf 1_{\rm admissible}(\omega)$, explicitly retaining the hard exclusion. Then the normalized Poisson free and periodic partition rates exist and equal
$$-\min_{P\in\mathcal K_B}\{I(P)-\rho(P)\log z\},$$
where $\mathcal K_B$ is the set of stationary laws with no forbidden pair almost surely. The minimizer set is nonempty and compact in $\tau_L$. The periodically continued grand laws are relatively compact in $\tau_L$, all their accumulation points are minimizers, and if this minimizer is unique they converge to it for every measurable local observable of at-most-linear count growth. If $B=\varnothing$, this is the Poisson activity-$z$ model. For $B\ne\varnothing$, it is not an unrestricted Poisson law and does not assign a value to the undefined product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

citations.quote:
Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with finite slope $P_i(x)$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for every simple state $x$, the forward sector $A_x=\{y\in\Gamma_i:x\prec y\}$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$. For collinear $y=tx+(1-t)z$, $0<t<1$, $y\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$, and $x\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$.
Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], every forward sector $A_x$ has nonempty interior in its ambient simple domain $\Gamma_i$.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], each simple domain has one orientation sign $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$, constant across the domain, such that at fixed work coordinate $v$, $x\prec y$ exactly when $\varepsilon_i(u_y-u_x)\ge0$. In coordinates oriented so $\varepsilon_i=1$, for each $x\in\Gamma_i$ the projection $\rho_x$ of $\partial_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ onto work coordinates is open and connected; the boundary is the graph $(u_x(v),v)$ of a $C^1$ function with locally Lipschitz derivative

$$Du_x(v)=-P_i(u_x(v),v).$$

If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y=A_x$ and their boundary graphs agree.

Let $C$ be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$. Its relative interior $\operatorname{ri}_H C$ is the interior in $H=\operatorname{aff}C$. Then $\operatorname{ri}_H C$ is nonempty. If $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$, $y\in\overline{C}^{\,H}$, and $0\le t<1$, then $(1-t)w+ty\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$.

derivations.claim: If $y\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_y\subseteq A_x$. If also $y\in\partial A_x$, [F3] gives equality. Suppose instead $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. If $A_y$ met $\partial A_x$ at $z$, then $z\in A_y$ and [F3] would give $A_z=A_x$. Since $z\in A_y$, transitivity gives $A_z\subseteq A_y\subseteq A_x$, so $A_y=A_x$. But S2 puts $y$ on $\partial A_y$, contradicting $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. Thus $A_y$ avoids $\partial A_x$ and, being a subset of the closed sector $A_x$, lies in $\operatorname{int}A_x$.

Suppose neither $y\in A_x$ nor $x\in A_y$. Choose $z\in\operatorname{int}A_x$ using [F2]. The segment from $y$ to $z$ lies in $\Gamma_i$ and meets $\partial A_x$ at a point $w$ strictly between its endpoints. By [F3], $A_w=A_x$, so $w\prec z$. The collinear implication in [F1], applied to $w=ty+(1-t)z$, gives $y\prec w\prec z$. Hence every $z\in\operatorname{int}A_x$ lies in $A_y$. Reversing $x,y$ gives $\operatorname{int}A_y\subseteq A_x$.

Because $A_x$ is full-dimensional by [F2], its affine hull is the ambient space. Fix $w\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. For any $q\in A_x$, relative closedness gives $q\in\overline{A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$, and [F4] puts $(1-t)w+tq$ in $\operatorname{int}A_x$ for every $0\le t<1$. Letting $t\uparrow1$ shows $q\in\overline{\operatorname{int}A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$. The reverse inclusion follows because $A_x$ is relatively closed. Hence $A_x=\overline{\operatorname{int}A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$; the same holds for $A_y$. Relative closedness from [F1] therefore extends the two interior inclusions in step 1.2 to $A_x\subseteq A_y$ and $A_y\subseteq A_x$. Equality would put $x\in A_y$, contradicting the supposition. Thus at least one of $x\prec y$ or $y\prec x$ always holds.

If $x\prec y$, then $y\in A_x$. If $y$ is a boundary point, step 1.1 gives $A_x=A_y$, hence $x\prec y$ and $y\prec x$. Otherwise step 1.1 gives $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}A_x$, and $x\notin A_y$ because S2 places $x$ on $\partial A_x$. Thus $x\prec\prec y$. Conversely, if $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$, step 1.1 and S2 show $x\notin A_y$, so $x\prec\prec y$.

derivations.claim: Let $S_N=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}^d$ be the cell indices in $\Lambda_N$. For $i\in S_N$, set $A_{i,N}=\{j-i:j\in S_N,\ j<_{\rm lex}i\}$; this is a finite subset of the past of the reference cell. Repeated conditional-density factorization from [F3] gives, $P$-almost surely, $$\log h_N(\omega)=\sum_{i\in S_N}\log k_{A_{i,N}}(T_{-i}\omega).$$ Every finite factor is defined $P$-almost surely because the corresponding local relative entropy is finite by [F1].

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By the directed convergence in [F2], choose a finite past $A_*$ such that every finite $B\supseteq A_*$ satisfies $E_P|\log k_B-Z|<\varepsilon$. Put $R=\max\{|a_j|:a\in A_*,1\leq j\leq d\}$, with $R=0$ if $A_*=\varnothing$. Let $S_N^\circ$ consist of cells at least $R$ cells from each face of $S_N$. If $i\in S_N^\circ$, then $A_*\subseteq A_{i,N}$, so by stationarity $E_P|\log k_{A_{i,N}}(T_{-i}\omega)-Z(T_{-i}\omega)|<\varepsilon$. The boundary has $N^d-(N-2R)^d=o(N^d)$ cells (for $N>2R$). For every finite past $B$, $E_P\log k_B=g(B)\leq\gamma$ and $E_P(-\log k_B)^+\leq1/e$, hence $E_P|\log k_B|\leq\gamma+2/e$. For $Z=\log k_\infty$, $E_P(-\log k_\infty)^+=\int_{0<k_\infty<1}k_\infty(-\log k_\infty)\,dR_0\leq1/e$ on its reference probability $R_0=P_{F_+}\otimes Q_C$, so [F2] gives $E_P|Z|\leq\gamma+2/e$ as well. Summing the interior errors and bounding each boundary error by $2(\gamma+2/e)$ yields $$\left\|N^{-d}\log h_N-N^{-d}\sum_{i\in S_N}Z(T_{-i}\cdot)\right\|_{L^1(P)}\longrightarrow0,$$ since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary.

For $j=1,\ldots,d$, the shift $U_jf=f\circ T_{-e_j}$ is a linear isometry on complex $L^2(P)$ by stationarity. Apply [F4] to $N^{-1}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}U_j^n$, obtaining strong convergence to the orthogonal projection $P_j$ onto the $U_j$-invariant subspace. The coordinate shifts commute, so every average for coordinate $j$ commutes with every average for coordinate $k$; taking strong limits shows that the $P_j$ commute with each other and with the other coordinate averages. Since all these operators have norm at most one, a finite telescoping estimate gives strong convergence of the product of the $d$ averages to $P_1\cdots P_d$. This product is the orthogonal projection onto the intersection of the coordinate-invariant subspaces, because the $P_j$ are commuting orthogonal projections. The product averages are exactly the rectangular cube averages $N^{-d}\sum_{i\in S_N}Z_M(T_{-i}\cdot)$, so these converge in $L^2$ for bounded $Z_M$ to a function invariant under every integer shift.

Since $Z\in L^1(P)$, dominated convergence gives $\|Z-Z_M\|_1\to0$. Cube averages are $L^1$ contractions, so the averages of $Z$ are Cauchy in $L^1$: for large $M$ their distance from the convergent averages of $Z_M$ is at most $\|Z-Z_M\|_1$. Let their $L^1$ limit be $s$. Every cube average has mean $E_PZ=\gamma$, hence $E_Ps=\gamma$. For each coordinate shift $e_j$, the averaging index cube and its translate have symmetric difference of exactly $2N^{d-1}$ indices, so $\|U_j A_NZ-A_NZ\|_1\leq2\|Z\|_1/N$. Passing to the $L^1$ limit gives $U_js=s$. These generators imply invariance under every integer translation.

Fix $r\in\mathbb R^d$, put $G=\Lambda_N$, $G'=G+r$, and $B=G\cap G'$. For $N>2\|r\|_\infty$, $B$ contains a cube $J$ of side $N-2\|r\|_\infty$. By [F1] and restriction monotonicity, $D(P_G\Vert Q_G)\leq\gamma N^d$ and $D(P_B\Vert Q_B)\geq D(P_J\Vert Q_J)$; the latter divided by $N^d$ tends to $\gamma$. Therefore $N^{-d}(D(P_G\Vert Q_G)-D(P_B\Vert Q_B))\to0$. The conditional chain rule [F3] identifies $\log h_G-\log h_B$ with a conditional log density. Its mean is this entropy difference, and [F3] bounds its negative-part expectation by $1/e$; thus its $L^1(P)$ norm is at most the entropy difference plus $2/e$. The same bound applies to $G'$. Translation covariance gives $\log h_{G'}=(\log h_G)\circ T_{-r}$; thus the normalized information in $G$ and $G'$ have the same $L^1$ limit. Since $N^{-d}\log h_G\to s$, it follows that $s\circ T_{-r}=s$ $P$-almost surely for this $r$.

Step 5.1 applies to every fixed $r\in\mathbb R^d$. For each rational $q$, the event $\{s\leq q\}$ is therefore invariant modulo null sets under every translation. Full-translation ergodicity makes each such event have probability $0$ or $1$. If $s$ were not almost surely constant, some rational sublevel set would have probability strictly between $0$ and $1$; hence $s$ is constant. Its mean from step 4.1 is $\gamma$, so $s=\gamma$. Combining with step 2.1 proves the asserted $L^1(P)$ limit.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Assume AC. Let $d\geq1$, let $P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$, with this class defined in [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], be ergodic under the full translation group $\mathbb R^d$, and suppose its specific relative entropy $I(P)=\gamma$ relative to the unit-intensity Poisson law $Q$ is finite. Ergodic means that every measurable event invariant modulo $P$-null sets under each translation has probability $0$ or $1$. For an integer $N\geq1$, let $\Lambda_N=[0,N)^d$, and let $h_N=dP_{\Lambda_N}/dQ_{\Lambda_N}$, which exists because $D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})<\infty$. Then
$$\frac{1}{N^d}\log h_N\longrightarrow\gamma\qquad\text{in }L^1(P).$$
Without the full-translation ergodicity hypothesis the proof yields an invariant $L^1(P)$ limit of mean $\gamma$; it need not be constant.

The statement uses aligned half-open cubes; translations may create boundary strips, whose normalized contribution is controlled by the overlap argument.

derivations.claim: If $G_1,G_2$ are disjoint bounded Borel sets, [F1] decomposes $D(P_{G_1\cup G_2}\Vert Q_{G_1}\otimes Q_{G_2})$ into $D(P_{G_1}\Vert Q_{G_1})$ plus the mean conditional relative entropy of $G_2$ given $G_1$. That conditional increment is at least $D(P_{G_2}\Vert Q_{G_2})$ by the conditioning monotonicity in [F1], comparing observation by $G_1$ with no observation. Thus relative entropy is superadditive over disjoint regions; if the left side is infinite the inequality is immediate, and otherwise all terms in the chain rule are finite.

Fix an integer $m\geq1$ and let $q_N=\lfloor N/m\rfloor$. Tile $[0,q_Nm)^d$ by $q_N^d$ disjoint translates of $\Lambda_m$, leaving the Borel remainder $\Lambda_N\setminus[0,q_Nm)^d$. Iterating step 1.1 and using nonnegativity on the remainder gives $$D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})\geq q_N^dD(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m}),$$ because stationarity gives the same entropy for each translated $m$-cube. If $D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})=+\infty$, this forces $D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})=+\infty$ for every $N\geq m$.

Put $s=\sup_{m\geq1}m^{-d}D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})$. If $s=+\infty$, step 2.1 makes the liminf of $N^{-d}D_N$ exceed every finite bound, so the integer-cube limit is $+\infty=s$. If $s<+\infty$, step 2.1 gives $$\liminf_{N\to\infty}N^{-d}D_N\geq m^{-d}D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})$$ for every $m$, since $q_N^d/N^d\to m^{-d}$. Taking the supremum gives liminf at least $s$, while the definition of $s$ gives $N^{-d}D_N\leq s$ for every integer $N$. Hence the integer-cube limit exists and equals $s$.

For real $L\to\infty$, let $N=\lfloor L\rfloor$. The inclusions $\Lambda_N\subseteq\Lambda_L\subseteq\Lambda_{N+1}$ and [F3] give $D_N\leq D_L\leq D_{N+1}$. Since $N/L\to1$ and $(N+1)/L\to1$, step 3.1 squeezes $L^{-d}D_L$ to the same extended limit $s$; if some integer-cube entropy is infinite, monotonicity gives the same conclusion directly.

If $I(P)<\infty$ and $A$ is bounded, choose an integer cube $\Lambda_N+x$ containing $A$. Stationarity [F2] and restriction monotonicity [F3] give $$D(P_A\Vert Q_A)\leq D(P_{\Lambda_N+x}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N+x})=D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})\leq N^d I(P)<\infty.$$ Thus every bounded restriction has finite relative entropy.

Assume AC and let $P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$, with this class defined in [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], be stationary for the translations of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. For a bounded Borel set $G$, write $P_G$ and $Q_G$ for the restrictions of $P$ and the unit-intensity Poisson reference $Q$ to configurations in $G$. For $L>0$, put $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$ and
$$D_L:=D(P_{\Lambda_L}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L}).$$
Then the specific relative entropy density
$$I(P):=\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{D_L}{L^d}$$
exists in $[0,+\infty]$ and satisfies
$$I(P)=\sup_{m\in\mathbb N,\ m\geq1}\frac{D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})}{m^d}.$$
If $I(P)<\infty$, every bounded Borel restriction has finite relative entropy. This is an information functional relative to the specified unit-intensity Poisson law; changing the reference changes its value.
