citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For the type set $\mathcal G$ and cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]], define the relation $\Gamma\approx_0\Gamma'$ by $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')=F(\Gamma',\Gamma)=0$. Let $\mathcal P:=\mathcal G\times\mathcal G$ be the set of raw type pairs. Define a relation on raw pairs by

$$(A,B)\equiv(A',B')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists C\text{ such that }A\times B'\times C\approx_0 A'\times B\times C.$$

The separate well-definedness lemma proves that $\approx_0$ is an equivalence compatible with composition and positive scaling, that $\equiv$ is an equivalence on $\mathcal P$, and that the following operations are well-defined on its classes. After that proof, write $V_F:=\mathcal P/\equiv$. Define addition by $[(A,B)]+[(D,E)]:=[(A\times D,B\times E)]$, negation by $-[(A,B)]:=[(B,A)]$, and positive scaling by $t[(A,B)]:=[(tA,tB)]$. Set zero to $[(1,1)]$, where $1$ is the empty unit type. The same lemma establishes that these operations make $V_F$ a real vector space; no vector-space law is assumed by this Definition.

For the construction in [[def-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space]], $\approx_0$ is an equivalence compatible with product and positive scaling; $V_F$ is a real vector space and its displayed operations are representative-independent.

For the cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]], $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, $F$ is positively homogeneous, invariant under adding the same catalyst to both endpoints, and satisfies the triangle inequality whenever the extended-real sum on its right is defined. It is subadditive under composition whenever $F(\Gamma_1,\Gamma'_1)+F(\Gamma_2,\Gamma'_2)$ is defined. Every pair of actual forward and reverse decorated-chain witnesses has nonnegative total cost. A finite reverse witness therefore bounds all forward costs below; $F=-\infty$ can occur only when the reverse direction has no witness.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $V$ be a real vector space and $p:V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ satisfy $p(0)=0$, $p(tx)=tp(x)$ for every $t>0$, and $p(x+y)\le p(x)+p(y)$ in extended-real arithmetic. Assume **no sinks**: $p(x)<+\infty$ if and only if $p(-x)<+\infty$. Put $W:=\{x\in V:p(x)<+\infty\}$. Then $W$ is a linear subspace and there exists a real-linear $L:V\to\mathbb R$ such that

$$-p(-x)\le L(x)\le p(x)\qquad(x\in V),$$

with $-\infty\le r\le+\infty$ interpreted in the usual extended order. The result is valid in arbitrary dimension and allows $p=+\infty$ outside $W$.

For the conditional offset application, let $V=V_{\mathcal G}$ from [[def-tdmath-type-offset-vector-space]], let $F:\mathcal G\times\mathcal G\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ satisfy $p([e_\Gamma]-[e_{\Gamma'}])=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$, and define $B(\Gamma):=L([e_\Gamma])$. Then $B(\Gamma\times\Gamma')=B(\Gamma)+B(\Gamma')$, $B(t\Gamma)=tB(\Gamma)$ for $t>0$, and

$$-F(\Gamma',\Gamma)\le B(\Gamma)-B(\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma,\Gamma').$$

For each $\Gamma\in\mathcal G$, let $X_\Gamma$ be a state set and $\sigma_\Gamma:X_\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ a baseline state function. If every admitted transition $(\Gamma,x)\to(\Gamma',y)$, with $x\in X_\Gamma$ and $y\in X_{\Gamma'}$, satisfies $\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)\ge F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$, then $\sigma_\Gamma(x)+B(\Gamma)$ is nondecreasing across those transitions. The existence or properties of such a cost $p$, including no-sinks, are hypotheses and are not proved by this theorem.

Assume the calibrated entropy family of [[thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration]], the cross-type accessibility axioms A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], and the decorated cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]]. For every pair of types $\Gamma,\Gamma'$ and states $x\in X_\Gamma$, $y\in X_{\Gamma'}$,

$$x\prec y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sigma_\Gamma(x)+F(\Gamma,\Gamma')\le \sigma_{\Gamma'}(y).$$

The infimum defining $F$ need not be attained. If $F=+\infty$, the right side is false; if $F=-\infty$, the right side is true.

derivations.claim: If $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')<+\infty$, no-sinks gives a finite reverse witness of some real cost $c$. Concatenating it with any forward witness makes a closed chain, so [F2] gives forward cost at least $-c$. Thus $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')>-\infty$ whenever it is finite; all cost values are in $\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$.

For a pair class $v=[\Gamma,\Gamma']\in V_F$, define $p(v):=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. Suppose $(\Gamma,\Gamma')\equiv(\Lambda,\Lambda')$ via $C$, so $P=\Gamma\times\Lambda'\times C\approx_0 Q=\Lambda\times\Gamma'\times C$. Put $D=\Gamma'\times\Lambda'\times C$. Since $P\approx_0 Q$, the triangle inequality gives $F(P,D)\le F(Q,D)$ and $F(Q,D)\le F(P,D)$; the costs have no $-\infty$ by step 1.1, so these inequalities imply equality. Catalyst invariance from [F2] gives $F(P,D)=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ and $F(Q,D)=F(\Lambda,\Lambda')$. Therefore $p$ is independent of the pair representative.

The identity $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$ gives $p(0)=0$. Homogeneity of $F$ gives $p(tv)=tp(v)$ for $t>0$, and its product subadditivity gives $p(v+w)\le p(v)+p(w)$. The no-sinks condition says $p(v)<+\infty$ exactly when $p(-v)<+\infty$. By step 1.1, $p$ has no $-\infty$ value.

Apply [F3] to $V_F$ and $p$. It gives a real-linear $L:V_F\to\mathbb R$ with $-p(-v)\le L(v)\le p(v)$ for all $v$. Put $B(\Gamma)=L([\Gamma,1])$, where $1$ is the empty unit type. Since $[\Gamma\times\Gamma',1]=[\Gamma,1]+[\Gamma',1]$, $B$ is additive. Since $[t\Gamma,1]=t[\Gamma,1]$ (the unit type satisfies $t1=1$), $B(t\Gamma)=tB(\Gamma)$ for $t>0$. Also $[\Gamma,\Gamma']=[\Gamma,1]-[\Gamma',1]$, so applying the sandwich to this pair gives the displayed two-sided cost bound.

For an admitted transition, [F4] gives $\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)\ge F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$, while step 3.1 gives $B(\Gamma)-B(\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. Subtracting the latter from the former yields
$[\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)+B(\Gamma')]-[\sigma_\Gamma(x)+B(\Gamma)]\ge0.$
Thus the offset entropy is nondecreasing across every admitted transition.

Fix a positive integer $d$ and use the Euclidean space $\mathbb R^d$ with norm
$\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A
pair potential is an even Borel-measurable function
$\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ whose image is contained in
$\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. Here $\overline{\mathbb R}$ is the extended real
line ([[def-extended-reals]]). Borel measurability means the inverse image of
each Borel subset of $\overline{\mathbb R}$ belongs to the Borel sigma-algebra
generated by open sets in the Euclidean topology on $\mathbb R^d$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Even means $\phi(-x)=\phi(x)$. The value
$+\infty$ represents a forbidden pair separation. Coordinates and
potential values are numerical values in fixed reference length and energy
units.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $d\ge1$, let $\phi$ be a stable pair
potential as in [[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]] with

measure (rectangle formula and uniqueness in [F6]) make the assignment
integrals equal.

citations.quote: Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$; then $(p_i)$ is a countable probability law. For any real observable $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

derivations.claim: On a compact interval $K\subset J$, let $Z_N$, $D_N$, and $Q_N$ be the first $N$ partial sums of $\sum_i g_i e^{-\beta E_i}$, $-\sum_i g_iE_ie^{-\beta E_i}$, and $\sum_i g_iE_i^2e^{-\beta E_i}$. Since $|E_i|^r\le1+|E_i|^2$ for $r=0,1,2$, each tail is bounded uniformly on $K$ by the corresponding tail of $\sum_i a_i$, which tends to zero [A1]. Thus all three sequences converge uniformly; call their limits $Z,D,Q$. Each finite partial sum has the displayed derivatives by the chain rule [F5] and the exponential derivative [F2]. Each partial sum is continuous, so the uniform limits are continuous by the $\varepsilon/3$ definition of continuity.

For an interior $\beta$ and sufficiently small $h\ne0$, apply [F4] to $Z_N$ on the interval with endpoints $\beta$ and $\beta+h$: its difference quotient is $D_N(\xi_{N,h})$ for some intermediate $\xi_{N,h}$. Choose $N=N(h)$ so that $\sup_K|Z_N-Z|<h^2$ and $\sup_K|D_N-D|<|h|$. The difference quotient for $Z$ then differs from $D(\beta)$ by at most $2|h|+|h|+\sup_{|t-\beta|\le|h|}|D(t)-D(\beta)|$, which tends to zero by continuity of $D$. Hence $Z'=D$. Applying the same argument to $D_N$ and $Q_N$ proves $D'=Q$, so the displayed derivatives hold.

The summands of $Z$ are positive and at least one is present, hence $0<Z<\infty$ on $K$; summing the definition of $p_i$ gives $\sum_i p_i=1$. The envelope also gives $\sum_i p_i|E_i|$ and $\sum_i p_iE_i^2$ finite. Differentiating $\log Z$ using [F3] yields $-Z'/Z=\bar E$ and $Z''/Z-(Z'/Z)^2=\langle E^2\rangle-\bar E^2=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$.

Since $p_i/g_i=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$, its logarithm is $-\beta E_i-\log Z$. The finite first moment makes $\sum_i p_i|\log(p_i/g_i)|\le |\beta|\sum_i p_i|E_i|+|\log Z|\sum_i p_i<\infty$; summing the identity gives $H_g=\beta\bar E+\log Z$.

case_scope.source_excerpt: Let $I,E_i,g_i,J,Z$ be as in [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]. Suppose that for every compact interval $K\subset J$ there is a summable sequence $a_i\ge0$ such that $g_i(1+|E_i|^2)\exp(-\beta E_i)\le a_i$ for every $i\in I$ and $\beta\in K$. Moreover $H_g(p)=\log Z+\beta\bar E$, and its defining series is absolutely convergent.

With fixed numerical length and energy units, the canonical positional partition is
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}dq_1\cdots dq_N,\quad Z(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
where $\beta>0$, and the grand partition is $\Xi(L;a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$ for numerical activity $a>0$.

For a bounded set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $R>0$, define its two-sided boundary layer
$$\partial_R\Omega=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)\leq R\},$$
where distance is Euclidean distance and $|\cdot|$ denotes $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

For the unit cells $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$, there are constants $A>0$ and $B\geq0$ such that every finite configuration satisfies
$$H_\phi(\omega)\geq A\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}N_{C_i}(\omega)^2-BN(\omega).$$
Only finitely many summands are nonzero.
For free-boundary cubes define $\Xi_L(a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable.

derivations.claim:
First take a finite union $\mathcal R$ of unit cells and its free Gibbs law. By [L1] and Tonelli [F5],
$$E N_i^2=E N_i+E[N_i(N_i-1)] \leq \xi |C_i\cap\mathcal R|+\xi^2|C_i\cap\mathcal R|^2 \leq M:=\xi+\xi^2.$$
Let the cells be partitioned into boxes of side $\ell$. For each cell $i$, let $e_i$ be the sum of the lower-regular lattice envelope over cells $j$ in other boxes. The negative cross-box energy obeys $W^-\leq\tfrac12\sum_i e_iN_i^2$, because $N_iN_j\leq(N_i^2+N_j^2)/2$. Therefore $E W^-\leq(M/2)\sum_i e_i$. If $\sum_i e_i>0$, then $P(W^->M\sum_i e_i)\leq E W^-/(M\sum_i e_i)\leq1/2$; if the sum is zero, $W^-=0$ almost surely. Thus the event $W^-\leq M\sum_i e_i$ has probability at least $1/2$.

For each $\Omega_k$, let $\mathcal R_k$ be the union of unit cells meeting $\Omega_k$. Then $\Xi_{\Omega_k}\leq\Xi_{\mathcal R_k}$ by domain monotonicity, and $|\mathcal R_k|/|\Omega_k|\to1$ by the van Hove boundary condition. Partition $\mathcal R_k$ into boxes of $\ell$ unit cells per side. The probability event from step 1.1 has full Gibbs probability at least $1/2$; on it, $H_{\mathrm{total}}\geq H_{\mathrm{in}}-M\sum_i e_i$, where $H_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the sum of within-box energies. Therefore
$$\Xi_{\mathcal R_k}/2\leq e^{\beta M\sum_i e_i}\prod_B\Xi_{\mathcal R_k\cap B}.$$
Indeed, $\Xi_{\mathcal R_k}\mu_{\mathcal R_k}(E)=\int_Ee^{-\beta H_{\mathrm{total}}}d\Pi\leq e^{\beta M\sum_i e_i}\int_Ee^{-\beta H_{\mathrm{in}}}d\Pi$, and the last integral is bounded by the unrestricted product over boxes. Each partial-box partition is at most the full $\ell$-cube partition. For one full box, $E_\ell=\sum_{i\in B,j\notin B}\Psi(|i-j|)$ satisfies $E_\ell/\ell^d\to0$: cells within fixed distance $R$ of the boundary are $O_R(\ell^{d-1})$; all other cells contribute at most the summable tail beyond $R$. Thus
$$\limsup_k|\Omega_k|^{-1}\log\Xi_{\Omega_k} \leq\ell^{-d}\bigl[\log\Xi_{\Lambda_\ell}+\beta M E_\ell\bigr].$$
Let $\ell\to\infty$ and use [F4].

For the lower bound, fix core side $\ell$ and gap $g$, and retain every whole $(\ell+g)$-cell whose core lies in $\Omega_k$. By the van Hove property [F2], the retained count divided by $|\Omega_k|$ tends $(\ell+g)^{-d}$. Restrict each core to at most $K\ell^d$ particles. Exact $N!$ cancellation factorizes their grand weights. The lattice-shell count and [F1] bound positive cross energy per core by $C K^2(\ell/g)^d\eta(g)$, with $\eta(g)\to0$ from the integrable tail. This gives the same separated-core lower bound as the free-cube packing proof. First let $k\to\infty$, then choose $g=g(\ell)$ from [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]] and let $\ell\to\infty$; packing fraction tends one and the cross penalty vanishes. The resulting liminf is at least the cube pressure [F4].

$$|\Omega_k|^{-1}\log\Xi_{\Omega_k}(z,\beta)\longrightarrow p(z,\beta),$$
the free-cube limit from [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. The extra superstability hypothesis is essential to this proof's uniform cell-occupation bound; no arbitrary-shape theorem under stability alone is claimed.

citations.quote:
Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with finite slope $P_i(x)$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

Let $I$ be a nonempty set of primitive simple-system labels containing a distinguished meter label $m$. Assume every finite separated product is explicitly represented by its finitely many tagged elementary factors; positive scaling and finite product are the only identifications. Suppose the join-closed family satisfies the hypotheses of [[thm-tdmath-conditional-contact-calibrator]], and fix a strict meter pair $z_0\prec\prec z_1$ in $\Gamma_m$. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Then one can choose, for every $i\in I$, an additive constant and positive scale for its same-type entropy so that

$$S\big((t_1i_1,x_1),\ldots,(t_ni_n,x_n)\big)=\sum_{\ell=1}^n t_\ell S_{i_\ell}(x_\ell)$$

is additive, extensive, and characterizes every same-composition comparison on every finite separated product. No conclusion is asserted for transitions that change composition.

Let $\mathcal G$ be a set of tagged system types closed under finite composition $T\times T'$ and positive scaling $tT$. Scaling is associative and acts componentwise on products: $s(tT)=(st)T$ and $t(T\times T')=(tT)\times(tT')$. Each type $T$ has a nonempty state set $X_T$ of finite tagged compounds, every state in $X_T$ is represented by the coefficient-map interpretation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and has total coefficient mass $m(T)=w_T\ge0$, and $m(T\times T')=m(T)+m(T')$, $m(tT)=t\,m(T)$. The entropy $\sigma_T:X_T\to\mathbb R$ is the finite additive extensive entropy from [[thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration]]; in particular $\sigma_{tT}(ta)=t\sigma_T(a)$.

Include the formal empty unit type $1$, with $X_1=\{*\}$, $m(1)=0$, $\sigma_1(*)=0$, $T\times1=T$, and $t1=1$. A transition edge from type $T$ to type $T'$ is a pair $a\in X_T$, $b\in X_{T'}$ such that the underlying equal-mass compounds satisfy $a\prec b$ under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Thus an edge can exist only when $m(T)=m(T')$. Its cost is the finite real number $\sigma_{T'}(b)-\sigma_T(a)$.

A decorated finite chain from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma'$ consists of a catalyst type $C\in\mathcal G$, an integer $N\ge1$, types $T_0=\Gamma\times C,T_1,\ldots,T_N=\Gamma'\times C$, and states $a_k\in X_{T_k}$, $b_{k+1}\in X_{T_{k+1}}$ with an edge $a_k\prec b_{k+1}$ for every $0\le k<N$. Its cost is the finite real sum

$$c=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bigl(\sigma_{T_{k+1}}(b_{k+1})-\sigma_{T_k}(a_k)\bigr).$$

Define $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ as the infimum of all such witness costs. Set $F=+\infty$ if there is no witness and $F=-\infty$ if the witness costs are unbounded below. The infimum is over real witness costs, so no subtraction of extended-real infima is used. Type permutations, reassociation, reversible identifications, and the identity $T\times1=T$ are part of the declared type structure. The cost identities and inequalities require a separate proof.

For the cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]], $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, $F$ is positively homogeneous, invariant under adding the same catalyst to both endpoints, and satisfies the triangle inequality whenever the extended-real sum on its right is defined. It is subadditive under composition whenever $F(\Gamma_1,\Gamma'_1)+F(\Gamma_2,\Gamma'_2)$ is defined. Every pair of actual forward and reverse decorated-chain witnesses has nonnegative total cost. A finite reverse witness therefore bounds all forward costs below; $F=-\infty$ can occur only when the reverse direction has no witness.

Under A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for compounds $A,B$ with $m(A)=m(B)$ and every finite spectator compound $C$, $A+C\prec B+C$ if and only if $A\prec B$. Consequently, for finite-support signed maps $u,v$ of equal total coefficient, define $u\preceq_s v$ by $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$. This relation is well-defined, agrees with $\prec$ on nonnegative maps, is invariant under adding a common signed map, is transitive, and is closed under addition of two comparisons. No comparison hypothesis is used.

derivations.claim: If $x\prec y$, the one-edge witness with an identity catalyst has cost $\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)$. Hence $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')\le\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)$, which is the forward inequality, including the case $F=+\infty$ where no such transition can exist.

Conversely assume the displayed entropy inequality. It is impossible when $F=+\infty$. For each integer $n\ge1$, choose a decorated witness of real cost $c_n\le\Delta\sigma+h/n$, where $\Delta\sigma=\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)$ and $h=\sigma(z_1)-\sigma(z_0)>0$ is the entropy gap of a fixed strict meter pair from [F1]. Such witnesses exist from the definition of infimum, also if $F=-\infty$. Write their types as $T_0=\Gamma\times C,T_1,\ldots,T_N=\Gamma'\times C$, their edges as $a_k\prec b_{k+1}$, and their endpoints as $a_0=(\widetilde x,c_0)$, $b_N=(\widetilde y,d_0)$.

Put $\delta_n=1/n$. In one finite compound type form
$L_n=(x,b_N,b_1,\ldots,b_{N-1},\delta_n z_0),\qquad R_n=(a_0,y,a_1,\ldots,a_{N-1},\delta_n z_1).$
These have the same composition: both contain $\Gamma$, $\Gamma'$, the catalyst $C$, every intermediate type $T_1,\ldots,T_{N-1}$, and one scaled meter state, up to reassociation and permutation. Additivity of $\sigma$ and the definition of chain cost give
$\sigma(R_n)-\sigma(L_n)=\Delta\sigma-c_n+\delta_n h\ge0.$
Thus the same-composition entropy representation [F1] gives $L_n\prec R_n$.

Starting from $R_n$, use consistency on $a_0\prec b_1$ with $y,\delta_nz_1,a_1,\ldots,a_{N-1}$ as spectators. The result contains $b_1$ in place of $a_0$. Next use $a_1\prec b_2$ with $y,\delta_nz_1,b_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{N-1}$ as spectators, and continue in order. At stage $k$, the current compound contains $a_k$, the earlier outputs $b_1,\ldots,b_k$, all later inputs $a_{k+1},\ldots,a_{N-1}$, and the unchanged $y,\delta_nz_1$. After the last edge, transitivity gives $R_n\prec R'_n$, where $R'_n=(b_1,\ldots,b_N,y,\delta_nz_1)$. Compose this with $L_n\prec R_n$ from step 2.1. The compounds $L_n$ and $R'_n$ share the finite spectator $b_1+\cdots+b_N$; cancel it by [F4]. The result is $x+\delta_nz_0\prec y+\delta_nz_1$ for every $n$.

Since $\delta_n\downarrow0$, stability in [A1] with bases $x,y$ and fixed positive spectators $z_0,z_1$ yields $x\prec y$. This proves the reverse implication without assuming that any infimum is attained.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Assume the calibrated entropy family of [[thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration]], the cross-type accessibility axioms A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], and the decorated cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]]. For every pair of types $\Gamma,\Gamma'$ and states $x\in X_\Gamma$, $y\in X_{\Gamma'}$,

$$x\prec y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sigma_\Gamma(x)+F(\Gamma,\Gamma')\le \sigma_{\Gamma'}(y).$$

The infimum defining $F$ need not be attained. If $F=+\infty$, the right side is false; if $F=-\infty$, the right side is true.

boundaries.evidence: The positive meter scale tends to zero for stability (step 4.1).
A one-edge identity-catalyst witness proves the forward bound (step 1.1).
The F=+∞ and F=−∞ cases are separated (step 2.1).
Approximate witnesses suffice when the infimum is unattained (step 2.1).
A witness within tolerance is selected for each n (step 2.1).
Accessibility implies the entropy-cost inequality (step 1.1).
Approximate costs and stability prove the converse (step 4.1).

citations.quote: A pair potential is an even Borel function, measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra generated by open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]), $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where even means $\phi(-x)=\phi(x)$.
The tail of the cell envelope $\psi(|j|_\infty-1)$ over all sufficiently large integer offsets is summable.

Then there are a nonnegative nondecreasing $h:\mathbb N_0\to[0,+\infty]$ with $h(0)=0$ and $h(N)/N^2\to+\infty$, and a constant $b<\infty$, such that
$$H_\phi(\omega)\geq\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}h(N_{C_i}(\omega))-bN(\omega).$$
The hard-core alternative permits $h(N)=+\infty$ above the finite packing capacity of a unit cell.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

derivations.claim: Write $T_n=\sum_{i\subset\Lambda_n}N_i^2$ and $V_n=|\Lambda_n|$. From [F3], $T_n$ is controlled by $H_n+bN_n$ and the superquadratic penalty dominates $N_i^2$ for large cell counts. For exterior cells at distance at least $k$, the lattice tail gives an energy lower error at most $\delta_k(T_n+c_tV_n)$, where $\delta_k\to0$. For the finitely many near exterior cells, use $mN\leq g(N)+g^*(m)$ with $g(N)=N\sqrt{h(N)}$. Since $g(N)/N^2\to\infty$, its Legendre transform satisfies $g^*(m)/m^2\to0$: for each $\epsilon>0$, $g(N)\geq N^2/(4\epsilon)-C_\epsilon$, so $g^*(m)\leq\epsilon m^2+C_\epsilon$. The exterior square-count bound then makes the near-cell contribution at most $\epsilon T_n+\epsilon V_n+O(n^{d-1})$, uniformly over $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$.

Combining near and far estimates, for each $\epsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, the cross energy obeys $W(\omega,\zeta\setminus\Lambda_n)\geq-\epsilon T_n-\epsilon V_n$, uniformly in $\zeta$. Use $T_n\leq A_\epsilon(H_n+bN_n)+C_\epsilon V_n$ from [F3], and absorb the resulting linear-in-$N_n$ term into activity. This gives
$$\Xi_{n,\zeta}(\beta,z)\leq e^{c\epsilon V_n}\Xi_{n,\mathrm{free}}(\beta(1-c\epsilon),ze^{c\epsilon}),$$
for a fixed constant $c$ depending only on the coercivity constants.

For the lower bound, restrict interior particles to a smaller cube with an empty corridor of width $k$. All exterior pairs are then in the far tail, and the same shell estimate bounds the absolute cross energy by $\epsilon T_{n-k}+\epsilon V_n$. The cell penalty absorbs the count term and yields
$$\Xi_{n,\zeta}(\beta,z)\geq e^{-c\epsilon V_n}\Xi_{n-k,\mathrm{free}}(\beta(1+c\epsilon),ze^{-c\epsilon})$$
uniformly over $\zeta$. The removed corridor volume fraction vanishes for fixed $k$.

Divide steps 2.1–2.2 by $V_n$ and take $n\to\infty$; [F4] supplies the perturbed cube pressure limits. These limits are finite convex functions of $(\beta,\log z)$, by Hölder’s inequality [F5], since finite-volume log partition functions are convex and pointwise limits preserve convexity. A finite convex function on an open parameter rectangle is continuous, by bounding coordinate secant slopes on a smaller rectangle. Let $\epsilon\downarrow0$ in both bounds. The upper and lower limits coincide with the free-cube pressure, uniformly over the entire exterior class.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Assume a stable regular pair potential with the genuine positive-core condition of [[lem-tdmath-superquadratic-positive-core]]: a nonincreasing $\chi(r)>0$ satisfies $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ near zero and $\int_0^{r_0}\chi(r)r^{d-1}dr=\infty$. For fixed $z,\beta>0$, define the exterior class
$$\Omega(t)=\{\zeta:\sum_{i\in\Lambda_n\cap\mathbb Z^d}N_{C_i}(\zeta)^2\leq t(2n+1)^d\text{ for every }n\}.$$
Then the free-wall grand pressure in $\Lambda_n=[-n-\tfrac12,n+\tfrac12)^d$, with the exterior pair energy against any $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$, converges to the free-cube pressure uniformly in $\zeta$. This statement is conditional on the genuine positive core; it does not infer that condition from superstability alone.

L1.title: D. Ruelle, Superstable Interactions in Classical Statistical Mechanics
L1.source_section: Section 6, printed pp.188–191 / PDF pp.18–21; complete relevant arguments and the Ruelle moment proof were read.
L1.source_statement: For a superstable lower-regular interaction, finite-volume and tempered-law estimates control near-boundary and far-tail contributions uniformly over the stated square-count class.

citations.quote:
With fixed numerical length and energy units, the canonical positional partition is
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}dq_1\cdots dq_N,\quad Z(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
where $\beta>0$, and the grand partition is $\Xi(L;a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$ for numerical activity $a>0$.

A van Hove sequence is a sequence of bounded Lebesgue measurable sets $(\Omega_k)_{k\geq1}$ with $0<|\Omega_k|<\infty$, $|\Omega_k|\to\infty$, and
$$\frac{|\partial_R\Omega_k|}{|\Omega_k|}\longrightarrow0\qquad\text{for every fixed }R>0.$$
The condition controls both inner and outer boundary neighborhoods.

For sequences $L_j\to\infty$ and integers $N_j\geq0$ with $N_j/L_j^d\to\rho$, define
$$b(\rho)=\sup\left\{\limsup_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta):\frac{N_j}{L_j^d}\to\rho\right\}.$$
Let $F$ be the concave envelope of $b$ on $[0,\infty)$, namely the supremum of $\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i b(\rho_i)$ over finite lists with $\theta_i\geq0$, $\sum_i\theta_i=1$, $\rho_i\geq0$, and $\sum_i\theta_i\rho_i=\rho$; the empty supremum is $-\infty$.

Then
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\bigl(F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho\bigr),\qquad F_\beta(\rho)=\inf_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\bigl(P(\alpha,\beta)-\alpha\rho\bigr)$$
for every $\rho$ in the closed effective domain of $F_\beta$.

For every van Hove sequence $(\Omega_k)$, the free-wall physical grand pressure satisfies
$$|\Omega_k|^{-1}\log\Xi_{\Omega_k}(z,\beta)\longrightarrow p(z,\beta),$$
the free-cube limit from [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]].
Let $d\geq1$ and let $\phi$ be a regular potential with a nonnegative nonincreasing envelope $\psi:[R_0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, where $R_0<\infty$ and $\int_{R_0}^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr<\infty$.

derivations.claim: For any $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $e^{\alpha N_k}Z(\Omega_k,N_k)\leq\Xi_{\Omega_k}(e^\alpha,\beta)$. Divide by volume, use [F5], and take the infimum over $\alpha$. The duality [F4] gives $\limsup |\Omega_k|^{-1}\log Z(\Omega_k,N_k)\leq F_\beta(\rho)$.

Choose $\delta>0$ so $\rho-\delta,\rho+\delta$ lie in the attainable interior. For large core side $\ell$, choose integers $n_-,n_+$ with $n_\pm/\ell^d\to\rho\pm\delta$. Put a central $\ell$-cube inside each $(\ell+g)$-cell, with $g=g(\ell)$ from [F6]. The effective densities $n_\pm/(\ell+g)^d$ still bracket $\rho$ when $\ell$ is large.

At fixed $\ell,g$, pack every complete $(\ell+g)$-cell contained in $\Omega_k$. Its count $M_k$ satisfies $M_k/|\Omega_k|\to(\ell+g)^{-d}$ by [F2]. Assign $n_+$ particles to $j_k$ cores and $n_-$ to the remaining cores, except one correction core with remainder $r_k$ chosen to make the total exactly $N_k$. Bracketing ensures $0\leq j_k<M_k$ for large $k$; Euclidean division gives $0\leq r_k<n_+-n_- \leq n_+$. Every correction integral $Z(\ell,r)$, $0\leq r\leq n_+$, is positive: delete particles from a positive-measure finite-energy set realizing $Z(\ell,n_+)>0$. There are finitely many such $r$, so the correction contributes $O_\ell(1)$ to the log weight.

Exact assignment of labels cancels the global $N_k!$, leaving the product of core canonical integrals. The core lattice shell estimate bounds cross-energy per volume by $C K^2(\ell/g)^d\eta(g)$, where $K\ell^d\geq n_+$. Let $k\to\infty$ first, then $\ell\to\infty$. The packing fraction tends one, the cross error tends zero, and the two rates tend $F_\beta(\rho-\delta)$ and $F_\beta(\rho+\delta)$. The bracketing proportions tend one half, so the lower rate is at least their average. Finally $\delta\downarrow0$; finite concavity makes $F_\beta$ continuous at the interior density. Combined with step 1.1 this proves the limit.
